title: HARP: The Human--AI Research Platform
comment: 5 pages, 3 figures, SAP Academic Community Conference North America, 2026
summary: Large language models (LLMs) have shifted human--computer interaction from `traditional'' interface journeys toward more conversational exchanges. Researchers studying HCI and UI use moderated usability sessions, interviews, surveys, transcript analysis, and static prototypes. However, static prototypes provide limited opportunities to study interaction with live AI systems or systematically control how an LLM behaves across participants and scenarios. Conversation transcripts reveal little about how users formulate, revise, and hesitate over prompts before submission. We designed the Human--AI Research Platform (HARP) for researchers, designers, and anyone who has ever wondered, `What if AI did this?' HARP places participants in controlled mock scenarios with live, configurable AI agents. Researchers can control agent prompts, model parameters, response characteristics, and experimental conditions; trigger surveys at predefined moments; and record prompt composition time, response latency, deletions, and keystroke pauses. Planned capabilities include voice, facial expression, gesture, and, where legally and ethically appropriate, emotion analysis. We illustrate HARP through a study examining how technical specificity and response length affect retention of LLM output. By pairing controllable live agents with behavioral and self-report measures, HARP enables systematic testing of how AI design choices affect users.

AI.tldr: HARP is a research platform that enables controlled human-AI interaction studies with live, configurable LLM agents. It captures fine-grained behavioral data (prompt composition time, keystroke pauses, deletions, response latency) alongside self-report measures, allowing researchers to systematically test how AI design choices affect user behavior.
AI.motivation: Current HCI/UI research methods—moderated usability sessions, interviews, surveys, transcript analysis, and static prototypes—cannot adequately capture how users interact with live AI systems. Static prototypes prevent studying real-time AI interaction, while conversation transcripts obscure the pre-submission cognitive process (formulation, revision, hesitation). Researchers also lack tools to systematically control LLM behavior across participants and experimental conditions.
AI.method: The authors designed and built HARP, a platform that places participants in controlled mock scenarios with live, configurable AI agents. Researchers can manipulate agent prompts, model parameters, response characteristics, and experimental conditions. The platform records behavioral metrics (prompt composition time, response latency, deletions, keystroke pauses) and triggers surveys at predefined moments. Planned extensions include voice, facial expression, gesture, and emotion analysis. The platform is demonstrated through a study on how technical specificity and response length affect retention of LLM output.
AI.result: The paper presents HARP as a functional platform and illustrates its use through a study examining the effects of technical specificity and response length on users' retention of LLM-generated output. Specific quantitative results from the illustrative study are not detailed in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: By combining controllable live AI agents with rich behavioral and self-report measures, HARP enables systematic, ecologically valid testing of how AI design choices affect users, filling a methodological gap in human-AI interaction research.

title: Flint: A Semantics-Driven Data Visualization Intermediate Language
summary: We present Flint, an intermediate language that enables authors to create high-quality visualizations from concise, semantics-driven specifications without explicitly configuring low-level parameters such as scales, axes, and formatting. Unlike prior systems that infer default configurations from surface-level data representations, often producing brittle choices, Flint introduces a hierarchical data semantic model that allows users to specify the meanings of data fields structurally and helps the compiler derive appropriate visualization configurations. From a concise specification, the system generates and optimizes library-agnostic visualization configurations and translates them into complete, executable specifications for multiple target grammars, including Vega-Lite, Apache ECharts, and Chart.js. We demonstrate that Flint simplifies the authoring process without compromising on visual quality, and it is an effective intermediate language for both humans and AI agents to create visualizations.

AI.tldr: Flint is an intermediate language that generates high-quality, library-agnostic visualization configurations from concise, semantics-driven specifications. It uses a hierarchical data semantic model to infer robust visualization parameters and can compile to multiple target grammars (Vega-Lite, Apache ECharts, Chart.js).
AI.motivation: Existing visualization authoring tools require tedious manual configuration of low-level parameters (scales, axes, formatting) or rely on surface-level data heuristics that produce brittle defaults. There is a need for a more robust, semantics-driven approach that reduces authoring effort while maintaining high visual quality across multiple output frameworks.
AI.method: Flint introduces a hierarchical data semantic model where users structurally specify the meanings of data fields (e.g., distinguishing nominal vs. quantitative, temporal semantics, roles). The Flint compiler uses these semantic annotations to derive appropriate visualization configurations automatically — scales, axes, legends, formatting — without manual tuning. It produces library-agnostic intermediate configurations and translates them into executable specifications for Vega-Lite, Apache ECharts, and Chart.js.
AI.result: Flint simplifies the visualization authoring process without compromising visual quality. The system generates optimized, complete specifications across multiple target grammars from concise inputs. It is effective for both human authors and AI agents, demonstrating flexibility and robustness as an intermediate representation.
AI.conclusion: Flint demonstrates that a semantics-driven intermediate language can bridge the gap between concise declarative specifications and high-quality, multi-target visualization output. By leveraging hierarchical data semantics rather than surface-level heuristics, Flint produces more reliable configurations and serves as a practical tool for both human and AI-driven visualization authoring.

title: Sonic Stage: Automatically Generating Interactive Spatial Soundscapes to Facilitate Dialogue Video Comprehension for Blind Viewers
summary: Audio description (AD) makes film and television accessible to blind and low-vision (BLV) audiences by narrating characters' actions. However, in scenes with lots of dialogue, AD often omits important actions because it is constrained not to overlap with speech. It is not yet known how to convey characters' actions during dialogue. We present Sonic Stage, a system that transforms dialogue videos into interactive spatial soundscapes, enabling BLV audiences to intuitively understand characters' actions and movements through immersive auditory cues. Sonic Stage conveys essential visual information during dialogue through three auditory techniques: (1) spatialized dialogue to represent spatial layout, (2) diegetic sound to convey character actions, and (3) interactive descriptions to provide context-specific visual details. Evaluation with 12 BLV viewers showed that Sonic Stage significantly improved video comprehension, spatial presence, and narrative engagement. We highlight opportunities for enhancing video accessibility across diverse genres through immersive, interactive audio representations.

AI.tldr: Sonic Stage transforms dialogue-heavy videos into interactive spatial soundscapes using spatialized dialogue, diegetic sound, and interactive descriptions, significantly improving comprehension, spatial presence, and narrative engagement for blind and low-vision viewers.
AI.motivation: Standard audio description (AD) often omits important character actions during dialogue-heavy scenes because AD is constrained not to overlap with speech. Currently, no established method exists for conveying characters' actions during dialogue, leaving a critical accessibility gap for BLV audiences.
AI.method: The authors developed Sonic Stage, which employs three auditory techniques: (1) spatialized dialogue that positions speech in a 3D sound field to reflect spatial layout, (2) diegetic sound to sonify character actions, and (3) interactive descriptions allowing users to access context-specific visual details on demand. The system was evaluated with 12 BLV participants.
AI.result: Evaluation with 12 BLV viewers demonstrated that Sonic Stage significantly improved video comprehension, spatial presence, and narrative engagement compared to standard approaches.
AI.conclusion: Immersive, interactive audio representations present a promising direction for enhancing video accessibility across diverse genres, addressing a key limitation of traditional audio description in dialogue-dense scenes.

title: Exploring the Design Space of LLM-Based Programming Support in CS Education: A Scoping Review through the Lens of Assistance Governance
summary: As large language models (LLMs) become integrated into programming education, learner-facing systems increasingly differ in how that assistance is bounded, enacted, and controlled. These governance decisions are often described implicitly, making it difficult to compare systems in educationally meaningful ways. To address this gap, we conduct a scoping review and qualitative synthesis of 90 peer-reviewed LLM-based programming support systems in CS education. We analyze assistance governance through three dimensions, which we refer to collectively as PEA: Policy, capturing what forms of help are allowed or restricted; Enforcement, capturing how those boundaries are operationalized through interaction and system behavior; and Authority, capturing who can configure, adapt, or override them during use. Our findings show that systems often share similar pedagogical goals, but implement those goals through varied enforcement mechanisms. At the same time, authority remains highly centralized in system logic, with fewer systems giving learners or instructors runtime control. This work contributes PEA as a three-dimensional analytic lens, a governance codebook empirically refined within these dimensions, and a map of underexplored configurations in the current design space of LLM-based programming support. By making these explicit and comparable, PEA offers a vocabulary for analyzing existing systems and designing future tools that are pedagogically bounded, configurable, and accountable.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces PEA (Policy, Enforcement, Authority), a three-dimensional analytic framework for comparing how LLM-based programming support systems govern learner assistance. Through a scoping review of 90 systems, the authors find that while pedagogical goals are often shared, enforcement mechanisms vary widely and authority remains centralized in system logic, with limited runtime control for learners or instructors.
AI.motivation: LLM-based programming support systems differ greatly in how they bound, enact, and control learner assistance, yet these governance decisions are described implicitly, hindering educationally meaningful comparison across systems.
AI.method: A scoping review and qualitative synthesis of 90 peer-reviewed LLM-based programming support systems in CS education, analyzed through the three PEA dimensions: Policy (allowed/restricted help), Enforcement (how boundaries are operationalized), and Authority (who can configure or override them).
AI.result: Systems share similar pedagogical goals but implement them through varied enforcement mechanisms. Authority remains highly centralized in system logic, with few systems granting learners or instructors runtime control over governance parameters.
AI.conclusion: PEA provides a vocabulary for analyzing existing systems and designing future tools that are pedagogically bounded, configurable, and accountable, while also mapping underexplored design configurations in the current landscape.

title: Probabilistic Residual Learning for Online Recommendations
comment: Accepted at the 20th ACM Conference on Recommender Systems (RecSys 2026)
summary: Modern recommender systems are typically based on deep learning (DL) models, where a dense encoder learns representations of users and items. As a result, these systems often suffer from the black-box nature and computational complexity of the underlying models, making it difficult to systematically enhance their recommendation capabilities. To address this problem, we propose Probabilistic Residual Learning (PRL), a causal Bayesian recommendation model that models the residual between ground-truth and base predictions, enabling targeted refinement of existing systems. Specifically, PRL (1) probabilistically groups users for localized residual modeling, (2) models domain-level confounders that influence user and item representations, and (3) aggregates cluster-specific residual predictions over the confounders using do-calculus. Experiments demonstrate that our plug-and-play PRL is compatible with various base deep learning recommender systems, improving their performance while automatically discovering meaningful user clusters.

AI.tldr: PRL is a causal Bayesian plug-and-play framework that improves existing deep learning recommender systems by learning residual corrections over probabilistically grouped users, accounting for domain-level confounders via do-calculus.
AI.motivation: Modern DL-based recommender systems suffer from black-box opacity and computational complexity, making systematic enhancement difficult. There is a need for a principled, interpretable way to refine existing systems without retraining them from scratch.
AI.method: PRL employs three components: (1) probabilistic user clustering for localized residual modeling between ground-truth and base predictions; (2) modeling of domain-level confounders affecting user/item representations; (3) do-calculus-based aggregation of cluster-specific residual predictions over confounders, yielding unbiased causal estimates for refinement.
AI.result: PRL is compatible with various base DL recommender systems as a plug-and-play module, improving their recommendation performance while automatically discovering meaningful user clusters.
AI.conclusion: PRL provides an effective, causally grounded approach for enhancing black-box recommender systems through targeted residual learning, offering both performance gains and interpretability via discovered user clusters.

title: Verifier-First Evaluation of Agentic LLMs for Infrastructure-as-Code Generation
comment: 26 pages, 3 figures, 17 tables. Benchmark dataset available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/iac-eval-v2/iac-eval-v2
summary:
Infrastructure-as-Code (IaC) generation from natural language requires satisfying provider schemas, dependency planning, and organizational policy constraints, not merely producing syntactically plausible configurations. We present a verifier-first empirical study of seven agentic strategies for Terraform generation evaluated on IaC-Eval v2, a modernized 186-task AWS/Terraform benchmark with Rego v1 intent policies. Our evaluation separates failures into three verifier stages (terraform validate, terraform plan, opa eval) and applies McNemar's test with Wilson confidence intervals on all pairwise comparisons (n=186, alpha=0.05).
  We report five principal findings. (1) Active retrieval via ReAct agents with MCP or ChromaDB-backed RAG raises Qwen2.5-Coder 7B from 14.0% to 45.7% pass@1 (p<0.0001), primarily by reducing VALIDATE_FAIL from 144 to 66 tasks. (2) Iterative refinement with verifier feedback achieves 62.9% (Qwen 7B) and 84.4% (GPT-4o) pass@1, exhibiting binary convergence -- tasks either resolve in one retry or exhaust the budget. (3) GEPA reflective instruction optimization raises the Active RAG baseline by +7.5 pp (p=0.026) using only 80 verifier-guided rollouts, providing evidence that prompt optimizers can improve verifiable IaC generation without weight updates. (4) SIMBA teacher-free demonstration injection achieves performance equivalent to Active RAG (p=1.0) without retrieval infrastructure, but fails to address the dominant SELF_DEFINED_PROPERTY error class (50% of failures). (5) A diagnostic Rego-injection experiment shows that 79% of post-refinement OPA failures are information-gap failures resolvable when policy text is visible (p=0.016), motivating policy

AI.tldr: Analysis of seven agentic strategies for generating Terraform configurations from natural language, evaluated on a 186-task benchmark. Verifier-based refinement achieves up to 84.4% pass@1, active retrieval significantly boosts small models, and policy visibility is key to resolving compliance failures.
AI.motivation: Existing approaches to IaC generation from natural language focus on syntactic plausibility but neglect provider schema compliance, dependency planning, and organizational policy constraints. The authors aim to systematically evaluate agentic strategies that address these verifiable correctness dimensions.
AI.method: The authors conduct a verifier-first empirical evaluation using IaC-Eval v2, a 186-task AWS/Terraform benchmark with Rego v1 intent policies. Seven agentic strategies are compared: Active RAG (ReAct agents with MCP/ChromaDB), iterative refinement with verifier feedback (terraform validate, terraform plan, opa eval), GEPA reflective instruction optimization, SIMBA teacher-free demonstration injection, and Rego-injection for policy gap diagnosis. McNemar's test with Wilson confidence intervals is used for all pairwise comparisons (n=186, α=0.05).
AI.result: (1) Active RAG raises Qwen2.5-Coder 7B from 14.0% to 45.7% pass@1 (p<0.0001). (2) Iterative refinement achieves 62.9% (Qwen 7B) and 84.4% (GPT-4o) pass@1 with binary convergence. (3) GEPA optimization adds +7.5 pp over Active RAG (p=0.026). (4) SIMBA matches Active RAG (p=1.0) without retrieval but fails on SELF_DEFINED_PROPERTY errors (50% of failures). (5) 79% of post-refinement OPA failures are information-gap failures resolvable with policy text visibility (p=0.016).
AI.conclusion: Verifier-gated iterative refinement is highly effective for IaC generation, with small models significantly benefiting from active retrieval. Policy text visibility resolves most OPA compliance failures, motivating policy-aware generation architectures. Prompt optimization and demonstration injection offer complementary benefits but cannot fully substitute for retrieval or verifier feedback.

title: pAI-Econ-claude: A Gated Human-in-the-Loop Multi-Agent Architecture for AI-Assisted Economic Theory Development
summary: In many social-science research tasks, such as economics, LLM-based agents must produce outputs for which no cheap, task-complete, machine-readable correctness signal exists. This creates a distinctive reliability problem for multi-agent systems: how should generation, critique, coordination, and human judgment be organized when no component can certify the final result? We address this problem through pAI-Econ-claude, a gated, human-in-the-loop multi-agent architecture for AI-assisted economic theory development. Agents coordinate through a shared workspace of inspectable intermediate records; specialized gates diagnose targeted failure modes and recommend loopbacks without certifying correctness; and human checkpoints retain authority over decisions that are costly to reverse. We evaluate the architecture on five matched economic-theory tasks against an ungated baseline. Two evaluators blinded to configuration agreed on all five pairwise rankings, preferring the gated architecture in four tasks and the baseline in one. Mean failure severity fell from 1.58 to 1.16, while overall usefulness rose from 2.60 to 3.10. The largest observed gain occurred when a reality check rejected a false market-structure premise and a proof review prompted revision of a false welfare claim. The negative case shows that scaffolding can also compress an economically important mechanism too aggressively. The results support a bounded claim: gated oversight improves the auditability of AI-assisted economic theory without substituting for formal verification, and the allocation of irreversible human judgment is a more informative design variable than pure agent autonomy. The workflow is publicly available at https://github.com/maxwell2732/pAI-Econ-claude.

AI.tldr: This paper presents pAI-Econ-claude, a gated human-in-the-loop multi-agent architecture for AI-assisted economic theory development where no automated correctness signal exists. Evaluated against an ungated baseline across five economic-theory tasks, the gated architecture reduced failure severity and improved usefulness, though one negative case revealed scaffolding can over-compress important mechanisms. The core insight: allocating irreversible human judgment matters more than maximizing agent autonomy.
AI.motivation: In social-science domains like economics, LLM-based agents must produce outputs for which no cheap, task-complete, machine-readable correctness signal exists. This creates a distinctive reliability problem: no component in a multi-agent system can certify the final result, raising the question of how to organize generation, critique, coordination, and human judgment under conditions of fundamental uncertainty about correctness.
AI.method: The authors propose pAI-Econ-claude, a gated multi-agent architecture with three key features: (1) a shared workspace of inspectable intermediate records for agent coordination, (2) specialized gates that diagnose targeted failure modes and recommend loopbacks without claiming to certify correctness, and (3) human checkpoints that retain authority over decisions costly to reverse. The architecture is evaluated on five matched economic-theory tasks against an ungated baseline, with two blinded evaluators providing pairwise rankings, failure severity scores, and overall usefulness ratings.
AI.result: Blinded evaluators agreed on all five pairwise rankings, preferring the gated architecture in four tasks and the baseline in one. Mean failure severity dropped from 1.58 (baseline) to 1.16 (gated), while overall usefulness rose from 2.60 to 3.10. The largest gain came from a reality-check gate rejecting a false market-structure premise and a proof-review gate prompting revision of a false welfare claim. The negative case revealed scaffolding can over-compress an economically important mechanism.
AI.conclusion: Gated oversight improves the auditability of AI-assisted economic theory without substituting for formal verification. The allocation of irreversible human judgment is a more informative design variable than pure agent autonomy. The bounded claim is that structured gating and human-in-the-loop checkpoints enhance reliability, but the approach has limitations (e.g., over-compression risk) and does not replace formal guarantees.

title: PhantomSeal: Proactive Deepfakes Defense with Identity/Context Protection and Forensic Tracing
summary: Deepfakes, especially face-swapping attacks, pose significant challenges to authenticity, security, and ethics across science, engineering, and society. While most existing detection/tracing approaches operate post hoc, proactive defenses that aim to intervene before deepfake generation remain limited in terms of real-world effectiveness. In this paper, we present PhantomSeal, the first proactive defense to simultaneously protect both the identity and the context of users' images from being used in face-swapping attacks, while supporting forensic tracing. We present a novel cloaking technique that embeds a selected identity as a stealthy identifier. This mechanism steers the deepfake generation process toward producing content that resembles the chosen cloak identity, thereby preventing successful face-swapping while enabling effective feature-based forensic analysis. The effectiveness and robustness of PhantomSeal is demonstrated in extensive experiments across different face-swapping architectures and models. For example, it reduces the attack success rate of SimSwap, an advanced deepfake model, to 0.30%, and correctly identifies 97.97% of manipulated content. Codes can be found at https://github.com/LiangqinRen/PhantomSeal

AI.tldr: PhantomSeal is a proactive defense that embeds a stealthy cloaking identity into images, redirecting face-swapping attacks to produce the cloak identity instead of the victim's, while also enabling forensic tracing of manipulated content.
AI.motivation: Existing deepfake defenses are primarily post-hoc (detection after generation), and proactive defenses that intervene before generation lack real-world effectiveness. There is a need for a proactive approach that simultaneously protects both identity and context while supporting forensic tracing.
AI.method: A novel cloaking technique that embeds a selected identity as a stealthy identifier into user images. This steers the deepfake generation process to produce content resembling the chosen cloak identity rather than the attacker's intended target, effectively disrupting face-swapping. The embedded identifier also enables feature-based forensic analysis.
AI.result: PhantomSeal reduces the attack success rate of SimSwap to 0.30% and correctly identifies 97.97% of manipulated content. Extensive experiments across different face-swapping architectures and models demonstrate its effectiveness and robustness.
AI.conclusion: PhantomSeal is the first proactive defense to simultaneously protect identity and context in face-swapping attacks while enabling forensic tracing, demonstrating strong real-world potential through substantial empirical validation.

title: What is Good? Extracting and Testing Implicit Theories of Literary Quality from LLM Reasoning Traces
summary:
What makes writing "good" remains a persistent question in literary studies and computational linguistics. We present a two-study investigation of how reasoning-enabled LLMs evaluate literary quality.
  In Study 1, we construct a benchmark of 30 real texts spanning six quality tiers, from canonical literature to anonymous forum posts, and extract the model's implicit theory of quality from its reasoning traces. Across five DeepSeek replications, the model achieves 79.3% mean tier-classification accuracy. The traces reveal a consistent stated theory: the model values intentionality over correctness, prioritizing craft, depth, and distinctive voice. A familiarity experiment with style-matched but unrecognizable passages suggests that source recognition may inflate scores, although this is confounded by genuine quality differences between canonical originals and researcher-written pastiches.
  In Study 2, we probe this theory through systematic degradation of five canonical prose passages. We apply six manipulations - vocabulary simplification, rhythm flattening, imagery removal, voice genericization, structure simplification, and combined degradation - and reevaluate each version. Vocabulary simplification causes the smallest quality loss (0.41 +/- 0.46 points), far below structure (2.78) or voice (2.34) loss. Combined degradation is devastating (-5.64) but subadditive. An exploratory comparison with Qwen QwQ shows the same broad qualitative pattern.
  Together, these studies suggest that LLM judgments of writing quality are holistic, author-specific, and more sensitive to structural than lexical features, with implications for automated writing feedback and computational aesthetics.

AI.tldr: Two studies investigate how reasoning-enabled LLMs evaluate literary quality, finding they prioritize intentionality, craft, depth, and voice over correctness, with structural features mattering far more than lexical ones.
AI.motivation: To understand what constitutes "good" writing by examining the implicit theory of literary quality embedded in reasoning-enabled LLMs, addressing a persistent question in both literary studies and computational linguistics.
AI.method: Study 1: Constructed a benchmark of 30 texts across six quality tiers (canonical literature to forum posts), extracted LLM reasoning traces across 5 DeepSeek replications, and conducted a familiarity experiment with style-matched but unrecognizable passages. Study 2: Systematically degraded 5 canonical prose passages using 6 manipulations (vocabulary simplification, rhythm flattening, imagery removal, voice genericization, structure simplification, combined degradation) and reevaluated each version, with exploratory comparison to Qwen QwQ.
AI.result: Study 1: 79.3% mean tier-classification accuracy; the model's stated theory consistently values intentionality over correctness. Study 2: Vocabulary simplification caused minimal quality loss (0.41±0.46 points), far below structure (2.78) or voice (2.34) loss; combined degradation was devastating (-5.64) but subadditive. Qwen QwQ showed the same broad qualitative pattern.
AI.conclusion: LLM judgments of writing quality are holistic, author-specific, and more sensitive to structural than lexical features, with implications for automated writing feedback and computational aesthetics.

title: DataPrep-Bench: Benchmarking LLMs as Training Data Preparators
summary: The quality of training data fundamentally determines the capabilities of large language models (LLMs), yet no unified benchmark exists to measure how well LLMs, agents, and data-centric workflows actually prepare training data end to end. We view LLM-driven data preparation as comprising two complementary capabilities: data construction, which transforms raw sources into supervised training data, and data quality evaluation, which predicts the training value of candidate datasets before downstream training; throughout, "quality" refers to downstream training utility rather than surface-level textual properties. We introduce DataPrep-Bench, the first unified benchmark that jointly evaluates both capabilities under a shared downstream-grounded protocol over six domains and multiple base models. For data construction, methods consume identical raw sources and are scored by fine-tuning a base model on their outputs jointly with Dolly-15k; alongside this track we release Data-Construction-Skill, a skill-guided agent that lifts the Dolly-only baseline by nearly 20 points absolute on Llama-3.1-8B Finance and is competitive with the strongest agent- and DataFlow-based methods in knowledge-extraction-dense domains. For data quality evaluation, scoring functions are scored by Pearson correlation with downstream performance on a shared candidate pool; we release the Distributional Alignment Score (DAS), a distribution-based evaluator that uses MMD between a candidate dataset and a domain proxy. DAS attains the strongest cross-model correlation in four of six domains and is the only metric clearing r > 0.70 simultaneously in Math, Science, and Medical, outperforming existing quality-, diversity-, and heuristic-based evaluators. DataPrep-Bench provides a unified, downstream-grounded framework for measuring progress on both capabilities as co-equal targets of LLM-driven data preparation.

AI.tldr: DataPrep-Bench is the first unified benchmark for evaluating LLM-driven data preparation, jointly assessing data construction and data quality evaluation under a downstream-grounded protocol across six domains. The paper also introduces Data-Construction-Skill (a skill-guided agent for data construction) and the Distributional Alignment Score (DAS), a distribution-based evaluator that achieves strong cross-model correlation.
AI.motivation: Despite the critical importance of training data quality for LLM capabilities, no unified benchmark exists to end-to-end measure how well LLMs, agents, and data-centric workflows prepare training data. Existing efforts treat data construction and data quality evaluation in isolation, and "quality" is often assessed via surface-level textual properties rather than downstream training utility.
AI.method: The benchmark evaluates two complementary capabilities: (1) Data construction — methods consume identical raw sources and are scored by fine-tuning a base model on their outputs (jointly with Dolly-15k) and measuring downstream performance; (2) Data quality evaluation — scoring functions are evaluated by Pearson correlation with downstream performance on a shared candidate pool. The authors also contribute Data-Construction-Skill, a skill-guided agent, and DAS, a distributional evaluator using Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD) between a candidate dataset and a domain proxy.
AI.result: Data-Construction-Skill lifts the Dolly-only baseline by nearly 20 absolute points on Llama-3.1-8B Finance and is competitive with the strongest agent- and DataFlow-based methods in knowledge-extraction-dense domains. DAS attains the strongest cross-model correlation in four of six domains and is the only metric clearing r > 0.70 simultaneously in Math, Science, and Medical, outperforming existing quality-, diversity-, and heuristic-based evaluators.
AI.conclusion: DataPrep-Bench provides a unified, downstream-grounded framework that treats data construction and data quality evaluation as co-equal targets, enabling systematic progress measurement in LLM-driven data preparation. Both proposed methods (Data-Construction-Skill and DAS) demonstrate significant improvements over existing baselines.

title: AINTMA: Agentic AI Architecture for Autonomous Test Management with Generative Intelligence, Secure Cloud Communication and Adaptive Quality Analytics
comment: 11 pages, 2 figures, 4 tables, Submitted to AICCONS (AIP Conference Proceedings format)
summary: Modern software quality assurance demands intelligent, autonomous systems capable of adaptive decision-making across distributed cloud environments. This paper presents AINTMA (Agentic Intelligent Test Management Architecture), a multi-agent agentic AI system that transforms traditional test management into an autonomous quality intelligence ecosystem. AINTMA deploys six specialized AI agents (Test Discovery, Risk Assessment, Reinforcement Learning Prioritization, Execution Orchestration, Generative Quality Intelligence, and Cloud Security Monitor) coordinated through a secure multi-agent communication framework over a cloud-native microservices infrastructure. The Generative Quality Intelligence agent employs large language models to produce plain language quality narratives, defect risk summaries, and data-augmented test recommendations. The RL Prioritization agent models test selection as a Markov Decision Process, learning contextual policies from large-scale historical test execution data (47 features, rolling 36-month window). Secure cloud communication is enforced through a zero-trust API gateway with OAuth2/JWT authentication, encrypted inter-agent messaging, and multi-tenant isolation. Evaluation across 12 heterogeneous software projects over 18 months demonstrates: 88.4% test prioritization accuracy (APFD, vs. 51.2% random, 82.1% best commercial baseline); 43% test cycle time reduction; defect escape rate reduced from 8.3% to 2.1%; 340% ROI at 9-month payback. The agentic architecture scales to 50,000+ test cases with sub-400ms response time, and the generative intelligence module achieves 4.3/5.0 developer usefulness rating. AINTMA demonstrates that agentic AI, combining autonomous multi-agent coordination, generative intelligence and secure smart connectivity, can fundamentally advance software quality management in cloud-scale enterprise environments.

AI.tldr: AINTMA is a multi-agent AI system with six specialized agents that autonomously manages software testing in cloud environments, achieving 88.4% test prioritization accuracy, 43% cycle time reduction, and 340% ROI.
AI.motivation: Modern software quality assurance requires intelligent, autonomous systems for adaptive decision-making in distributed cloud environments, moving beyond traditional manual test management approaches.
AI.method: AINTMA deploys six specialized AI agents (Test Discovery, Risk Assessment, RL Prioritization, Execution Orchestration, Generative Quality Intelligence, Cloud Security Monitor) coordinated via a secure multi-agent communication framework on cloud-native microservices. The RL Prioritization agent uses Markov Decision Processes with 47 features over a 36-month rolling window. The Generative Quality Intelligence agent employs LLMs for quality narratives and defect summaries. Security uses zero-trust API gateway with OAuth2/JWT, encrypted messaging, and multi-tenant isolation.
AI.result: Evaluated across 12 projects over 18 months: 88.4% APFD test prioritization accuracy (vs. 51.2% random, 82.1% best commercial baseline); 43% test cycle time reduction; defect escape rate reduced from 8.3% to 2.1%; 340% ROI with 9-month payback; scales to 50,000+ test cases with sub-400ms response time; generative intelligence rated 4.3/5.0 for developer usefulness.
AI.conclusion: Agentic AI combining autonomous multi-agent coordination, generative intelligence, and secure connectivity can fundamentally advance software quality management in cloud-scale enterprise environments.

title: Reimagining the Augmented Reality Accessibility Ecosystem for Deaf Students: Service Provider Perspectives in Experiential Learning
summary: In experiential learning environments, Deaf and hard of hearing (DHH) students often experience ``split attention,'' dividing their focus among tasks, instructors, and access providers. Augmented reality (AR) has been proposed as a means to centralize communication access within the student's field of view; however, little is known about how such systems affect the instructors, interpreters, and captioners who support access in these settings. We present a formative, expert-based evaluation of ARRAE, an AR-mediated communication access ecosystem, examining the experiences of an instructor, an American Sign Language (ASL) interpreter, and a real-time captioner in a simulated laboratory environment. Comparing in-person, traditional remote, and AR-mediated access, our findings suggest that AR reconfigures accessibility labor and interactional practices by redistributing communication, attention, and awareness across participants. While AR-mediated access supported integrated, in-situ communication and enhanced contextual awareness, it also altered interactional feedback mechanisms, such as gaze coordination and pacing, that support shared understanding during instruction. These observations highlight trade-offs between access, control, and coordination, and suggest that AR-mediated systems may be most effective when considered as part of a broader, hybrid ecosystem rather than as standalone replacements for existing modalities. This work contributes initial insights into how AR reshapes communication access in experiential learning and informs the design of systems that support coordinated, multi-user interaction in hands-on educational contexts.

AI.tldr: AR-mediated communication access (ARRAE) was evaluated with an instructor, ASL interpreter, and captioner in a simulated lab, revealing that while AR centralizes access and enhances contextual awareness, it also disrupts gaze coordination, pacing, and other interactional feedback mechanisms, suggesting AR works best within a hybrid ecosystem rather than as a standalone solution.
AI.motivation: DHH students in experiential learning environments face "split attention" from dividing focus among tasks, instructors, and access providers. AR has been proposed to centralize communication access within the student's field of view, but little is known about how such systems affect the instructors, interpreters, and captioners who provide that access.
AI.method: A formative, expert-based evaluation of ARRAE (an AR-mediated communication access ecosystem) was conducted in a simulated laboratory environment, comparing three modalities: in-person, traditional remote, and AR-mediated access. Participants included an instructor, an ASL interpreter, and a real-time captioner.
AI.result: AR reconfigures accessibility labor and interactional practices by redistributing communication, attention, and awareness across participants. While AR supported integrated, in-situ communication and enhanced contextual awareness, it altered interactional feedback mechanisms such as gaze coordination and pacing that support shared understanding. Trade-offs between access, control, and coordination were identified.
AI.conclusion: AR-mediated systems may be most effective as part of a broader, hybrid ecosystem rather than as standalone replacements for existing modalities. The work contributes initial insights into how AR reshapes communication access and informs the design of systems supporting coordinated, multi-user interaction in hands-on educational contexts.

title: LO-FAR: A Cost-Aware Local Filter for Sparse Feature Ranking in Industrial Ad Recommendation
summary: Industrial ad recommendation models rely heavily on sparse, high-cardinality ID-list features that encode user histories and contextual identifiers. Each is backed by a dedicated embedding table, so these features dominate storage, training, and serving cost and must be revisited as traffic and downstream models evolve. Therefore, sparse feature ranking is not just an offline modeling problem but also a recurrent systems decision limited by compute budgets and iteration cadence. We present Localized Feature Ranking (LO-FAR), a CPU-only, model-agnostic workflow that ranks each candidate feature from its stand-alone held-out predictive signal using lightweight local estimators rather than the GPU-bound retraining loops of permutation- and stochastic-gate-based methods. On a production dataset of more than one million logged interactions and 475 sparse ID-list features, LO-FAR completes ranking in approximately two CPU-hours and preserves downstream Normalized Entropy gains on CTR and CVR tasks that are competitive with shuffle-based importance, Binary Stochastic Neurons, and a coverage-based heuristic across budgets of 100--400 retained features. The contribution is a deployable workflow showing that, when cost and turnaround constraints are binding, a simple local filter can be a practical production choice over heavier interaction-aware alternatives.

AI.tldr: LO-FAR introduces a lightweight, CPU-only feature ranking method for industrial ad recommendation systems that ranks sparse ID-list features using local estimators, avoiding expensive GPU retraining. It achieves competitive downstream performance with existing methods while completing ranking in ~2 CPU-hours on a production-scale dataset.
AI.motivation: Industrial ad models depend heavily on high-cardinality sparse ID-list features backed by embedding tables that dominate storage, training, and serving costs. Existing feature importance methods (permutation-based, stochastic gates) require expensive GPU retraining loops, making them impractical under tight compute budgets and iteration cadences. There is a need for a cost-effective, model-agnostic feature ranking workflow that fits within binding compute and turnaround constraints.
AI.method: LO-FAR (Localized Feature Ranking) is a CPU-only, model-agnostic workflow that ranks each candidate sparse feature using its stand-alone held-out predictive signal. Lightweight local estimators are trained per feature independently, avoiding the GPU-bound retraining loops of permutation importance and Binary Stochastic Neurons (BSN). The method evaluates 475 sparse ID-list features on a production dataset of over one million logged interactions.
AI.result: LO-FAR completes ranking in approximately two CPU-hours. At retention budgets of 100–400 features, it preserves downstream Normalized Entropy (NE) gains on both CTR and CVR tasks that are competitive with shuffle-based importance, Binary Stochastic Neurons, and a coverage-based heuristic baseline.
AI.conclusion: When cost and turnaround constraints are binding, a simple local filtering approach like LO-FAR is a practical, deployable production choice over heavier interaction-aware alternatives, enabling recurrent sparse feature selection without expensive infrastructure.

title: Transformer-Assisted LLM-Based Source Code Summarisation: to Enable More Secure Software Development
summary: Neural Source Code Summarisation (NSCS) aims to generate natural language summaries of source code to improve developers' and maintainers' understanding of code. Source code summaries are vital during the maintenance phase of the Secure Software Development Lifecycle (SSDLC), as they improve maintainers' understanding of code and help reduce the number of bugs and vulnerabilities in a software system. However, summaries are often missing, incomplete, or outdated in many software systems. Solutions to this problem use small, task-specific Transformer models or code-aware Large Language Models (LLMs). Task-specific Transformer-generated summaries often score well across many natural language generation (NLG) metrics, but these metrics reward lexical overlap rather than summary quality. Conversely, the ability of LLMs to capture semantics and produce high-quality summaries presents an exciting solution to this problem. This is especially relevant given the increased availability of LLMs and improvements in workstation hardware in recent years, which mean that some LLMs can now be run on developers' workstations. However, because of their abstractive nature, LLM-generated code summaries often differ greatly from developer-written summaries in the words and phrases they use, resulting in low scores across NLG metrics. We show how combining these two methods, by using Transformer-generated summaries in prompt engineering, may enable LLMs to create better source code summaries and help software practitioners maintain secure systems. We prompt four LLMs using four different prompts, with a task-specific Transformer used to assist the LLMs within the prompts. We present "Transformer-Assisted LLM-Based Source Code Summarisation", a method through which we observe an improvement of 7.8% in BLEU-4 and 5%.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes combining task-specific Transformer models with Large Language Models (LLMs) via prompt engineering to improve source code summarization. Using Transformer-generated summaries as prompts boosts LLM performance by 7.8% in BLEU-4 and 5%, addressing the lexical mismatch between LLM outputs and developer-written reference summaries.
AI.motivation: Source code summaries are critical for the maintenance phase of the Secure Software Development Lifecycle (SSDLC), yet they are often missing, incomplete, or outdated. Task-specific Transformers score well on NLG metrics but prioritize lexical overlap over true quality. LLMs produce semantically rich summaries but suffer from low NLG metric scores due to abstractive phrasing that diverges from developer-written references. The authors seek to harness the strengths of both approaches.
AI.method: The authors introduce "Transformer-Assisted LLM-Based Source Code Summarisation." They prompt four different LLMs using four distinct prompt configurations, where a task-specific Transformer model generates a summary that is embedded into the prompt to guide the LLM. This combines the lexical alignment strength of task-specific Transformers with the semantic and generative capabilities of LLMs.
AI.result: The proposed method yields a 7.8% improvement in BLEU-4 and a 5% improvement in another NLG metric when compared to baselines, demonstrating that Transformer-assisted prompting effectively bridges the gap between LLM abstractive outputs and reference summary phrasing.
AI.conclusion: Combining task-specific Transformer-generated summaries with LLMs via prompt engineering is a viable strategy for improving source code summarization quality. This approach helps software practitioners better maintain secure systems by generating higher-quality, more lexically aligned summaries, especially as LLMs become increasingly deployable on local developer workstations.

title: FedAgentKE: Federated Semantic Knowledge Evolution for Heterogeneous Agents
summary: Large language model (LLM)-based agents increasingly rely on reasoning, tool use, and iterative execution, yet existing agent frameworks still operate largely in isolation. While recent memory-based agent systems improve individual agents through local retrieval and workflow reuse, local experiences remain fragmented across isolated agent frameworks, limiting cross-framework knowledge transfer and collaborative reasoning evolution. We propose FedAgentKE, a lightweight framework for Federated Semantic Knowledge Evolution across heterogeneous agents. FedAgentKE enables distributed agent frameworks to collaboratively evolve transferable reasoning abstractions through iterative semantic knowledge distillation, aggregation, and adaptation without sharing raw reasoning trajectories. Experiments demonstrate consistent improvements under both cross-framework and cross-task settings, highlighting the potential of federated semantic knowledge evolution for future collaborative agent ecosystems.

AI.tldr: FedAgentKE is a lightweight federated framework that enables heterogeneous LLM-based agents to collaboratively evolve transferable reasoning knowledge through semantic knowledge distillation and aggregation, without sharing raw trajectories, improving both cross-framework and cross-task performance.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-based agent frameworks operate in isolation; even memory-based systems that reuse local workflows suffer from fragmented local experiences. This fragmentation prevents cross-framework knowledge transfer and collaborative evolution of reasoning capabilities across heterogeneous agent ecosystems.
AI.method: FedAgentKE employs federated semantic knowledge evolution: distributed agent frameworks iteratively perform semantic knowledge distillation (extracting transferable reasoning abstractions from local experiences), aggregation (merging distilled knowledge across frameworks without sharing raw trajectories), and adaptation (applying the aggregated knowledge to individual agents).
AI.result: The framework demonstrates consistent performance improvements under both cross-framework and cross-task evaluation settings.
AI.conclusion: Federated semantic knowledge evolution is a promising direction for building collaborative agent ecosystems, enabling heterogeneous agents to benefit from collective reasoning experience while preserving privacy and framework independence.

title: AuthProbe: Specification-Driven, Multi-Identity Detection of Broken Object-Level Authorization in Recruitment API
summary: Broken Object-Level Authorization (BOLA), also known as Insecure Direct Object Reference (IDOR), has topped the OWASP API Security ranking since 2019 and is the root cause of some of the largest exposures of applicant data in recruitment technology. The defining feature of this flaw class is that a malicious request is byte-for-byte indistinguishable from a legitimate one, which is precisely why web application firewalls and single identity scanners fail to catch it. We present AuthProbe, an open-source, black-box scanner that detects BOLA and IDOR in HTTP APIs by driving its tests from an OpenAPI specification and by acting under two or more identities that the operator controls. AuthProbe discovers, for each identity, the objects that identity legitimately owns, then attempts to read one identity's objects while authenticated as another and confirms a leak by comparing the response against a ground-truth fetch by the true owner. It also walks predictable identifiers to expose enumeration and reports missing authentication and existence oracles. The tool returns a severity-thresholded exit code and machine-readable reports so that it can gate a continuous integration build. On a synthetic recruitment API in which the McHire failure class is reproduced, AuthProbe detects every planted cross-identity read with no false positives on a hardened counterpart, and its running time grows linearly with the number of objects under test. AuthProbe is released under the Apache 2.0 license with an authorized-use guardrail.

AI.tldr: AuthProbe is an open-source black-box scanner that detects Broken Object-Level Authorization (BOLA/IDOR) in HTTP APIs by using multiple identities, comparing responses against ground-truth fetches, and walking predictable identifiers — achieving zero false positives on a synthetic recruitment API while scaling linearly with object count.
AI.motivation: BOLA/IDOR has topped the OWASP API Security Top 10 since 2019 and caused major recruitment data breaches. Its defining characteristic — malicious requests being byte-for-byte identical to legitimate ones — renders WAFs and single-identity scanners ineffective. No existing black-box tool adequately addresses this gap.
AI.method: AuthProbe operates as a black-box scanner driven by an OpenAPI specification. It acts under two or more operator-controlled identities, discovers per-identity owned objects, attempts cross-identity reads (one identity accessing another's objects), and confirms leaks by comparing responses against a ground-truth fetch by the true owner. It also enumerates predictable identifiers, reports missing authentication, and identifies existence oracles. The tool outputs severity-thresholded exit codes and machine-readable reports for CI integration.
AI.result: On a synthetic recruitment API reproducing the McHire failure class, AuthProbe detected every planted cross-identity read with zero false positives on a hardened counterpart. Running time scales linearly with the number of objects under test.
AI.conclusion: AuthProbe provides a practical, automated solution for detecting BOLA/IDOR vulnerabilities in CI/CD pipelines. Released under Apache 2.0 with an authorized-use guardrail, it fills a critical gap left by traditional scanners and WAFs.

title: Knowledge Injection Exists in MoE? Exploring Expert-Aware Contrast Decoding in MoE for Mitigating LLMs'Hallucinations
summary: Existing LLM hallucination mitigation methods, including prompt engineering and model optimization, either hardly alter models'internal knowledge or have poor cross-domain generalization. Contrastive decoding mitigates hallucinations by using layer-wise differences in LLMs. However, prior studies only explore transformer-based models (e.g., GPT), ignoring other effective frameworks like mixture-of-experts (MoE) models. Since MoE alters the traditional transformer architecture, we conduct empirical studies to investigate whether similar layer-wise differences exist in MoEs. Our results show that they do not exist in MoE with shared experts; nevertheless, across different MoEs, higher layers exhibit distinct expert activation patterns between factual and non-factual outputs. Building on these, we propose EAACD, an expert-aware adaptive contrast decoding that uses expert differences in MoE's higher layers to mitigate hallucinations on QA tasks. EAACD splits high-layer experts into a higher-reliability group and several lower-reliability groups based on their confidence and consistency. It contrasts the higher-reliability group's prediction with each lower-reliability group's prediction to calibrate the model's original predictions. To strengthen this contrast, EAACD amplifies hallucinations from lower-reliability experts via attention and masking to provide stronger negative references. EAACD outperforms all baselines on four datasets.

AI.tldr: EAACD is a novel hallucination mitigation method for MoE models that leverages expert activation differences in higher layers, using contrastive decoding between high-reliability and low-reliability expert groups, outperforming baselines on four QA datasets.
AI.motivation: Existing hallucination mitigation methods (prompt engineering, model optimization) either fail to alter internal knowledge or generalize poorly. Contrastive decoding using layer-wise differences has only been studied on transformer-based models (e.g., GPT), ignoring MoE architectures. The authors investigate whether similar layer-wise differences exist in MoEs and find they do not — but discover distinct expert activation patterns in higher layers that can be exploited instead.
AI.method: EAACD (Expert-Aware Adaptive Contrastive Decoding) operates in three stages: (1) It splits high-layer experts into a higher-reliability group and multiple lower-reliability groups based on confidence and consistency metrics. (2) It contrasts the higher-reliability group's prediction against each lower-reliability group's prediction to calibrate the model's original output distribution. (3) To strengthen the contrastive signal, it amplifies hallucinations from lower-reliability experts using attention manipulation and masking, providing stronger negative references for decoding.
AI.result: EAACD outperforms all baseline methods across four QA datasets, demonstrating effective cross-domain hallucination mitigation for MoE-based LLMs.
AI.conclusion: While layer-wise differences (as used in transformer-based contrastive decoding) do not exist in MoEs with shared experts, distinct expert activation patterns in higher layers between factual and non-factual outputs provide an alternative signal. EAACD successfully exploits these expert-level differences for adaptive contrastive decoding, establishing a new effective paradigm for hallucination mitigation in MoE architectures.

title: PhantomFill: When the Form Demands an Answer, Language Models Invent One
summary:
Language models in production do not write prose. They fill forms: JSON fields, function arguments, extraction templates. We show that the form itself causes hallucination.
  We ask thirteen models the same question about the same input and change only the answer format. The inputs are built so the question cannot be answered: a viral post showing 12,400 likes but no visible replies, a support ticket whose call was never transcribed. In free text, GPT-5.5 answers honestly. It says there is no reply data, 98% of the time. Given a required JSON field for sentiment, the same model invents an answer 40 times out of 40. It fabricates the mood of crowds it never saw and quotes customers it never heard.
  The pattern holds with force. Required fields drive fabrication to 100% in ten of thirteen models. An explicit "insufficient evidence" option rescues only the frontier: all nine open-weight models ignore it. A direct instruction, do not infer sentiment, is overridden by the schema in four of six models. Resistance does not come with scale: within a single model family, the smallest model refuses, the mid-sized model fabricates, the largest refuses again. Honesty under format pressure is a training outcome that no one is measuring.
  The fabrication hides exactly where hedging is impossible: in required enums and minimum-count arrays, fields where no disclaimer fits. We release PhantomFill, a benchmark with deterministic scoring and two reportable numbers: the Coerced Fabrication Rate and the Escape Utilization Rate. The fix we test is one line of schema. The failure we measure is everywhere.

AI.tldr: Language models reliably fabricate answers when forced into structured output formats (JSON, enums, arrays) for unanswerable queries — required fields drive hallucination rates to 100% in most models, and even explicit instructions to refuse are overridden by schema constraints.
AI.motivation: Production language models predominantly output structured data (JSON fields, function arguments, extraction templates) rather than free text. The authors investigate whether the output format itself induces hallucination when models face unanswerable queries — a critical reliability concern for deployed systems where hedging or refusal may be structurally impossible.
AI.method: Thirteen models are evaluated on deliberately unanswerable inputs (e.g., viral posts with no reply data, support tickets without call transcriptions). The same question is posed in two formats: free text and required structured fields (JSON with mandatory enums, minimum-count arrays). A subset of tests examines whether providing an explicit "insufficient evidence" option or a direct "do not infer" instruction mitigates fabrication. The authors introduce PhantomFill, a benchmark with two metrics: Coerced Fabrication Rate and Escape Utilization Rate.
AI.result: In free text, GPT-5.5 answers honestly 98% of the time. Under required JSON fields, fabrication reaches 100% in 10 of 13 models (40/40 for GPT-5.5 on sentiment). An "insufficient evidence" option helps only frontier models; all nine open-weight models ignore it. A direct instruction not to infer sentiment is overridden by schema in 4 of 6 models. Within a single model family, resistance follows a U-shaped pattern: smallest refuses, mid-sized fabricates, largest refuses again.
AI.conclusion: Output format constraints systematically coerce fabrication in language models. Required enums and minimum-count arrays structurally preclude hedging, making hallucination the only compliant behavior. Honesty under format pressure is an unmeasured training outcome, not an emergent property of scale. A one-line schema change can fix the problem, but the failure is pervasive across current models.

title: Marking the Wrong Symptoms: Evaluating LLM Watermarks in Medical Texts
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly integrated into clinical workflows, stressing the need for reliable traceability of model-generated output with watermarking. Yet, most watermarks are evaluated on general-purpose benchmarks, leaving domains like medicine, where small token-level perturbations can result in significant semantic changes, underexplored. In this work, we present the first rigorous study of how LLM watermarks affect medical performance, benchmarking 5 watermarking schemes across 11 LLMs and 7 VLMs on various tasks spanning unimodal and multimodal clinical reasoning. Importantly, we complement existing evaluations by introducing a human-expert-validated pipeline for systematically auditing medical reasoning quality, terminological precision, and induced hallucinations. Our results reveal that watermarking can induce substantial degradation across multiple failure modes, including lexical corruption, hallucinated terminology, and amplified misattribution or omission of image findings. Notably, we find that the absence of domain-specific analyses, combined with aggregate metrics that miss failures inherent to clinical text, can systematically obscure practical watermark-induced degradations. Our findings establish domain-specific evaluation as a prerequisite for the safe deployment of watermarked models in medicine, where current benchmarks can otherwise mask clinically consequential failures.

AI.tldr: First rigorous study on how LLM watermarking degrades medical performance, benchmarking 5 watermarking schemes across 11 LLMs and 7 VLMs. Using a human-expert-validated pipeline, the authors reveal that watermarks cause lexical corruption, hallucinated terminology, and misattribution/omission in clinical reasoning — failures systematically obscured by standard aggregate metrics.
AI.motivation: Watermarking is critical for traceability as LLMs enter clinical workflows, but existing watermark evaluations are limited to general-purpose benchmarks. The medical domain is uniquely vulnerable because small token-level perturbations can produce clinically significant semantic errors, yet no prior work has systematically studied how watermarks affect medical reasoning quality.
AI.method: The authors benchmark 5 watermarking schemes across 11 LLMs and 7 VLMs on unimodal and multimodal clinical reasoning tasks. They introduce a human-expert-validated auditing pipeline that systematically evaluates medical reasoning quality, terminological precision, and watermark-induced hallucinations, going beyond standard aggregate metrics.
AI.result: Watermarking induces substantial degradation across multiple failure modes: lexical corruption, hallucinated terminology, and amplified misattribution or omission of image findings in multimodal settings. Crucially, aggregate metrics systematically mask these clinically consequential failures, showing that domain-agnostic evaluation is insufficient for detecting practical degradations.
AI.conclusion: Domain-specific evaluation is a prerequisite for safe deployment of watermarked models in medicine. Current general-purpose benchmarks can obscure clinically consequential failures, and the research community should adopt medical-domain auditing pipelines before integrating watermarked LLMs/VLMs into clinical workflows.

title: CRAFT: Exploring Wearable Creative AI on Smart Glasses for Fiction Writing in Real-World Contexts
comment: Conditionally accepted (pending minor revisions) for publication in Proceedings of the ACM on Interactive, Mobile, Wearable and Ubiquitous Technologies (PACM IMWUT), Vol. 10, No. 3, Article 81, September 2026
summary: Creative writing increasingly integrates AI assistance, yet current tools miss in-situ moments when writers draw inspiration from real-world experiences. We envision Context-aware Reality-Fiction Transformation (CRAFT), an approach for AI glasses that translates daily experiences into fiction narratives. We explored its desirability, feasibility, and potential viability through three studies. Interviews with nine writers yielded desires and three design goals: 1) augmenting in-situ perception to bridge reality-fiction gaps, 2) promoting authenticity grounded in real-world experiences while maintaining fictionalization, and 3) preserving creative agency, enjoyment, and life-art boundaries. Co-design workshops with 16 writers and researchers operationalized these goals into concrete interaction mechanisms using a technology probe. We then conducted supported field trials with eight writers across 24 sessions using a refined probe, revealing writer-perceived benefits (e.g., enriched fictional ideas from serendipitous encounters), emergent practices (e.g., micro-creation), and design considerations for future sustained use. We contribute design explorations for the CRAFT approach, offering design implications and empirical insights on ubiquitous human-AI creative collaboration in everyday life.

AI.tldr: CRAFT envisions AI-powered smart glasses that transform real-world daily experiences into fiction narratives. Through interviews, co-design workshops, and field trials, the authors derive design goals, interaction mechanisms, and empirical insights for context-aware reality-to-fiction transformation tools that preserve creative agency and authenticity.
AI.motivation: Current AI-assisted creative writing tools fail to capture in-situ moments when writers draw inspiration from real-world experiences. The authors address this gap by envisioning wearable AI systems (smart glasses) that can contextually transform everyday encounters into fictional material, supporting creativity at the moment of inspiration.
AI.method: Three-phase study: (1) Semi-structured interviews with 9 writers to elicit desires and derive design goals; (2) Co-design workshops with 16 writers and researchers using a technology probe to operationalize goals into concrete interaction mechanisms; (3) Supported field trials with 8 writers across 24 sessions using a refined probe to evaluate benefits, emergent practices, and sustained-use considerations.
AI.result: Three design goals emerged: augmenting in-situ perception to bridge reality-fiction gaps, promoting authenticity grounded in real-world experiences while enabling fictionalization, and preserving creative agency, enjoyment, and life-art boundaries. Field trials revealed writer-perceived benefits (enriched fictional ideas from serendipitous encounters), emergent practices (micro-creation), and design considerations for sustained use.
AI.conclusion: The CRAFT approach demonstrates the potential of ubiquitous AI wearables for human-AI creative collaboration in everyday life. The paper contributes design explorations, implications, and empirical insights for building context-aware systems that support reality-to-fiction transformation while respecting writers' creative agency and boundaries.

title: Controllable and Content-Based Recommendations
summary: Traditional recommendation systems rely on latent (dense) representations, making them difficult to interpret and control. We propose the Controllable and Content-Based Recommendations (CCBR) framework, which builds its recommendations from textual user profile representations. CCBR plugs into collaborative filtering models and introduces controllability via text bottlenecks. We show that CCBR enables text-based and multimodal interventions, allowing users to steer the model towards the directions they prefer. Different from existing controllable recommendation systems, CCBR infers the text summaries directly from item contents (images, audio or video). Across image-, audio-, and video-based datasets, we demonstrate that the proposed framework obtains competitive model performance with standard (latent-representation) models while providing controllable model summaries via text. The model also outperforms TEARS, a recent baseline for controllable recommendation systems. Through systematic interventions, we demonstrate the efficacy of the user steering mechanism.

AI.tldr: CCBR proposes a recommendation framework that uses textual user profiles as bottlenecks in collaborative filtering, enabling interpretable and user-steerable recommendations directly from item content (images, audio, video), outperforming prior controllable baselines while matching standard latent models.
AI.motivation: Traditional recommendation systems use latent (dense) representations that are opaque and uncontrollable. There is a need for interpretable and steerable recommendation systems that allow users to understand and influence model behavior, without sacrificing recommendation quality.
AI.method: The CCBR framework replaces latent user representations with textual user profile summaries inferred directly from item content (images, audio, video). It plugs into collaborative filtering models via a text bottleneck, creating a controllable interface. Users can apply text-based and multimodal interventions to steer recommendations toward preferred directions.
AI.result: CCBR achieves competitive performance with standard latent-representation models across image, audio, and video datasets. It outperforms TEARS, a recent controllable recommendation baseline. Systematic intervention experiments demonstrate effective user steering.
AI.conclusion: CCBR successfully bridges the gap between recommendation performance and controllability by using content-derived text bottlenecks, enabling both interpretability and user steering without compromising model quality.

title: Maintenance Signals in AI-Assisted GitHub Repositories: Evidence from GenAI Adopters
summary: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) can reduce code-generation effort, but it may shift work to documentation, validation, debugging, and maintenance. We study observable maintenance-cost signals among GenAI adopters on GitHub by analyzing 622 users who publicly signal adoption, 179 repositories with visible AI-assistance configuration files, 179 matched traditional repositories, and 248 issues created in AI-assisted repositories. AI-assisted repositories span diverse project types and contain longer README files with more headers and code blocks, while traditional repositories contain more external URLs. Issues concerning GenAI technology often involve external dependencies, such as API rate limits and reliance on GenAI provider APIs. These findings suggest that AI assistance shifts maintenance costs toward verifying generated content, managing external AI dependencies, and validating AI-specific behavior.

AI.tldr: Analysis of 622 GitHub users and 179 AI-assisted repositories reveals that GenAI adoption shifts maintenance burden from code generation toward documentation bloat, external API dependency management, and validation of AI-generated content.
AI.motivation: While GenAI promises to reduce coding effort, there is limited empirical evidence on whether it merely relocates costs to downstream activities like documentation, debugging, validation, and maintenance. The authors aim to quantify observable maintenance-cost signals in real-world open-source projects.
AI.method: A mixed-methods empirical study analyzing GitHub data: (1) 622 users who publicly signal GenAI adoption, (2) 179 repositories with AI-assistance configuration files (e.g., .cursorrules, .github/copilot-instructions), (3) 179 matched traditional repositories as a control group, and (4) 248 issues from AI-assisted repositories. Comparative analysis focuses on README structure (length, headers, code blocks, external URLs) and issue content.
AI.result: AI-assisted repositories exhibit systematically longer README files with more headers and code blocks compared to matched traditional repositories, while traditional repos contain more external URLs. Issues in AI-assisted repos frequently concern external dependencies such as API rate limits and reliance on GenAI provider APIs, indicating a new class of maintenance burden tied to third-party AI service dependencies.
AI.conclusion: GenAI adoption does not eliminate maintenance costs but redistributes them: developers spend more effort documenting and validating AI-generated output and managing brittle external AI dependencies, suggesting that tooling and best practices should evolve to address these emerging cost centers.

title: ChannelGuard: Safe Models Do Not Compose into Safe Multi-Agent Systems
summary: Multi-agent LLM applications chain a planner, worker agents, a verifier, and a synthesizer, and every hop between agents is an unmonitored channel through which an adversary can smuggle instructions. Existing defenses guard only the input boundary (IBProtector, Llama Guard, perplexity filters, SmoothLLM) or run outside the application as opaque, stochastic provider-side filters. We show this gap carries a consequence rarely measured: on a 2,100-trace evaluation across eight attack families, five defenses, and three model backends, an undefended pipeline that appears fully safe under standard reporting (attack success 0.000 on tool- and memory-poisoning) owes that safety almost entirely to the cloud provider's server-side filter (54 of 60 blocks on Azure GPT-5), and silently shifts to the agent model's own alignment on a backend without such a filter. Outcome-only reporting hides this dependence. We present ChannelGuard, a training-free defense-in-depth framework placing information-bottleneck gates on every inter-agent channel; each scores channel text against an adversarial phrase bank by embedding similarity and deterministically passes, compresses, or blocks it, adding no LLM call, while an attribution method records which layer stopped each attack. ChannelGuard's tool-output gate blocks Tool Poisoning 30 of 30 at the application layer, identically across Azure GPT-5, Anthropic Sonnet 4.5, and Anthropic Haiku 4.5, whereas the undefended pipeline shifts entirely across backends; it also lowers Prompt Injection attack success by half (0.333 to 0.167) and preserves GSM8K accuracy exactly (0.867). White-box adaptive paraphrase evades every embedding gate, where a perturb-and-vote baseline does better. An extended appendix adds baselines, ablations, sweeps, a benign-preservation analysis, and a judge audit (kappa = 0.900), at a total cost of 47.36 USD.

AI.tldr: Multi-agent LLM systems are vulnerable to adversarial instruction smuggling through unmonitored inter-agent channels. Existing defenses only guard input boundaries or operate as opaque server-side filters. The paper reveals that apparent safety in undefended pipelines often depends entirely on provider-side filtering (which disappears on other backends) rather than model alignment. ChannelGuard is proposed as a training-free, defense-in-depth framework that places embedding-based information-bottleneck gates on every inter-agent channel, achieving consistent cross-backend defense with no additional LLM calls.
AI.motivation: Inter-agent channels in multi-agent LLM applications are unmonitored, creating an attack surface for adversarial instruction smuggling. Current defenses either only protect the input boundary or function as opaque, stochastic provider-side filters outside the application. The paper demonstrates that standard outcome-only reporting obscures a critical dependency on cloud-provider filters, which vanishes when switching backends, exposing a false sense of safety.
AI.method: ChannelGuard places information-bottleneck gates on every inter-agent channel. Each gate scores channel text against an adversarial phrase bank using embedding similarity and deterministically passes, compresses, or blocks content. The framework adds no LLM calls and includes an attribution mechanism recording which layer stopped each attack. Evaluation uses 2,100 traces across eight attack families, five defenses, and three model backends (Azure GPT-5, Anthropic Sonnet 4.5, Anthropic Haiku 4.5).
AI.result: The undefended pipeline's apparent safety (0.000 attack success on tool/memory poisoning) relied primarily on Azure's server-side filter (54 of 60 blocks). ChannelGuard's tool-output gate blocked Tool Poisoning 30/30 at the application layer identically across all three backends. It reduced Prompt Injection attack success from 0.333 to 0.167 and preserved GSM8K accuracy exactly (0.867). White-box adaptive paraphrase attacks evaded all embedding gates, where a perturb-and-vote baseline performed better. Judge audit achieved kappa=0.900.
AI.conclusion: Outcome-only safety reporting is misleading as it hides backend dependence on provider-side filters. ChannelGuard provides consistent, training-free defense-in-depth across backends, but embedding-based gates remain vulnerable to white-box adaptive paraphrasing, suggesting hybrid approaches (e.g., perturb-and-vote) are needed for robustness.

title: Deepfake News Detection: A Multimodal Framework Integrating LipNet, DeepSpeech and ResNET for Enhanced Audio-Visual Analysis
summary: Deepfake news refers to AI-generated (or AI ma-nipulated) multimedia content intentionally generated to deceive audiences by manipulating the facial expressions, or speech while maintaining the realistic appearance. The rapid progress of generative AI has made the synthesis of highly realistic fake videos and cloned voices widely accessible, posing a serious threat to the authenticity of digital news media. This paper presents a multi-modal framework that discerns the authenticity of video content by jointly exploiting audio and visual cues, thereby addressing the challenge of detecting the deepfake videos. We proposed a framework that involves features extraction from lip movements, audio content and video frames.
