Lip movements and speech content are encoded using the LipNet and DeepSpeech2 models, while facial features are extracted by leveraging the use of BlazeFace and represented with ResNet18. The extracted feature vectors are concatenated into a holistic video representation and classified with an ensemble of machine learning and deep learning models, including Random Forest (RF), Multi-layer Perceptron (MLP) and Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks. Exten-sive experiments performed on the FakeAVCeleb dataset shows that the proposed approach attains an accuracy of 94% using augmented audio features, outperforming a state-of-the-art multi-modal ensemble baseline. The results confirm the robustness and practical potential of the proposed framework for deepfake news detection.

AI.tldr: A multi-modal framework that detects deepfake videos by combining lip movement, audio, and facial features, using LipNet, DeepSpeech2, BlazeFace, and ResNet18 for feature extraction, with ensemble classifiers (RF, MLP, LSTM). Achieves 94% accuracy on FakeAVCeleb, outperforming baselines.
AI.motivation: The rapid advancement of generative AI enables highly realistic fake videos with manipulated facial expressions and speech, threatening the authenticity of digital news media. Existing detection methods may not fully exploit the complementary audio-visual cues jointly, motivating a multi-modal approach.
AI.method: A three-stream framework: (1) Lip movement features extracted via LipNet; (2) Audio/speech features extracted via DeepSpeech2; (3) Facial features extracted via BlazeFace and encoded with ResNet18. All feature vectors are concatenated into a unified representation and classified using an ensemble of Random Forest, MLP, and LSTM networks. Data augmentation is applied to audio features.
AI.result: The proposed method achieves 94% accuracy on the FakeAVCeleb dataset using augmented audio features, outperforming a state-of-the-art multi-modal ensemble baseline.
AI.conclusion: The multi-modal framework demonstrates robust performance and practical potential for deepfake news detection, confirming that jointly leveraging audio, visual, and lip-movement cues significantly improves detection accuracy.

title: Is MoE Routing a Huffman Code? Discovering the Frequency-Diversity Law in Chain-of-Thought
summary: Mixture-of-Experts architectures have revolutionized scaling, yet the underlying logic of their routing remains a black box. In this paper, we uncover a fundamental governing principle: MoE routing is not merely selection, but a manifestation of Huffman Coding. We introduce the Frequency-Diversity Law, revealing that state-of-the-art models, such as Phi-3.5-MoE and Gemma-4-27B-A4B, spontaneously act as information-theoretic engines. These models allocate sparse expert resources for common tokens while invoking high-diversity expert committees for rare, complex tasks found in chain-of-thought trajectories. However, we identify a critical redundancy trap in Qwen3.5-35B-A3B: when effective sparsity (k/E_eff) is sufficiently low, load-balancing inadvertently imposes functional redundancy, masking the underlying Huffman efficiency signal. To bridge this gap, we propose Subset Difference Pruning, a surgical strategy to eliminate functional duplicates. We demonstrate that pruning does not degrade reasoning; instead, it unleashes the model's latent Huffman efficiency, forcing the logic to collapse into streamlined, high-density paths. Our findings suggest that the next generation of MoEs should move beyond forced load-balancing toward Minimum Description Length (MDL) optimality, assigning shorter expert-routing codes to high-frequency information and longer, more diverse codes to low-frequency information, thereby transforming routing from a heuristic into a principled compression engine.

AI.tldr: MoE routing is shown to be an emergent instance of Huffman coding: models spontaneously assign sparse expert sets to frequent tokens and diverse expert committees to rare, complex tokens. A redundancy trap is identified when load-balancing forces functional duplication under low effective sparsity. Subset Difference Pruning is proposed to eliminate duplicates and restore latent Huffman efficiency without degrading reasoning.
AI.motivation: MoE routing mechanisms remain poorly understood despite their widespread use in scaling large models. The authors seek to uncover the fundamental information-theoretic principle governing how experts are allocated, and to identify and correct pathologies that obscure this principle in practice.
AI.method: The authors introduce the Frequency-Diversity Law, showing that routing behavior in models like Phi-3.5-MoE and Gemma-4-27B-A4B follows Huffman coding: common tokens activate few experts (short codes), while rare tokens in chain-of-thought trajectories activate diverse expert committees (long codes). They diagnose a "redundancy trap" in Qwen3.5-35B-A3B where low effective sparsity (k/E_eff) combined with load-balancing imposes functional redundancy. To address this, they propose Subset Difference Pruning, which surgically removes functionally duplicate experts, restoring the Huffman efficiency signal.
AI.result: State-of-the-art MoEs (Phi-3.5-MoE, Gemma-4-27B-A4B) naturally exhibit Huffman-like routing. Qwen3.5-35B-A3B suffers from a redundancy trap when k/E_eff is low, masking this efficiency. Subset Difference Pruning eliminates functional duplicates without degrading reasoning performance, instead allowing the model to collapse into streamlined, high-density routing paths that recover latent Huffman efficiency.
AI.conclusion: Future MoE design should move beyond forced load-balancing toward Minimum Description Length (MDL) optimality: assigning short expert codes to high-frequency information and longer, diverse codes to low-frequency information, thereby transforming routing from a heuristic into a principled compression engine.

title: The Active Ingredient in Muon's Grokking
summary: The Muon optimizer reaches the grokking threshold on modular arithmetic faster than AdamW. Prior work attributes this to "spectral-norm constraints plus orthogonalized momentum" but does not isolate which mechanism matters. To better understand Moun's behavior, we run multi-seed and multi-learning-rate sweeps to decompose and stress-test the effect. First, an ablation shows the speedup comes from orthogonalization (the Newton-Schulz iteration): orthogonalize-only matches full Muon, whereas spectral-only is no faster than AdamW and is unreliable, and this verdict holds across learning rates. Second, a mechanistic analysis finds that orthogonalizing optimizers reach generalization at roughly 3x lower spectral norm and, controlling for how much the embedding actually moves, settle into a lower-norm solution rather than simply perturbing the embedding less. Third, reducing the Newton-Schulz iteration count from five to one accelerates reaching the threshold but makes the grokked solution fragile, prone to transient collapse, with fragility that grows with learning rate; a single iteration is fast and stable only at small learning rate, while the canonical five iterations are the learning-rate-robust choice. We also show spectral scaling can be dropped at no measured cost. A methodological thread runs throughout: under a stability-aware metric, "faster" claims about grokking optimizers can invert, so we report both first-crossing and sustained-grok times. To support reproducibility, we release our full training and analysis code at https://github.com/louiswang524/muon-grokking-frontier

AI.tldr: This paper dissects the Muon optimizer's grokking speed advantage over AdamW on modular arithmetic tasks. Through systematic ablations, the authors identify that orthogonalization (via Newton-Schulz iteration), not spectral normalization, drives the speedup. They further show that reducing iteration count accelerates grokking but introduces fragility, and that spectral scaling is unnecessary. The paper also advocates for reporting both first-crossing and sustained-grok times to avoid misleading "faster" claims.
AI.motivation: Prior work credits Muon's grokking speedup to "spectral-norm constraints plus orthogonalized momentum" without isolating which mechanism is causal. The authors aim to decompose these intertwined components, stress-test them across learning rates, and establish robust evaluation methodology for grokking optimizers.
AI.method: Multi-seed and multi-learning-rate sweeps on modular arithmetic grokking tasks with three sets of experiments: (1) ablation study comparing full Muon, orthogonalize-only, spectral-only, and AdamW; (2) mechanistic analysis measuring spectral norm and embedding displacement at generalization; (3) sensitivity analysis varying Newton-Schulz iteration count (1–5) and evaluating stability via both first-crossing time and sustained-grok time.
AI.result: Orthogonalize-only matches full Muon; spectral-only performs no better than AdamW and is unreliable. Orthogonalizing optimizers reach generalization at ~3× lower spectral norm. Reducing Newton-Schulz iterations from 5 to 1 accelerates first-crossing but causes transient collapse at higher learning rates; only 5 iterations is learning-rate-robust. Spectral scaling can be dropped at no measured cost. Under stability-aware metrics, "faster" claims sometimes invert.
AI.conclusion: The Newton-Schulz orthogonalization is the sole driver of Muon's grokking speed advantage, operating by steering solutions toward lower spectral norm. Five iterations represent a robustness–speed trade-off favoring reliability across learning rates. The field should adopt sustained-grok metrics alongside first-crossing times to prevent misleading optimizer comparisons.

title: ClickGuard: Detecting and Spoiling Clickbait News with Informativeness Measures and Large Language Models
summary: This paper presents an AI-driven browser extension that identifies clickbait to help users avoid misleading Internet articles. Moving beyond traditional detection, the application employs a hybrid machine learning architecture that combines transformer-based embeddings with linguistically motivated features and a custom "baitness" score. After evaluating various natural language processing techniques -- from classic vectorizers to large language model (LLM) embeddings -- an XGBoost-based model was developed that achieves an F1-score of 91% on the open combined dataset. Most importantly, the tool can warn users before and after they access a clickbait article. After opening an article, the user receives a percentage score indicating the likelihood that it is clickbait. The prediction is explained based on the analyzed metrics, including those specifically developed within the proposed system. The browser extension also provides a clickbait spoiler -- a one- to two-sentence summary of the entire article. Demo video:https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IJ1gkQV82C4}{https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IJ1gkQV82C4

AI.tldr: An AI browser extension that detects clickbait articles using a hybrid XGBoost model (91% F1-score), combining transformer embeddings with linguistic features and a custom "baitness" score, while also providing explanations and a concise spoiler summary to users.
AI.motivation: To help users avoid misleading Internet articles by moving beyond traditional clickbait detection to a practical, real-time browser-based tool that warns users both before and after accessing clickbait content.
AI.method: A hybrid machine learning architecture using XGBoost that integrates transformer-based embeddings (LLM embeddings), linguistically motivated features, and a custom "baitness" score. Various NLP techniques were evaluated, from classic vectorizers to LLM embeddings, trained on an open combined dataset.
AI.result: The XGBoost-based model achieved an F1-score of 91% on the open combined dataset. The browser extension provides pre- and post-access warnings, a percentage-based clickbait likelihood score with metric-based explanations, and a one- to two-sentence article spoiler summary.
AI.conclusion: The proposed system successfully integrates high-performance clickbait detection into a practical browser extension, offering real-time warnings, interpretable predictions, and concise article summaries to enhance user awareness and mitigate exposure to misleading content.

title: Thinkink: 2D Spatial Ink-native Interaction with LLMs
summary: People often use handwritten notes and sketches to externalize ideas for ideation. To integrate large language models (LLMs) into this practice, we propose Thinkink. Prompts can be handwritten text or drawn sketches with LLM-generated responses visualized as ink-like text and sketches spatially integrated into a shared canvas. A semantic tree streamlines ink interpretation, and a lightweight UI provides explicit control using a state machine. The tool was designed using a three-stage process. A formative study (N=12) examined current practices with conventional and digital inking methods. The results informed a technical probe for a diagnostic study (N=6) identifying usability and human-LLM interaction challenges. This motivated the design of Thinkink, with a final study (N=10) examining how people incorporate it into their ideation practices. We contribute design implications and a tool for ink-native LLM interaction where the user and LLM write and draw in a shared 2D canvas.

AI.tldr: Thinkink is a tool that integrates LLMs into ideation workflows by allowing users to write and sketch handwritten prompts on a shared 2D canvas, with LLM responses rendered as ink-like text and drawings. A three-stage design process—formative study, diagnostic probe, and evaluation study—informed its development, yielding design implications for ink-native LLM interaction.
AI.motivation: People frequently use handwritten notes and sketches for ideation, but existing tools do not seamlessly integrate LLM capabilities into this fluid, spatial, ink-based workflow. The goal is to bridge the gap between natural inking practices and LLM-powered assistance without disrupting the user's creative process.
AI.method: A three-stage design process: (1) a formative study (N=12) investigating current practices with conventional and digital inking; (2) a technical probe used in a diagnostic study (N=6) to uncover usability and human-LLM interaction challenges; (3) design and implementation of Thinkink, followed by an evaluation study (N=10) examining how users incorporate it into ideation. Thinkink features a semantic tree for ink interpretation and a lightweight UI with a state machine for explicit control.
AI.result: The formative study characterized current inking practices and unmet needs. The diagnostic study identified specific usability and interaction challenges in combining LLMs with ink-based interfaces. The final evaluation demonstrated how users adopt Thinkink into their ideation workflows, validating the ink-native LLM interaction paradigm.
AI.conclusion: Thinkink demonstrates a viable approach for ink-native LLM interaction, where both user and model co-create on a shared 2D canvas. The paper contributes design implications and a functional tool that integrates LLM responses as spatially situated, ink-like text and sketches, preserving the fluidity of handwritten ideation.

title: Fast and Efficient Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search for High-Dimensional LLM Embeddings
summary:
The annual SISAP Indexing Challenge benchmarks Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search (ANNS) algorithms under rigorous constraints. This paper presents our submissions for the 2026 edition, addressing both $k$-Nearest Neighbor Graph (kNNG) construction on 1024-dimensional BGE-M3 embeddings (Task 1) and Maximum Inner Product Search (MIPS) on unnormalized Llama-3.2-8B features (Task 2). To optimize construction speed, we utilize Equi-Voronoi Polytopes (EVP) for efficient quantization, supplemented by targeted reranking strategies to maintain high recall. For MIPS, we transform the asymmetric inner product problem into a Euclidean search space via dimensionality augmentation. To reduce query latency and optimize memory access, we introduce a 1D presorting mechanism via Fast Linear Assignment Sorting (FLAS) prior to graph construction. This significantly improves spatial locality and cache hit rates during subsequent graph traversal.
  Source Code: https://github.com/Visual-Computing/sisap26-deglib

AI.tldr: Submission to SISAP 2026 Indexing Challenge: uses EVP quantization + reranking for fast k-NNG construction on BGE-M3 embeddings, and dimensionality augmentation + FLAS presorting for efficient MIPS on Llama-3.2-8B features.
AI.motivation: Addresses the SISAP Indexing Challenge 2026, which benchmarks ANNS algorithms under strict constraints. The two tasks — k-NNG construction on high-dimensional dense embeddings and MIPS on unnormalized language model features — demand solutions that balance construction speed, query latency, recall, and memory efficiency.
AI.method: For Task 1 (kNNG construction): employs Equi-Voronoi Polytopes (EVP) for efficient vector quantization, combined with targeted reranking to recover recall lost during approximate indexing. For Task 2 (MIPS): converts the asymmetric inner product problem into Euclidean ANNS via dimensionality augmentation, and introduces Fast Linear Assignment Sorting (FLAS) — a 1D presorting step applied before graph construction — to improve spatial locality and cache hit rates during graph traversal.
AI.result: Not explicitly stated in the abstract; the paper describes the submitted approaches but does not provide quantitative results.
AI.conclusion: The proposed methods — EVP-based quantization with reranking and FLAS-based presorting with dimensionality augmentation — offer principled approaches to the dual challenges of fast graph construction and efficient MIPS under competition constraints. Source code is publicly available.

title: Improving Communication of Changes in Model-Based Engineering with Model-Independent Change Descriptions
summary: In model-based engineering, inter-disciplinary teams collaborate through models, which change over time for purposes of system development, what makes the proper description of such changes crucial for engineers. However, any change made by the engineer of one discipline will be difficult to understand by the engineers of other disciplines. To overcome this limitation, model-independent change descriptions can be derived instead, which preserve semantics of the changes and do not require model-specific knowledge. The two opposing approaches here are to describe changes using either informal language or formal notions of change. While informal language lacks objectivity and standardisation, formal notions of change lack human interpretability, and thus offering no support for inter-disciplinary communication. In this paper, we propose functions to map formally specified changes, represented in the approach of delta modelling, to change descriptions in model-independent language. In an exhaustive mixed-methods evaluation, we bridge the gap between the theoretical and the practical representation of changes. We quantitatively assess technical feasibility, with an implementation framework, and technical applicability, along a case study; and we qualitatively assess plausibility, practical applicability, and extensibility, in a user study. Our work shows a promising starting point for automated, model-independent description of changes in model-based engineering projects.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes mapping functions that translate formally specified model changes (delta modelling) into model-independent natural language descriptions, bridging formal precision with human interpretability for interdisciplinary communication in model-based engineering.
AI.motivation: In model-based engineering, cross-disciplinary teams struggle to understand each other's model changes. Informal descriptions lack objectivity; formal change notations lack human interpretability. A solution is needed that preserves semantic precision while being accessible to engineers from any discipline.
AI.method: The authors propose functions to map formally specified changes (using delta modelling) to model-independent natural language change descriptions. They evaluate this through a mixed-methods approach: quantitative assessment via an implementation framework and a case study (technical feasibility and applicability), and qualitative assessment via a user study (plausibility, practical applicability, and extensibility).
AI.result: The implementation framework and case study demonstrate technical feasibility and applicability of the mapping approach. The user study confirms plausibility, practical applicability, and extensibility of the generated model-independent change descriptions.
AI.conclusion: The work establishes a promising foundation for automated, model-independent description of changes in model-based engineering, effectively bridging the gap between formal change representations and practical, human-interpretable communication across disciplines.

title: Human-in-the-Loop Large Language Model Framework for Identification of Cutaneous Immune-Related Adverse Events
summary: This study evaluated a retrieval-augmented, multi-agent large language model (LLM)-driven, human-in-the-loop framework for detecting cutaneous immune-related adverse events (cirAEs) from clinical notes. Compared with unassisted manual review, the LLM-assisted workflow improved accuracy (F1 = 0.88 vs 0.77), inter-rater agreement measured by Cohen's kappa (kappa = 0.82 vs 0.50), and reduced average review time by approximately half. This framework pilots how LLMs can be applied to identify immune-related toxicities across organ systems and, more broadly, enable accurate, scalable, and transparent adverse event data extraction.

AI.tldr: A retrieval-augmented, multi-agent LLM framework with human-in-the-loop was tested for detecting cutaneous immune-related adverse events from clinical notes, outperforming manual review in accuracy (F1: 0.88 vs 0.77), inter-rater agreement (κ: 0.82 vs 0.50), and review time (halved).
AI.motivation: Manual review of clinical notes for adverse event detection is time-consuming, inconsistent, and poorly scalable. There is a need for accurate, efficient, and transparent methods to identify immune-related toxicities across organ systems from unstructured clinical text.
AI.method: The authors developed a retrieval-augmented, multi-agent LLM-driven, human-in-the-loop framework for detecting cutaneous immune-related adverse events (cirAEs) from clinical notes. The system was evaluated against unassisted manual review on metrics including F1 score, Cohen's kappa for inter-rater agreement, and average review time.
AI.result: The LLM-assisted workflow achieved an F1 score of 0.88 (vs. 0.77 manual), Cohen's kappa of 0.82 (vs. 0.50 manual), and reduced average review time by approximately half compared to unassisted manual review.
AI.conclusion: The framework demonstrates that LLMs can be effectively applied to identify immune-related toxicities across organ systems, enabling accurate, scalable, and transparent adverse event data extraction. This pilot supports broader adoption of LLM-assisted workflows for pharmacovigilance and clinical data abstraction.

title: Geometric Configurations of Perturbed Jailbreak Prompts
comment: 21 pages, 9 figures, 7 tables, 2nd Workshop on Safe AI (SafeAI)
summary: Perturbation techniques that turn unsuccessful jailbreak prompts into successful ones are continuously evolving, constituting a major security threat to LLM safety. In this paper, we investigate the internal representations of such string-level perturbed jailbreak inputs in the small weight models of the Qwen-2.5-1.5B/-3B/-7B-Instruct and Llama-3.2-1B/-3B/-3.1-8B-Instruct families. We select two representation spaces: the last-layer-last-token embedding space and the top-50 next-token probability space. The former space separates prompts based on their spelling and format, while the latter space is effectively one-dimensional but appears more complex to cluster. Within our refusal-dominated answer set we find no behavioral hyperplane in either space. Only the next token "Sure" in the 1.5B Qwen model, and both tokens "," and "ĊĊ" in the 1$ Llama model, display a significant association with a compliant-labeled answer.

AI.tldr: Analysis of internal representations in small-weight LLMs reveals that perturbed jailbreak prompts do not form separable clusters or behavioral hyperplanes in embedding or next-token probability spaces, challenging assumptions about detectable safety boundaries.
AI.motivation: Jailbreak perturbation techniques are evolving and pose a serious security threat to LLM safety. The authors aim to understand whether string-level perturbations leave detectable signatures in the internal representations of small models, which could inform defense mechanisms.
AI.method: The authors investigate two representation spaces — the last-layer-last-token embedding space and the top-50 next-token probability space — across six small-weight instruction-tuned models from the Qwen-2.5 (1.5B, 3B, 7B) and Llama-3.2 (1B, 3B, 3.1-8B) families. They analyze whether perturbed jailbreak prompts cluster separately from non-jailbreak prompts and search for behavioral hyperplanes separating refusal from compliance.
AI.result: The embedding space separates prompts by spelling and format rather than by safety outcome. The next-token probability space appears effectively one-dimensional and resists meaningful clustering. No behavioral hyperplane separating refusal from compliance was found in either space. Only the token "Sure" in Qwen-2.5-1.5B and tokens "," and "ĊĊ" in the 1B Llama model showed significant association with compliant-labeled answers.
AI.conclusion: String-level jailbreak perturbations do not produce easily detectable separation in the studied internal representations of small-weight LLMs, suggesting that safety monitoring based solely on these representation spaces may be insufficient for robust defense.

title: Scaling Closed-Loop Feature Channel Configuration with LLMs
summary: Promising initial results in closed-loop large-language-model-based channel-configuration search demonstrated that neural-network widths can be optimized directly through executable code generation and accuracy feedback. However, those results were obtained from a relatively sparse set of valid evaluations, leaving open whether the observed optimization behavior transfers to a denser sampling regime and whether additional architectural regularities emerge when more generated networks are evaluated. To test this, the same search setting is scaled to 250 candidate networks per fine-tuning cycle. The analysis covers 2000 generated candidates from 8 complete cycles, yielding 462 verified CIFAR-100 evaluations after task and metadata filtering. Per-cycle mean accuracy exhibits a positive linear trend with slope 9.87e-4 (p=0.043), while the high-performing frontier improves more strongly: the best observed accuracy increases from 0.3144 to 0.3676, and both the top-5 and top-10 cycle-level means exhibit positive trends. The scaled run also reveals improved parameter efficiency. The best model reaches 0.3676 with 11.8M parameters, compared with an early high-performing model at 0.3144 with 166.5M parameters. Beyond accuracy, the larger sample exposes architectural regularities that were difficult to assess from sparse observations. Non-power-of-two channel widths occur in 41.8% of verified candidates, and the strongest models share structured channel-allocation patterns characterized by moderate early widths and expanded middle or later blocks. These findings indicate that the channel-search signal observed in the initial study transfers

AI.tldr: Scaling up LLM-based channel-configuration search to 250 candidates per cycle (2000 total, 462 verified) confirms that the optimization signal transfers to denser sampling. Mean accuracy trends positively (slope 9.87e-4, p=0.043), the best model improves from 0.3144 to 0.3676 with far fewer parameters (11.8M vs 166.5M), and structured architectural regularities emerge — notably non-power-of-two channel widths in 41.8% of candidates and a pattern of moderate early widths with expanded middle/later blocks.
AI.motivation: The original LLM-based channel-width search used sparse evaluations, raising questions about whether the observed optimization behavior would hold under denser sampling and whether additional architectural patterns would surface with more candidate networks evaluated.
AI.method: The same closed-loop LLM-based search setting (executable code generation with accuracy feedback) was scaled to 250 candidate networks per fine-tuning cycle across 8 complete cycles, producing 2000 generated candidates. After task and metadata filtering, 462 verified CIFAR-100 evaluations were analyzed for accuracy trends, parameter efficiency, and architectural regularities.
AI.result: Per-cycle mean accuracy showed a positive linear trend (slope 9.87e-4, p=0.043). The best accuracy rose from 0.3144 to 0.3676, with top-5 and top-10 cycle-level means also improving. Parameter efficiency improved dramatically: the best model achieved 0.3676 with 11.8M parameters vs. an early high-performer at 0.3144 with 166.5M parameters. Non-power-of-two channel widths appeared in 41.8% of verified candidates. The strongest models shared a structured pattern: moderate early widths with expanded middle or later blocks.
AI.conclusion: The channel-search signal from the initial sparse study transfers robustly to a denser sampling regime. Scaling up reveals clear parameter-efficiency gains and emergent architectural regularities — specifically, non-power-of-two widths and a moderate-early/expanded-late channel allocation pattern — that were not discernible from sparse observations.

title: Stochastic Sampling is Epistemically Shallow: The Dimensionality Gap Between Temperature Variation and Model Diversity in LLMs
comment: 8 pages, 4 figures, 3 tables. Accepted at EIML@ICML 2026
summary: When a language model gives different answers on repeated runs, does that variation reveal what it does not know? Self-consistency turns the variation into a per-question uncertainty estimate via majority voting. But does the same variation reveal cross-question structure -- related questions flipping together, the way a diverse ensemble does? We compare two regimes on the same questions: one model run $100$ times at $τ=1$ versus an ensemble of $24$ LLMs run once each at $τ=0$. A Marchenko--Pastur random-matrix test separates signal from sampling noise on both sides. Within any single model, at most one dimension rises above noise across five families and three benchmarks (MMLU, HellaSwag, GSM8K). Across the ensemble, four eigenvalues clear the noise edge, while a matched-difficulty Bernoulli null produces at most one in $500$ Monte Carlo draws. Self-consistency gives accurate per-question uncertainty but no detectable cross-question structure; only a diverse ensemble surfaces what a model does not know.

AI.tldr: Self-consistency (repeated sampling from a single model) yields reliable per-question uncertainty estimates but reveals no cross-question structure. Only a diverse ensemble of different models surfaces shared patterns in what models collectively fail to know, as evidenced by eigenvalue analysis using Marchenko–Pastur random-matrix theory.
AI.motivation: To determine whether the variation observed when a language model is repeatedly queried (at temperature τ=1) reflects meaningful cross-question structure — i.e., groups of questions that flip together, analogous to a diverse ensemble — or whether that variation is essentially unstructured sampling noise.
AI.method: Two regimes are compared on the same set of questions: (1) one model run 100 times at τ=1 (self-consistency), and (2) an ensemble of 24 LLMs run once each at τ=0. For both, the authors construct a binary correctness matrix (questions × runs/models) and apply Marchenko–Pastur random-matrix theory to separate signal eigenvalues from sampling noise. A matched-difficulty Bernoulli null is used as a baseline, and results are evaluated across five model families and three benchmarks (MMLU, HellaSwag, GSM8K).
AI.result: Within any single model, at most one eigenvalue rises above the Marchenko–Pastur noise edge across all settings. Across the 24-model ensemble, four eigenvalues clear the noise edge. The matched-difficulty Bernoulli null produces at most one eigenvalue above noise in 500 Monte Carlo draws. Self-consistency thus yields accurate per-question uncertainty but no detectable cross-question structure.
AI.conclusion: Self-consistency captures per-question epistemic uncertainty but fails to uncover latent cross-question structure. Only a diverse ensemble of different models reveals systematic patterns in what models do not know, suggesting that model diversity — not repeated sampling from a single model — is necessary to surface shared knowledge gaps.

title: A Needs Assessment for Measuring Geographic - Legislative Associations in the U.S. House of Representatives
comment: 35 pages, 9 figures, 6 tables. Link to map: https://doi.org/10.6084/m9.figshare.32680776. Research Team: Ashu Gupta, Cameron Owens, Benjamin Wilson-Langman, Max Hill, Jason Cox, Ian Arnold, Santiago Velez, Quinn Pearson, Yunhe Cui, Isaac Felix, Ryan Luong, Priya Parikh, Shubham Purish, Vivek Rao, Cat Tran, Mingkuan Yan, Christopher Yang, Clio Andris
summary:
Political legislation affects the well-being and livelihoods of constituents. In the U.S. Congress a representative's voting record on bills and legislation is public. These bills have themes associated with them, such as veterans' affairs, coastal monitoring, agricultural appropriations, etc. A bill on veterans' affairs may affect a constituency differently if they have a high percentage of veterans. In this work, we demonstrate how congressional vote outcomes can be merged with typical geographic information systems (GIS) data to help compare a legislator's votes with the geographies of their constituencies to measure the association between district features and legislators' decisions.
  We retrieved and tagged bills from the 118th U.S. House of Representatives (Jan. 2023 - Jan. 2025) by manually assigning each bill a set of themes. We then retrieved spatial data at the congressional district level related to each theme. We built a backend database to connect bill information and spatial data, and an interactive map prototype displayed the spatial data related to each theme associated with each bill. Our work helps identify challenges to creating a more accessible and complete system that would facilitate the visualization and analysis of the nature of contemporary Congressional representation. This technical report is primarily written for members of the data science community, and specifically those interested in legislative and geographic data.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a prototype system that merges U.S. congressional voting records with GIS data to spatially analyze how district-level demographic and geographic features correlate with legislators' voting decisions, using manually themed bills from the 118th House of Representatives (2023–2025).
AI.motivation: Legislators' votes on themed bills (e.g., veterans' affairs, agriculture) may be influenced by the demographic and geographic characteristics of their constituencies. Existing systems do not readily integrate congressional roll-call data with spatial district-level data, making it difficult to systematically measure the association between district features and voting behavior.
AI.method: The authors (1) retrieved bills from the 118th U.S. House (Jan. 2023–Jan. 2025) and manually assigned thematic tags to each bill; (2) collected congressional-district-level spatial data corresponding to each theme; (3) built a backend database linking bill metadata to spatial datasets; and (4) developed an interactive map prototype that visualizes theme-relevant spatial data alongside voting outcomes.
AI.result: The prototype demonstrates feasibility of integrating legislative and GIS data and surfaces challenges in building a comprehensive, accessible system for visualizing and analyzing the relationship between district characteristics and congressional representation.
AI.conclusion: The work serves as a technical report for the data science community, highlighting both the potential and the infrastructural challenges of creating a complete platform for geo-legislative analysis of contemporary congressional representation.

title: Bridging the Structural Gap: Adapting Autoregressive Generation for Recommendation
summary: Generative Recommendation (GR) has emerged as a new paradigm for sequential recommendation, in which a representative line of work encodes items into hierarchical semantic IDs via residual quantization and predicts the IDs token by token. However, this generative formulation still exhibits structural gaps with respect to the recommendation task: flattening multi-token IDs into a single sequence destroys item-level structure, and the inconsistency between training and inference over a hierarchical codebook gives rise to semantic drift. To bridge these two gaps, we propose BARGE, which employs Item Context-Aware Attention (ICA) to restore item-level structure during encoding, and Hierarchical Path Reranking (HPR) together with Dual-Path Decoding (DPD) to suppress semantic drift from two complementary angles during decoding. Extensive experiments and analytical studies on public benchmarks and a large-scale offline test demonstrate that BARGE achieves superior recommendation performance. An online A/B test on a Tencent platform yields improvements of 0.60% in click-through rate, 1.34% in click unique visitors, and 1.70% in total reading time, confirming the practical value of BARGE in industrial-scale recommendation.

AI.tldr: BARGE improves generative sequential recommendation by restoring item-level structure during encoding (via Item Context-Aware Attention) and suppressing semantic drift during decoding (via Hierarchical Path Reranking and Dual-Path Decoding), achieving SOTA results and verified industrial gains on a Tencent platform.
AI.motivation: Existing generative recommendation methods encode items as hierarchical semantic IDs and predict them token-by-token, but suffer from two structural gaps: (1) flattening multi-token IDs destroys item-level structure, and (2) train-inference inconsistency over hierarchical codebooks causes semantic drift.
AI.method: BARGE introduces three components: (1) Item Context-Aware Attention (ICA) to restore item-level structure during encoding; (2) Hierarchical Path Reranking (HPR) and (3) Dual-Path Decoding (DPD) to suppress semantic drift from complementary angles during decoding.
AI.result: BARGE achieves superior performance on public benchmarks and a large-scale offline test. An online A/B test on a Tencent platform shows +0.60% CTR, +1.34% click unique visitors, and +1.70% total reading time.
AI.conclusion: BARGE effectively bridges the structural gaps in generative sequential recommendation, delivering both academic SOTA results and verified industrial value at scale.

title: Information is all you need: Requirements Engineering Quality Reframed
summary: To move beyond this vague appeal to context, this vision proposes a novel holistic theory of requirements engineering (RE) quality. This theory models how information particles, i.e., discrete pieces of domain knowledge, are transferred between roles and artifacts. Since the RE process is ultimately an information transfer, holistic RE quality depends on the properties of information flow, i.e., how effectively and efficiently information is transferred from sources (like stakeholders) to targets (like developers and testers), uniting both artifact- and process-based perspectives on RE quality. In an exemplary simulation of the theory we illustrate why a high-quality specification gets bypassed in an agile context, thereby demonstrating that a simulation can provide actionable insights into calibrating the RE process to optimize the information flow. Beyond organizational applications, we envision that the theory can serve as a coherent theoretical framework for understanding the success or failure of RE processes and artifacts.

AI.tldr: Proposes a holistic theory of RE quality based on information transfer, modeling how discrete knowledge particles flow between roles and artifacts to unify artifact- and process-based quality perspectives.
AI.motivation: Existing appeals to "context" in RE are vague and unsatisfactory. There is a need for a coherent theoretical framework that explains why RE processes and artifacts succeed or fail, bridging the gap between artifact quality and process quality perspectives.
AI.method: Develops a novel theory modeling RE as information transfer, where discrete pieces of domain knowledge ("information particles") flow between roles (stakeholders, developers, testers) and artifacts. An exemplary simulation demonstrates the theory's application in an agile context.
AI.result: The simulation illustrates why a high-quality specification can be bypassed in agile settings, showing that the theory can yield actionable insights for calibrating RE processes to optimize information flow.
AI.conclusion: The theory serves two purposes: (1) organizational — enabling simulation-driven calibration of RE processes, and (2) theoretical — providing a unified framework for understanding RE success or failure beyond vague appeals to context.

title: Workload-Aware Caching for Multi-Agent Systems
summary: Multi-agent systems decompose complex tasks into directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) of specialized agent executions, creating natural opportunities for caching intermediate results across queries. However, existing cache eviction policies treat all cached entries uniformly based on access history, ignoring structural and workload signals uniquely available in agentic execution environments. We present a workload-aware eviction policy that combines three signals, namely recomputation cost, DAG dependency count, and agent invocation frequency, into a unified scoring function that retains the most valuable entries under memory constraints. Evaluated across three multi-agent benchmarks spanning diverse reuse regimes, our policy reduces latency by up to 64.7% relative to the uncached baseline and achieves on average a 31.1% latency reduction over the next best finite-capacity baseline, while approaching the performance of an unbounded cache and maintaining accuracy on par with or exceeding all competing finite-capacity methods. We further show that workload-aware content caching is complementary to other agentic system optimization methods, including plan-level caching and parallel agent execution, with each technique targeting a distinct efficiency bottleneck in multi-agent pipelines.

AI.tldr: A workload-aware cache eviction policy for multi-agent systems that combines recomputation cost, DAG dependency count, and agent invocation frequency into a unified scoring function, achieving up to 64.7% latency reduction over uncached baselines and 31.1% improvement over the next best finite-capacity cache.
AI.motivation: Multi-agent systems decompose tasks into DAGs of agent executions, creating reuse opportunities for intermediate results. Existing cache eviction policies are workload-agnostic—treating all entries uniformly based solely on access history—and fail to exploit structural and workload signals unique to agentic execution environments (e.g., recomputation cost, dependency topology, invocation patterns).
AI.method: A unified scoring function for cache eviction that integrates three workload-aware signals: (1) recomputation cost of the cached entry, (2) DAG dependency count (how many downstream agents depend on the result), and (3) agent invocation frequency. Entries with higher scores are retained under memory constraints.
AI.result: Evaluated across three multi-agent benchmarks with diverse reuse regimes, the policy achieves up to 64.7% latency reduction versus uncached baselines, a 31.1% average latency reduction over the next best finite-capacity baseline, near-unbounded-cache performance, and accuracy on par with or exceeding all competing finite-capacity methods. The approach is also complementary to plan-level caching and parallel agent execution.
AI.conclusion: Workload-aware content caching, informed by recomputation cost, dependency structure, and invocation frequency, significantly outperforms traditional eviction policies in multi-agent systems. It is orthogonal to other optimizations like plan caching and parallelism, with each addressing distinct bottlenecks in agentic pipelines.

title: Enhancing Attack Detection Capabilities in BACnet/IP Networks Using Machine-Learning Models
summary: Building Automation Systems (BAS) manage critical building functions using protocols such as BACnet/IP, yet defenders have limited tooling and few labeled datasets for detecting BACnet-specific attacks. This work addresses these gaps through three contributions. First, CISA's Zeek BACnet parser is modified to produce a unified per-packet log, simplifying feature engineering for machine-learning (ML) pipelines. Second, a simulated BACnet/IP testbed is developed using bacpypes3 to model a small commercial HVAC system with physics-based device behavior, schedule-aware controller logic, and per-packet attack labeling. Third, five unsupervised anomaly detection models are evaluated using baseline traffic and six BACnet attack types, including denial of service, reconnaissance, property tampering, and false data injection. Results show that One-Class SVM achieved the strongest overall performance, with an average F1 score of 0.864 across all attacks and F1 scores above 0.99 for high-volume denial-of-service and reconnaissance attacks. Detection is much stronger for high-volume attacks, such as DoS attacks and reconnaissance, than stealthier techniques such as tampering and false data injection, which scored around 77%.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a BACnet/IP intrusion detection framework featuring a modified Zeek parser for unified logging, a physics-based HVAC testbed (bacpypes3) with per-packet attack labeling, and an evaluation of five unsupervised anomaly detection models against six attack types. One-Class SVM achieved the best results (avg F1=0.864), excelling on high-volume attacks (F1>0.99) but struggling with stealthy attacks (~77% F1).
AI.motivation: Defenders lack adequate tooling and labeled datasets for detecting BACnet-specific attacks in Building Automation Systems (BAS), despite BACnet/IP being critical for managing building functions. This gap hinders the development and evaluation of ML-based intrusion detection for BAS environments.
AI.method: Three contributions: (1) CISA's Zeek BACnet parser is modified to produce a unified per-packet log for streamlined ML feature engineering; (2) a simulated BACnet/IP testbed is built using bacpypes3, modeling a small commercial HVAC system with physics-based device behavior, schedule-aware controller logic, and per-packet attack labeling; (3) five unsupervised anomaly detection models are evaluated against baseline traffic and six BACnet attack types (DoS, reconnaissance, property tampering, false data injection, etc.).
AI.result: One-Class SVM achieved the strongest overall performance with an average F1 score of 0.864 across all attacks. High-volume attacks (DoS, reconnaissance) yielded F1 scores above 0.99. Stealthier attacks (property tampering, false data injection) scored around 77% F1, indicating substantially weaker detection for low-volume, subtle attack techniques.
AI.conclusion: Unsupervised anomaly detection is viable for BACnet/IP intrusion detection, particularly effective against high-volume attacks. However, significant performance gaps remain for stealthy attacks, highlighting the need for improved detection methods targeting subtle manipulation techniques like tampering and false data injection in BAS environments.

title: More Is Not More: What Matters for Diversity in LLM Opinions?
summary: Large language models are increasingly used to simulate diverse human opinions in open-ended tasks such as synthetic surveys, focus group modeling, and public opinion prediction. However, LLM outputs exhibit systematic opinion homogenization. Practitioners have explored various interventions to increase diversity, but the landscape remains fragmented: different methods are evaluated in isolation with incomparable metrics, and in practice they are typically deployed and upgraded simultaneously, making it difficult to attribute gains to specific components. To advance a more scientific understanding of LLM output diversity, we design a factorial experiment that separates two primary intervention dimensions: input conditioning (operationalized through persona depth) and interaction architecture. We evaluate all conditions on 100 real-user open-ended questions across 7 models, measuring diversity with multiple complementary metrics. Our findings challenge several common assumptions. First, more persona detail does not monotonically increase diversity. The initial step of persona conditioning already captures the majority of the gain, while further elaboration with demographic detail does not consistently improve and can reduce diversity on some models. Second, rather than seeking a single best interaction architecture, we find that different architectures explore largely non-overlapping opinion regions. Combining multiple architectures yields broader coverage than optimizing any one. Third, commonly attempted low-cost alternatives such as raising sampling temperature and adding diversity instructions produce negligible effects compared to structured interventions. Overall, our work demonstrates that diversity is not a product of scaling along any single dimension, but is highly sensitive to the structural form and combination of interventions.

AI.tldr: A factorial experiment across 7 LLMs and 100 open-ended questions reveals that output diversity is not monotonically driven by persona detail, that different interaction architectures cover non-overlapping opinion regions, and that low-cost interventions (temperature, diversity prompts) have negligible effects compared to structured methods.
AI.motivation: LLMs are increasingly used to simulate human opinions in surveys, focus groups, and public opinion prediction, but suffer from systematic opinion homogenization. The landscape of diversity-enhancing interventions is fragmented: methods are evaluated in isolation with incomparable metrics and deployed simultaneously, obscuring attribution of gains to specific components.
AI.method: A factorial experiment design separating two primary intervention dimensions: (1) input conditioning, operationalized as persona depth (none → basic persona → persona + demographics), and (2) interaction architecture (multiple distinct prompting/agent structures). Evaluated across 7 models on 100 real-user open-ended questions, using multiple complementary diversity metrics.
AI.result: Key findings: (1) Initial persona conditioning captures most diversity gains; adding demographic detail does not consistently improve and can reduce diversity on some models. (2) Different interaction architectures explore largely non-overlapping opinion regions, so combining architectures yields broader coverage than optimizing any single one. (3) Low-cost alternatives (higher temperature, diversity instructions) produce negligible effects compared to structured interventions.
AI.conclusion: Diversity in LLM outputs is not a product of scaling along any single dimension but is highly sensitive to the structural form and combination of interventions. A scientific, factorial approach to studying diversity mechanisms is essential for advancing the field beyond ad hoc method stacking.

title: Multimodal CoLRAG-TF: Triple-Filtered Retrieval for Complex PDFs
summary: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) over heterogeneous PDF collections remains challenging due to multimodal content, domain-specific terminology, and the need for multi-hop reasoning across dispersed evidence. We present Multimodal CoLRAG-TF, a four-axis fusion architecture that integrates dense text embeddings, BM25 keyword matching, knowledge-graph triple filtering, and image-based similarity for robust retrieval over complex documents. Our system constructs a multimodal index of 2,403 blocks extracted from 43 Japanese disaster lesson PDFs, supported by a hybrid OCR pipeline and LLM-based caption generation. To enhance compositional reasoning, we extract 11,414 OpenIE triples and index them with FAISS, enabling sub-second triple lookup and hierarchical propagation of relevance signals. A HippoRAG2-inspired coarse-to-fine retriever (volume $\to$ chapter $\to$ block) narrows the search space before final fusion scoring. Bayesian optimization over fusion weights reveals that the triple axis must dominate ($α_\text{triple} = 0.44$) to counteract lexical bias and sustain multi-hop retrieval quality. Evaluated on a 457-pair benchmark, Multimodal CoLRAG-TF achieves a Retrieval Recall of 0.9909 and a 71.6$\%$ improvement in multi-hop answer similarity over single-hop queries. An image-to-lesson pipeline using a vision LLM further demonstrates the applicability of the approach to visual inputs. These results show that triple-filtered multimodal fusion is essential for structured reasoning over noisy, heterogeneous PDFs and provides a general framework applicable beyond the disaster domain.

AI.tldr: Multimodal CoLRAG-TF is a four-axis fusion RAG architecture combining dense text embeddings, BM25, knowledge-graph triple filtering, and image similarity for multi-hop retrieval over heterogeneous PDFs. Tested on Japanese disaster lesson documents, it achieves 0.9909 retrieval recall and a 71.6% improvement in multi-hop answer similarity, with Bayesian optimization showing that the triple axis must dominate fusion weights.
AI.motivation: Retrieval-augmented generation over heterogeneous PDF collections is challenging due to multimodal content (text, images, tables), domain-specific terminology, and the need for multi-hop reasoning across dispersed evidence scattered throughout documents. Existing approaches struggle to integrate these diverse signals effectively.
AI.method: The authors propose Multimodal CoLRAG-TF, a four-axis fusion architecture that: (1) constructs a multimodal index of 2,403 blocks from 43 Japanese disaster lesson PDFs via hybrid OCR and LLM-based caption generation; (2) extracts 11,414 OpenIE triples indexed with FAISS for sub-second triple lookup; (3) employs a HippoRAG2-inspired coarse-to-fine retriever (volume → chapter → block); (4) fuses four axes — dense text embeddings, BM25 keyword matching, knowledge-graph triple filtering, and image-based similarity — with weights optimized via Bayesian optimization, yielding a dominant triple weight (α_triple = 0.44). An image-to-lesson pipeline using a vision LLM extends the system to visual inputs.
AI.result: Evaluated on a 457-pair benchmark, Multimodal CoLRAG-TF achieves a Retrieval Recall of 0.9909 and a 71.6% improvement in multi-hop answer similarity over single-hop queries. Bayesian optimization reveals that the triple filtering axis must dominate (α_triple = 0.44) to counteract lexical bias and sustain multi-hop retrieval quality.
AI.conclusion: Triple-filtered multimodal fusion is essential for structured reasoning over noisy, heterogeneous PDFs. The framework generalizes beyond the disaster domain and demonstrates that knowledge-graph–centric weighting is critical for compositional, multi-hop retrieval tasks.

title: JAXBench: Benchmarking Autonomous TPU Kernel Optimization
summary: Rigorous benchmarks have driven progress in autonomous GPU kernel performance optimization by establishing a shared target to hillclimb on, but no equivalent exists for TPUs. We present JAXBench, a TPU-native benchmark suite for AI-generated kernel optimization on Google Cloud TPUs. JAXBench comprises 50 JAX workloads that are both relevant and provide headroom for optimization. We extract 17 production ML operators from architectures in the public MaxText library such as Llama-3.1, DeepSeek-V3, Mixtral, Mamba-2, and AlphaFold2, and translate 33 operators from KernelBench that are validated for correctness and set with new problem sizes that achieve high TPU v6e MXU utilization. Eight of the 17 production operators ship with hand-optimized Pallas kernels from the public Tokamax library and block-size tuned to establish an expert upper-bound baseline. We evaluate four feedback-driven methods on generating candidate Pallas kernels for JAXBench. Across the full suite with Gemini 3 Flash, we find that target-specific context matters more than model scale on a sparsely-documented DSL like Pallas. Conditioning on curated TPU documentation raises per-sample correctness from 5.8% to 37.3% and solves 48 of 50 benchmarks at a 1.28x geomean speedup. Search structure yields significant gains once correctness is achieved, with Autocomp's beam-search pipeline reaching a 1.36x geomean speedup over XLA. On the 8 hand-tuned kernels, Autocomp reaches 1.60x geomean over XLA, recovering most of the 2.08x Tokamax upper bound but trailing on the specialized paged and ragged attention operators. High-quality TPU kernel optimization remains a challenging task, and we release the JAXBench benchmark, evaluation harness, and baseline results to support open source contributions.

AI.tldr: JAXBench is a new benchmark suite of 50 JAX workloads for evaluating AI-driven TPU kernel optimization. It includes 17 production ML operators and 33 translated operators, with 8 hand-optimized Pallas kernels as expert baselines. Experiments show that curated TPU documentation dramatically improves correctness (5.8%→37.3%), and Autocomp's beam search achieves up to 1.36x geomean speedup over XLA.
AI.motivation: GPU kernel optimization has benefited from rigorous benchmarks (e.g., KernelBench) that enable systematic progress via feedback-driven methods. No equivalent exists for TPUs, limiting reproducible research on AI-generated TPU kernel optimization.
AI.method: The authors construct JAXBench with 50 workloads: 17 extracted from production ML architectures (Llama-3.1, DeepSeek-V3, Mixtral, Mamba-2, AlphaFold2) and 33 translated from KernelBench with TPU-appropriate problem sizes. Eight kernels have hand-optimized Pallas baselines from Tokamax. Four feedback-driven methods (including Autocomp's beam search) are evaluated using Gemini 3 Flash, ablating the impact of TPU-specific documentation and search structure.
AI.result: Target-specific context is critical: curated TPU documentation raises per-sample correctness from 5.8% to 37.3% and solves 48/50 benchmarks at 1.28x geomean speedup. Autocomp's beam search achieves 1.36x geomean speedup over XLA overall and 1.60x on the 8 hand-tuned kernels, approaching but not matching the 2.08x Tokamax upper bound, particularly lagging on paged/ragged attention.
AI.conclusion: High-quality TPU kernel optimization remains challenging. Documentation quality and search structure are both essential for AI-driven kernel generation. JAXBench, along with its evaluation harness and baselines, is released to spur open-source research.

title: Transparent by Design, Usable in Practice? A Formative Usability Study of a Conversational Product Advisor
summary: Large language models can make conversational product advisors fluent but opaque. If they hide the logic behind a ranking and the evidence for a recommendation inside natural-language replies, they challenge users' ability to understand, trust, and steer the results. One response is to build transparency into the advisor. We report a formative, moderated think-aloud usability study of one such system: a chatbot for laptop search with constrained natural-language generation, an on-demand ranking explanation, and a comparison feature. Seven participants completed three laptop-search tasks and reported post-task usability measures. We coded their sessions into severity-rated usability problems. Ease and satisfaction during the tasks were high, but two findings stand out. First, transparency by design did not guarantee understanding: several participants valued the ranking explanation in principle, yet it caused the most severe problem. Second, participants valued the effort the advisor saved, but some wanted additional direct-manipulation controls. We contribute a severity-prioritized set of usability problems and design implications for human-centered conversational product advisors.

AI.tldr: A usability study of a transparent conversational laptop advisor found that while ease and satisfaction were high, designed transparency features (especially ranking explanations) sometimes caused severe usability problems, and users desired more direct-manipulation controls.
AI.motivation: LLM-based conversational product advisors risk being opaque — hiding ranking logic and recommendation evidence behind fluent natural-language replies, which undermines user understanding, trust, and control. The study investigates whether designing transparency into such systems can address these challenges.
AI.method: A formative, moderated think-aloud usability study with seven participants completing three laptop-search tasks on a chatbot featuring constrained NLG, on-demand ranking explanations, and a comparison feature. Sessions were coded into severity-rated usability problems, supplemented by post-task usability measures.
AI.result: Ease and satisfaction were high, but two key findings emerged: (1) transparency by design did not guarantee understanding — the ranking explanation caused the most severe usability problem despite being valued in principle; (2) participants appreciated the advisor's effort-saving qualities but desired additional direct-manipulation controls.
AI.conclusion: The paper contributes a severity-prioritized set of usability problems and design implications for building human-centered conversational product advisors, highlighting the gap between transparency as a design feature and actual user comprehension.

title: SHIFT: Self-reconstruction Harnesses Implicit Fine-grained Thinking for Retrieval
summary: LLM-based retrievers have become a fundamental component of modern information retrieval systems. The paradigm of "rewrite-then-retriev" introduces explicit reasoning before retrieval. In addition, implicit-reasoning retrievers such as GIRCSE and LaSER improve efficiency by replacing explicit reasoning with soft tokens. Although these methods demonstrated competitive performance on reasoning-intensive retrieval benchmarks, they struggle to address the mismatch between the objectives of retrieval and generation. In this work, we propose SHIFT ($\textbf{S}$elf-reconstruction $\textbf{H}$arnesses $\textbf{I}$mplicit $\textbf{F}$ine-grained $\textbf{T}$hinking for Retrieval), a retrieval training framework based on LLMs. Firstly, we transfer LLMs into reasoning-efficient retrievers with residual projection and task-oriented bidirectional attention aggregation in the latent space. Secondly, we alleviate the mismatch between contrastive learning and implicit reasoning using fine-grained next-token-prediction-based reconstruction. Extensive experiments on reasoning-intensive retrieval benchmarks show that SHIFT consistently outperforms other widely used retrievers. We also carried out a detailed analysis to illustrate how our method works.

AI.tldr: SHIFT is an LLM-based retrieval training framework that improves reasoning-intensive retrieval by combining implicit reasoning in latent space with fine-grained next-token-prediction reconstruction to resolve the mismatch between contrastive learning and generation objectives.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-based retrievers using either explicit "rewrite-then-retrieve" or implicit reasoning (e.g., GIRCSE, LaSER) face a fundamental mismatch between contrastive retrieval objectives and the generative pretraining of LLMs, limiting their effectiveness on reasoning-intensive queries.
AI.method: SHIFT proposes three components: (1) transferring LLMs into reasoning-efficient retrievers via residual projection and task-oriented bidirectional attention aggregation in latent space; (2) fine-grained next-token-prediction-based reconstruction to align contrastive learning with implicit reasoning; (3) a self-reconstruction mechanism that harnesses implicit fine-grained thinking signals.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on reasoning-intensive retrieval benchmarks demonstrate that SHIFT consistently outperforms widely used retrievers, with detailed analyses illustrating the mechanism's inner workings.
AI.conclusion: SHIFT effectively bridges the gap between retrieval-oriented contrastive learning and generation-oriented LLM pretraining by integrating implicit reasoning with self-reconstruction, achieving state-of-the-art performance on reasoning-intensive retrieval tasks.

title: Teaching Business Process Modeling to Leverage Soft Skills of Computing Students
summary: Background and Context: Organizations have highly depended on software systems to realize their business processes and achieve strategic business goals and competitive advantage; hence, computing professionals who can understand these processes could more effectively build such systems. At the same time, while Artificial Intelligence (AI) has increased the productivity in developing these and other systems, professionals should be better prepared due to the competitiveness of the job market; thus, soft skills could be an important factor to ensure their position in this market. Objective: This paper aims to analyze and present the impact of teaching business process modeling to leverage key soft skills of future computing professionals. Method and Findings: Our method involved an industry-driven, project-based approach with 53 computing students who actively interacted with stakeholders and modeled the organization's business process. We systematically collected the students' feedback, including the soft skills practiced and demonstrating that professionalism, initiative, motivation, communication, and teamwork can be leveraged. Implications: The main implication of this work for the Computer Science Education research community is to provide evidence that teaching business process modeling subjects is particularly beneficial for future professionals, as it could contribute to preparing them regarding their soft skills for the era of AI-assisted software development.

AI.tldr: Teaching business process modeling to computing students through industry-driven, project-based learning effectively develops soft skills such as communication, teamwork, professionalism, initiative, and motivation—skills increasingly vital in the era of AI-assisted software development.
AI.motivation: Organizations depend on software systems aligned with business processes, yet computing professionals often lack the business-process understanding needed to build them effectively. Concurrently, AI is boosting development productivity, intensifying job market competition and making soft skills critical for employability. The authors seek to investigate whether business process modeling education can address both gaps.
AI.method: An industry-driven, project-based pedagogical approach was applied with 53 computing students. Students actively engaged with real organizational stakeholders to model authentic business processes. Feedback was systematically collected to identify which soft skills were practiced and developed through the experience.
AI.result: The study demonstrated that business process modeling instruction successfully leveraged five key soft skills: professionalism, initiative, motivation, communication, and teamwork. Student feedback confirmed these competencies were meaningfully exercised through the stakeholder-interactive, project-based format.
AI.conclusion: Teaching business process modeling provides dual benefits for computing education: it imparts domain-relevant technical knowledge while simultaneously cultivating soft skills. This is especially valuable as AI tools increasingly handle routine coding tasks, shifting the differentiating value of human professionals toward business understanding and interpersonal competencies.

title: MKEvolve: A Modular Multi-Agent Framework for Kernel Code Generation
summary: Despite rapid progress in LLM-based code generation, writing correct and performant kernels for hardware accelerators remains a key bottleneck in scaling modern ML workloads. We present MKEvolve (Modular Kernel Evolve), a framework that iteratively co-evolves a modular decomposition of complex PyTorch modules and the LLM-generated kernel for each submodule, refining the decomposition by splitting and fusing across iterations while independently improving each subkernel via LLM-driven beam search. The resulting kernels are programmatic compositions of independently verified subkernels, making them configurable (subkernel implementations are swappable), interpretable (errors and speedups are traceable to specific subkernels), and readily adaptable to related model architectures. Experiments with Triton on KernelBench L2 and L3, spanning multi-operator sequences and full model architectures, show that MKEvolve improves both correctness and speedup over end-to-end direct synthesis baselines while reducing LLM token usage by up to 35%.

AI.tldr: MKEvolve is a framework that co-evolves modular decomposition of PyTorch modules with LLM-generated kernels, using iterative splitting/fusing and beam search to produce configurable, interpretable, and adaptable hardware kernels that outperform end-to-end synthesis baselines in correctness and speedup while using 35% fewer LLM tokens.
AI.motivation: Writing correct, high-performance kernels for hardware accelerators remains a critical bottleneck in scaling ML workloads. Existing LLM-based code generation approaches struggle with the complexity of full model architectures, motivating a modular, iterative approach that can independently optimize subcomponents.
AI.method: MKEvolve iteratively co-evolves (1) a modular decomposition of complex PyTorch modules (splitting and fusing submodules across iterations) and (2) LLM-generated kernels for each submodule. Each subkernel is independently improved via LLM-driven beam search. The final output is a programmatic composition of independently verified, swappable subkernels. Evaluated using Triton on KernelBench L2 and L3 benchmarks.
AI.result: MKEvolve improves both correctness and speedup over end-to-end direct synthesis baselines on KernelBench L2 (multi-operator sequences) and L3 (full model architectures). Additionally, it reduces LLM token usage by up to 35%.
AI.conclusion: Modular co-evolution of decomposition and kernel generation is an effective strategy for producing high-quality accelerator kernels. The resulting kernels are not only more performant and correct but also more configurable, interpretable, and adaptable to related architectures, while being more token-efficient.

title: Buzz to Boom: Detecting Message Progression Vulnerabilities in Electron Applications via Segmented Directed Fuzzing
summary: Electron is a popular framework for building cross-platform desktop applications using web technologies. Such applications consist of multiple processes with different privilege levels that communicate via message passing. When inter-process messages carry attacker-controlled inputs, they can propagate across processes and reach privileged APIs, e.g., command execution. Such a message propagation behavior is characterized as Message Progression Vulnerabilities (MPVs). The exploitation of MPVs is challenging because it often requires multiple steps, e.g., first arbitrary code execution in one process via message passing, and then command injection in another process using another message crafted in the first process. To our knowledge, existing works on Electron security only study unsafe configurations and malicious Document Object Model (DOM) content, i.e., they cannot detect or exploit these vulnerabilities that need to be triggered by complex cross-process exploits via message passing. We present Proton, a segmented directed fuzzing framework for detecting MPVs. Our key insight is to decompose end-to-end fuzzing into per-process segments along message-passing boundaries, where the goals of fuzzing each segment are either: (i) reaching a sink in the current process or (ii) propagating the payload to the next process, to enable the exploration of another process. In the second case, the messages seed the corpus of the next segment. Finally, Proton synthesizes crash inputs from each process to validate end-to-end exploits. We evaluate Proton against 589 real-world Electron applications, resulting in 23 zero-day MPVs. Among them, 22 lead to OS command execution, including projects with over 50k GitHub stars. We responsibly disclosed all findings. To date, we have received 13 acknowledgments, 11 fixes, and 11 CVEs, including a bug bounty from Vercel.

AI.tldr: Proton is a segmented directed fuzzing framework that detects Message Progression Vulnerabilities (MPVs) in Electron applications by decomposing cross-process fuzzing into per-process segments. Evaluated on 589 real-world apps, it found 23 zero-day MPVs (22 enabling OS command execution), yielding 11 CVEs and a bug bounty.
AI.motivation: Electron applications use multi-process architectures with privilege separation and message-passing communication. Existing security tools only study unsafe configurations or malicious DOM content, failing to detect or exploit vulnerabilities requiring complex, multi-step cross-process message propagation. There is a gap in automated detection of Message Progression Vulnerabilities (MPVs).
AI.method: Proton, a segmented directed fuzzing framework. The key insight is decomposing end-to-end fuzzing into per-process segments along message-passing boundaries. Each segment's fuzzing goal is either: (i) reaching a sink in the current process, or (ii) propagating the payload to the next process to enable further exploration. Propagated messages seed the next segment's corpus. Finally, Proton synthesizes crash inputs across processes to validate end-to-end exploits.
AI.result: Evaluated on 589 real-world Electron applications. Discovered 23 zero-day MPVs, of which 22 lead to OS command execution, including projects with over 50k GitHub stars. Received 13 acknowledgments, 11 fixes, 11 CVEs, and a bug bounty from Vercel.
AI.conclusion: Proton effectively automates the detection of complex, multi-step MPVs in Electron apps that prior approaches miss. The high yield of critical vulnerabilities (22/23 resulting in command execution) and positive vendor response (11 CVEs, bug bounty) demonstrate both the prevalence of MPVs and the practical impact of segmented directed fuzzing for cross-process vulnerability discovery.

title: LLM-INSTRUCT at UZH Shared Task 2026: Constraint-Aware Retrieval and Selective Debate for Paragraph-Level Argument Mining
comment: Accepted to the 13th Workshop on Argument Mining (ArgMining 2026) at ACL 2026
summary: We present LLM-INSTRUCT, the winning system for the UZH Shared Task at ArgMining 2026 on paragraph-level argument mining in UN and UNESCO resolutions. The task requires paragraph-type classification, prediction of a subset of 141 official tags, and directed relation prediction under a strict JSON schema setting using only open-weight models up to 8B parameters. We frame the task as constrained structured prediction. The system first narrows the candidate tag space with metadata-aware dense retrieval, then applies constrained decoding with per-dimension caps, escalates only uncertain cases to a three-agent debate branch, and finally validates the output schema. On the official leaderboard, LLM-INSTRUCT ranked 1st overall, with 1st in F1 and 5th in LLM-as-a-Judge. During development, our configuration search further improved Task 1b Micro-F1 from 35.83% to 40.08% while keeping the internal Task 2 score at 4.421. The main lesson is simple: reducing the decision space before generation improves both accuracy and submission robustness. Our code and supporting scripts are publicly available at: https://github.com/LLM-Instruct-at-UZH-Shared-Task-2026/Method

AI.tldr: LLM-INSTRUCT won the ArgMining 2026 shared task on paragraph-level argument mining in UN/UNESCO resolutions by framing the problem as constrained structured prediction, combining metadata-aware dense retrieval for tag space reduction, constrained decoding, a three-agent debate for uncertain cases, and output schema validation — achieving 1st place overall with further gains during development configuration search.
AI.motivation: Argument mining in UN and UNESCO resolutions is challenging due to three subtasks (paragraph-type classification, prediction from 141 official tags, and directed relation prediction), all under strict JSON schema constraints using only open-weight models ≤8B parameters. The core insight is that reducing the decision space before generation improves both accuracy and robustness.
AI.method: The system employs a multi-stage constrained structured prediction pipeline: (1) metadata-aware dense retrieval narrows the candidate tag space; (2) constrained decoding enforces per-dimension caps; (3) uncertain cases are escalated to a three-agent debate branch; (4) final output undergoes schema validation. The entire approach uses only open-weight models up to 8B parameters.
AI.result: LLM-INSTRUCT ranked 1st overall on the official leaderboard, achieving 1st in F1 and 5th in LLM-as-a-Judge. During development, configuration search improved Task 1b Micro-F1 from 35.83% to 40.08% while maintaining an internal Task 2 score of 4.421.
AI.conclusion: The core lesson is that reducing the decision space prior to generation significantly improves both predictive accuracy and submission robustness in constrained structured prediction tasks. The system's code is publicly available on GitHub.

title: Adaptive Depth in Looped Transformers: Diagnosing Learned Halting Gates and Trajectory Readouts
summary: Looped Transformers increase test-time computation by repeatedly applying a shared recurrent block. Learned halting objectives in looped Transformers typically use a single exit distribution both as the inference-time stopping rule and as the training-time weighting of per-depth losses. This entangles exit selection with trajectory formation: the gate not only chooses which recurrent state to use, but also determines how strongly each intermediate state is supervised. Consequently, poor adaptive-compute performance can arise from the readout, the induced trajectory, or their interaction. We study adaptive depth in looped Transformers through this trajectory--readout lens, across controlled synthetic tasks (modular arithmetic and binary parity) and large-scale Ouro-1.4B and 2.6B checkpoints.
