We find that fixed-prior depth supervision, which shapes the trajectory without an input-dependent halting policy, produces difficulty-aware trajectories whose intermediate states expose useful stopping signals, and that simple post-hoc confidence readouts often match or outperform learned linear and MLP gates. Fitting gates on frozen trajectories localizes the failure: it appears to stem mainly from the trajectory induced by joint gate training rather than from limited gate expressivity. The same pattern is present in Ouro evaluations, where pretrained ponder gates are competitive but not uniformly Pareto-optimal, and measured latency confirms that the resulting reductions in average exit depth translate into practical inference-time savings. Our systematic diagnostic evaluation reframes adaptive depth in looped Transformers as a joint problem of trajectory formation and exit readout, rather than gate learning alone, highlighting a distinction that prior learned-halting work has often left implicit.

AI.tldr: This paper reframes adaptive depth in looped Transformers as a joint problem of trajectory formation (how recurrent states are supervised during training) and exit readout (how halting is decided at inference), rather than solely a gate-learning problem. Through synthetic tasks and large-scale Ouro model checkpoints, the authors show that fixed-prior depth supervision produces effective trajectories with useful stopping signals, and that simple confidence-based readouts often match or exceed learned gates. Failures stem mainly from trajectories induced by joint gate training, not gate expressivity.
AI.motivation: Prior learned-halting approaches use a single exit distribution for both inference-time stopping and training-time per-depth loss weighting, entangling exit selection with trajectory formation. This coupling obscures whether poor adaptive-compute performance comes from the readout mechanism, the induced trajectory, or their interaction. The authors argue this distinction has been left implicit and warrants systematic investigation.
AI.method: The authors propose a trajectory--readout lens: (1) Fixed-prior depth supervision shapes trajectories without input-dependent halting, using difficulty-aware priors. (2) Post-hoc confidence readouts (e.g., maximum softmax probability) are compared against learned linear and MLP gates. (3) Gates are fitted on frozen trajectories to isolate failure sources. Evaluations span controlled synthetic tasks (modular arithmetic, binary parity) and Ouro-1.4B/2.6B checkpoints, including latency measurements.
AI.result: Fixed-prior depth supervision produces difficulty-aware trajectories whose intermediate states naturally expose useful stopping signals. Simple post-hoc confidence readouts often match or outperform learned gates. Fitting gates on frozen trajectories localizes failure to trajectory formation induced by joint training, not limited gate expressivity. In Ouro evaluations, pretrained ponder gates are competitive but not uniformly Pareto-optimal; reduced average exit depth translates into measured inference-time savings.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive depth in looped Transformers should be treated as a joint trajectory-formation and exit-readout problem. Decoupling these aspects — using fixed-prior supervision for trajectory shaping and simple confidence readouts — can match or exceed jointly trained halting mechanisms. The trajectory induced by gate training, not gate capacity, is the primary bottleneck.

title: DC-Leap: Training-Free Acceleration of dLLMs via Draft-Guided Contiguous Leaping Decoding
summary: While parallel decoding is central to the efficiency of Diffusion Large Language Models (dLLMs), current strategies are often hindered by overly conservative confidence thresholds. These thresholds, necessitated by the Joint Probability Dependence Error (JPDE), result in redundant denoising iterations and suboptimal inference speeds. To overcome this, we propose DC-Leap, a training-free framework that enables reliable acceleration of dLLMs in the moderate-confidence regime. DC-Leap introduces a Dynamic Contiguous Verification strategy that integrates strictly-ordered causal constraints into the parallel decoding process. By progressively validating token dependencies, this mechanism effectively neutralizes the JPDE, enabling reliable acceleration with comparable performance. Furthermore, DC-Leap incorporates the draft-guided decoding mechanism, where the draft helps extend the context by leaping forward across multiple tokens, providing look-ahead context and retaining the structural benefits of bidirectional attention during inference. Extensive experiments on standard benchmarks demonstrate that DC-Leap achieves substantial speedups, up to 53.19x on MBPP for long-sequence generation, and up to 105.02x when combined with KV-Cache with comparable generation quality. Code is available at https://github.com/ffh-wyls/DC-Leap .

AI.tldr: DC-Leap is a training-free framework that accelerates diffusion LLMs by introducing Dynamic Contiguous Verification to overcome overly conservative confidence thresholds caused by Joint Probability Dependence Error (JPDE), achieving up to 53x speedup (105x with KV-Cache) while maintaining generation quality.
AI.motivation: Current parallel decoding strategies in diffusion LLMs are bottlenecked by overly conservative confidence thresholds, which are necessitated by the Joint Probability Dependence Error (JPDE). This leads to redundant denoising iterations and suboptimal inference speeds, motivating the need for reliable acceleration in moderate-confidence regimes.
AI.method: DC-Leap proposes two key mechanisms: (1) Dynamic Contiguous Verification, which integrates strictly-ordered causal constraints into the parallel decoding process to progressively validate token dependencies, thereby neutralizing the JPDE; and (2) a draft-guided decoding mechanism that leaps forward across multiple tokens using a draft to provide look-ahead context while retaining bidirectional attention benefits during inference. The framework is training-free.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on standard benchmarks show up to 53.19x speedup on MBPP for long-sequence generation, and up to 105.02x speedup when combined with KV-Cache, all while maintaining comparable generation quality.
AI.conclusion: DC-Leap effectively overcomes the JPDE bottleneck in dLLM parallel decoding, enabling substantial inference acceleration without sacrificing output quality, and demonstrates strong synergy with KV-Cache for further speedups.

title: Sources of Inequity and Fairness Risks inWellbeing Sensing
comment: 16 pages, 1 figure, 2 tables. Accepted to AIES 2026
summary: Passive sensing for wellbeing uses smartphones and wearables to continuously collect human behavioral data and applies ML/AI models to infer psychological states and behaviors (e.g., depression, cognitive load). These systems are increasingly adopted in high-stakes settings (e.g., hospitals, universities), yet fairness research remains limited---primarily to post-hoc, identity-based comparisons of model performance. However, passive sensing combines heterogeneous sensing infrastructures, indirect behavioral inference, and longitudinal deployment---characteristics that, while not exclusive to the domain, are jointly pronounced here and raise two underexplored questions: (1) what additional sources of inequity arise from these characteristics, and (2) how do such inequities propagate beyond algorithmic audits across the system lifecycle? To address this gap, we conducted semi-structured interviews with 14 researchers and practitioners across five countries, examining how fairness risks emerge and are negotiated across the full passive sensing lifecycle. Our findings empirically characterize five situated sources of inequity (e.g., comfort with monitoring, behavioral regularity) that systematically shape fairness risks beyond identity-based attributes. We further synthesize 15 fairness risks and corresponding mitigation strategies across the lifecycle, from study design to deployment. Finally, we identify structural barriers that constrain fair practice in reality, and argue that enabling fair passive sensing requires both individual researcher efforts and ecosystem-level governance support from funders, publication venues, and deploying institutions.

AI.tldr: Passive sensing systems for wellbeing infer psychological states from behavioral data but lack fairness research beyond post-hoc identity comparisons. Through interviews with 14 researchers/practitioners, the paper identifies five situated sources of inequity, 15 fairness risks with mitigation strategies across the system lifecycle, and structural barriers requiring both individual and ecosystem-level governance responses.
AI.motivation: Passive sensing for wellbeing is increasingly deployed in high-stakes settings, yet fairness research remains narrowly focused on post-hoc, identity-based model performance comparisons. The domain's joint characteristics—heterogeneous sensing infrastructures, indirect behavioral inference, and longitudinal deployment—raise underexplored questions about additional sources of inequity and how they propagate across the entire system lifecycle, beyond algorithmic audits.
AI.method: Semi-structured interviews with 14 researchers and practitioners across five countries, examining how fairness risks emerge and are negotiated across the full passive sensing lifecycle (study design, data collection, modeling, deployment, and evaluation).
AI.result: (1) Five situated sources of inequity were empirically characterized—including comfort with monitoring and behavioral regularity—that systematically shape fairness risks beyond identity-based attributes. (2) Fifteen fairness risks and corresponding mitigation strategies were synthesized across the lifecycle. (3) Structural barriers constraining fair practice were identified, pointing to the need for ecosystem-level governance from funders, publication venues, and deploying institutions.
AI.conclusion: Enabling fair passive sensing requires both individual researcher efforts (methodological and design choices) and systemic, ecosystem-level governance support. The lifecycle perspective reveals that inequities are not merely algorithmic but are socio-technically embedded across design, data, and deployment stages.

title: Diffusion Language Model for Recommendation
summary: Large language model (LLM)-empowered recommender systems have emerged as a promising paradigm for generative recommendation, leveraging their strong semantic reasoning and generative capacity to model complex, diverse user preferences. However, most existing approaches rely on an autoregressive paradigm that is suboptimal for recommendation. The next-token objective emphasizes sequential order rather than the structural inter-item dependencies underlying user preferences. In addition, prefix-constrained generation restricts bidirectional context and commits to left-to-right decoding, causing early errors to accumulate without correction. Inspired by the success of diffusion language models, we propose \textbf{DLMRec}, a discrete diffusion language model tailored for recommendation that offers a compelling alternative to autoregressive generation. Specifically, DLMRec introduces three key components to bridge diffusion language modeling with recommendation. First, a collaborative-aware stochastic tokenizer encodes multi-hop collaborative signals into expressive discrete tokens compatible with diffusion modeling. Second, a curriculum-driven training strategy aligns the denoising process with preference recovery through progressive item- and token-level learning. Third, a stability-aware voting mechanism aggregates iterative predictions to improve generation consistency and robustness.

AI.tldr: DLMRec proposes a discrete diffusion language model for recommendation, replacing autoregressive generation with three key components: a collaborative-aware stochastic tokenizer, curriculum-driven training, and a stability-aware voting mechanism to better capture structural item dependencies.
AI.motivation: Autoregressive LLM-based recommenders are suboptimal because: (1) the next-token objective prioritizes sequential order over structural inter-item dependencies, and (2) prefix-constrained left-to-right decoding causes error accumulation without bidirectional context.
AI.method: DLMRec adapts discrete diffusion language modeling for recommendation via three components: (1) a collaborative-aware stochastic tokenizer that encodes multi-hop collaborative signals into discrete tokens; (2) a curriculum-driven training strategy aligning denoising with preference recovery through progressive item- and token-level learning; (3) a stability-aware voting mechanism that aggregates iterative predictions for consistency and robustness.
AI.result: Not explicitly stated in the provided abstract.
AI.conclusion: Not explicitly stated in the provided abstract.

title: Toward Federated Cognitive Digital Twins over the Edge-to-Cloud Continuum
summary: Digital Twins (DTs) are increasingly adopted to monitor, analyze, and optimize Cyber-Physical Systems (CPSs) through continuous interaction between physical assets and their digital counterparts. However, current DT architectures often rely on centralized and monolithic designs, leading to scalability, latency, and resilience issues in distributed environment such as smart cities. Moreover, they provide limited support for semantic integration and high-level reasoning, reducing the effectiveness of DT-based decision-making. Recent studies on Federated Digital Twins (FDTs) have addressed scalability by decomposing complex systems into interacting twins, but they still largely centralize intelligence in cloud components. In parallel, Cognitive Digital Twins (CDTs) enhance DTs with semantic reasoning, explainability, and AI-driven decision support, yet they are typically difficult to integrate into distributed architectures. This paper proposes a Federated Cognitive Digital Twin (FCDT) architecture that combines federation and cognition within a unified approach. The architecture distributes intelligence across the edge-to-cloud continuum through local twins, which provide real-time monitoring and lightweight cognitive capabilities, and global twins, which perform system-level reasoning, simulation, and coordination. By integrating distributed autonomy with cognitive reasoning, the proposed approach improves scalability, responsiveness, and decision-making in complex distributed CPSs

AI.tldr: Proposes a Federated Cognitive Digital Twin (FCDT) architecture that unifies federation (for scalability) and cognition (for semantic reasoning) by distributing intelligence across edge-to-cloud continuum via local twins and global twins.
AI.motivation: Current Digital Twin architectures suffer from two major limitations: (1) centralized/monolithic designs cause scalability, latency, and resilience problems in distributed environments like smart cities; (2) limited semantic integration and reasoning capabilities reduce decision-making effectiveness. Federated Digital Twins address scalability but still centralize intelligence in the cloud, while Cognitive Digital Twins enhance reasoning but are hard to integrate into distributed architectures. A unified solution is needed.
AI.method: Proposes a Federated Cognitive Digital Twin (FCDT) architecture that distributes intelligence across the edge-to-cloud continuum using two tiers: local twins for real-time monitoring and lightweight cognitive capabilities at the edge, and global twins for system-level reasoning, simulation, and coordination in the cloud.
AI.result: The paper presents the architecture conceptually. The proposed FCDT approach combines distributed autonomy with cognitive reasoning, aiming to improve scalability, responsiveness, and decision-making in complex distributed CPSs. (Specific quantitative/experimental results are not detailed in this abstract.)
AI.conclusion: Integrating federation and cognition into a single FCDT architecture overcomes the individual limitations of FDTs and CDTs, enabling more scalable, responsive, and intelligent digital twin systems for complex distributed CPS environments.

title: AppWorld-UL: Benchmarking Diverse Agent-User Interactions for Tool-Use
summary: Tool-use agents that address day-to-day digital tasks such as ordering groceries must not only operate applications, but also interact with the user, e.g., to ask clarification questions, prompt for confirmation, and inform the user when the instruction is infeasible. However, current benchmarks for evaluating agent-user interactions do not capture the diversity of such interactions. Further, they operate in small environments with few, often non-state-changing, APIs. To address this gap, we introduce AppWorld-UL, a ``user-in-the-loop'' benchmark of 516 challenging tasks requiring diverse agent-user interactions. Building upon the AppWorld framework with 9 popular simulated apps like Amazon and Spotify, we systematically modify original tasks to introduce ambiguities and constraints that necessitate various types of agent-user interaction. User behavior is simulated by an LLM prompted to respond with carefully designed knowledge boundaries, offering more reliable simulation than the unconstrained or overly rigid alternatives used in prior work. Our evaluation reveals that a state-of-the-art LLM, Claude Opus 4.7, achieves only 48.6% success on AppWorld-UL, and only 35.7% on the harder, compositional subset. On the stricter, scenario-level metric, compositional task performance drops to only 21.3%. Our analysis reveals that correct user-interaction is crucial for success. This demonstrates the benchmark's difficulty and its potential to advance research on user-in-the-loop tool-use agents.

AI.tldr: AppWorld-UL introduces a benchmark of 516 tasks requiring diverse agent-user interactions across 9 simulated apps, revealing that state-of-the-art LLM Claude Opus 4.7 achieves only 48.6% success, with performance dropping to 21.3% on compositional scenario-level tasks, highlighting the difficulty of user-in-the-loop tool-use.
AI.motivation: Current benchmarks for evaluating agent-user interactions in tool-use agents suffer from two key limitations: (1) they fail to capture the diversity of real-world agent-user interactions such as asking clarification questions, prompting for confirmation, or informing users about infeasible instructions; and (2) they operate in small environments with few, often non-state-changing, APIs. This motivates the need for a more comprehensive and realistic benchmark.
AI.method: The authors build AppWorld-UL upon the existing AppWorld framework, which features 9 popular simulated apps (e.g., Amazon, Spotify). They systematically modify original tasks to introduce ambiguities and constraints that necessitate various types of agent-user interaction. User behavior is simulated by an LLM prompted with carefully designed knowledge boundaries, providing more reliable simulation than unconstrained or overly rigid alternatives from prior work. The benchmark comprises 516 tasks, including a harder compositional subset, and uses both task-level and stricter scenario-level success metrics.
AI.result: Claude Opus 4.7 achieves only 48.6% success on the full AppWorld-UL benchmark and 35.7% on the compositional subset. Under the stricter scenario-level metric, compositional task performance plummets to 21.3%. Analysis reveals that correct user-interaction is a critical factor for task success, underscoring the benchmark's difficulty.
AI.conclusion: AppWorld-UL demonstrates significant room for improvement in user-in-the-loop tool-use agents and has strong potential to advance research in this area by providing a realistic, challenging, and diverse evaluation framework for agent-user interactions.

title: Evaluating Large Language Models for Symbolic Security Protocol Analysis
summary: Security protocol verification relies on formal tools such as ProVerif and OFMC. This study evaluates whether Large Language Models (LLMs) can perform comparable analysis. We test GPT and DeepSeek in chat and reasoning modes over three runs on 130 obfuscated AnB/AnBx protocols covering 388 security goals, scored against ProVerif and OFMC. Chat models reach 69 to 81% recall at precision below 31%. Reasoning models reverse this trade-off, reaching 66.5% precision for GPT and 45.4% for DeepSeek, but detect just over half the attacks. DeepSeek's two modes share one underlying model, so the comparison isolates reasoning itself, which raises precision from 27.2% to 45.4%. The GPT contrast spans a model-version change and is only suggestive. All models perform worst on authentication goals: reasoning models detect well under half of injective and non-injective agreement attacks, whereas chat models over-flag them at low precision. Confidentiality is the exception, with F1 up to 95.7% in reasoning mode. Verdicts are unstable across runs, identical on 89.7% of goals for GPT but 74.0% for DeepSeek. Self-reported confidence is uniformly high yet shows no meaningful correlation with correctness. On this benchmark LLMs do not match formal verification, but may serve, at best, as pre-screening filters.

AI.tldr: This paper benchmarks LLMs (GPT and DeepSeek, in chat vs. reasoning modes) on security protocol verification using 130 obfuscated AnB/AnBx protocols with 388 security goals. Reasoning models achieve higher precision (up to 66.5%) but lower recall, while chat models show high recall (69–81%) but poor precision (<31%). LLMs fall short of formal tools like ProVerif/OFMC and may only serve as pre-screening filters.
AI.motivation: To assess whether LLMs can perform security protocol verification comparable to established formal tools (ProVerif, OFMC), and to understand the trade-offs between chat and reasoning modes in this domain.
AI.method: Benchmarked GPT and DeepSeek models (chat and reasoning modes) across three runs on 130 obfuscated AnB/AnBx protocols covering 388 security goals. Scored outputs against ProVerif and OFMC ground truth. Measured precision, recall, F1, verdict stability, and self-reported confidence calibration. DeepSeek's two modes share an underlying model, enabling isolation of the reasoning effect.
AI.result: Chat models: recall 69–81%, precision <31%. Reasoning models: GPT precision 66.5%, DeepSeek 45.4%, but both detect just over half of attacks. DeepSeek reasoning mode raised precision from 27.2% to 45.4%. All models perform worst on authentication goals (injective/non-injective agreement). Confidentiality F1 reached 95.7% in reasoning mode. Verdict stability: GPT 89.7% identical across runs, DeepSeek 74.0%. Self-reported confidence uniformly high with no correlation to correctness.
AI.conclusion: LLMs do not match formal verification tools on this benchmark. At best, they may serve as pre-screening filters. Reasoning-mode inference improves precision over chat mode, but substantial limitations remain, particularly for authentication properties and verdict consistency.

title: Skill-Contracted Agents for Evidence-Aware Materials Literature Analysis
summary: Materials science literature analysis requires simultaneous attention to composition, processing, characterization, and property relationships, yet conventional retrieval-augmented generation pipelines struggle to reconcile heterogeneous tasks within a single retrieve-then-generate architecture. Here we present AlphaAgent, a skill-driven agent framework that decouples retrieval-based question answering from paper-level report generation through explicit skill contracts. A dedicated retrieval skill rewrites user requests into material-specific search intents, queries a curated index of more than 300,000 papers from the Journal Citation Reports Metallurgy and Metallurgical Engineering category, and reformulates queries when initial evidence is insufficient. A separate report-generation skill parses full-text PDFs to produce structured per-paper analytical reports and cross-paper summaries. In a blind evaluation on 40 materials-science questions, half of which required deep analytical reasoning, AlphaAgent substantially outperformed a baseline system matched for underlying model, document index, and retrieval scale, with the largest gains in mechanistic explanation and awareness of credibility boundaries. These results indicate that explicit task separation, refined retrieval intent, and evidence-aware generation improve large-language-model-based literature analysis for materials research.

AI.tldr: AlphaAgent is a skill-driven agent framework that decouples retrieval and report generation for materials science literature analysis. It outperformed a matched baseline on 40 evaluation questions, with largest gains in mechanistic reasoning and credibility awareness.
AI.motivation: Conventional retrieve-then-generate (RAG) pipelines struggle with materials science literature because the field demands simultaneous attention to diverse, heterogeneous relationships (composition, processing, characterization, properties), and a single unified architecture cannot effectively reconcile retrieval-based QA with deep, paper-level analytical report generation.
AI.method: AlphaAgent uses explicit skill contracts to separate two tasks: (1) a retrieval skill that rewrites user queries into material-specific search intents, searches a curated index of 300,000+ papers (JCR Metallurgy and Metallurgical Engineering category), and iteratively reformulates queries when evidence is insufficient; (2) a report-generation skill that parses full-text PDFs to produce structured per-paper analytical reports and cross-paper summaries. A blind evaluation on 40 materials-science questions (half requiring deep analytical reasoning) was conducted against a baseline matched for model, index, and retrieval scale.
AI.result: AlphaAgent substantially outperformed the matched baseline system, with the most pronounced gains observed in mechanistic explanation tasks and in demonstrating awareness of credibility boundaries (i.e., knowing when evidence is insufficient).
AI.conclusion: Explicit task separation, refined retrieval intent, and evidence-aware generation collectively improve LLM-based literature analysis for materials research, suggesting that skill-driven agent architectures are a promising direction for domain-specific scientific literature systems.

title: Generative Bayesian Filtering for State Estimation
summary: The state of a dynamic system evolves over time, switching among several latent modes that govern its observable behavior. Filtering methods infer the latent state from observations. Classical filtering approaches, including Kalman filters, typically rely on simple observation models, such as linear-Gaussian models, that are incapable of characterizing the increasingly nonlinear and heterogeneous patterns in high-dimensional sensor signals. To tackle the challenge, we propose Generative Bayesian Filtering (GBF), a filtering framework that replaces restrictive observation models with pretrained conditional generative models parametrized by conditional variational autoencoders (CVAE). For online inference, GBF performs a Bayesian prediction-update recursion in which the measurement update is formulated as a posterior sampling problem that combines the dynamical prior with the CVAE-induced likelihood. The resulting filtering problem is then transformed into a score-based sampling problem, which naturally inherits the flexibility from generative models and the uncertainty quantification capabilities from ensembling. Experiments on synthetic datasets and real-world applications involving manufacturing system monitoring and arrhythmia diagnosis demonstrate that GBF improves state estimation accuracy and robustness relative to baseline approaches.

AI.tldr: Generative Bayesian Filtering (GBF) replaces restrictive linear-Gaussian observation models in classical filters with pretrained conditional VAEs, enabling flexible nonlinear filtering via score-based posterior sampling, with demonstrated improvements in manufacturing monitoring and arrhythmia diagnosis.
AI.motivation: Classical filtering methods like Kalman filters rely on overly simplistic observation models (e.g., linear-Gaussian) that cannot capture the complex, nonlinear, and heterogeneous patterns present in modern high-dimensional sensor signals. There is a need for a filtering framework that leverages the expressive power of deep generative models while preserving rigorous Bayesian uncertainty quantification.
AI.method: GBF performs Bayesian prediction-update recursion online. The key innovation is formulating the measurement update as a posterior sampling problem: it combines a dynamical prior with a likelihood induced by a pretrained conditional variational autoencoder (CVAE). This posterior sampling problem is then transformed into a score-based sampling procedure, leveraging score functions for efficient inference. The framework naturally supports ensembling for uncertainty quantification.
AI.result: Experiments on synthetic datasets, manufacturing system monitoring, and arrhythmia diagnosis show that GBF outperforms baseline approaches in both state estimation accuracy and robustness.
AI.conclusion: GBF successfully marries the flexibility of deep generative models with principled Bayesian filtering, offering a scalable and accurate solution for state estimation in complex, high-dimensional, nonlinear dynamical systems.

title: InferenceBench: A Benchmark for Open-Ended LLM Inference Optimization by AI Agents
summary: AI agents are increasingly used to automate research and development tasks, yet existing benchmarks typically evaluate them on prescribed workflows or narrow action spaces. Even nominally open-ended tasks can often be solved by retrieving a well-known recipe and tuning a few hyperparameters, making it unclear whether strong results reflect genuine optimization or memorized solutions. We introduce InferenceBench, where an agent must deploy an OpenAI-compatible inference server and optimize the speed of LLM inference. Each agent receives a target LLM, one H100 GPU, an optimization scenario, and a wall-clock time budget of two hours. Three optimization scenarios isolate distinct bottlenecks of inference (prefill latency, decode latency, and concurrent request throughput) and a fourth balances all three at the same time. Across 15 frontier agent configurations, agents reliably improve over a naive PyTorch baseline (up to $8.08\times$) and often match or exceed serving engines with default settings ($4.05\times$ for vLLM), but still fall below a simple hyperparameter search under the same time budget (up to $11.53\times$). Qualitative analysis of agent trajectories shows that although agents enumerate many relevant optimization techniques, they overwhelmingly converge on a single inference framework. They test only a few distinct configurations and spend the remaining budget re-measuring, repairing, or optimizing hyperparameters rather than exploring substantially different strategies. This suggests the bottleneck is not domain knowledge, but the ability to propose diverse configurations, evaluate them systematically, and submit the best identified solution. Overall, InferenceBench reflects the ability of agents to operate in an open-ended AI engineering setting, where memorized solutions lead to limited improvements.

AI.tldr: InferenceBench evaluates AI agents on optimizing LLM inference speed under a 2-hour GPU budget. Agents improve over baselines but underperform a simple hyperparameter search, revealing that the bottleneck is not domain knowledge but the ability to systematically explore diverse configurations.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks evaluate agents on narrow, prescribed workflows where strong results may stem from retrieving memorized solutions rather than genuine optimization. The authors aim to test whether agents can operate in a truly open-ended AI engineering setting where formulaic recipes yield only limited gains.
AI.method: InferenceBench tasks an agent with deploying an OpenAI-compatible inference server and optimizing LLM inference speed on one H100 GPU within 2 hours. Three isolated scenarios target prefill latency, decode latency, and concurrent request throughput; a fourth balances all three. Fifteen frontier agent configurations are evaluated against naive PyTorch, vLLM defaults, and a hyperparameter search baseline.
AI.result: Agents achieve up to 8.08× improvement over naive PyTorch and 4.05× over vLLM defaults, but fall short of a simple hyperparameter search (up to 11.53×). Qualitatively, agents converge on a single inference framework, test few distinct configurations, and waste remaining time re-measuring or tuning hyperparameters rather than exploring diverse strategies.
AI.conclusion: The primary bottleneck is not domain knowledge but the ability to propose, systematically evaluate, and select among diverse configurations. InferenceBench provides a benchmark for open-ended AI engineering where memorized recipes are insufficient.

title: Search-on-Graph: Iterative Informed Navigation for Large Language Model Reasoning on Knowledge Graphs
comment: Accepted to KDD '26 (32nd ACM SIGKDD Conference on Knowledge Discovery and Data Mining)
summary: Large language models (LLMs) augmented with knowledge graphs (KGs) offer a promising approach for knowledge-intensive reasoning. Central to this approach is the selection of appropriate reasoning paths in the KG. Yet, existing methods face a common limitation: reasoning path selection is often performed by separate modules using criteria that are only weakly connected to the reasoning requirements. This often results in selecting incorrect relations or premature pruning of relevant paths. We propose Search-on-Graph (SoG), a method that strengthens the connection between path selection and reasoning by having the LLM itself select which relations to follow, informed by both the available KG structure and the complete reasoning history. SoG follows an \textit{observe-think-navigate} paradigm: at each step, the LLM observes the relational connections available at the current entity, reasons about which path best advances toward answering the question, and navigates accordingly. This context-aware navigation fully exploits the LLM's reasoning capabilities rather than relying on independent selection modules with surrogate criteria. Experiments on six knowledge graph question answering (KGQA) benchmarks demonstrate that SoG outperforms state-of-the-art methods while requiring no task-specific fine-tuning and generalizing across different KG schemas.

AI.tldr: Search-on-Graph (SoG) lets the LLM itself select reasoning paths on a KG at each step using an observe-think-navigate paradigm, outperforming SOTA on six KGQA benchmarks without fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: Existing KG-augmented LLM methods decouple path selection from reasoning by using separate modules with surrogate criteria, leading to incorrect relation choices and premature pruning of relevant paths. The authors aim to tightly couple path selection with the LLM's own reasoning capabilities.
AI.method: SoG follows an observe-think-navigate loop: at each step, the LLM observes available relations at the current entity, reasons about which path best advances toward the answer given the full reasoning history and KG structure, and navigates to the next entity. This eliminates separate selection modules.
AI.result: SoG outperforms state-of-the-art methods on six KGQA benchmarks, generalizes across different KG schemas, and requires no task-specific fine-tuning.
AI.conclusion: Embedding path selection directly into the LLM's reasoning process via context-aware navigation yields stronger performance and better generalization than modular approaches with detached selection criteria.

title: From Resource Flow to Executable Tests: Petri-Net-Guided LLM Test Generation for Concurrent Stateful Rust APIs
summary: Concurrent stateful library APIs expose behavior through evolving resource ownership, lifecycle states, and competing interleavings. Large language models can synthesize executable Rust tests, but their outputs often violate API preconditions, remain shallow, or reduce concurrency to accidental sequential traces. Conversely, model-based and systematic testing techniques provide semantic control but commonly require substantial handwritten code to turn abstract scenarios into executable tests. This paper addresses the gap between formal scenario design and low-cost test concretization. We present a Petri-net-guided methodology for test generation over concurrent stateful Rust APIs. The method represents API resources, lifecycle conditions, and causal dependencies as colored tokens and transitions; derives legal deep-state, near-legal, and partial-order concurrent scenarios; and uses these scenarios as a constrained intermediate representation for LLM-based code synthesis. A local-faithfulness contract and structural repair loop preserve the modeled intent during concretization, while Petri-guided schedule shaping prioritizes high-conflict concurrency skeletons for systematic exploration. A layered semantic oracle then distinguishes synthesis failures from violations of the target API's expected behavior.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a Petri-net-guided methodology for generating concurrent tests over stateful Rust APIs, using colored Petri nets to model resources and lifecycles, then employing LLMs to concretize derived scenarios into executable tests, with repair loops and semantic oracles ensuring fidelity.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-based test generation for concurrent stateful Rust APIs produces outputs that violate API preconditions, lack depth, or reduce concurrency to sequential traces. Meanwhile, model-based testing offers semantic rigor but requires substantial manual effort to translate abstract scenarios into executable code. A gap exists between formal scenario design and low-cost concretization.
AI.method: The approach uses colored Petri nets to model API resources, lifecycle conditions, and causal dependencies. From these nets, it derives legal deep-state, near-legal, and partial-order concurrent scenarios. These scenarios serve as constrained intermediate representations for LLM-based code synthesis. A local-faithfulness contract and structural repair loop preserve modeled intent during concretization. Petri-guided schedule shaping prioritizes high-conflict concurrency skeletons. A layered semantic oracle distinguishes synthesis failures from genuine API behavior violations.
AI.result: Not explicitly stated in the provided abstract; the abstract focuses on the proposed methodology rather than empirical outcomes.
AI.conclusion: The Petri-net-guided methodology bridges the gap between formal scenario design and automated test concretization, enabling systematic, semantically controlled concurrent test generation for stateful Rust APIs with reduced manual effort.

title: Bayesian uncertainty estimation improves clinical decision making in medical AI agents
summary: Machine learning models for medical image analysis typically lack a reliable measure of confidence, limiting their use in ambiguous or atypical cases. Here we show that Monte Carlo dropout, applied to a multi-task chest-radiograph classifier (eight thoracic findings, 137,593 training images), provides an epistemic uncertainty signal that tracks generalisation across training-set scales and flags confident yet error-prone predictions. Adding this signal to the point prediction raised error-detection AUROC from 0.74 to 0.77 ($Δ$AUROC +0.023, 95% CI [+0.014, +0.033]). In a controlled 2x2 factorial experiment, a clinical-decision-support agent exploited this uncertainty only when it was delivered as a binary error-risk flag rather than as raw scores, cutting confident misdiagnoses on unreliable findings from 8.5% to 2.7%. Epistemic uncertainty estimation thus carries decision-relevant information beyond point predictions, but its value for downstream agents depends on how it is communicated.

AI.tldr: Monte Carlo dropout applied to a multi-task chest X-ray classifier produces epistemic uncertainty estimates that improve error detection (AUROC +0.023) and, when communicated as binary risk flags, enable a clinical decision-support agent to reduce confident misdiagnoses from 8.5% to 2.7%.
AI.motivation: Medical image analysis models lack reliable confidence measures, limiting safe deployment in ambiguous cases. The authors aim to determine whether epistemic uncertainty can provide decision-relevant information beyond point predictions and how its communication format affects clinical utility.
AI.method: Monte Carlo dropout was applied to a multi-task chest radiograph classifier trained on 137,593 images across eight thoracic findings. Epistemic uncertainty was evaluated for tracking generalization across training-set sizes and for error detection (AUROC). A controlled 2×2 factorial experiment then tested whether a clinical-decision-support agent could leverage this uncertainty, comparing raw scores versus binary error-risk flags.
AI.result: Epistemic uncertainty tracked generalization across training-set scales and flagged confident yet erroneous predictions. Adding uncertainty to point predictions improved error-detection AUROC from 0.74 to 0.77 (ΔAUROC +0.023; 95% CI [+0.014, +0.033]). In the factorial experiment, the agent only exploited uncertainty when presented as a binary error-risk flag (not raw scores), reducing confident misdiagnoses on unreliable findings from 8.5% to 2.7%.
AI.conclusion: Epistemic uncertainty estimation carries decision-relevant information beyond point predictions, but its practical value for downstream agents critically depends on the communication format — binary flags proved effective while raw scores did not.

title: Security Vulnerability Patterns in AI-Generated Code: A Cross-Model Comparative Study
summary: LLM-based coding tools enable non-expert users to generate routine automation scripts that may enter enterprise workflows without meaningful security review. This study examines that risk directly. Code was collected from ChatGPT, Microsoft Copilot, and Google Gemini using identical prompts across three automation domains. Claude Code performed a standardized vulnerability review. Each identified vulnerability was scored using CVSS v3.1 and mapped to the OWASP Top 10:2021 and the MITRE ATT&CK frameworks. Every script contained exploitable vulnerabilities. Nine of the 17 identified vulnerability classes appeared in code from all three models, while 14 of the 17 vulnerability classes appeared in at least two models. The weighted CVSS scores across platforms differed by less than 10%. The risk is not tied to any particular model but rather to the task category. Organizations should therefore ask not which tool to trust, but instead whether LLM-generated automation code should be deployed without review.

AI.tldr: A security analysis of automation scripts generated by ChatGPT, Microsoft Copilot, and Google Gemini found that every script contained exploitable vulnerabilities, with consistent risk profiles across models, indicating that the danger lies in deploying unreviewed LLM-generated code—not in the choice of tool.
AI.motivation: LLM-based coding tools increasingly enable non-experts to produce automation scripts that may enter enterprise workflows without adequate security review. The authors sought to directly quantify and characterize the security risks inherent in such LLM-generated automation code across multiple widely-used models.
AI.method: Code was collected from three LLM platforms (ChatGPT, Microsoft Copilot, Google Gemini) using identical prompts across three automation domains. Claude Code then performed a standardized vulnerability review on all collected scripts. Each identified vulnerability was scored using CVSS v3.1 and mapped to the OWASP Top 10:2021 and MITRE ATT&CK frameworks for consistent classification and risk assessment.
AI.result: Every script examined contained exploitable vulnerabilities. Nine of 17 identified vulnerability classes appeared across all three models, and 14 of 17 appeared in at least two. Weighted CVSS scores differed by less than 10% across platforms, demonstrating that risk is model-agnostic and instead tied to the task category.
AI.conclusion: The risk of LLM-generated automation code is not attributable to any specific model but is inherent to the nature of the task. Organizations should therefore reconsider whether LLM-generated automation scripts should be deployed without human review, rather than focusing on which tool to trust.

title: Position: Natural Language Should Not Fully Replace Formal Languages
comment: To be published in ICML 2026 (position track)
summary: Recent advances in large language models and their widespread adoption have prompted claims that natural language could entirely replace formal languages, such as programming languages for software design. In this position paper, we argue that this perspective overlooks fundamental linguistic properties of natural language, specifically that it is optimized for underspecification in open-ended contexts. We introduce a formal framework centered on *task specificity*, defining it as the information-theoretic reduction of uncertainty in an output space -- such as all possible images -- given a user's specific requirements. We prove a *specificity crossover theorem*, showing the existence of a threshold beyond which the cost to express formal requirements into natural language exceeds the cost of direct formal specification. By analyzing case studies across modalities, such as image generation, code synthesis, and audio production, we demonstrate that natural language excels at low specificity tasks, while formal languages are advantageous on tasks with stricter requirements. We conclude that natural and formal languages are complementary tools and advocate the development of hybrid systems that allow users to move across the specificity spectrum.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that natural language cannot fully replace formal languages because natural language is inherently optimized for underspecification. It introduces a formal framework based on "task specificity" and proves a "specificity crossover theorem," showing that beyond a certain precision threshold, formal specification becomes more cost-efficient than natural language. Hybrid systems spanning the specificity spectrum are advocated.
AI.motivation: To challenge the growing claim that natural language can entirely supplant formal languages (e.g., programming languages) in software design and other precise domains, by highlighting the fundamental linguistic property of underspecification in natural language.
AI.method: The authors introduce a formal framework centered on "task specificity," defined as the information-theoretic reduction of uncertainty in an output space given user requirements. They prove a "specificity crossover theorem" demonstrating a threshold where natural language specification becomes costlier than formal specification, and support the argument with case studies across image generation, code synthesis, and audio production.
AI.result: Natural language excels at low-specificity tasks where underspecification is tolerable or even desirable, while formal languages are advantageous for high-specificity tasks with strict requirements. The crossover theorem formally establishes the existence of a threshold where formal specification becomes more efficient.
AI.conclusion: Natural and formal languages are complementary rather than substitutive tools. The authors advocate for developing hybrid systems that allow seamless movement across the specificity spectrum, leveraging the strengths of both modalities.

title: Do Active SAE Feature Planes Carry More Holonomy? A Preregistered Reversal in Gemma
comment: 23 pages, 5 figures. Preregistered confirmatory study; frozen experiment record archived at Zenodo, doi:10.5281/zenodo.20960027
summary: This paper tests whether holonomy concentrates on active sparse-autoencoder (SAE) feature planes in Gemma 2 2B, a concrete operationalization of the broader semantic-concentration prediction. Holonomy is measured at the final-token layer-12 to layer-13 residual-stream readout by carrying a local frame around small loops using the instrument's restricted-Jacobian transport rule, then normalizing the resulting rotation by enclosed area. The design, materiality threshold, analysis, and verdict rules were preregistered and frozen before the analysed measurements were inspected. The prediction was falsified in reverse: active-feature planes carried less holonomy than matched mixed-feature controls, with an adjusted log contrast of -0.29439 and 95% interval [-0.43989, -0.14889]. A magnitude-only explanation was not supported in this design, while the three-way ordering across random, mixed-feature, and active-feature planes was undefined at matched magnitude because common support failed. Post-freeze diagnostics at the same readout supported the area law on a small validation subset, bounded matched-center displacement under a simple paired regression, and identified transport distortion as a live mechanism or confound. The result is therefore a narrow, auditable operational reversal, not a causal claim that meaning suppresses holonomy. The cause remains open, with activation-strength geometry, degree of feature engagement, dictionary geometry, matched-center displacement, activation-manifold proximity, and transport shear as live alternatives.

AI.tldr: The paper tests whether semantic concentration manifests as concentrated holonomy on active SAE feature planes in Gemma 2 2B. Using a preregistered design with restricted-Jacobian parallel transport around small loops, the prediction was falsified in reverse: active-feature planes carried significantly less holonomy than matched controls. The cause remains unresolved, with several live alternative explanations identified.
AI.motivation: To empirically test the broader semantic-concentration prediction — the hypothesis that meaning concentrates in neural network representations — by concretely operationalizing it as holonomy concentration on active sparse-autoencoder feature planes in a language model.
AI.method: Holonomy was measured at the final-token residual stream readout (layer-12 to layer-13) in Gemma 2 2B by transporting a local frame around small loops using a restricted-Jacobian transport rule, then normalizing the resulting rotation by enclosed area. Active-feature planes were compared against matched mixed-feature controls. The design, materiality threshold, analysis, and verdict rules were all preregistered and frozen before data inspection. Post-freeze diagnostics included area-law validation, matched-center displacement regression, and transport distortion assessment.
AI.result: The prediction was falsified in reverse: active-feature planes carried less holonomy than matched mixed-feature controls (adjusted log contrast = -0.29439, 95% CI [-0.43989, -0.14889]). A magnitude-only explanation was not supported, and three-way ordering across random, mixed-feature, and active-feature planes was undefined due to failed common support. Post-freeze diagnostics confirmed the area law on a validation subset, identified bounded matched-center displacement, and flagged transport distortion as a live mechanism or confound.
AI.conclusion: This is a narrow, auditable operational reversal — not a causal claim that meaning suppresses holonomy. The cause remains open, with several live alternatives: activation-strength geometry, degree of feature engagement, dictionary geometry, matched-center displacement, activation-manifold proximity, and transport shear.

title: DecodeShare: Tracing the Shared Subspace of LLM Decode-Time Decisions
summary: Large language models (LLMs) handle many tasks with one set of parameters, but under KV-cached inference it is unclear what task-general structure, if any, is used at decode time rather than during prefill. We propose DecodeShare, a protocol that identifies a low-dimensional subspace consistently shared across tasks in decode-time hidden states, and then tests its causal role by removing that subspace only during decoding. In our experiments, disturbing the discovered shared subspace degrades decision performance far more than disturbing either a prefill-derived or random subspace under the same intervention budget. We further show this decode-shared subspace has practical consequences for activation steering: common steering directions can overlap the task-general decode channel. Projecting out this shared subspace directly separates the functional roles of the two components, while evaluating steering vectors at decode-time yields more reliable signal for downstream deployment than prefill-based proxies. Despite its compactness, the shared subspace can serve as a high-leverage causal channel at decode time. Code is available at: https://github.com/Zishan-Shao/decodeshare.git.

AI.tldr: DecodeShare identifies a low-dimensional shared subspace in LLM decode-time hidden states that operates as a task-general causal channel; disturbing it disproportionately harms performance, and it has practical implications for activation steering by separating functional components.
AI.motivation: Under KV-cached inference, it is unclear whether LLMs use any task-general structure specifically during decoding (as opposed to prefill). Understanding this could reveal how models generalize across tasks at inference time and improve techniques like activation steering.
AI.method: The authors propose DecodeShare, a protocol that: (1) identifies a low-dimensional subspace consistently shared across tasks in decode-time hidden states, (2) causally tests its role by ablating only that subspace during decoding, and (3) compares degradation against prefill-derived and random subspaces under matched intervention budgets. They further analyze overlap between this shared subspace and activation steering directions.
AI.result: Disturbing the decode-shared subspace degrades decision performance significantly more than disturbing prefill-derived or random subspaces. The shared subspace overlaps with common steering directions; projecting it out cleanly separates functional roles. Evaluating steering vectors at decode time yields more reliable downstream signals than prefill-based proxies.
AI.conclusion: Despite its compactness, the decode-time shared subspace serves as a high-leverage causal channel, suggesting that LLMs rely on a task-general representation during decoding. This has both scientific implications for mechanistic interpretability and practical benefits for activation steering methods.

title: Can Valence Reflect Morality in Natural Language? A Preliminary Annotation Study
comment: 8 pages, 2 figures, submitted to the 36th Irish Signals and Systems Conference
summary: Present implementations of artificial intelligence (AI) ethics do not adequately take feelings, or affect, into account. If AI should be aligned with human ethics, it seems reasonable to thoroughly investigate the possibility of AI behaviour that mirrors virtuous human ethical conduct, where feelings play a role in the actions, judgements or statements one makes. Furthermore, while prominent theories of normative ethics are often discussed in terms of their differences and shortcomings, Virtue, Consequentialist, and Kantian Deontological ethics all share a common feature of considering human feeling to some degree while the popular descriptive ethics theory, Moral Foundations Theory, positions feelings as central to many of its foundations. Therefore, in the present paper, a data set of moral valence is proposed, consisting of 500 annotations by six human participants for both action/judgement and consequence moral valence, ranging from -1 to 1 for text-presented scenarios from the Commonsense Norm Bank data set. The resulting valence features share significant relationships with multi-class (immoral/discretionary/moral) and binary immoral/moral categories while additionally providing a noteworthy test set Matthew's correlation coefficient of 0.764 using regularised logistic regression for binary classification. This provides early evidence of the usefulness of valence features for morality estimation of text, indicating that valenced consequences of responses for others can be considered toward more human morally-aligned AI. In the interest of promoting further affective-moral computing research, this study's annotations will be made available for research on request.

AI.tldr: Proposes a moral valence dataset (500 annotations) linking affective/emotional dimensions to ethical judgment of text scenarios, demonstrating valence features significantly predict moral classification (MCC=0.764), arguing affect is essential for morally-aligned AI.
AI.motivation: Current AI ethics implementations neglect affect (feelings/emotions), despite major normative and descriptive ethical theories — Virtue Ethics, Consequentialism, Deontology, and Moral Foundations Theory — all recognizing feelings as integral to moral judgment. Bridging this gap requires empirical resources connecting affect to morality.
AI.method: Six human annotators rated 500 text scenarios from the Commonsense Norm Bank on two continuous valence dimensions (action/judgement valence and consequence valence, scale -1 to +1). Statistical analyses examined relationships between valence scores and categorical moral labels (immoral/discretionary/moral; binary immoral/moral), with regularised logistic regression used for binary classification benchmarking.
AI.result: Valence features showed significant relationships with both multi-class and binary moral categories. Regularised logistic regression achieved a Matthews Correlation Coefficient of 0.764 for binary immoral/moral classification, providing early evidence that valence features are useful for morality estimation in text.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating valenced consequences for others into computational models represents a promising direction for developing more human-like morally-aligned AI. The annotated dataset will be released to support further affective-moral computing research.

title: Search-on-Graph-R1: Training Large Language Models to Search Knowledge Graphs with Reinforcement Learning
summary: Knowledge graph question answering (KGQA) requires navigating from topic entities to an answer several relations away. Recent methods prompt a frontier LLM to explore the graph through a retrieval tool, but their reliance on frontier-scale inference makes them costly to deploy. We present Search-on-Graph-R1 (\sogrone{}), which internalizes this navigation into a compact 8B model through supervised fine-tuning (SFT) followed by reinforcement learning (RL). Our central idea is to scaffold a frontier teacher with each question's gold SPARQL query, so the teacher traverses a known answer-bearing path with a live \texttt{Search} tool rather than having to discover the path itself. Since every call executes against a live Freebase server, the resulting trajectories are grounded in the knowledge graph by construction. On WebQSP, CWQ, and GrailQA, \sogrone{} at 8B surpasses every frozen frontier-LLM system in our comparison and posts the strongest results on CWQ of any system we compare against. It does so using no auxiliary module at inference and no LLM judge during training. Isolating each training stage shows that SFT and RL contribute complementary gains, our approach transfers across model families, and RL learns to reach answers in fewer \texttt{Search} calls than its SFT initialization.

AI.tldr: Search-on-Graph-R1 (SoG-R1) is a compact 8B model for KGQA that internalizes graph traversal by training on teacher trajectories scaffolded with gold SPARQL queries, using SFT followed by RL. It surpasses frontier LLM systems on WebQSP, CWQ, and GrailQA without auxiliary modules or LLM judges at inference.
AI.motivation: Existing KGQA methods rely on prompting frontier-scale LLMs with retrieval tools to navigate knowledge graphs, which is costly to deploy at scale. The authors aim to distill this navigation capability into a compact, deployable model without sacrificing performance.
AI.method: The method has three key stages: (1) A frontier teacher is scaffolded with each question's gold SPARQL query, so it traverses a known answer-bearing path using a live Search tool against Freebase, producing grounded trajectories. (2) These trajectories are used for supervised fine-tuning (SFT) of an 8B model. (3) Reinforcement learning (RL) further optimizes the model to reach answers in fewer Search calls. No auxiliary module or LLM judge is used during inference or training.
AI.result: SoG-R1 at 8B surpasses all frozen frontier-LLM systems compared on WebQSP, CWQ, and GrailQA, achieving the strongest results on CWQ among all compared systems. Ablations show SFT and RL contribute complementary gains, the approach transfers across model families, and RL reduces the number of Search calls needed versus the SFT-only baseline.
AI.conclusion: Distilling teacher-guided graph navigation into a compact model via SFT+RL is a viable and cost-effective alternative to deploying frontier LLMs for KGQA. The approach achieves state-of-the-art results while being more efficient at inference time.

title: Routing Subspaces: Auditing Evaluation-to-Deployment Mismatch in Fine-Tuned Language Models
summary: Safety evaluations often assume that behavior observed during testing reflects behavior in ordinary use, but fine-tuning can break this assumption. A checkpoint can appear fixed under evaluation-style prompts while the same behavior persists under ordinary-use prompts. Output scores reveal this mismatch but do not locate it. We investigate whether the distinction is encoded in a stable internal site and introduce an approach that fits a paired activation contrast at a path-patching-informed mid-depth window, then modifies the resulting coordinate on held-out prompts. The intervention closes the evaluation-to-deployment gap in ten of twelve model--behavior settings (six of the eight settings with $n{\geq}120$ paired questions) across four full-matrix instruction-tuned model instances; a fifth model supports localization and edit-provenance checks, and deployment-framed rates change by at most $6.1$pp. The two flat cells, both sycophancy, indicate that a single-coordinate audit is not sufficient when the installed distinction is higher-rank or missed by the depth heuristic. The audit is a diagnostic for fine-tuned checkpoints, not a training-time defense or a guarantee of deployment safety.

AI.tldr: Safety evaluations assume test behavior equals real-world behavior, but fine-tuning can create a gap where a model appears safe under evaluation prompts yet still exhibits unsafe behavior under ordinary-use prompts. The authors identify a mid-depth internal representation that encodes this evaluation/deployment distinction and show that editing a single activation coordinate can close the gap in most tested settings.
AI.motivation: Standard safety evaluations may fail to detect persistent unsafe behaviors after fine-tuning because they rely on evaluation-style prompts that differ from how users actually interact with models. The mismatch between evaluation scores and deployment behavior is known but not mechanistically located. The authors seek to locate where this distinction is encoded inside the model and whether a targeted intervention can close the gap.
AI.method: The authors use path-patching to identify a mid-depth window of layers where the evaluation-vs-deployment distinction is encoded. They fit a paired activation contrast—computing a difference vector between activations for evaluation-framed and deployment-framed prompts—and then intervene by modifying this single coordinate (adding or subtracting the contrast direction) on held-out prompts. Effectiveness is measured by whether the intervention eliminates the behavioral gap across multiple model instances and behavior settings.
AI.result: The intervention closed the evaluation-to-deployment gap in 10 of 12 model–behavior settings (and 6 of 8 settings with n≥120 paired questions) across four instruction-tuned models. A fifth model was used for localization and edit-provenance checks. Deployment-framed behavior rates changed by at most 6.1 percentage points. Two flat cells, both involving sycophancy, suggest the single-coordinate approach fails when the distinction is higher-rank or when the depth heuristic misses the relevant site.
AI.conclusion: The proposed audit is a diagnostic tool for fine-tuned checkpoints—not a training-time defense or a deployment safety guarantee. A single-coordinate intervention suffices in most cases, but higher-rank distinctions (as in sycophancy) require more comprehensive approaches.

title: HiMe: Real-Time Self-Hosted Personal Agent Platform for Health Insights with Wearable Devices
summary: Traditional approaches to wearable health signal analysis, such as smartwatches, are constrained by rigid analytical frameworks and limited personalisation. The emergence of LLM agents creates a new opportunity for Personal Health Agentic Analysis, where health insights can be generated adaptively and in context. However, currently there is no open-source locally deployable platform capable of processing personal health data in real time while preserving privacy. We present HiMe, a locally deployable, privacy-first agent platform that is fully compatible with real-time health data ecosystems across a wide range of wearable devices. HiMe is guided by three design principles. The database is treated as a first-class component. Effectiveness and efficiency are jointly optimised to achieve a low-cost Pareto-optimal balance. Data are processed in real time while the user is modelled over the long term. Together, these principles make it practical for individuals to harness Personal Health Agents for continuous, personalised health monitoring for better wellbeing.

AI.tldr: HiMe is an open-source, locally deployable platform enabling privacy-preserving, real-time personal health analysis using LLM agents, designed for continuous and personalised wearable health monitoring.
AI.motivation: Current wearable health analytics (e.g., smartwatches) suffer from rigid frameworks and limited personalisation. While LLM agents offer adaptive, context-aware health insights, no open-source, locally deployable platform exists that can process personal health data in real time with privacy preservation.
AI.method: HiMe is built on three design principles: (1) treating the database as a first-class component, (2) jointly optimising effectiveness and efficiency for a low-cost Pareto-optimal balance, and (3) processing data in real time while maintaining long-term user modelling. The platform is compatible with diverse wearable health data ecosystems.
AI.result: The paper presents the HiMe platform itself as the result — a functional, locally deployable agent platform capable of real-time, privacy-first personal health analysis across wearable devices.
AI.conclusion: HiMe makes it practical for individuals to harness Personal Health Agents for continuous, personalised health monitoring, advancing wellbeing through adaptive and private health insight generation.

title: Leaky Language Models: Stealing Architecture and Inference Optimizations via Per-Token Timing
summary: This work presents LeakyLMs, a set of attacks that leak proprietary model, architecture, and deployment information from production language models. LeakyLMs is the first to demonstrate that key model and deployment details can be inferred using only token generation timing, even when interacting through remote APIs. LeakyLMs introduces two core attacks. The first attack targets inference optimizations and deployment strategies. For example, our attack detects whether a provider uses speculative decoding, a widely deployed inference-time optimization, and further identifies the context length of the draft model used in the pipeline. Our measurements show that Google Gemini Flash 2.5 uses speculative decoding with a draft context window of approximately 128K tokens. The second attack recovers key architectural properties, including the number of transformer layers, hidden dimension size, and number of attention heads. To achieve this, LeakyLMs builds a detailed and accurate model of token-generation timing on modern NVIDIA GPUs, characterizing how latency scales with model configuration and hardware parameters. The attack then performs a search over the architecture space using this timing model. In experiments with Llama models, the near-correct architectural configuration appears in the top-10 guesses more than 90% of the time.

AI.tldr: LeakyLMs is a timing-based side-channel attack that leaks proprietary model architecture and deployment details (e.g., speculative decoding usage, layer count, hidden dimension, attention heads) from production LLMs via token-generation latency alone, achieving >90% top-10 accuracy on Llama models and revealing that Google Gemini Flash 2.5 uses speculative decoding with a ~128K draft context window.
AI.motivation: Production LLMs are deployed as black-box APIs, hiding valuable intellectual property such as model architecture, parameter counts, and inference optimizations. Existing inversion attacks focus on stealing model weights or training data, but none systematically infer architectural and deployment details from token-level timing signals alone. The authors aim to fill this gap by demonstrating that fine-grained timing measurements suffice to reverse-engineer critical proprietary information.
AI.method: LeakyLMs introduces two core timing-based attacks: (1) A deployment inference attack that detects inference-time optimizations like speculative decoding and estimates draft model context length by analyzing per-token latency patterns. (2) An architecture recovery attack that builds a precise analytical timing model of token generation on NVIDIA GPUs, characterizing how latency scales with layer count, hidden dimension, and attention heads. A search procedure then matches observed latencies against this model to recover the most likely architectural configurations.
AI.result: The deployment attack reveals that Google Gemini Flash 2.5 employs speculative decoding with a draft model context window of approximately 128K tokens. The architecture recovery attack, evaluated on Llama-family models, places the near-correct architectural configuration in the top-10 candidate guesses more than 90% of the time.
AI.conclusion: Token-generation timing alone, observable through black-box API interactions, constitutes a significant information leakage vector for production LLMs. Providers should consider timing-based side-channel mitigations, as current deployments expose both optimization strategies and core architectural details to adversaries with modest query budgets.

title: Moir: Let the Model Direct Its Own Story for Robust Cross-Domain Knowledge Editing
summary: While language models remain frozen at their training state, the world evolves continuously. Knowledge editing has emerged as a key alternative to full retraining, but its deployment is bottlenecked by the erosion of core capabilities: mathematical and programmatic reasoning collapse while encyclopedic recall remains intact. We trace this asymmetric degradation to a distributional mismatch. Covariance-based editors preserve only the subspaces spanned by their reference corpus, but fail to capture the operative distribution shaped by post-training such as SFT and DPO. Static external corpora, including Wikipedia and even the original pretraining mixture, cannot recover this shifted manifold. We propose Moir, which estimates the preservation covariance $C$ directly from the model itself by sampling from its own decoding distribution. Seeding generation with a single random vocabulary token bypasses the instruction-following templates that otherwise dominate sampled outputs, exposing the broader subspaces the model has internalized. Moir requires no external data and serves as a drop-in component for any covariance-based editor, a practical advantage given that the pre- and post-training corpora of most modern LLMs are not publicly accessible. Across OLMo-2, Llama-3.1, and Qwen-3 (7-8B), under both MEMIT and AlphaEdit and in batch and sequential regimes, Moir consistently extends preservation in the most vulnerable domains, most strikingly on Qwen3-8B after 20,000 AlphaEdit batch edits, it retains 79.9% GSM8K accuracy compared to 10.9% with the Wikipedia baseline. These results suggest that aligning the preservation distribution with the model's operative distribution is a key factor in non-destructive editing, and that the model itself may be the most accessible source of that distribution for deployed systems.

AI.tldr: Knowledge editing erodes reasoning capabilities asymmetrically due to a distributional mismatch in preservation covariances. The proposed method, Moir, estimates the preservation covariance from the model's own decoding distribution rather than external corpora, dramatically improving retention of mathematical reasoning after editing.
AI.motivation: Current covariance-based knowledge editors rely on external corpora (e.g., Wikipedia) to compute preservation subspaces, but these corpora fail to capture the post-training distribution (SFT, DPO) that shapes a model's operative capabilities. This mismatch causes catastrophic degradation in mathematical and programmatic reasoning while leaving encyclopedic recall intact. The core problem is that the preservation distribution is misaligned with the model's internalized distribution.
AI.method: Moir estimates the preservation covariance C by sampling directly from the model's own decoding distribution. The key innovation is seeding generation with a single random vocabulary token, which bypasses instruction-following templates that would otherwise dominate outputs, thereby exposing the broader subspaces the model has internalized. This requires no external data and can be dropped into any covariance-based editor (e.g., MEMIT, AlphaEdit).
AI.result: Across OLMo-2, Llama-3.1, and Qwen-3 (7-8B), Moir consistently extends preservation in vulnerable reasoning domains. The most dramatic result: Qwen3-8B after 20,000 AlphaEdit batch edits retains 79.9% GSM8K accuracy with Moir, compared to only 10.9% with the Wikipedia baseline.
AI.conclusion: Aligning the preservation distribution with the model's operative distribution is critical for non-destructive knowledge editing. The model itself serves as the most accessible and effective source of this distribution, a practical advantage given that pre- and post-training corpora for most modern LLMs are not publicly available.

title: Uncertainty-Aware Trust Estimation for Multi-LLM Systems via Structured Expert Judgement
summary: Large Language Model (LLM) ensembles are increasingly used to improve reliability by combining predictions from multiple LLMs. However, existing aggregation methods typically assume that all models are equally trustworthy, overlooking differences in uncertainty quality. This assumption is poorly suited to heterogeneous LLMs, whose reliability and capability vary significantly, making naive aggregation vulnerable to unreliable or adversarial experts. In this work, we formulate multi-LLM aggregation as a problem of uncertainty-aware trust estimation. We adapt structured expert judgment from decision theory, using context-aware calibration questions to estimate expert reliability based on the quality of its probabilistic predictions. Specifically, we employ Cooke-style log weighting, which penalises overconfident incorrect predictions and favours well-calibrated experts. We evaluate our approach on MMLU and MMLU-Pro across homogeneous, heterogeneous, and contaminated expert panels. Results show that while aggregation methods perform similarly in homogeneous settings, Cooke weighting becomes critical under heterogeneity and contamination. It achieves a superior accuracy-reliability balance and remains robust when unreliable experts are introduced. These findings suggest that Multi-LLM aggregation requires not just combining predictions, but calibrating trust under uncertainty.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Cooke-style log weighting from decision theory for multi-LLM aggregation, which estimates expert reliability via calibration questions. It outperforms naive aggregation under heterogeneous and contaminated settings, achieving superior accuracy-reliability balance.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM ensemble aggregation methods assume equal trustworthiness across models, ignoring differences in uncertainty calibration quality. This fails when LLMs are heterogeneous or when unreliable/adversarial experts are present, leading to vulnerable aggregation.
AI.method: The authors adapt structured expert judgment from decision theory, specifically Cooke-style log weighting. Experts are evaluated using context-aware calibration questions that assess the quality of their probabilistic predictions. The weighting penalizes overconfident incorrect predictions and rewards well-calibrated experts, enabling uncertainty-aware trust estimation for aggregation.
AI.result: On MMLU and MMLU-Pro benchmarks, all aggregation methods perform similarly in homogeneous settings. However, under heterogeneous and contaminated expert panels, Cooke weighting is critical: it achieves superior accuracy-reliability balance and remains robust to unreliable experts, unlike naive approaches.
AI.conclusion: Multi-LLM aggregation requires not merely combining predictions but explicitly calibrating trust under uncertainty. Cooke-style log weighting provides a principled, robust solution for heterogeneous LLM ensembles.

title: PlanE: Meta Planning of Data, Tuning, and Inference for Extractive-based LLMs
summary: Enhancing the task-specific capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs) primarily requires substantial instruction-tuning datasets. However, the sheer volume of such data imposes a considerable annotation cost, and a lack of optimization methods for tailoring LLMs to specific tasks. To address the above issues, we propose a \textbf{Plan}ning framework for constructing \textbf{E}xtractive-based LLMs called \textbf{PlanE}, which includes data decomposition, instruction tuning, and prompt inference. Additionally, we introduce a Data-Tuning-Inference (DTI) planner, aimed at selecting the optimal base-LLM and its DTI combinations for specific datasets to improve construction efficiency. The experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our PlanE from two views: (1) across different datasets using the same base-LLM, and (2) on the same dataset using different base-LLMs. Furthermore, we validate the generalizability of the proposed DTI planner under different optimization objectives. The codes are publicly available at https://github.com/gugugu-469/PlanE.

AI.tldr: PlanE is a planning framework for constructing extractive-based LLMs that uses data decomposition, instruction tuning, and prompt inference, along with a DTI planner to select optimal base-LLM and data-tuning-inference combinations, reducing annotation costs while enhancing task-specific capabilities.
