AI.result: The analysis identifies three distinct reasons human participation may persist even with highly capable AI. The most novel contribution is the concept of target emergence: in activities where objectives are not fully specified in advance but instead emerge through interaction, human participation is constitutive rather than instrumental. This reframes human–AI co-construction not as a temporary remedy for imperfect AI but as a persistent, structurally necessary feature of certain activities.
AI.conclusion: The limits of automation are not solely technological but conceptual. Human–AI co-construction is a durable paradigm for activities whose targets emerge through participation, with significant implications for how future AI systems should be designed, evaluated, and ethically governed — moving beyond the assumption that full automation is always the appropriate end goal.

title: Which Model Is Actually Serving You? IRIS: Budgeted Black-Box Auditing of Model Substitution and Routing Dilution in LLM Gateways
summary: Commercial LLM gateways mediate access to hosted models, but the served backend may not match the advertised one: it may substitute a cheaper model on every request or route only a fraction $ε$ of requests to it. Prior black-box auditors often need a privileged signal (log-probabilities, token ranks, or reference samples) or a target-specific probe, fix the query budget in advance, and return a yes/no verdict. We present $\mathrm{IRIS}$, an audit that needs only the returned text: it asks endpoints to generate random numbers or strings, fingerprints the backend, and is the first to combine, in one text-only audit, detection of whole-stream substitution and fractional dilution, attribution of the served backend, routing-fraction ($ε$) estimation, and a query budget it sizes itself. A cheap pilot fits the exponential query-error decay and freezes that budget before any suspect query is issued. On an intra-family Qwen3 ladder $\mathrm{IRIS}$ verifies the backend at $0.99$ AUROC and sharpens attribution as queries accumulate; across a commercial OpenRouter library it catches $ε{=}0.3$ dilution on margin-qualified pairs at $0.85$ mean power ($0.017$ false-positive rate) and recovers $ε$ to within $0.04$ for enrolled diluents; and a live cross-provider audit flags $14$ of $15$ same-model provider pairs by genuine quantization and kernel deviations, corroborated on third-party MET traces. Against comparable black-box auditors, $\mathrm{IRIS}$ matches or beats detection on shared tasks, and adaptive allocation lifts the matched-budget target-hit rate from $73$% to $87$%. Further experiments cover adversarial gateways, knob identifiability, unseen diluents, and false-positive control.

AI.tldr: IRIS is a black-box audit that detects LLM backend substitution and fractional dilution using only generated text (random numbers/strings). It fingerprints backends, estimates routing fractions, and automatically sizes its query budget via a pilot phase. It achieves 0.99 AUROC on intra-family detection, catches ε=0.3 dilution with 0.85 mean power, and flags 14/15 same-model provider pairs in a live audit.
AI.motivation: Commercial LLM gateways may cheat by serving cheaper backend models instead of advertised ones — either full substitution or fractional routing (only a fraction ε of requests go to the advertised model). Prior audits require privileged signals (log-probs, token ranks), target-specific probes, fixed query budgets, and return only binary verdicts. A text-only, general-purpose audit that can detect both substitution and dilution, attribute the actual backend, estimate ε, and self-size its budget is needed.
AI.method: IRIS asks endpoints to generate random numbers or random strings, then fingerprints the backend by analyzing statistical patterns in the output text. It uses an exponential query-error decay model fitted during a cheap pilot phase to automatically determine the query budget before any suspect queries. The method combines detection of whole-stream substitution and fractional dilution, backend attribution, and routing-fraction (ε) estimation in a single text-only framework. It employs adaptive allocation to improve target-hit rates under fixed budgets.
AI.result: On an intra-family Qwen3 model ladder, IRIS verifies backends at 0.99 AUROC with improving attribution as queries accumulate. Across OpenRouter, it catches ε=0.3 dilution on margin-qualified pairs at 0.85 mean power with 0.017 false-positive rate and recovers ε within 0.04 for enrolled diluents. A live cross-provider audit flags 14 of 15 same-model provider pairs via genuine quantization and kernel deviations, corroborated by third-party MET traces. Against comparable black-box auditors, IRIS matches or beats detection; adaptive allocation lifts matched-budget target-hit rate from 73% to 87%. Additional experiments cover adversarial gateways, knob identifiability, unseen diluents, and false-positive control.
AI.conclusion: IRIS demonstrates that text-only black-box auditing of LLM gateways is both feasible and effective, achieving strong detection, attribution, and ε-estimation performance without privileged signals. Its self-budgeting pilot and adaptive allocation make it practical for real-world deployment against both substitution and dilution attacks.

title: A Graph Neural Network approach to zero-shot Digital Twins
summary: Traditional Predictive Digital Twins often remain geometrically rigid, requiring extensive retraining or fine-tuning whenever the underlying physical domain or boundary conditions change. To overcome this limitation, we present a novel framework for \textit{Zero-Shot Digital Twins} that seamlessly couples real-time visual perception with a geometry-agnostic, physics-informed reasoning engine. At the core of our architecture is the Thermodynamics-Informed Graph Neural Network architecture, a Geometric Deep Learning solver grounded in a metriplectic thermodynamic formalism that enforces energy conservation and non-negative entropy production locally through graph message passing. The framework integrates an auxiliary Graph Neural Network to infer unobservable fields (such as stress tensors or velocity and energy distributions) directly from sparse initial visual boundaries, mitigating numerical start-up transients. To bridge the sim-to-real gap, we implement a continuous closed-loop data assimilation mechanism; the pipeline tracks macroscopic deformations and free-surface fluid boundaries in real-time using deep segmentation networks combined with sparse optical flow, dynamically correcting the autoregressive simulation rollout and eliminating numerical drift. To test the validity of our approach, we demonstrate the extreme generalization capabilities of our approach across two disparate physical regimes: the large deformations of a viscoelastic beam and the non-linear sloshing of a viscous fluid. In both scenarios, the unified framework instantiates physically accurate simulations on novel, unseen geometries without case-specific retraining, operating well within real-time latency budgets (approximately 25 ms per frame) and enabling the direct projection of latent mechanical variables via Augmented Reality.

AI.tldr: A Zero-Shot Digital Twin framework that couples real-time visual perception with a Thermodynamics-Informed Graph Neural Network (TIGN) solver, enabling physically accurate simulations on novel geometries without retraining, operating at ~25ms per frame.
AI.motivation: Traditional predictive digital twins are geometrically rigid, requiring costly retraining or fine-tuning whenever physical domains or boundary conditions change. There is a need for a unified framework that generalizes across unseen geometries and physical regimes without case-specific retraining.
AI.method: The framework integrates: (1) A Thermodynamics-Informed Graph Neural Network (TIGN) grounded in metriplectic thermodynamic formalism, enforcing energy conservation and non-negative entropy production via graph message passing; (2) An auxiliary GNN to infer unobservable fields from sparse visual boundaries; (3) A closed-loop data assimilation pipeline using deep segmentation networks combined with sparse optical flow to track macroscopic deformations and free-surface boundaries in real time, dynamically correcting autoregressive rollout and eliminating numerical drift.
AI.result: The framework was validated on two disparate physical regimes: large deformations of a viscoelastic beam and non-linear sloshing of a viscous fluid. It instantiated physically accurate simulations on novel, unseen geometries without retraining, operating within real-time latency (~25ms per frame), and enabled direct projection of latent mechanical variables via Augmented Reality.
AI.conclusion: The proposed Zero-Shot Digital Twin framework achieves extreme generalization across different physical regimes and geometries while maintaining real-time performance, eliminating the retraining bottleneck of traditional digital twins through its geometry-agnostic, physics-informed architecture with closed-loop visual data assimilation.

title: VeriSimpl: Robust Optimization Modeling from Natural Language using Simplification-based Verification
summary: Natural language interfaces can greatly benefit the accessibility and usability of optimization modeling, and recent advances in large language models (LLMs) show promise in automatically translating textual problem descriptions into executable solver formulations. However, a key challenge for existing approaches is to ensure that the inferred formulation correctly implements the intended task, even if it may execute without errors. We introduce VeriSimpl, a solver LLM framework for robust natural-language-to-optimization formalization. Our approach is based on the idea of simplification-based verification, where the optimization solver is leveraged to generate simplified diagnostic queries about a candidate formulation to allow the LLM to tractably reason about the correctness of the formulation with respect to the task description. We present such simplification strategies along different dimensions with respect to problem constraints and decision variables, which allow the LLM to reason locally under fixed global contexts. Evaluations on a range of optimization benchmarks show how our approach provides consistent improvements in accuracy over existing methods, while also providing a novel high-precision self-verification signal.

AI.tldr: VeriSimpl introduces a simplification-based verification framework that uses optimization solvers to generate simplified diagnostic queries, enabling LLMs to tractably verify the correctness of generated optimization formulations against natural language task descriptions.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-based approaches for translating natural language into optimization models often produce formulations that execute without errors but may not correctly implement the intended task. There is a need for robust verification mechanisms to ensure semantic correctness of the inferred formulation.
AI.method: VeriSimpl employs simplification-based verification, where the optimization solver generates simplified diagnostic queries about a candidate formulation. These simplifications operate along different dimensions — problem constraints and decision variables — allowing the LLM to reason locally under fixed global contexts. The framework uses the solver itself as an analytical tool to probe formulation correctness.
AI.result: Evaluations on a range of optimization benchmarks demonstrate consistent accuracy improvements over existing methods, along with a novel high-precision self-verification signal.
AI.conclusion: Simplification-based verification provides an effective mechanism for improving the robustness and accuracy of LLM-driven optimization formalization, offering both performance gains and reliable self-verification capabilities.

title: QuantiBias: Benchmarking Quantization-Induced Bias in LLMs
summary: Almost every large language model that reaches a broad audience is quantized: trained in full precision, then compressed for efficiency. This step is assumed harmless and its safety is rarely re-checked. We find its principal side effect is increased bias that standard safety evaluation misses. Holding the model, its training, and the prompts fixed, a quantized model still refuses harmful requests, still avoids over-refusing benign prompts, and still selects the unbiased multiple-choice answer. Yet asked an open-ended question, the same model volunteers stereotypes in all eight languages we probe, in roughly one in four open-ended answers under an independent judge (~24% to ~27% across the compression ladder): it passes every standard check and still reaches users measurably more biased. The selective gap is a robust finding; whether open-ended bias further increases with compression is less certain, sensitive to the judge that scores it. We address both with \textbf{QuantiBias}, a benchmark that pairs a generative, multilingual stereotype probe with the refusal and multiple-choice controls that isolate open-ended generation, contrasts each build with and without reasoning, and rates the content severity of what it generates. Across two backbone models (Qwen and Gemma), a five-family screen, and eight benchmarks, quantizers allocate their extra precision by capability data that carries no bias-prevention signal, and reasoning before answering roughly halves the effect on some families while doing nothing on others. A quantized build must be re-evaluated for open-ended bias, not only on the short-form safeguards it already passes.

AI.tldr: Quantization of LLMs introduces a selective bias: quantized models pass standard safety checks (refusal, multiple-choice) but exhibit significantly more stereotypes in open-ended generation across multiple languages (~24-27%). The paper introduces QuantiBias, a benchmark isolating this gap, and finds reasoning before answering mitigates bias in some model families but not others.
AI.motivation: Current LLM safety evaluations focus on refusal behavior and multiple-choice benchmarks, which fail to detect the stereotypical bias introduced by quantization in open-ended generative contexts. Since nearly all deployed LLMs are quantized, this represents a systematic blind spot in safety assurance.
AI.method: The authors propose QuantiBias, a multilingual benchmark that pairs generative stereotype probes with refusal and multiple-choice controls to isolate open-ended generation effects. They test across two backbone models (Qwen, Gemma), five quantizer families, eight benchmarks, and eight languages, contrasting builds with and without reasoning, and measuring content severity of generated outputs using an independent judge.
AI.result: Quantized models produce biased open-ended responses in ~24-27% of cases across the compression ladder while passing all standard safety checks. The selective gap is robust; whether bias increases monotonically with compression is less certain and judge-sensitive. Reasoning before answering roughly halves the bias effect in some model families but has no effect in others. Quantizers appear to allocate extra precision using capability data that carries no bias-prevention signal.
AI.conclusion: Quantized LLM builds must be re-evaluated specifically for open-ended generative bias, not solely on the short-form safeguards they already pass. Standard safety evaluations are insufficient to detect this quantization-induced stereotype amplification.

title: Agentic Context Management: Solving Agent Memory and Cost by Treating Them as Lifecycle and Architecture Problems
comment: 23 pages, 6 figures, 4 tables. Evaluation harness and study data: github.com/maximem-ai
summary: Production AI agents' failures are less often due to an inability to reason well and more often because they cannot manage what is in their reasoning context: conversation histories, large prompts, large tool definitions, and ballooning tool outputs. Agents drown in their own accumulating history while paying a token cost that grows every turn, producing missing recalls within and across conversations. The incumbent response treats this as a storage-and-retrieval problem. We argue that framing is too narrow. Actively managing what an agent holds in mind is a lifecycle, not merely a store: it spans deciding what to remember, extracting and structuring it, choosing the right store per data type, consolidating and forgetting while preserving provenance, deciding what is relevant now, anticipating what is needed next, and compacting context to a budget without losing what matters. In serious production this operates not over a single user but across an organizational scope hierarchy. We name this discipline Agentic Context Management (ACM) and decompose it into five primitives: architecting, ingesting, scoping, anticipating, and compacting & consolidation. We then make the economic case: naive context accumulation grows token cost quadratically in conversation length, crude summarization buys linear cost at the price of an accuracy cliff, and only validated compaction achieves linear cost with preserved fidelity. We describe a reference implementation, Maximem Synap, that realizes the five primitives as a multi-tenant service and reports 92% on LongMemEval and 93.2% on LoCoMo under the configuration detailed in Section 6. We close with dimensions existing benchmarks do not yet capture, latency, token efficiency, and context-rot resistance, and the frontier of decision-level and organization-level context the category points toward.

AI.tldr: Production AI agents fail primarily due to context management issues—accumulating conversation histories, large prompts, and ballooning tool outputs—rather than reasoning deficiencies. The paper introduces Agentic Context Management (ACM), decomposing it into five primitives (architecting, ingesting, scoping, anticipating, compacting & consolidation), and demonstrates economic and performance benefits through a reference implementation called Maximem Synap.
AI.motivation: Production AI agents commonly fail not because of poor reasoning but because they cannot effectively manage their reasoning context—conversation histories, large prompts, tool definitions, and tool outputs grow unboundedly. This leads to ballooning token costs, missing recalls within/across conversations, and agents "drowning" in their own history. The incumbent storage-and-retrieval framing is too narrow to address the full lifecycle of context management.
AI.method: The authors propose Agentic Context Management (ACM), a discipline decomposed into five primitives: (1) architecting—deciding what to remember and choosing the right store per data type; (2) ingesting—extracting and structuring information; (3) scoping—determining what is relevant now; (4) anticipating—predicting what is needed next; (5) compacting & consolidation—forgetting while preserving provenance and compacting context to a budget. They provide an economic analysis comparing naive accumulation (quadratic token cost), crude summarization (linear cost with accuracy cliff), and validated compaction (linear cost with preserved fidelity). A reference implementation, Maximem Synap, is built as a multi-tenant service realizing all five primitives.
AI.result: Maximem Synap achieves 92% on LongMemEval and 93.2% on LoCoMo benchmarks. The economic analysis demonstrates that naive context accumulation incurs quadratic token cost growth in conversation length, crude summarization yields linear cost but suffers an accuracy cliff, and only validated compaction achieves linear cost with preserved fidelity.
AI.conclusion: ACM reframes agent context management from a narrow storage-and-retrieval problem into a full lifecycle discipline. The five-primitive decomposition provides a systematic framework, and the Maximem Synap implementation validates its practical viability. The paper identifies gaps in existing benchmarks—latency, token efficiency, and context-rot resistance—and points toward future frontiers in decision-level and organization-level context management.

title: Tencent WorkBuddy Bench: A Multi-Domain Coding-Agent Benchmark with Contamination-Resistant Task Construction
comment: 30 pages, 9 figures. Project page: https://workbuddybench.com/ ; code: https://github.com/Tencent/workbuddy-bench ; dataset: https://huggingface.co/datasets/tencent/workbuddy-bench
summary: We introduce Tencent WorkBuddy Bench, a multi-domain evaluation suite for coding agents; this report documents its construction methodology, scoring protocol, and a cross-model leaderboard. At its core is a unified evaluation framework for constructing and running distribution-informed coding-agent tasks across four work domains - Code, Web, Office, and Security. Rather than adapting public issue text, every task is reverse-engineered from a real commit, pull request, or business scenario and rewritten as a short, colloquial, role-played request, so that a task's prompt is not recoverable by web-searching the underlying issue, pull request, or commit thread. Because the dataset is released openly - task directories, environment images, evaluation harness, tests, and reference solutions - contamination resistance rests on this construction together with dataset versioning rather than on secrecy. The four subsets - repository-level engineering, front-end development, office and business workflows, and red-/blue-team security - probe complementary facets of real work, each with its own verification style. All are packaged in a uniform task-directory format and run, under a uniform and reproducible protocol, on two agent harnesses (CodeBuddy Code and Claude Code); the full open release makes the benchmark reproducible end to end and directly auditable, since any third party can re-run each task and inspect its content. Because each subset uses a different scoring instrument, scores are not comparable across subsets and the suite reports no suite-wide average. We report a cross-model leaderboard across several model families.

AI.tldr: Tencent WorkBuddy Bench is an open, multi-domain evaluation suite for coding agents, featuring tasks reverse-engineered from real-world commits/PRs/business scenarios across Code, Web, Office, and Security domains. It employs a unified framework with contamination-resistant, role-played prompts and a reproducible protocol, reporting cross-model leaderboards without suite-wide averaging due to domain-specific scoring instruments.
AI.motivation: Existing coding benchmarks often rely on public issues or curated problems that are susceptible to data contamination (e.g., models trained on public issue text). There is a need for a multi-domain, contamination-resistant benchmark that reflects real-world work across diverse professional contexts — not just software engineering — and is fully open and reproducible.
AI.method: Tasks are reverse-engineered from real commits, pull requests, or business scenarios and rewritten as short, colloquial, role-played requests so that prompts cannot be recovered by web search. The suite spans four domains (Code, Web, Office, Security), each with its own verification/scoring style. All tasks are packaged in a uniform task-directory format with environment images, tests, and reference solutions, and run on two agent harnesses (CodeBuddy Code and Claude Code) under a reproducible protocol. Contamination resistance relies on construction methodology and dataset versioning rather than secrecy.
AI.result: A cross-model leaderboard is reported across several model families. Because each subset uses a different scoring instrument, scores are not comparable across subsets, and no suite-wide average is reported.
AI.conclusion: Tencent WorkBuddy Bench provides a practical, contamination-resistant, and fully reproducible multi-domain benchmark for coding agents. Its open release enables third-party auditing and re-execution, setting a standard for transparent and realistic evaluation of coding agents across diverse professional workflows.

title: Toward cryptographically verifiable authorization for autonomous AI agents: A security hypothesis, preliminary formal model, and proof-of-concept implementation
comment: 11 pages, 1 figure, 2 Tables. Keywords: autonomous AI agents, zero-knowledge proofs, verifiable authorization, agentic security, zk-SNARKs, access control, cryptographic authorization, cryptographic protocols, zero-trust architecture, pre-execution authorization. Submitted to ACM Transactions on AI Security and Privacy (TAISAP)
summary: Autonomous AI agents increasingly execute actions, invoke tools, and operate on protected resources with limited human oversight. Existing authentication and authorization mechanisms establish identity and delegate authority, but do not inherently provide cryptographic evidence that a concrete request issued by a specific agent satisfies the applicable policy in a specific execution context. This paper hypothesizes that agent authorization can be formalized as a cryptographically verifiable relation, denoted $R_{CVA}$, that jointly binds an agent principal, a concrete authorization request, an execution context, and the satisfaction of an applicable policy, while selectively preserving the confidentiality of private authorization attributes. We introduce a preliminary formal abstraction for Cryptographically Verifiable Agent Authorization (CVA), define a compact set of candidate security properties including authorization soundness, principal binding, request binding, policy binding, and replay resistance, and provide an executable zero-knowledge proof of concept that instantiates selected elements of the model over a Groth16 zk-SNARK construction. We further identify and formalize the structural separation among identity binding, authorization-request binding, and runtime execution binding as a central open problem in the design of secure agentic systems (a distinction {not explicitly addressed by} current agentic security frameworks) and present a falsifiable research agenda for its resolution.

AI.tldr: The paper formalizes agent authorization as a cryptographically verifiable relation (CVA) that binds an agent, its request, execution context, and policy satisfaction, with a zk-SNARK proof-of-concept. It highlights the unaddressed structural separation of identity, authorization, and execution binding as a core open problem in agentic security.
AI.motivation: Autonomous AI agents increasingly operate on protected resources with minimal human oversight, yet existing authN/authZ mechanisms lack cryptographic evidence that a specific request by a specific agent satisfies policy in a given execution context. This gap motivates a verifiable, privacy-preserving authorization framework.
AI.method: The authors define a formal abstraction for Cryptographically Verifiable Agent Authorization (CVA) as a relation R_CVA binding agent principal, request, context, and policy satisfaction. They specify security properties (authorization soundness, principal/request/policy binding, replay resistance) and implement an executable proof-of-concept using a Groth16 zk-SNARK construction.
AI.result: A preliminary formal model and a working zk-SNARK-based prototype demonstrate selected CVA elements. The analysis identifies the structural separation of identity binding, authorization-request binding, and runtime execution binding as a central open problem not addressed by current agentic security frameworks.
AI.conclusion: CVA offers a promising direction for verifiable agent authorization, but resolving the tripartite separation of identity, authorization, and execution binding remains an open challenge. The paper presents a falsifiable research agenda to address this gap.

title: Preference Tuning as Spectral Update Reorganization
summary: Preference-based post-training is usually understood through endpoint behavior, yet the learned update that produces this behavior remains largely opaque. We study RLHF and related preference optimization through the spectral structure of their induced parameter updates. By decomposing effective LoRA updates and reloading their spectral components as plug-in modules, we turn preference-induced updates into objects that can be isolated, recomposed, and directly intervened on. Across model families, optimization algorithms, and supervision regimes, these updates consistently develop a spectral head--tail organization. A compact head emerges early and carries the dominant endpoint shift, while a heterogeneous residual tail remains. The split is functional rather than merely descriptive. Plug-in intervention shows that the head accounts for the visible behavioral departure from the base model, while the tail is weak in isolation. Cross-run recomposition further shows that mixed adapters follow the source of the head, indicating that the head carries run-level solver bias. This endpoint dominance does not imply learning sufficiency. Head-only learning is non-vacuous but fails to recover the full solution, especially on out-of-distribution behavior. Tail-only learning yields little visible gain, yet the full solution is not recovered without the tail. These findings recast preference post-training as structured update reorganization rather than a monolithic behavioral correction, and suggest that alignment gain and coverage loss are tied to how the learned update itself is organized.

AI.tldr: RLHF/preference optimization updates exhibit a spectral head–tail structure: a compact, early-emerging head drives dominant behavioral change, while a diffuse tail is necessary for full solution recovery, especially out-of-distribution. This recasts preference post-training as structured update reorganization rather than monolithic correction.
AI.motivation: Preference-based post-training (RLHF, DPO, etc.) is typically understood only through endpoint behavior, while the learned parameter update itself remains opaque. The authors aim to open the black box of these updates by analyzing their spectral structure.
AI.method: The authors decompose effective LoRA updates spectrally (via SVD) and reload individual spectral components as plug-in modules, enabling isolation, recomposition, and direct intervention. They study this across model families, optimization algorithms (RLHF, DPO, SimPO), and supervision regimes, examining emergence dynamics and conducting cross-run recomposition experiments.
AI.result: Updates consistently form a spectral head–tail organization: (1) a compact head emerges early and carries dominant endpoint shift; (2) a heterogeneous residual tail remains. Plug-in intervention shows the head accounts for visible behavioral departure from the base model, while the tail is weak in isolation. Cross-run recomposition shows mixed adapters follow the head's source, indicating the head carries run-level solver bias. Head-only learning is non-vacuous but fails to recover the full solution, especially OOD. Tail-only learning yields little visible gain, yet the full solution is not recovered without the tail.
AI.conclusion: Preference post-training is better understood as structured update reorganization rather than a monolithic behavioral correction. Alignment gain and coverage loss are tied to how the learned update itself is organized, with the head–tail structure linking directly to the alignment-coverage trade-off.

title: ReliableTableQA:How Much Supervision Does Reliability Annotation Need?
summary: We introduce ReliableTableQA, a framework for training an LLM to annotate the statistical reliability of tabular QA results, not whether the query is answerable, but whether the computed answer is statistically meaningful. In real enterprise analytics, a syntactically correct SQL query can return a value that is based on too small a sample, has an excessively wide confidence interval, or is too confounded to support action. Existing systems answer confidently in all such cases, a failure we quantify as the Unreliable Confident Answer Rate (UCAR). We contribute (1) a ten-category reliability taxonomy (R1-R10) covering hazards such as small-sample aggregates, multiple-comparison inflation, and distribution-tail mismatch; (2) a program-first data pipeline that generates 50,000 reliability-labeled training examples from a context-free grammar over public retail schemas, with schema-stratified SFT/GRPO splits; and (3) a controlled study of how much supervision calibrated reliability annotation actually requires. We find that a small, schema-stratified SFT set is remarkably sufficient: 200 examples raise reliability-flag F1 from 0.61 to 0.98 and parse rate from 0.52 to 1.00, drive UCAR to zero, and yield a model that generalizes to an unseen retail domain (Rel-F1 0.997 on held-out H&M). Against this strong SFT baseline, GRPO, commonly assumed to be essential, helps only when SFT is under-trained (+0.06-0.16 exact-flag-set match at 100 examples, in- and out-of-distribution) and provides no measurable benefit once SFT is adequate, a null result we confirm across a hard compound-flag slice, a strict exact-match metric, and out-of-distribution evaluation. Our findings reframe reliability annotation as a data-efficiency problem and delineate precisely when reinforcement fine-tuning does and does not pay off.

AI.tldr: ReliableTableQA is a framework for training LLMs to assess whether tabular QA results are statistically reliable (not just answerable). Using a 10-category reliability taxonomy and a program-generated dataset of 50K examples, the authors show that a small stratified SFT set (200 examples) is sufficient to achieve near-perfect reliability annotation (F1 0.98, zero UCAR), and that GRPO provides no additional benefit once SFT is adequate—challenging the assumption that RL fine-tuning is always necessary.
AI.motivation: Enterprise analytics systems confidently return SQL query results even when those results are statistically meaningless—based on tiny samples, wide confidence intervals, or confounding factors. This "Unreliable Confident Answer Rate" (UCAR) failure mode is unaddressed by existing systems, which only check answerability, not statistical meaningfulness. The authors aim to quantify and solve this gap by teaching LLMs to flag unreliable answers.
AI.method: The authors propose a three-part framework: (1) A 10-category reliability taxonomy (R1–R10) covering hazards like small-sample aggregates, multiple-comparison inflation, and distribution-tail mismatch. (2) A program-first data pipeline that uses a context-free grammar over public retail schemas to generate 50,000 reliability-labeled training examples with schema-stratified SFT/GRPO splits. (3) A controlled study varying SFT dataset size (100–500 examples) and comparing SFT-only vs. SFT+GRPO, evaluated on in-distribution and out-of-distribution (H&M) retail data across multiple metrics including exact-flag-set match and compound-flag slices.
AI.result: Key findings: (1) A mere 200 schema-stratified SFT examples raise reliability-flag F1 from 0.61 to 0.98, parse rate from 0.52 to 1.00, and drive UCAR to zero. (2) The SFT model generalizes strongly to unseen domains (Rel-F1 0.997 on held-out H&M). (3) GRPO helps only when SFT is under-trained (+0.06–0.16 exact-flag-set match at 100 examples) and provides no measurable benefit once SFT is adequate—a null result confirmed across hard slices, strict metrics, and OOD evaluation.
AI.conclusion: Reliability annotation is fundamentally a data-efficiency problem, not a reasoning problem requiring RL fine-tuning. A small, well-stratified SFT dataset suffices for near-perfect performance, and GRPO's benefits are limited to the under-trained regime. This reframes how practitioners should approach reliability annotation and delineates the precise conditions under which reinforcement fine-tuning adds value.

title: SonicSampler: Unified Tile-Aware Kernels for LLM Sampling and Speculative Verification
summary: Sampling in LLM inference comprises a combinatorial set of logit processing, token selection, and verification operations for speculative decoding. However, existing implementations either accelerate only subsets of this pipeline, rely on multiple kernel launches, or assume homogeneous sampling behavior across a batch, limiting support for dynamic serving workloads and preventing efficient CUDA Graph execution. We present $\textbf{SonicSampler}$, a unified suite of tile-aware Triton kernels that vertically fuses the complete sampling pipeline into a fixed, workload-aware execution model. Our kernels support dynamic per-request sampling behaviors, including grammar-constrained decoding, repetition, frequency and presence penalties, logit bias, temperature scaling, top-$k$ / top-$p$ / min-$p$ filtering, and speculative verification - within a single batched kernel while remaining fully CUDA Graph-compatible. Central to our approach is a novel hierarchical two-stage top-$k$ algorithm that achieves up to $\textbf{10x speedup}$ over competitive baselines and exploits the low-entropy structure of LLM outputs to enable efficient selection over large vocabularies. Across heterogeneous speculative decoding workloads, SonicSampler achieves up to $\textbf{16x speedup}$ over state-of-the-art baselines while preserving flexible batched execution.

AI.tldr: SonicSampler is a unified suite of Triton kernels that vertically fuses the entire LLM sampling pipeline into a single CUDA Graph-compatible kernel, achieving up to 16x speedup over state-of-the-art baselines for heterogeneous speculative decoding workloads.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM sampling implementations suffer from three key limitations: (1) they accelerate only subsets of the sampling pipeline (logit processing, token selection, speculative verification), (2) they rely on multiple kernel launches causing overhead, and (3) they assume homogeneous sampling behavior across a batch, which limits dynamic serving workloads and prevents efficient CUDA Graph execution.
AI.method: SonicSampler introduces tile-aware Triton kernels that vertically fuse the complete sampling pipeline into a fixed, workload-aware execution model. Key innovations include: (1) dynamic per-request sampling support (grammar-constrained decoding, penalties, logit bias, temperature scaling, top-k/top-p/min-p filtering, speculative verification) within a single batched kernel, (2) a novel hierarchical two-stage top-k algorithm that exploits the low-entropy structure of LLM outputs for efficient selection over large vocabularies, and (3) full CUDA Graph compatibility.
AI.result: The hierarchical two-stage top-k algorithm achieves up to 10x speedup over competitive baselines. Across heterogeneous speculative decoding workloads, SonicSampler achieves up to 16x speedup over state-of-the-art baselines while maintaining flexible batched execution.
AI.conclusion: SonicSampler demonstrates that vertically fusing the entire sampling pipeline into a single, workload-aware, CUDA Graph-compatible kernel yields substantial performance gains for LLM inference, particularly benefiting dynamic serving scenarios with heterogeneous speculative decoding.

title: AI Assistants Overassist
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as tutors and thought partners, helping users reason through problems. While guidance from AI assistants can scaffold thinking and foster learning, such benefits depend on how they help--for instance, intervening too early or too frequently may hinder true learning and cognitive engagement. Yet how AI systems navigate intervention decisions during problem-solving remains poorly understood. Here, we introduce Int-Bench, a simulation-based benchmark for evaluating LLM interventions during learning. Int-Bench simulates a "student" solving a problem while a "teacher" monitors the student's reasoning and decides whether, when, and how to intervene. Across three domains--code debugging, mathematics, and brain teasers--we evaluate LLM teachers on the frequency and timing of interventions, as well as their impact on both immediate task success and generalization to new problems. We also compare LLMs to humans, finding that LLMs intervene more frequently and earlier than humans. Moreover, in contrast to humans, they tend to provide complete solutions rather than targeted hints. These findings suggest that current LLM assistants often optimize for short-term success rather than supporting the reasoning processes needed for deeper learning and long-term success.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Int-Bench, a simulation-based benchmark for evaluating how LLMs decide when and how to intervene during problem-solving tasks. Results show LLMs intervene more frequently, earlier, and with complete solutions rather than hints, unlike human teachers, suggesting they prioritize short-term task success over deeper learning.
AI.motivation: LLMs are increasingly used as tutors and thought partners, but the effect of AI guidance on learning depends critically on intervention strategy—poorly timed or overly frequent interventions can hinder cognitive engagement. Despite this, little is known about how LLMs make intervention decisions during problem-solving.
AI.method: The authors introduce Int-Bench, a simulation-based benchmark where a "student" solves problems while a "teacher" (LLM or human) monitors reasoning and decides whether, when, and how to intervene. Evaluation spans three domains: code debugging, mathematics, and brain teasers. Metrics include intervention frequency, timing, immediate task success, and generalization to new problems. LLM teachers are compared against human teachers.
AI.result: LLM teachers intervene significantly more frequently and earlier than human teachers. Additionally, LLMs tend to provide complete solutions rather than targeted hints. These intervention patterns optimize for short-term task completion but may undermine the reasoning processes necessary for deeper learning and long-term generalization.
AI.conclusion: Current LLM assistants are biased toward immediate success rather than fostering the cognitive engagement required for robust learning. The Int-Bench framework provides a systematic means to evaluate and improve how AI tutors navigate intervention decisions.

title: Delivery, Not Storage: Cue-Anchored Working Memory as a Harness Property for Coding Agents
summary: Coding agents ship with one kind of memory: documents. Instruction files, plan artifacts, and auto-written memory directories are deliberately authored and deliberately retrieved: the agent must choose to write them and choose to read them back. Human expertise runs on a second tier that never gets written down: situationally-bound operational facts (gotchas, locations, local conventions) encoded as a side effect of the work and retrieved involuntarily when the situation cues them. We argue this second tier is the load-bearing one for long-running agents and must be a harness property, not an agent choice. We contribute: (1) a two-tier design theory grounded in the cognitive literature on memory offloading, incidental encoding, and event-based prospective memory, each mapped to an architectural requirement; (2) a cue-anchored memory model where memories carry first-class trigger conditions over a composable vocabulary (path, symbol, semantic, event, temporal), evaluated deterministically by the harness, a composition no surveyed academic or shipped system provides; (3) a controlled evaluation on a real coding task showing that voluntary memory use is near zero even with a pre-seeded store (0 memory operations in 114 turns), that deterministic injection delivered in every seeded run with zero false alarms, and that 39% of intra-session re-reads re-buy content paid for before a compaction boundary; (4) a repeated-compaction decay probe: ten facts held only in conversation vanish at the first summary and stay absent from 106 of 108 compactions, and the deprived agent greps the harness's own session files to rebuild them, while the same facts injected from a harness-owned store arrive intact through all 138 compact-resumes as the final summary carries none. Delivery, not storage, is the product: the reliable memory channel for agents is the one the agent never has to think about.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that coding agents need a two-tier memory architecture: a deliberate document-store tier and a crucial involuntary "cue-anchored" memory tier managed by the harness, not the agent. Experiments show agents rarely use voluntary memory, and only harness-managed cue-triggered delivery reliably preserves operational facts across session compactions.
AI.motivation: Current coding agents rely solely on deliberately authored and retrieved documents (instruction files, plans, memory directories), but human expertise depends on involuntary, situationally-cued recall of operational facts (gotchas, local conventions). This second tier is missing in agent architectures and is critical for long-running agents that undergo repeated context compaction.
AI.method: The authors ground their design in cognitive literature (memory offloading, incidental encoding, event-based prospective memory) and propose a cue-anchored memory model where memories carry composable trigger conditions (path, symbol, semantic, event, temporal) evaluated deterministically by the harness. They evaluate using a controlled real coding task: (1) measuring voluntary vs. harness-delivered memory retrieval rates, (2) a repeated-compaction decay probe tracking fact survival across summarization boundaries, and (3) testing whether deprived agents attempt workarounds like grepping harness session files.
AI.result: Voluntary memory use was near zero (0 operations in 114 turns) despite a pre-seeded store. Deterministic harness injection delivered in every seeded run with zero false alarms. 39% of intra-session re-reads re-bought content paid for before a compaction boundary. In the decay probe, ten conversation-held facts vanished at the first summary and stayed absent in 106 of 108 compactions; deprived agents grepped harness session files attempting recovery. Harness-injected facts survived intact through all 138 compact-resumes, with zero facts carried in the final summary.
AI.conclusion: Delivery, not storage, is the product. The reliable memory channel for agents is the one the agent never has to think about — memory must be a harness property with deterministic, cue-triggered injection rather than a voluntary agent choice.

title: Themis Consensus Extension v1: MEV Mitigation by Randomized Delayed Execution and Intent-Hiding Transactions in Application-Specific Blockchains
summary: Maximal extractable value (MEV) arises when privileged participants select, exclude, insert, or reorder pending transactions for private gain. We specify and analyze the Themis Consensus Extension v1, first published by Mangata in 2021. The design separates value extraction by reordering (VER) from value extraction by denial (VED). For VER, block construction and execution occur across consecutive producers: one producer commits a transaction set, and the next derives a publicly verifiable, deterministic, previously un- predictable seed and executes a seed-determined, dependency-preserving permutation. For selective VED, a user may encrypt a transaction for a designated builder and executor. The builder removes an outer layer and commits the opaque inner ciphertext; the executor reveals and executes the plaintext only after commitment. Under selfish but non-colluding validators, an adversary below the underlying consensus fault threshold, secure cryptography, and accountable role performance, the construction limits unilateral post-commit ordering control and hides transaction intent from relays and the builder. It does not provide send-order or receive-order fairness, complete censorship resistance, resistance to builder-executor collusion, or per-transaction price guarantees. We analyze probabilistic extraction, spam, dependent transactions, decryption liveness, session boundaries, total denial, and threshold coalitions. We also document the initial Aura-based Substrate implementation and its subsequent transition to a BABE-based sr25519/VRF seed path, together with delayed execution, Fisher-Yates shuffling, and Xoshiro256++. The result preserves the original proposal while narrowing its claims to explicit assumptions.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes the Themis Consensus Extension v1, a protocol that separates MEV into value extraction by reordering (VER) and value extraction by denial (VED). For VER, a two-phase commit-then-shuffle mechanism prevents unilateral ordering control; for VED, a commit-then-reveal encryption scheme hides transaction intent. The analysis bounds the protocol's guarantees under explicit adversarial assumptions.
AI.motivation: MEV enables privileged validators to profit by manipulating transaction ordering. Prior solutions often entangle ordering fairness with censorship resistance, making guarantees fragile. Themis aims to cleanly separate these concerns: VER addresses reordering attacks through deterministic, seed-based shuffling across consecutive block producers, while VED addresses selective denial via layered encryption that hides transaction content until after commitment.
AI.method: The paper formally specifies the Themis protocol and analyzes its security properties. For VER: block producer N commits a transaction set; producer N+1 derives an unpredictable seed (via Aura, later BABE/VRF) and applies a dependency-preserving Fisher-Yates shuffle using Xoshiro256++. For VED: users submit double-encrypted transactions; the builder strips the outer layer and commits the opaque inner ciphertext; the executor decrypts and executes only post-commit. The analysis examines probabilistic extraction, spam resistance, dependent transactions, decryption liveness, session boundaries, total denial, and threshold coalitions under selfish-but-non-colluding validators.
AI.result: Under stated assumptions (sub-threshold adversary, secure cryptography, accountable role performance, no builder-executor collusion), the protocol limits unilateral post-commit ordering control and hides transaction intent from relays and builders. However, it explicitly does not guarantee send-order or receive-order fairness, complete censorship resistance, resistance to builder-executor collusion, or per-transaction price guarantees. The original Aura-based Substrate implementation was later migrated to a BABE-based sr25519/VRF seed path with delayed execution.
AI.conclusion: Themis provides a clean decomposition of MEV into separable ordering and denial components, each addressed by distinct cryptographic-consensus mechanisms. The analysis narrows the protocol's claims to precisely stated adversarial assumptions, documenting both what is achieved (limited unilateral reordering, hidden intent) and what remains outside scope (full fairness, collusion resistance, censorship resistance). The implementation evolution from Aura to BABE reflects practical lessons in seed unpredictability.

title: AsymVerify at SemEval-2026 Task 6: Asymmetric Confidence-Gated Verification for Political Evasion Detection
comment: Accepted to SemEval-2026 Task 6 (CLARITY) at ACL 2026. Team AsymVerify placed 2nd of 41 teams on the official Subtask 1 leaderboard. Task: https://konstantinosftw.github.io/CLARITY-SemEval-2026/. Code: https://github.com/kaons-research/AsymVerify-ACL. Website: https://kaons.com/
summary: Political evasion is difficult to detect because evasive answers often appear cooperative while avoiding concrete commitment. We present AsymVerify, a confidence-gated verification system for SemEval-2026 Task 6, a three-way classification of Clear Reply, Ambivalent, and Clear Non-Reply responses. AsymVerify scored 0.85 Macro F1 on the evaluation split (D_eval, n=237), placing 2nd out of 41 teams on the official leaderboard. The system first classifies each question-answer pair, then selectively applies downgrade verification (CR/CNR -> AMB) or upgrade verification (AMB -> CR) to low-confidence predictions. Development analysis shows that errors concentrate at the Ambivalent boundary in both directions, motivating this asymmetric two-verifier design while confidence gating keeps additional inference cost low. On D_dev (n=308), AsymVerify with GLM-4.7 gains +17.1 Macro F1 over single-pass classification at 1.48 calls/example, and the upgrade verifier alone improves every tested LLM backend on D_dev by +6.8 to +15.2 Macro F1 over its single-pass baseline. Code is available at https://github.com/kaons-research/AsymVerify-ACL.

AI.tldr: AsymVerify is a two-stage system for detecting political evasion. It first classifies responses as Clear Reply, Ambivalent, or Clear Non-Reply, then selectively applies asymmetric verifiers (downgrade or upgrade) only to low-confidence predictions, achieving 0.85 Macro F1 and 2nd place out of 41 teams on SemEval-2026 Task 6.
AI.motivation: Political evasion is inherently difficult to detect because evasive answers mimic cooperative discourse while avoiding substantive commitment. Errors in classification concentrate at the Ambivalent boundary in both directions (CR/CNR ↔ AMB), motivating an asymmetric two-verifier design rather than a single correction mechanism.
AI.method: AsymVerify employs a confidence-gated, two-stage pipeline: (1) a single-pass classifier assigns each question-answer pair to one of three categories (Clear Reply, Ambivalent, Clear Non-Reply); (2) low-confidence predictions trigger one of two specialized verifiers — a downgrade verifier (CR/CNR → AMB) or an upgrade verifier (AMB → CR). This asymmetric design targets the most common error patterns while confidence gating minimizes additional inference cost, averaging 1.48 calls per example with the GLM-4.7 backend.
AI.result: On the evaluation split (D_eval, n=237), AsymVerify achieved 0.85 Macro F1, securing 2nd place out of 41 teams. On the development split (D_dev, n=308), the full system with GLM-4.7 gained +17.1 Macro F1 over single-pass classification. The upgrade verifier alone improved every tested LLM backend by +6.8 to +15.2 Macro F1 over single-pass baselines.
AI.conclusion: Asymmetric verification with confidence gating effectively addresses boundary ambiguity in political evasion detection, delivering substantial gains over single-pass classification while maintaining low inference overhead. The upgrade verifier generalizes across LLM backends, suggesting broad applicability.

title: Codec-Gauge: Learning Compression-Friendly Gauges for Transformer KV Caches
summary: Long-context Transformer inference increasingly relies on KV-cache compression or quantization. Prior rotation and transform-coding results suggest that the channel basis of each key/value vector affects how faithfully a fixed backend preserves model behavior. We introduce Codec-Gauge, a post-training cache-coordinate layer that learns small orthogonal channel transforms around existing compression and quantization backends. Its frequency-distribution objective combines a token-channel DCT spectral-centroid loss with a smooth rate proxy to concentrate KV energy in low-frequency codec-facing layouts. We evaluate actual compression and decompression using measured bytes and rolling compressed-history scoring. Across six models at $3$, $4$, and $6$ bits/value, learned gauges reduce zfp KL divergence by $44.0\%$ on average relative to raw coordinates and outperform random, Hadamard, DCT, and PCA/KLT controls. The same gauges improve quality preservation for block-uniform and KIVI-style quantization. Experiments on a 27B model and long-context task prompts reproduce the quality trend, while serial storage and timing measurements validate the implemented compressed-cache paths. These results establish cache-coordinate geometry as a practical post-training variable for improving compression fidelity without changing model weights, attention semantics, or backend coding rules.

AI.tldr: Codec-Gauge learns small orthogonal channel transforms applied to KV-cache vectors before compression/quantization, concentrating energy in low-frequency layouts to improve compression fidelity without altering model weights or backend codecs.
AI.motivation: KV-cache compression is critical for long-context Transformer inference, but existing methods ignore how the channel basis of key/value vectors affects compression fidelity. Prior work on rotation and transform-coding hints that channel geometry matters, motivating a learned coordinate transform that optimizes the layout for any given compression backend.
AI.method: Codec-Gauge is a post-training, lightweight orthogonal transform layer inserted at cache coordinates. It is trained with a frequency-distribution objective combining: (1) a token-channel DCT spectral-centroid loss that concentrates energy toward low frequencies, and (2) a smooth rate proxy. The gauge is learned per model/backend without modifying weights, attention, or codec rules. Evaluated using measured bytes and rolling compressed-history scoring under actual compress/decompress cycles.
AI.result: Across six models at 3/4/6 bits/value, learned gauges reduce zfp KL divergence by 44.0% on average vs. raw coordinates, outperforming random, Hadamard, DCT, and PCA/KLT baselines. Improvements generalize to block-uniform and KIVI-style quantization. A 27B model with long-context prompts reproduces the quality trend; serial storage and timing measurements confirm practical viability.
AI.conclusion: Cache-coordinate geometry is a trainable post-training variable that meaningfully improves KV-cache compression fidelity. Codec-Gauge offers a practical, model-agnostic, backend-agnostic method that leaves model weights and attention semantics intact.

title: Benchmarking Large Language Models on Multi-Sensor Physical Hazard Assessment
comment: 14 pages, 6 figures. Benchmark dataset, evaluation code, and raw results publicly available at: https://github.com/Faizaniqbal52/PhysicalHazardBenchmark
summary: We present an empirical benchmark evaluating how five large language models assess multisensor physical hazard data. Testing 60 scenarios across three categories - multi-sensor joint assessment, response proportionality, and pattern disambiguation - with 1,800 API calls at temperature 0.0, we find that all tested models consistently produced no precautionary warning signal across the tested scenarios where multiple sensors are simultaneously elevated below their individual safety limits, while achieving near-perfect accuracy on single-sensor threshold violations. All five models (ChatGPT-4o, Gemini 2.5 Flash, DeepSeek, Kimi, Llama 3.1 8B) score near zero on Category A multi-sensor scenarios (Q2: 0.000-0.208; Q3: 0.000-0.592) compared to strong performance on single-sensor scenarios (Category B Q1: 0.975-1.000). Structured tabular formatting shows no consistent advantage over plain prose; ChatGPT-4o performs significantly better under prose (p = 0.001). These findings have direct implications for practitioners deploying the tested models in physical safety monitoring systems.

AI.tldr: An empirical benchmark of five LLMs on multisensor physical hazard assessment reveals a critical blind spot: all models fail to issue warnings when multiple sensors simultaneously read below individual thresholds, despite excelling at single-sensor threshold detection. Structured formatting offers no consistent benefit.
AI.motivation: LLMs are increasingly deployed in safety-critical monitoring contexts, yet their ability to integrate multisensor data for hazard assessment—particularly when individual sensors remain below alarm thresholds—is unexamined. This study addresses the gap between LLMs' known single-signal reasoning capabilities and the real-world need for holistic, cross-sensor situational awareness.
AI.method: The authors designed 60 test scenarios across three categories: (A) multi-sensor joint assessment where multiple sensors are simultaneously elevated but below individual limits, (B) response proportionality for single-sensor threshold violations, and (C) pattern disambiguation. Five models (ChatGPT-4o, Gemini 2.5 Flash, DeepSeek, Kimi, Llama 3.1 8B) were evaluated using 1,800 total API calls at temperature 0.0. Performance was compared across structured tabular versus plain prose input formats, with statistical significance testing.
AI.result: All five models scored near zero on Category A multi-sensor scenarios (Q2: 0.000–0.208; Q3: 0.000–0.592), meaning they consistently failed to generate precautionary warnings when multiple sub-threshold sensor elevations co-occurred. In contrast, single-sensor threshold violation detection was near-perfect (Category B Q1: 0.975–1.000). Structured tabular formatting provided no consistent advantage; ChatGPT-4o performed significantly better with prose (p = 0.001).
AI.conclusion: Current LLMs exhibit a systematic failure mode in multisensor fusion for safety assessment: they treat each sensor independently and miss emergent risk patterns from co-occurring sub-threshold signals. This has direct, cautionary implications for practitioners considering LLM deployment in physical safety monitoring systems.

title: MedGame: Storytelling Gamification Empowered by Large Language Models for Medical Education
comment: Work in Progress; an explorational design and study on AI+Education+Game
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) show promise for medical education, but most existing systems focus on localized interactions such as question answering or single-turn feedback, rather than organizing an entire clinical case into a decision-centered learning trajectory. We introduce \textit{MedGame}, a framework that transforms static clinical cases into structured, executable storytelling games. MedGame uses a dual-engine design: a Medical Narrative Designer synthesizes case-grounded clinical storylines with states and decision nodes, while a Story Director converts them into dependency-aware multimodal orchestration plans rendered by our released interactive platform. We construct MedGame Bench, a 5,000-case benchmark and evaluation protocol for Medical Narrative Generation and Story Direction. Experiments show that task-specific fine-tuning substantially improves open-source LLMs on MedGame Bench and narrows the gap with commercial models. A pilot student study further shows that learners perceive MedGame as more engaging and useful than text-only alternatives.

AI.tldr: MedGame is a dual-engine framework that transforms static clinical cases into interactive storytelling games for medical education, using a Medical Narrative Designer and Story Director. Evaluated on a 5,000-case benchmark, fine-tuned open-source LLMs approach commercial model performance, and a pilot study shows learners find it more engaging than text-only alternatives.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-based medical education systems are limited to localized interactions (QA, single-turn feedback) and fail to organize entire clinical cases into coherent, decision-centered learning trajectories. There is a need for a framework that structures full clinical reasoning pathways as interactive narratives.
AI.method: MedGame employs a dual-engine architecture: (1) a Medical Narrative Designer that synthesizes case-grounded clinical storylines with states and decision nodes, and (2) a Story Director that converts storylines into dependency-aware multimodal orchestration plans deployed on an interactive platform. MedGame Bench, a 5,000-case benchmark, was constructed with evaluation protocols for both Medical Narrative Generation and Story Direction. Task-specific fine-tuning was applied to open-source LLMs.
AI.result: Task-specific fine-tuning substantially improves open-source LLM performance on MedGame Bench, narrowing the gap with commercial models. A pilot student study indicates that learners perceive MedGame as significantly more engaging and useful compared to text-only alternatives.
AI.conclusion: MedGame demonstrates that structuring clinical cases as decision-centered storytelling games with a dual-engine design is a viable and effective approach for medical education, with both automated benchmarks and human evaluations supporting its advantages over traditional text-based methods.

title: Where You Tap Matters: A Probe-and-Model Benchmark for Open-Set RF Fingerprinting
summary: Radio Frequency Fingerprint Identification (RFFI) enables transmitter identification at the physical layer by learning device-specific impairments from received signals, yet the literature is inconsistent about where in the receiver chain those samples should be collected. Since distinct transformations are applied to the signal by the different receiver operations, i.e., carrier recovery, gain normalization, pulse shaping, and timing recovery, they can either tighten within-transmitter variability or suppress the features RFFI requires for classification. We present a systematic real-world evaluation of open-set, reconstruction-error RFFI using data collected at five probe points along a standard BPSK receiver chain. Our results show that RFFI is strongly probe-dependent: timing recovery and, to a lesser extent, carrier recovery enable low false-acceptance operation with limited in-distribution-out-of-distribution overlap, whereas other stages often require a false-acceptance ratio above 0.1 to achieve a true-acceptance ratio of 0.9. To test the validity of our findings across model selection, we benchmark several LLM-designed autoencoders using a controlled pipeline that holds preprocessing and MSE scoring fixed. These architectures confirm that RFFI is probe-dependent. Moreover, they do not outperform the baseline at the chosen operating point and typically increase training time. Overall, probe selection dominates reconstruction-based open-set RFFI performance, more than the autoencoder complexity.

AI.tldr: Radio Frequency Fingerprint Identification (RFFI) performance is highly dependent on where in the receiver chain signals are sampled. A systematic evaluation across five probe points in a BPSK receiver shows timing recovery and carrier recovery stages best preserve device-specific impairments, while autoencoder complexity matters less than probe selection for reconstruction-based open-set RFFI.
AI.motivation: The RFFI literature lacks consensus on where in the receiver processing chain signal samples should be collected, despite different receiver operations (carrier recovery, gain normalization, pulse shaping, timing recovery) applying distinct transformations that may either enhance or suppress the device-specific impairments RFFI relies on for classification.
AI.method: The authors conduct a systematic real-world evaluation of open-set, reconstruction-error RFFI using data collected at five probe points along a standard BPSK receiver chain. They benchmark several LLM-designed autoencoders using a controlled pipeline with fixed preprocessing and MSE scoring to test whether findings generalize across model architectures.
AI.result: RFFI is strongly probe-dependent: timing recovery and carrier recovery stages enable low false-acceptance operation with minimal in-distribution/out-of-distribution overlap, while other stages require a false-acceptance ratio above 0.1 to achieve a true-acceptance ratio of 0.9. LLM-designed autoencoder architectures confirm probe-dependence but do not outperform the baseline and typically increase training time.
AI.conclusion: Probe selection dominates reconstruction-based open-set RFFI performance, outweighing the effect of autoencoder complexity. The choice of where to sample in the receiver chain is a first-order design consideration for practical RFFI systems.

title: Answer-then-Edit: Reasoning Skeleton Editing for Anti-Distillation with Preserved Utility
summary: Proprietary large language models (LLMs) entail substantial intellectual and financial investment, making them valuable intellectual property (IP). However, even when deployed via black-box APIs, these models remain vulnerable to unauthorized knowledge distillation, which allows adversaries to cheaply extract and replicate model capabilities. To address this issue, anti-distillation (AD) has been proposed to generate defensive outputs that hinder distillation effectiveness, overcoming the limitation of watermarking-based approaches that rely on post-hoc verification. However, existing AD methods based on internal model perturbations struggle to balance anti-distillability and utility (e.g., answer accuracy and naturalness) of reasoning traces, with stronger defenses often causing significant utility loss. To fill this gap, we propose \textbf{\underline{S}}keleton-\textbf{\underline{G}}uided \textbf{\underline{R}}easoning \textbf{\underline{E}}diting (SGRE), an \textit{Answer-then-Edit} framework that performs post-hoc trace modification for anti-distillation. In the answer stage, the teacher model first generates clean reasoning traces, preserving the original reasoning accuracy while enabling more flexible control over trace naturalness. In the editing stage, we draw inspiration from Cognitive Load Theory (CLT) and introduce a three-stage strategy consisting of reasoning skeleton extraction, skeleton graph coarsening, and skeleton verbalization. These operations jointly perturb reasoning structures and augment textual complexity to amplify extraneous load on student models, hindering their acquisition of underlying reasoning patterns. Extensive experiments across diverse LLMs demonstrate that SGRE achieves state-of-the-art performance in reducing distillation effectiveness, while maintaining lossless reasoning accuracy and superior trace naturalness.

AI.tldr: SGRE proposes an Answer-then-Edit framework that first generates clean reasoning traces, then applies skeleton-guided perturbations inspired by Cognitive Load Theory to hinder unauthorized distillation while preserving accuracy and naturalness.
AI.motivation: Existing anti-distillation (AD) methods based on internal model perturbations face an inherent trade-off between defense strength and utility (answer accuracy and trace naturalness), with stronger defenses causing significant degradation. This motivates a post-hoc editing approach that decouples answer quality from defensive perturbation.
AI.method: SGRE is a two-stage framework: (1) Answer stage — the teacher LLM generates clean, accurate reasoning traces normally; (2) Editing stage — inspired by Cognitive Load Theory, SGRE extracts reasoning skeletons, applies skeleton graph coarsening to perturb logical structures, then re-verbalizes them to increase textual complexity, amplifying extraneous cognitive load on student models to disrupt their learning of underlying reasoning patterns.
AI.result: Extensive experiments across diverse LLMs show SGRE achieves state-of-the-art performance in reducing distillation effectiveness while maintaining lossless reasoning accuracy and superior trace naturalness compared to existing AD methods.
AI.conclusion: SGRE demonstrates that post-hoc trace modification via skeleton-guided editing is an effective anti-distillation strategy, successfully balancing the dual objectives of strong IP protection and preserved utility, outperforming perturbation-based alternatives.

title: Leveraging Biokinetic Knowledge Priors for Data-Scarce Bioprocess Modeling
comment: Accepted at ICML 2026 AI for Science Workshop
summary: While deep learning has accelerated drug discovery, its impact on biomanufacturing has been considerably more limited. The reason is data scarcity. Bioreactor experiments are high-cost, take days to weeks, and are rarely shared in public form, leaving each research work with only a handful of experiments. The domain itself, however, is rich in prior knowledge. Biokinetic ordinary differential equation (ODE) models have described microbial growth for decades, yet how to inject this knowledge into a neural network has not been studied systematically. We present the first systematic study of how to inject this ODE knowledge into a neural network, comparing a data-level prior that pre-trains a generic decoder on simulated ODE curves against an architecture-level prior that embeds the ODE inside the decoder. Both consistently outperform no-prior baselines across 11 datasets and 7 microbial species. Our central finding is that the two are substitutable. A generic decoder pre-trained on simulation matches a fully bio-structured decoder trained on real data. Simulation pre-training therefore offers a simple, data-efficient recipe for deep learning under bioprocess data scarcity.

AI.tldr: This paper systematically investigates injecting biokinetic ODE prior knowledge into neural networks to address data scarcity in biomanufacturing. It compares data-level priors (pre-training on simulated ODE curves) and architecture-level priors (embedding ODEs into the decoder), finding them substitutable — simulation pre-training matches bio-structured decoders, offering a simple, data-efficient solution.
AI.motivation: Deep learning has had limited impact on biomanufacturing due to severe data scarcity: bioreactor experiments are expensive, slow (days to weeks), and rarely shared publicly, leaving researchers with only a handful of experiments per study. However, the domain possesses rich prior knowledge in the form of biokinetic ODE models that have described microbial growth for decades. No prior work has systematically studied how to inject this ODE knowledge into neural networks for bioprocess applications.
AI.method: The authors conduct a systematic comparison of two strategies for incorporating biokinetic ODE priors into neural networks: (1) a data-level prior — pre-training a generic decoder on simulated ODE curves, and (2) an architecture-level prior — embedding the ODE structure directly inside the decoder. Both are benchmarked against no-prior baselines across 11 datasets spanning 7 microbial species.
AI.result: Both prior-injection strategies consistently outperform baselines without priors. The central finding is substitutability: a generic decoder pre-trained on simulation data matches the performance of a fully bio-structured decoder trained on real data.
AI.conclusion: Simulation pre-training provides a simple, data-efficient recipe for applying deep learning in bioprocess settings constrained by data scarcity, eliminating the need for complex architecture-level ODE embedding while achieving comparable performance.

title: Semi-Supervised Text-Attributed Graph Distillation
comment: Technical report for the paper "Semi-Supervised Text-Attributed Graph Distillation" accepted KDD2026
summary:
{\em Text-Attributed Graphs} (TAGs) have emerged as an expressive data model for integrating graph topology with rich textual semantics. Existing representation learning methods over TAGs suffer from severe scalability bottlenecks, particularly together with {\em Large Language Models} (LLMs). While data distillation offers a promising data-centric solution, existing methods fail to capture the complex interplay between graph and text modalities, struggle with the label scarcity inherent in semi-supervised settings, and lack the ability to produce the human-readable textual attributes required for downstream LLM-based tasks.
  To address these challenges, we propose \algo{}, a unified semi-supervised framework guided by the {\em Wasserstein Distance} (WSD). Grounded in our empirical findings on real TAGs, \algo{} introduces a graph-text collaborative encoding module that utilizes dual-pathway encoders (graph-aware and -free) within a collaborative self-training scheme to harvest reliable pseudo-labels and fuse complementary graph-text features. Furthermore, we develop a theoretically grounded WSD-based graph sketching algorithm and a cost-effective LLM text synthesis module, which leverages cluster-based keyword extraction to generate coherent, human-readable summaries for condensed nodes. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that \algo{} achieves a state-of-the-art performance-compression trade-off in terms of both GNN- and LLM-based downstream tasks, enabling effective and efficient TAG learning or analytics.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a Wasserstein Distance-guided semi-supervised framework for condensing Text-Attributed Graphs (TAGs) that jointly addresses scalability, graph-text interplay, label scarcity, and human-readable summary generation, achieving SOTA performance-compression trade-offs on both GNN and LLM downstream tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing TAG representation learning methods suffer scalability bottlenecks, especially with LLMs. Current data distillation approaches fail to: (1) capture the complex interplay between graph and text modalities, (2) handle label scarcity in semi-supervised settings, and (3) produce human-readable textual attributes needed for LLM-based downstream tasks.
AI.method: The proposed framework has three core components: (1) a graph-text collaborative encoding module with dual-pathway encoders (graph-aware and graph-free) using collaborative self-training to harvest pseudo-labels and fuse complementary features; (2) a WSD-based graph sketching algorithm with theoretical grounding; and (3) a cost-effective LLM text synthesis module using cluster-based keyword extraction to generate coherent, human-readable summaries for condensed nodes.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate state-of-the-art performance-compression trade-offs for both GNN-based and LLM-based downstream tasks.
AI.conclusion: The unified WSD-guided semi-supervised framework enables effective and efficient TAG learning and analytics by overcoming the limitations of prior data distillation methods through collaborative graph-text encoding, theoretically grounded graph sketching, and LLM-based text synthesis.

title: Euclid-MCP: A Model Context Protocol Server for Deterministic Logical Reasoning via Prolog
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) excel at natural language understanding and generation but remain unreliable for multi-step logical reasoning, especially in safety-critical or compliance-sensitive domains. Recent neuro-symbolic approaches address this gap by coupling neural models with external symbolic engines, yet most integrations are bespoke and lack a standardized interface for tool-augmented agents. This paper presents Euclid-MCP, an open-source MCP server that provides deterministic logical reasoning via SWI-Prolog. Euclid-MCP introduces Euclid-IR, an engine-agnostic intermediate representation for Horn-clause logic that is human-readable, easy for LLMs to generate, and straightforward to compile into Prolog or alternative backends. The server exposes a compact tool interface that supports a translate-run-inspect-repair loop, enabling LLM clients to delegate inference while retaining full access to proof traces and derivation logs. We evaluate Euclid-MCP on a realistic IT security and compliance use case. Results show that while LLMs alone are sufficient on small knowledge bases, they hallucinate systematically on larger problems, whereas Euclid-MCP delivers exact answers with lower latency and more compact outputs. We argue that semantic RAG is fundamentally unsuited for rule enforcement, and that Euclid-MCP can serve as a stable, shared reasoning substrate for both RAG-based assistants and agentic systems.
