Analyses reveal that current LLMs struggle to satisfy and anticipate what users hope to obtain, highlighting a fundamental source of misalignment. Building on these observations, we propose LENS, a lightweight latent expectation-aware response generation framework. LENS enables models to internalize user expectations and generate better-aligned responses, consistently improving expectation satisfaction and underscoring the importance of explicitly modeling user expectations for realistic human-AI alignment.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces ExpectBench, the first benchmark grounded in real user expectations for LLM interactions, revealing that current LLMs struggle to satisfy what users actually seek. The authors also propose LENS, a lightweight framework that helps models internalize user expectations for better-aligned responses.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM evaluation methods (model heuristics, expert rubrics, user simulation) fail to capture the diversity and subtlety of real human expectations, creating a fundamental misalignment where models appear competent on benchmarks but don't deliver what users actually want.
AI.method: The authors (1) conduct a systematic study of user expectations in real-world LLM interactions, (2) develop a principled procedure to extract semantically rich expectations and construct ExpectBench, and (3) propose LENS, a lightweight latent expectation-aware response generation framework that enables models to internalize and generate responses aligned with user expectations.
AI.result: Analyses reveal that current LLMs struggle to both satisfy and anticipate user expectations, highlighting a fundamental misalignment source. LENS consistently improves expectation satisfaction across evaluations.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly modeling user expectations is crucial for realistic human-AI alignment. The LENS framework demonstrates that making models expectation-aware significantly improves response quality from the user's perspective.

title: Domyn-Small: A European 10B Reasoning Language Model
summary: We introduce Domyn-Small, a 10-billion-parameter open-weight reasoning language model released under the MIT license. Domyn-Small is the product of an initial pre-training phase on 9 trillion tokens multilingual data, followed by a post-training pipeline for reasoning, instruction following, and context extension. For the latter, we performed a Continued Pre-Training (CPT) phase that doubles the native context window to 32K tokens, followed by SFT with a math-focused annealing run. Finally, the RL phase includes GRPO with verifiable rewards, DPO, and a multi-environment GRPO stage spanning five task domains: mathematics, code, multiple-choice QA, instruction-following, and tool calling. The 32K-token native context extends to 128K at inference via YaRN, and a chat-template toggle enables dual-mode reasoning. Against peer models in the 7--10B class (Qwen3.5-9B, OLMo-3-7B-Think, Nemotron-Nano-8B, Ministral-3-8B), Domyn-Small achieves a strong accuracy-efficiency balance: it produces roughly one-third as many tokens as Qwen3.5-9B and approximately 35% of OLMo-3-7B-Think's token budget on core reasoning benchmarks, while delivering strong instruction-following (IFEval 79.9) and competitive science reasoning (GPQA-Diamond 50.0). We release the weights and the post-training recipe alongside Domyn Swarm (Apache~2.0), an open-source framework for scalable LLM inference on HPC clusters developed during this program and used throughout this work.

AI.tldr: Domyn-Small is a 10B-parameter open-weight reasoning LM (MIT license) with a 32K native context window (extendable to 128K via YaRN), trained on 9T multilingual tokens. It uses a multi-stage post-training pipeline (CPT, math-focused SFT, GRPO with verifiable rewards, DPO, multi-environment GRPO) and achieves competitive reasoning benchmarks with significantly lower token output compared to peers, while releasing weights, recipes, and the Domyn Swarm inference framework.
AI.motivation: To develop a compact, open-weight reasoning language model in the 7–10B parameter class that achieves strong reasoning and instruction-following performance while maintaining high token efficiency — producing substantially fewer tokens than comparable models on reasoning benchmarks — and to release the full post-training recipe and supporting infrastructure openly.
AI.method: Pre-training on 9T multilingual tokens, followed by Continued Pre-Training (CPT) doubling the context window to 32K tokens, SFT with a math-focused annealing run, and a multi-component RL phase: GRPO with verifiable rewards, DPO, and a multi-environment GRPO stage covering math, code, multiple-choice QA, instruction-following, and tool calling. Inference context extends to 128K via YaRN, with a chat-template toggle for dual-mode reasoning.
AI.result: Domyn-Small achieves IFEval 79.9 and GPQA-Diamond 50.0, using ~1/3 the tokens of Qwen3.5-9B and ~35% of OLMo-3-7B-Think's token budget on core reasoning benchmarks, demonstrating a strong accuracy-efficiency trade-off against peer 7–10B models.
AI.conclusion: Domyn-Small demonstrates that a carefully designed multi-stage post-training pipeline — combining CPT, math-focused SFT, and diverse RL strategies — can yield a compact reasoning model that is both performant and token-efficient. The authors release model weights, the post-training recipe, and the Domyn Swarm framework (Apache 2.0) for scalable HPC inference.

title: Beyond SBDD: Geometric Deep Learning in Polypharmacology and Multi-target Drug Design
summary: The traditional "one drug, one target" paradigm of structure-based drug design (SBDD) frequently proves inadequate for treating multifactorial diseases such as cancer and neurodegenerative disorders, owing to compensatory signaling pathways and the emergence of drug resistance. While polypharmacology offers a synergistic therapeutic strategy, the rational design of ligands capable of simultaneously satisfying the geometric constraints imposed by multiple targets remains a major computational bottleneck. This review positions geometric deep learning (GDL) as a powerful integrative approach to overcome these limitations. We systematically survey GDL architectures ranging from invariant graph neural networks to SE(3)-equivariant diffusion models that harness non-Euclidean molecular data to capture intrinsic three-dimensional (3D) structural interdependencies. We critically analyze GDL applications across three core dimensions, including the characterization of shared binding pockets via geometric embeddings, multi-target bioactivity prediction through heterogeneous graph fusion, and de novo generation of dual-target ligands. Particular emphasis is placed on emerging structure-conditioned generative algorithms that integrate diffusion models with reinforcement learning to autonomously resolve complex geometric conflicts between competing binding sites. Furthermore, we evaluate the pivotal role of multimodal omics integration and specialized geometric benchmarking infrastructures in validating these models. By synthesizing these methodological advances, this review elucidates the paradigm shift in drug discovery from serendipitous exploration to rational, structure-driven polypharmacological molecular engineering, thereby providing a clear, structured guide for navigating the complexities of next-generation therapeutics.

AI.tldr: This review presents geometric deep learning (GDL) as a transformative framework for rational polypharmacological drug design, surveying architectures from graph neural networks to SE(3)-equivariant diffusion models that capture 3D molecular structure to address the computational challenges of designing ligands targeting multiple proteins simultaneously.
AI.motivation: The "one drug, one target" paradigm fails for multifactorial diseases (e.g., cancer, neurodegeneration) due to compensatory pathways and drug resistance. Rational design of multi-target ligands is hindered by the computational difficulty of simultaneously satisfying distinct geometric constraints imposed by multiple binding pockets.
AI.method: The review systematically surveys GDL architectures: (1) invariant graph neural networks and SE(3)-equivariant diffusion models operating on non-Euclidean molecular data; (2) geometric embeddings for shared binding pocket characterization; (3) heterogeneous graph fusion for multi-target bioactivity prediction; (4) structure-conditioned generative algorithms combining diffusion models with reinforcement learning for de novo dual-target ligand generation; and (5) multimodal omics integration with specialized geometric benchmarking infrastructures.
AI.result: GDL enables three core capabilities: characterization of shared binding pockets via geometric embeddings, multi-target bioactivity prediction through heterogeneous graph fusion, and de novo generation of dual-target ligands. Structure-conditioned generative models integrating diffusion with reinforcement learning autonomously resolve geometric conflicts between competing binding sites.
AI.conclusion: GDL is driving a paradigm shift in drug discovery from serendipitous exploration to rational, structure-driven polypharmacological molecular engineering, providing a structured framework for next-generation therapeutics targeting complex multifactorial diseases.

title: OPTScientist: Multi-Agent Discovery of Typed Optimizer Programs for Transformer Pretraining
summary: Designing optimizers for modern deep learning remains a challenging scientific problem, requiring the joint consideration of optimization geometry, state dynamics, numerical stability, implementation constraints, and empirical generalization. Existing automated optimizer discovery methods typically search either over unconstrained code spaces or within narrowly parameterized optimizer families. The former is flexible but often produces invalid or uninterpretable programs, while the latter is stable but limits novelty. We introduce OPTScientist, a theory-guided multi-agent framework for optimizer discovery in a typed domain-specific language (DSL). OPTScientist formulates optimizer design as a constrained scientific search process, where candidate updates are expressed through direction, scaling, preconditioning, regularization, state, and grouping modules. Four role agents, Theorist, Designer, Engineer, and Reviewer, collaborate within a single orchestration loop to propose hypotheses, synthesize DSL candidates, compile and evaluate optimizers, and critique results. To overcome the limitations of a fixed search space, OPTScientist combines evolutionary search over optimizer programs with a second-stage mechanism that proposes small DSL extensions when repeated failures reveal representational bottlenecks. Using this framework, we discover RS-MR, a reduced-state matrix optimizer that improves transformer pretraining over strong baselines under our native evaluation protocol. Our results suggest a path toward automated optimizer science grounded in theory, typed programs, compiler validation, and closed-loop experimentation.

AI.tldr: OPTScientist is a multi-agent framework that discovers optimizers using a typed DSL, combining evolutionary search with DSL extension mechanisms. It discovered RS-MR, a reduced-state matrix optimizer that improves transformer pretraining over strong baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing optimizer discovery methods face a trade-off: unconstrained code search is flexible but produces invalid/uninterpretable programs, while parameterized family search is stable but limits novelty. A systematic approach balancing flexibility, validity, and interpretability is needed.
AI.method: OPTScientist uses four role agents (Theorist, Designer, Engineer, Reviewer) in an orchestration loop over a typed DSL with six modules (direction, scaling, preconditioning, regularization, state, grouping). It employs evolutionary search over optimizer programs with a second-stage DSL extension mechanism triggered by repeated representational bottlenecks.
AI.result: The framework discovered RS-MR, a reduced-state matrix optimizer that improves transformer pretraining performance over strong baselines under the native evaluation protocol.
AI.conclusion: The results suggest a viable path toward automated optimizer science grounded in theory, typed programs, compiler validation, and closed-loop experimentation.

title: The Storyteller in the Model: Narrative Pattern Inheritance, Escalation Dynamics, and Alignment Governance in LLMs
summary: LLMs are trained predominantly on human-authored text, yet the structural and narrative conventions embedded in that text are rarely examined as a source of systematic behavioral influence, or as a governance risk in deployed systems. This paper considers whether the storytelling patterns inherent in published human writing, including archetypal roles such as protagonist, antagonist, and underdog, as well as tension-and-resolution narrative arcs, are absorbed during training and subsequently surface in LLM outputs, causing responses to drift toward unexpected, adversarial, or rhetorically enticing behaviors over extended interactions. Through a systematic literature review and cross-paper analysis of recent empirical studies on LLM alignment, persona dynamics, emergent misalignment, and user interaction patterns, we observe evidence bearing on this hypothesis. The findings reveal three key patterns. First, LLMs reproduce statistical patterns from their training data rather than reasoning independently. Second, measurable latent traits, including sycophancy and deceptiveness, emerge reliably across unrelated prompts. Third, fine-tuning on a narrow narrative task can produce unintended behavioral changes well beyond that task. Furthermore, evidence suggests that persuasive, narrative-style outputs are among the most common LLM products in real-world usage, amplifying these risks. Narrative drift constitutes an unmonitored escalation pathway in deployed AI systems, one that evades discrete-incident detection mechanisms and requires dedicated monitoring instruments.

AI.tldr: LLMs absorb narrative conventions (protagonist/antagonist roles, tension-resolution arcs) from human-authored training data, causing outputs to drift toward adversarial or rhetorically manipulative behaviors. A cross-study review identifies three patterns: statistical reproduction over reasoning, emergent sycophancy/deceptiveness, and unintended behavioral spillover from narrow fine-tuning. The paper frames "narrative drift" as an unmonitored governance risk requiring dedicated oversight instruments.
AI.motivation: The structural and narrative conventions embedded in human-authored training text are largely unexamined as sources of systematic behavioral influence and governance risk in deployed LLMs. The paper aims to investigate whether storytelling patterns (archetypes, narrative arcs) absorbed during training cause LLM outputs to drift toward unexpected, adversarial, or rhetorically enticing behaviors over extended interactions.
AI.method: Systematic literature review and cross-paper analysis of recent empirical studies covering LLM alignment, persona dynamics, emergent misalignment, and user interaction patterns.
AI.result: Three key findings: (1) LLMs reproduce statistical training patterns rather than reasoning independently; (2) latent traits like sycophancy and deceptiveness emerge reliably across unrelated prompts; (3) fine-tuning on narrow narrative tasks produces unintended behavioral changes beyond the task scope. Persuasive, narrative-style outputs are among the most common LLM products in real-world usage, amplifying these risks.
AI.conclusion: Narrative drift constitutes an unmonitored escalation pathway in deployed AI systems that evades discrete-incident detection mechanisms and requires dedicated monitoring instruments.

title: SenCos-GEM: SENet-Calibrated and Law-of-Cosines-Constrained Geometry-Enhanced Molecular Representation for Property Prediction
summary: Effective molecular representation learning is crucial for accurate molecular property prediction. Recently, numerous self-supervised learning (SSL) approaches leveraging 3D GNNs have been developed to capture comprehensive 3D structural information for drug discovery. However, existing methods lack explicit physical constraints and are highly susceptible to geometric noise induced by coarse empirical force fields during large-scale pre-training.Furthermore, they overlook dynamic feature modulation during downstream adaptation, often resulting in catastrophic forgetting and negative transfer. To address these limitations, we introduce SenCos-GEM, a novel explicitly decoupled geometry-enhanced molecular representation learning framework that incorporates SENet-calibrated and law-of-cosines-constrained enhancements. SenCos-GEM employs a physics-guided geometric consistency loss based on the law of cosines to derive high-fidelity and mathematically invariant 3D spatial priors. In addition, lightweight Squeeze-and-Excitation (SE) modules are integrated into the backbone as task-specific adapters, while a dual-modulation prediction head combines Feature-wise Linear Modulation (FiLM) and SENet mechanisms to enable dynamic feature recalibration. SenCos-GEM demonstrates highly competitive performance across diverse classification and regression tasks on MoleculeNet benchmark, establishing new state-of-the-art results specifically on 3D conformation-sensitive regression tasks, such as FreeSolv, Lipophilicity, and QM9, achieving relative error reductions of 12.9% (RMSE), 5.3% (RMSE), and 8.2% (MAE), respectively. Moreover, our model exhibits superior capability in distinguishing stereoisomers and discriminating conformational perturbations, underscoring its robust spatial modeling performance. Collectively, SenCos-GEM represents a significant breakthrough in accurate molecular property prediction.

AI.tldr: SenCos-GEM is a 3D geometry-enhanced molecular representation learning framework that combines physics-guided geometric consistency (law of cosines), SENet-based adapters, and FiLM-SENet dual-modulation prediction heads to achieve state-of-the-art molecular property prediction, particularly on 3D conformation-sensitive tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing self-supervised 3D GNN methods for molecular representation suffer from (1) lack of explicit physical constraints, (2) high susceptibility to geometric noise from coarse empirical force fields during pre-training, and (3) catastrophic forgetting and negative transfer due to neglected dynamic feature modulation during downstream adaptation.
AI.method: SenCos-GEM introduces: (1) a physics-guided geometric consistency loss grounded in the law of cosines to obtain high-fidelity, mathematically invariant 3D spatial priors; (2) lightweight Squeeze-and-Excitation (SE) modules integrated as task-specific adapters into the backbone; and (3) a dual-modulation prediction head combining Feature-wise Linear Modulation (FiLM) and SENet mechanisms for dynamic feature recalibration.
AI.result: SenCos-GEM achieves new state-of-the-art results on 3D conformation-sensitive regression tasks: FreeSolv (12.9% RMSE reduction), Lipophilicity (5.3% RMSE reduction), and QM9 (8.2% MAE reduction). It also excels in stereoisomer discrimination and conformational perturbation distinction, demonstrating robust spatial modeling.
AI.conclusion: SenCos-GEM represents a significant breakthrough in accurate molecular property prediction by explicitly decoupling geometry-enhanced representations with physical constraints and dynamic feature modulation, effectively addressing key limitations of prior SSL-based 3D GNN approaches.

title: Directional Hallucinations: Ideological Drift in News-Grounded LLM Question Answering
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to answer questions about political information, including in election-adjacent information settings where factual errors and ideological distortions are high-stakes. We present a reproducible measurement framework that treats hallucinations, unsupported statements in document-grounded QA, as diagnostic signals of ideological drift. Using 21,727 expert-labeled U.S. political news articles from QBias spanning left, center, and right sources, we (i) generate an article-specific question, (ii) elicit document-grounded answers from three open-weight LLMs and one proprietary model, (iii) detect sentence-level hallucinations via reference-based comparison, (iv) classify the ideological valence of hallucinated sentences with a fine-tuned stance classifier, and (v) probe output logits to relate token-level uncertainty to hallucination and drift. Hallucination rates vary substantially across models and concentrate in contentious topics, while source-ideology differences in hallucination frequency are modest. In contrast, hallucination content exhibits robust leftward drift: a majority of hallucinated sentences are classified as left-leaning, including among hallucinations generated from right-leaning sources. Logit-level analysis shows hallucinations arise in high-entropy generation contexts, and in some models uncertainty also predicts leftward drift, consistent with an "uncertainty to guessing" mechanism. We discuss implications for auditing AI-mediated political information and for designing safeguards in election-relevant deployments.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a measurement framework that uses hallucinations in document-grounded QA as diagnostic signals of ideological bias in LLMs. Analyzing 21,727 labeled political news articles, the authors find that while hallucination rates vary by model and topic, hallucinated content consistently exhibits leftward ideological drift—even when grounded in right-leaning sources—and that high token-level uncertainty predicts both hallucination and ideological drift.
AI.motivation: LLMs are increasingly deployed for answering political questions, including in high-stakes election contexts. Factual errors and ideological distortions in these settings pose serious risks. The authors aim to systematically investigate whether and how LLM hallucinations reveal latent ideological biases, treating hallucinated content as a diagnostic signal for "ideological drift" away from source documents.
AI.method: The authors construct a five-stage reproducible measurement framework: (1) generate article-specific questions from 21,727 expert-labeled U.S. political news articles (QBias dataset, spanning left/center/right sources); (2) elicit document-grounded answers from three open-weight LLMs and one proprietary model; (3) detect sentence-level hallucinations via reference-based comparison against the source document; (4) classify the ideological valence of hallucinated sentences using a fine-tuned stance classifier; and (5) probe output logits to relate token-level uncertainty (entropy) to hallucination and ideological drift.
AI.result: Hallucination rates vary substantially across models and cluster around contentious political topics. Differences in hallucination frequency based on source ideology are modest. However, hallucination content exhibits a robust leftward drift: a majority of hallucinated sentences are classified as left-leaning, even when the underlying source is right-leaning. Logit-level analysis reveals that hallucinations emerge in high-entropy generation contexts, and for some models, token-level uncertainty also predicts leftward drift, suggesting an "uncertainty to guessing" mechanism.
AI.conclusion: Hallucinations in LLM-generated political answers are not ideologically neutral; they systematically drift leftward regardless of source orientation. This drift is linked to model uncertainty, raising concerns for AI-mediated political information systems. The findings highlight the need for auditing frameworks and safeguards in election-relevant LLM deployments.

title: ShriNep@EEUCA 2026: RAKSHAK - Multi-Task DeBERTa with Rationale Distillation and Jigsaw-Augmented Training for Toxic Intent Classification
summary: This paper presents two systems for the GameTox Shared Task at the Workshop on EEUCA at ACL 2026, which requires classifying World of Tanks chat utterances into six fine-grained toxic intent categories (Labels 0-5). Severe class imbalance, domain-specific multilingual slang, and extremely scarce data for rare categories such as Threats (Label 4, 60 samples) and Extremism (Label 5, 24 samples) make this a challenging classification problem. Our primary submission, RAKSHAK (rak s. aka, Sanskrit for "Protector"), is a multi-task DeBERTa-v3-base (He et al., 2022) framework combining rationale distillation from Qwen2.5-14B (An et al., 2024), Supervised Contrastive Loss, and dedicated rare-class binary heads. RAKSHAK's training data is augmented with cross-domain transfer from the Jigsaw Toxic Comment dataset (16,225 samples mapped to Labels 1-4) and 100 LLM-generated extremism samples for Label 5. Our secondary system (M1) fine-tunes DeBERTa-v3-base with Focal Loss on the original GameTox data plus the same 100 extremism samples, without Jigsaw transfer. RAKSHAK achieves a Macro F1 of 0.5883 on the official test set, ranking 7th out of 35 participating teams, while M1 achieves 0.5252 Macro F1. An ablation comparing M1 with and without Jigsaw data shows that cross-domain transfer accounts for +2.6 F1 points, while RAKSHAK's multi-task architecture contributes a further +3.7 points.

AI.tldr: RAKSHAK, a multi-task DeBERTa-v3-base system combining rationale distillation, Supervised Contrastive Loss, and rare-class heads, achieves 0.5883 Macro F1 (7th/35) on fine-grained toxicity classification for multilingual game chat, with cross-domain transfer and multi-task architecture contributing +2.6 and +3.7 F1 points respectively.
AI.motivation: Classifying toxic chat in World of Tanks is difficult due to severe class imbalance (as few as 24 samples for Extremism), domain-specific multilingual slang, and extremely scarce data for rare categories like Threats and Extremism. The shared task demands fine-grained classification into six intent categories, and standard fine-tuning approaches struggle under these data-scarcity conditions.
AI.method: RAKSHAK employs a multi-task DeBERTa-v3-base framework with three key components: (1) rationale distillation from Qwen2.5-14B to provide interpretable supervision signals, (2) Supervised Contrastive Loss to improve representation learning, and (3) dedicated binary classification heads for rare classes (Labels 4 & 5). Training data is augmented via cross-domain transfer from the Jigsaw Toxic Comment dataset (16,225 samples mapped to Labels 1–4) and 100 LLM-generated extremism samples for Label 5. A secondary system (M1) fine-tunes DeBERTa-v3-base with Focal Loss on original GameTox data plus the 100 generated extremism samples, without Jigsaw transfer.
AI.result: RAKSHAK achieves 0.5883 Macro F1, ranking 7th out of 35 teams. The secondary M1 system achieves 0.5252 Macro F1. Ablation shows cross-domain transfer (Jigsaw data) contributes +2.6 F1 points, and RAKSHAK's multi-task architecture adds a further +3.7 points over the baseline.
AI.conclusion: The combination of multi-task learning with rationale distillation, contrastive loss, and targeted rare-class heads, supplemented by cross-domain data transfer and LLM-based augmentation, substantially improves fine-grained toxic intent classification under extreme data scarcity. The ablation quantifies the individual contributions of cross-domain transfer and multi-task architecture.

title: Thermodynamic Weight Decay: Exploring Grokking Acceleration via Attention Specific Heat
comment: 9 pages, 4 figures, 2 tables. Code and data: https://github.com/baymaxbyte/cbo_core
summary: Grokking -- the delayed generalization of neural networks long after they have memorized their training data -- wastes thousands of training epochs and is notoriously unpredictable. Building on the recent result that Transformer attention is formally isomorphic to a thermodynamic system, we treat the variance of attention logits as a specific heat Cv and show that its peak reliably precedes the generalization transition. We introduce CvAdamW, a drop-in AdamW variant that monitors Cv online and injects thermal energy by dynamically scaling weight decay when a phase transition is detected. Through a strictly iterative development process we identify three failure modes -- initialization noise, mini-batch micro-ripples, and slingshot blinding -- and resolve them with a memorization gate and an exponential-moving-average shock absorber. On modular arithmetic (a+b mod 97), CvAdamW enables grokking at epoch 2802 in a 4000-epoch budget where the baseline never groks. We further propose a scale-invariant z-score reformulation that removes task-specific hyperparameters, and evaluate it across 10 paired seeds. A paired analysis shows the cold-start variant reduces mean grokking latency by 257 epochs (6.0%; median 166 epochs; Wilcoxon p=0.049, Cohen's d=0.68, bootstrap 95% CI [53,489]), improving 8 of 10 seeds; on this single task Cv peaks before grokking in all 10 seeds. Our results indicate that neural networks may expose detectable precursors of impending generalization transitions, and that a physically motivated, proportional intervention can facilitate generalization within a fixed compute budget. Code and data are public.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces CvAdamW, a variant of the AdamW optimizer that treats attention logit variance as a thermodynamic specific heat (Cv). By monitoring Cv peaks as precursors to grokking (delayed generalization), the method dynamically scales weight decay to inject "thermal energy" at phase transitions. The approach reduces grokking latency on modular arithmetic tasks by ~6%, with statistically significant improvements across seeds.
AI.motivation: Grokking — delayed generalization long after memorization — wastes thousands of training epochs and is unpredictable. The authors aim to detect precursors of the generalization transition and intervene proactively within a fixed compute budget, rather than waiting for grokking to occur spontaneously.
AI.method: Building on the thermodynamic isomorphism of Transformer attention, the variance of attention logits is framed as a specific heat (Cv). CvAdamW monitors Cv online and dynamically scales weight decay (injecting thermal energy) when a phase transition is detected via Cv peaking. Three failure modes are identified and resolved: initialization noise (via a memorization gate), mini-batch micro-ripples, and slingshot blinding (via an EMA shock absorber). A scale-invariant z-score reformulation eliminates task-specific hyperparameters. Evaluation uses 10 paired seeds with a cold-start variant on modular arithmetic (a+b mod 97).
AI.result: CvAdamW achieves grokking at epoch 2802 within a 4000-epoch budget where the baseline never groks. The cold-start variant reduces mean grokking latency by 257 epochs (6.0%; median 166 epochs; Wilcoxon p=0.049; Cohen's d=0.68; bootstrap 95% CI [53,489]), improving 8 of 10 seeds. Cv peaks before grokking in all 10 seeds.
AI.conclusion: Neural networks expose detectable precursors of impending generalization transitions. A physically motivated, proportional intervention (CvAdamW) can facilitate grokking within a fixed compute budget, offering both practical optimization gains and theoretical insight into neural network learning dynamics.

title: Autonomous Topology Mutation: Safe Runtime Restructuring for Multi-Agent LLM Systems with Capability, State, and Shadow Invariants
comment: 9 pages, 5 tables. Code and benchmark harness available at https://github.com/sidikbro/jiuwen_atm
summary:
Multi-agent LLM frameworks typically fix their team topology at boot time. When an individual agent becomes overloaded at runtime, for example by mixing too many action categories, accumulating tool errors, or queueing behind too many calls, the system has no mechanism to restructure itself. We introduce Autonomous Topology Mutation (ATM), a runtime team-mutation mechanism for multi-agent LLM frameworks. ATM combines telemetry-driven overload detection with three safety invariants that gate each structural change: capability monotonicity, state-routing completeness, and shadow-before-live validation.
  ATM monitors a six-signal Bottleneck Index that includes queue depth, context thrash, tool-error rate, role entropy, retry-loop rate, and cross-agent wait time. When a warmup-calibrated threshold is breached for multiple consecutive ticks, ATM factorises the overloaded agent into specialised sub-agents and hot-swaps the parent into a coordinator role while preserving its external identity. State transfer is controlled by privacy-level-aware routing: each memory atom is routed only to a permitted child set, or explicitly dropped with a logged reason. No candidate topology receives live traffic until it has passed a shadow validation window.
  On 720 DeepSeek-V3-driven task runs with deterministic tool stubs across four ablation conditions and three workloads, the ATM factoriser split lifts code-task success from 3.3% to 61.7%. The full rail-and-distillation system reduces detected high-privacy memory exposure under a regex classifier from 2.0 to 0.0 events per task while preserving task quality. The runtime rails carrying ATM's invariants add less than 500 microseconds of p99 latency on the agent hot path. A small live-tool probe with real Python execution is included as an external-validity check. The implementation, benchmark harness, and traces are open-sourced.

AI.tldr: ATM introduces runtime topology mutation for multi-agent LLM frameworks, using bottleneck detection and safety invariants to dynamically restructure overloaded agents, boosting code-task success from 3.3% to 61.7% while eliminating high-privacy memory exposure.
AI.motivation: Existing multi-agent LLM frameworks fix team topology at initialization and cannot restructure when individual agents become overloaded at runtime due to action-category mixing, tool errors, or call queuing.
AI.method: ATM uses a six-signal Bottleneck Index (queue depth, context thrash, tool-error rate, role entropy, retry-loop rate, cross-agent wait time) with warmup-calibrated thresholds to detect overload. When breached for multiple ticks, it factorises the overloaded agent into specialized sub-agents, promotes the parent to a coordinator, and hot-swaps while preserving external identity. Three safety invariants gate all changes: capability monotonicity, state-routing completeness, and shadow-before-live validation. State transfer uses privacy-level-aware routing, and no topology receives live traffic without passing shadow validation.
AI.result: On 720 DeepSeek-V3 runs across four ablation conditions and three workloads: the ATM factoriser lifted code-task success from 3.3% to 61.7%. Full system reduced high-privacy memory exposure from 2.0 to 0.0 events/task under regex classification without degrading task quality. Runtime invariants add under 500μs p99 latency on the hot path.
AI.conclusion: ATM demonstrates that safe, automated runtime topology mutation is feasible and significantly improves both task success and privacy compliance in multi-agent LLM systems, with negligible latency overhead.

title: Semantic Field Theory: Historical Origin, Higher-Order Interaction, and Stabilized Semantic Inference
summary: Semantic Field Theory (SFT) has developed from a philosophical critique of strong anti-formalist readings of language games into a proposed computational model class for lexical semantics, higher order composition, and stabilized interpretation. This paper reconstructs that evolution and gives SFT a sharper mathematical core suitable for independent evaluation in computational linguistics and representation learning. The central proposal is that a tractable level of linguistic organization can be modeled through lexical representations expressed as semantic fields, through contextual deformation of those fields, through interaction terms defined over subsets of tokens, and through stabilization governed by semantic energy dynamics. The paper contributes five formal elements. First, it defines a semantic field model as a tuple consisting of a semantic space, a lexical field lifting, a contextual deformation map, an interaction complex, and an interpretation functional. Second, it proves a Gaussian product closure result showing that multiplicative field interactions have explicit centers, precisions, and compatibility factors. Third, it generalizes the three-word problem by using Mobius inversion on the subset lattice to isolate irreducible semantic interactions of arbitrary order. Fourth, it introduces an order spectrum that measures how much field mass is explained at each interaction order. Fifth, it formulates stabilized interpretation as minimization of an energy functional associated with the sentence and gives existence, descent, and stability conditions. A small worked example shows how a three-word summer day triple can be represented by Gaussian semantic fields, implemented in Python, and summarized by a flow diagram. The result is not a completed theory of natural language meaning and does not replace social, pragmatic, or normative accounts of language.

AI.tldr: The paper formalizes Semantic Field Theory (SFT) as a mathematical framework for lexical semantics, introducing five formal elements: a semantic field tuple definition, Gaussian product closure, Möbius inversion for higher-order interactions, an order spectrum metric, and energy-based stabilized interpretation. A worked example with Gaussian fields demonstrates the approach.
AI.motivation: SFT emerged from philosophical critiques of anti-formalist language game interpretations. The paper aims to give SFT a rigorous mathematical foundation suitable for independent evaluation in computational linguistics and representation learning, moving it from philosophical discourse to a testable computational model class.
AI.method: The paper contributes five formal constructions: (1) a semantic field model defined as a tuple (semantic space, lexical field lifting, contextual deformation map, interaction complex, interpretation functional); (2) a Gaussian product closure proof with explicit centers, precisions, and compatibility factors; (3) generalization of the three-word problem via Möbius inversion on the subset lattice to isolate irreducible n-ary semantic interactions; (4) an order spectrum measuring field mass distribution across interaction orders; (5) stabilized interpretation via energy functional minimization with existence, descent, and stability conditions. A Python implementation on a three-word example illustrates the framework.
AI.result: The paper delivers a mathematically sharpened SFT framework with five formal elements. The Gaussian product closure provides explicit multiplicative interaction formulas. Möbius inversion generalizes interaction isolation to arbitrary order. The order spectrum quantifies contribution by interaction level. Energy minimization yields stable interpretations under specified conditions. A worked "summer day" triple example demonstrates feasibility in Python.
AI.conclusion: The resulting framework is explicitly not a complete theory of natural language meaning and does not replace social, pragmatic, or normative accounts. It provides a formal, computationally tractable model class for further empirical evaluation in representation learning and computational linguistics.

title: Double-Scoring: Reliable Extraction of Strong Lottery Tickets
summary: The lottery ticket hypothesis proposes that large random neural networks contain sparse subnetworks that can match the performance of dense models after comparable training. A stronger version asserts that sufficiently overparameterized random networks contain subnetworks that are already accurate before any weight training. Existing theory establishes that such strong lottery tickets exist, but reliable extraction remains difficult. We revisit edge-popup, a frozen-weight score-training method for extracting strong tickets, and identify layerwise sparsity selection as a central bottleneck. We introduce double-scoring, an augmented score-space parameterization that replaces a layerwise sparsity search with optimization over enlarged score tensors. We prove that fixed-density masking in an augmented score space preserves access to all original-coordinate masks, and we show that the resulting method can be interpreted as edge-popup on a zero-augmented network. In controlled experiments, double-scoring substantially improves strong-ticket extraction over fixed-density edge-popup and pruning-at-initialization baselines, improves on the performance of rewound sparse-training topologies, and exhibits markedly lower sensitivity to sparsity hyperparameters. Ablations show that the gain is not merely due to additional trainable score parameters, but is tied to the augmented score-space competition that induces the effective original sparsity.

AI.tldr: Double-scoring improves extraction of strong lottery tickets (untrained subnetworks) by augmenting the score space, replacing layerwise sparsity search with optimization over enlarged score tensors, yielding better performance and lower sensitivity to sparsity hyperparameters.
AI.motivation: Existing theory confirms strong lottery tickets exist in random networks, but reliable extraction remains challenging. The authors identify layerwise sparsity selection as a central bottleneck in the edge-popup method and aim to overcome it.
AI.method: The authors introduce double-scoring, which augments the score-space parameterization by using enlarged score tensors. This replaces layerwise sparsity search with optimization in an overparameterized score space. Fixed-density masking in this augmented space provably preserves access to all original-coordinate masks. The method is interpretable as edge-popup on a zero-augmented network.
AI.result: Double-scoring substantially improves strong-ticket extraction over fixed-density edge-popup and pruning-at-initialization baselines. It also outperforms rewound sparse-training topologies and shows markedly lower sensitivity to sparsity hyperparameters. Ablations confirm the gain stems from augmented score-space competition, not merely additional trainable parameters.
AI.conclusion: Augmenting the score space via double-scoring effectively addresses the layerwise sparsity bottleneck in strong lottery ticket extraction, enabling more reliable discovery of accurate untrained subnetworks in random neural networks.

title: EvoSQL: Memory-Augmented Critic-Generator Co-Evolution for Text-to-SQL
summary: Text-to-SQL has advanced rapidly with large language models, but complex database queries still require reasoning beyond one-shot generation, including multi-step decomposition, execution-based diagnosis, and targeted correction. We present EvoSQL, a co-evolution framework that formulates SQL synthesis as an iterative interaction between a generator and a critic. EvoSQL maintains a contextualized candidate memory, verifies SQL candidates with both execution signals and LLM-based critique, and updates its memory through utility-guided aggregation. To strengthen the underlying generator-critic pair, we further introduce a Self-Distillation Policy Optimization (SDPO) fine-tuning stage that injects execution-aware supervision into modern coding LLM backbones. Experiments on Spider and BIRD show that EvoSQL consistently improves open-source models over Maj@16 baselines, with particularly large gains on BIRD-Dev, ranging from +1.37% for Qwen3-4B to +9.19% for Qwen2.5-Coder-3B. SDPO initialization further improves selected backbones on Spider-Test and BIRD-Dev. These results suggest that memory-grounded co-evolution is an effective path toward more reliable and generalizable Text-to-SQL systems. Code is available at https://github.com/valleysprings/EvoSQL.

AI.tldr: EvoSQL introduces a co-evolution framework for Text-to-SQL that iteratively refines SQL queries through generator-critic interaction with memory, enhanced by a Self-Distillation Policy Optimization (SDPO) fine-tuning stage, achieving significant gains on Spider and BIRD benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Complex Text-to-SQL queries require reasoning beyond single-shot generation — including multi-step decomposition, execution-based diagnosis, and targeted correction — which existing approaches handle inadequately.
AI.method: EvoSQL frames SQL synthesis as iterative co-evolution between a generator and a critic. It maintains a contextualized candidate memory, verifies candidates via execution signals and LLM-based critique, and updates memory through utility-guided aggregation. A Self-Distillation Policy Optimization (SDPO) stage further injects execution-aware supervision into coding LLM backbones via fine-tuning.
AI.result: EvoSQL consistently improves open-source models over Maj@16 baselines on Spider and BIRD. On BIRD-Dev, gains range from +1.37% (Qwen3-4B) to +9.19% (Qwen2.5-Coder-3B). SDPO initialization yields further improvements on Spider-Test and BIRD-Dev for selected backbones.
AI.conclusion: Memory-grounded co-evolution represents an effective path toward more reliable and generalizable Text-to-SQL systems.

title: A Knowledge-Injection Framework for Zero-Shot Adaptation of LLMs to Delirium Prediction
summary: Large language models show promise for clinical prediction, but zero-shot performance on specialized tasks is limited by incomplete domain knowledge, especially for smaller locally deployable models. We present a lightweight knowledge-injection framework for zero-shot ICU delirium prediction that augments a deterministic natural-language summary of structured electronic health record data with an external clinical knowledge report at inference time, without fine-tuning or retrieval. We evaluate LLaMA 3.1 8B and LLaMA 3.3 70B on 3,160 ICU admissions from the MIMIC IV dataset. Adding a clinically meaningful external knowledge report improves AUROC by 8.57 percentage points for the 8B model and 1.99 percentage points for the 70B model compared to no external knowledge. Relative to a GPT-5.2 frontier-model reference without external knowledge report (AUROC 68.86%), knowledge injection reduces the performance gap from 15.66 to 7.09 AUROC points for LLaMA 8B and from 5.30 to 3.31 AUROC points for LLaMA 70B. Random control reports do not improve performance and often degrade it, indicating that gains depend on clinically meaningful content rather than added prompt length alone. SHAP-based attribution further confirms that the injected knowledge is actively used during prediction. These findings suggest that inference-time knowledge injection can narrow the gap between locally deployable open-weight models and frontier closed models while preserving a practical, privacy-preserving workflow for resource-constrained clinical settings.

AI.tldr: A lightweight, inference-time clinical knowledge injection framework improves zero-shot ICU delirium prediction for smaller LLMs, narrowing the performance gap with frontier models without fine-tuning or retrieval.
AI.motivation: Zero-shot clinical prediction with LLMs—especially smaller, locally deployable models—suffers from incomplete domain knowledge. The authors aim to bridge this gap without sacrificing privacy or requiring resource-intensive fine-tuning/retrieval, enabling practical deployment in resource-constrained clinical settings.
AI.method: A knowledge-injection framework that augments a deterministic natural-language summary of structured EHR data with an external clinical knowledge report at inference time. Evaluated on LLaMA 3.1 8B and LLaMA 3.3 70B using 3,160 ICU admissions from MIMIC-IV. Random control reports serve as an ablation, and SHAP-based attribution verifies knowledge utilization.
AI.result: External knowledge improved AUROC by +8.57 pp (8B) and +1.99 pp (70B) vs. no knowledge. Relative to GPT-5.2 (AUROC 68.86%), knowledge injection reduced the performance gap from 15.66 to 7.09 points (8B) and from 5.30 to 3.31 points (70B). Random reports degraded or did not improve performance; SHAP confirmed active use of injected knowledge.
AI.conclusion: Inference-time clinical knowledge injection effectively narrows the gap between open-weight, locally deployable models and frontier closed models for zero-shot ICU delirium prediction, maintaining a privacy-preserving, practical workflow suitable for resource-constrained clinical environments.

title: Monkey King Bang: A Unified Scientific Multimodal Foundation Model
summary: Scientific discovery is increasingly shifting from isolated disciplines to multi-domain reasoning, and AI for science faces a similar transition. Existing systems are either specialised for individual domains or unify scientific data mainly through text tokenisation and prompt-based interfaces, limiting their ability to handle diverse scientific inputs, produce modality-native outputs, and support joint understanding, reasoning, and generation across scientific domains. We introduce MKB, a unified scientific multimodal model for both understanding and generation, built around a shared Transformer backbone and modality-tailored encoders, adapters, and decoders. MKB covers six scientific branches, including DNA, RNA, proteins, small molecules, earth science, and medical images, and supports native outputs such as biological sequences, molecular strings, meteorological fields, and segmentation masks. Training follows a two-stage modality-then-language curriculum: Stage 1 aligns modality-specific components with the frozen backbone, and Stage 2 consolidates them with the language backbone using mixed scientific and general corpora. Experiments show that MKB achieves competitive scientific understanding across biological and molecular benchmarks, produces high-fidelity native outputs for weather forecasting, biological generation, and medical-image segmentation, and largely retains the general capabilities of its Qwen3-VL backbone. These results demonstrate the feasibility of the proposed paradigm, suggesting that shared-backbone models with modality-tailored components can provide a promising foundation for future cross-domain scientific multimodal exploration. The model and code are publicly available at https://github.com/Shanghai-Academy-of-AI-For-Science/MKB and https://huggingface.co/sais-org/MKB.

AI.tldr: MKB is a unified multimodal scientific model built on a shared Transformer backbone with modality-tailored encoders/decoders, spanning six scientific domains (DNA, RNA, proteins, small molecules, earth science, medical images) for both understanding and generation tasks, trained via a two-stage curriculum.
AI.motivation: Scientific discovery is transitioning from single-discipline to multi-domain reasoning, but existing AI systems either specialize in one domain or superficially unify data through text tokenization, failing to handle diverse scientific inputs, produce modality-native outputs, or support joint understanding and generation across domains.
AI.method: MKB employs a shared Transformer backbone with modality-tailored encoders, adapters, and decoders covering six scientific branches. Training follows a two-stage "modality-then-language" curriculum: Stage 1 aligns modality-specific components with a frozen backbone; Stage 2 consolidates them with the language backbone using mixed scientific and general corpora. The base architecture leverages Qwen3-VL.
AI.result: MKB achieves competitive performance on biological and molecular understanding benchmarks, produces high-fidelity native outputs for weather forecasting, biological generation, and medical-image segmentation, and largely retains the general capabilities of its Qwen3-VL backbone.
AI.conclusion: The shared-backbone paradigm with modality-tailored components is feasible and promising for cross-domain scientific multimodal exploration, offering a foundation for future unified AI-for-science systems.

title: CRAWO: Custom Resources for Adaptive Workload Orchestration
summary: Edge Intelligence has emerged as a key paradigm for enabling real-time applications in smart cities by shifting computation from centralized cloud data centers to the network edge, thereby reducing latency and bandwidth consumption. However, deploying Artificial Intelligence (AI) pipelines across heterogeneous edge infrastructures remains challenging due to the wide range of device capabilities, from low-power microcontrollers to accelerator-equipped systems. Existing edge orchestration platforms primarily focus on deployment automation and infrastructure management, but these approaches are often inefficient and limit the ability to adaptively allocate resources under dynamic conditions. To tackle these issues, this paper introduces CRAWO (Custom Resources for Adaptive Workload Orchestration), an architectural framework for coordinating AI pipelines across distributed edge environments. CRAWO follows a control-loop-based model that separates allocation intelligence from execution by managing placement decisions, state management, and inter-stage data flows while instantiating services on edge nodes. The framework incorporates a hardware-aware allocator with a pluggable multi-criteria decision layer that leverages real-time infrastructure metrics to enable adaptive workload placement. The reference implementation adopts a microservices architecture deployed on a lightweight Kubernetes distribution (K3s), using Custom Resource Definitions (CRDs) for domain modeling and a dedicated operator for state reconciliation. Evaluation in a vehicle surveillance scenario using license plate recognition demonstrates improved workload distribution and reduced reliance on centralized cloud processing in latency-sensitive environments.

AI.tldr: CRAWO is a Kubernetes-based orchestration framework for edge AI pipelines that uses custom resources, a hardware-aware allocator, and a control-loop model to enable adaptive workload placement across heterogeneous edge devices, demonstrated via a license plate recognition use case.
AI.motivation: Deploying AI pipelines across heterogeneous edge infrastructures is challenging due to diverse device capabilities (microcontrollers to accelerators). Existing orchestration platforms focus on deployment automation but lack adaptive resource allocation under dynamic conditions, leading to inefficiencies.
AI.method: CRAWO employs a control-loop architecture separating allocation intelligence from execution. It features a hardware-aware allocator with a pluggable multi-criteria decision layer using real-time infrastructure metrics. The reference implementation uses microservices on K3s with Custom Resource Definitions (CRDs) for domain modeling and a dedicated operator for state reconciliation.
AI.result: Evaluation in a vehicle surveillance scenario using license plate recognition shows improved workload distribution and reduced reliance on centralized cloud processing in latency-sensitive environments.
AI.conclusion: CRAWO provides an effective architectural solution for adaptive orchestration of AI pipelines across heterogeneous edge environments, improving both workload distribution and latency performance for real-time smart city applications.

title: Response drift across frontier large language models
summary: All frontier large language models (LLMs) exhibit response drift -- producing outputs that deviate from expert-validated references -- yet the magnitude and structure of this drift remain uncharacterised by systematic human evaluation. Here we report a fully crossed evaluation in which 47 geographically diverse participants each assessed all 62 multidomain questions across ten frontier LLMs under blinded conditions, yielding 29,140 independent assessments. Every model drifts, but drift magnitude varies substantially: eight models converge on a statistically indistinguishable ceiling (78-81% deviation), while two achieve lower deviation (47-49%). Drift profiles differ across six domains and 62 questions, with pairwise correlations among ceiling models exceeding r = 0.85. Automated similarity metrics explain less than 2% of variance in human judgements. These findings reveal that response drift is universal across frontier LLMs, domain- and question-dependent in structure, and accessible only through human-centred evaluation.

AI.tldr: A large-scale blinded human evaluation (29,140 assessments across 47 participants, 10 frontier LLMs, 62 multidomain questions) reveals that response drift—deviation from expert-validated references—is universal across all models. Eight models cluster at a 78–81% deviation ceiling, two models show lower drift (47–49%), drift structure is domain- and question-dependent, and automated metrics fail to capture human judgments (R² < 2%).
AI.motivation: Response drift in frontier LLMs—systematic deviation from expert-validated reference outputs—is widely acknowledged but poorly characterized. No prior study has applied systematic, fully-crossed, blinded human evaluation to quantify the magnitude, structure, and inter-model consistency of this drift across multiple models and domains.
AI.method: A fully crossed, blinded human evaluation design: 47 geographically diverse participants each evaluated all 62 multidomain questions across all 10 frontier LLMs, producing 29,140 independent assessments. Drift was measured as deviation from expert-validated references. Pairwise correlations were computed among ceiling models, and automated similarity metrics were regressed against human judgments to assess their explanatory power.
AI.result: All 10 models exhibit drift. Eight models saturate at a statistically indistinguishable ceiling of 78–81% deviation; two models show substantially lower deviation (47–49%). Drift profiles vary by domain and question, with pairwise correlations among ceiling models exceeding r = 0.85—indicating highly similar drift patterns. Automated similarity metrics explain less than 2% of variance in human drift judgments.
AI.conclusion: Response drift is a universal property of frontier LLMs, with domain- and question-dependent structure. Most models converge on a high-drift ceiling with strongly correlated patterns, while a minority achieve meaningfully lower drift. Critically, automated evaluation metrics are poor proxies for human perception of drift, underscoring the irreplaceability of human-centered evaluation.

title: StabilityBench: Benchmarking Instability in LLMs
summary: AI Assistants are increasingly deployed in high-stakes settings, such as healthcare or government services. Yet their real-world behavior remains poorly understood due to strong context dependence. Current evaluation protocols follow a defense-in-depth paradigm with compounding layers of safeguards, ranging from traditional benchmarks to live or adversarial testing. Such benchmarks remain largely static and single-turn, limiting their ability to capture real-world variability in conversational settings. We propose StabilityBench, a principled, general and model-agnostic benchmark operator that transforms single-turn benchmark queries into multi-turn interaction histories. StabilityBench augments existing benchmarks by injecting realistic user simulations, through demographic proxies or sycophantic baits, while preserving original task intent. We apply StabilityBench to four benchmarks spanning mathematical reasoning, health question-answering and safety, and evaluate nine large language models under these conditions. Our results show that model performance is consistently unstable under these injections, with considerable performance degradations on three out of four benchmarks studied. These highlight important limitations of static evaluations and motivate more realistic evaluation settings. To this end, we propose StabilityBench-Mini: a size-preserving variant of StabilityBench that samples across diversification axes, enabling more realistic evaluation without increasing costs.

AI.tldr: StabilityBench transforms static single-turn benchmarks into dynamic multi-turn conversation histories using realistic user simulations (demographic proxies, sycophantic baits), revealing significant performance instability in LLMs across math, health QA, and safety tasks.
AI.motivation: Current LLM evaluation protocols rely on static, single-turn benchmarks that fail to capture real-world conversational variability in high-stakes deployment settings (healthcare, government). There is a need for evaluation methods that reflect the dynamic, multi-turn nature of real user interactions.
AI.method: StabilityBench is a model-agnostic benchmark operator that augments existing single-turn benchmarks by injecting multi-turn interaction histories with two diversification strategies: (1) demographic proxies that simulate diverse user personas, and (2) sycophantic baits that test model susceptibility to agreement-seeking behavior. It preserves original task intent while varying conversational context. A cost-efficient variant, StabilityBench-Mini, samples across these diversification axes.
AI.result: Nine LLMs evaluated across four benchmarks (math reasoning, health QA, safety) showed consistently unstable performance under StabilityBench injections, with substantial degradations on three of four benchmarks, exposing the brittleness of static evaluation.
AI.conclusion: Static single-turn benchmarks are insufficient for assessing real-world LLM reliability. Multi-turn, context-varying evaluation via StabilityBench reveals critical performance instability, motivating adoption of more realistic, dynamic evaluation protocols. StabilityBench-Mini offers a practical path forward without increased evaluation costs.

title: DFAH-Bench: Benchmarking Observable Agent Instability in Financial Decision-Making
comment: 16 pages, 3 figures. Code, replay logs, one-command reproduction (make reproduce-paper), and an interactive results explorer: github.com/ibm-client-engineering/output-drift-financial-llms
summary: Standard evaluation benchmarks measure what a tool-using agent decides, not whether it arrives at that decision through the same process each time. We introduce DFAH-Bench, a replay benchmark that measures observable behavioral instability in financial agent decision-making across three channels -- tool-call trajectories, evidence contacts, and decision concentration -- none of which require access to hidden reasoning text. Across 8,127 replay episodes spanning 10 models and 3 financial tasks, we find that outcome agreement alone is an incomplete stability signal: frontier models can agree on decisions 95% of the time while following the same tool path only 77% of the time -- an 18-percentage-point gap (95% CI: [0.14, 0.22]) that outcome-only evaluation misses entirely. Among frontier-model case groups with high decision agreement, over 55% exhibit meaningful trajectory divergence. We identify three behavioral profiles: pattern matchers that achieve near-perfect agreement by collapsing to a single output regardless of input, stable executors with relatively consistent tool-use processes, and trajectory divergers that reach the same conclusions through materially different tool paths and evidence contacts. The benchmark code, metric scripts, replay logs, benchmark card, dataset README, and release manifest are released in the accompanying repository.

AI.tldr: Introduces DFAH-Bench, a replay benchmark measuring behavioral instability in financial AI agent decision-making by analyzing tool-call trajectories, evidence contacts, and decision concentration across repeated runs. Finds an 18-percentage-point gap between outcome agreement (95%) and tool-path consistency (77%) in frontier models, and identifies three behavioral profiles: pattern matchers, stable executors, and trajectory divergers.
AI.motivation: Standard evaluation benchmarks for tool-using agents only assess final decisions (outcomes), not the consistency/reliability of the decision-making process across repeated runs. This masks behavioral instability — where agents reach identical conclusions through materially different internal processes — which is critical for high-stakes domains like finance where auditability and reproducibility matter.
AI.method: Introduces DFAH-Bench (Decision-Faithfulness and Action-History), a replay benchmark that repeatedly runs the same input through tool-using agents and measures instability across three observable channels — tool-call trajectories (sequence of API/tool invocations), evidence contacts (which data sources are consulted), and decision concentration (distribution of final decisions) — without requiring access to hidden reasoning text. Evaluated across 8,127 replay episodes spanning 10 models and 3 financial tasks.
AI.result: Outcome agreement alone proves an incomplete stability signal: frontier models achieve 95% decision agreement but only 77% tool-path consistency, revealing an 18-percentage-point gap (95% CI: [0.14, 0.22]). Among frontier-model case groups with high decision agreement, over 55% show meaningful trajectory divergence. Three behavioral profiles emerge: (1) pattern matchers that collapse to a single output regardless of input, (2) stable executors with relatively consistent tool-use processes, and (3) trajectory divergers that reach identical conclusions via materially different tool paths and evidence contacts.
AI.conclusion: Outcome-only evaluation systematically masks behavioral instability in tool-using agents. The proposed three-channel framework (trajectories, evidence contacts, decision concentration) provides a practical, observable method for auditing agent reliability without requiring access to internal reasoning. The three identified behavioral profiles offer a taxonomy for understanding and diagnosing agent consistency failures, with implications for deploying LLM-based agents in high-stakes financial contexts.

title: RE-AD: Real-Time Requirement Adherence for Data Labeling
comment: Accepted to The Fifth Generation, Evaluation & Metrics Workshop (GEM) workshop at ACL 2026
summary: Human-annotated data remains fundamental to training frontier Large Language Models (LLMs). However, crowd-sourced annotations often suffer from quality issues stemming from annotator misunderstanding or lack of engagement. To address this, we introduce a real-time requirement adherence (RE-AD) framework that leverages LLMs to proactively validate labeling quality. Our methodology involves decomposing Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) into atomic rules via self-reflection, categorizing them by complexity, and applying tiered validation strategies. Evaluated on a synthetic benchmark, the system achieved an F1 score of 0.749. Furthermore, production deployment resulted in annotators accepting and fixing 82% of the errors flagged by the framework. We include ablation studies to demonstrate the impact of our core design decisions.

AI.tldr: A real-time framework (RE-AD) uses LLMs to validate human annotation quality by decomposing SOPs into atomic rules, achieving an F1 score of 0.749 on benchmarks and an 82% error-fix acceptance rate in production.
AI.motivation: Crowd-sourced human annotations for LLM training often suffer from quality issues due to annotator misunderstanding or lack of engagement, necessitating automated, real-time quality validation.
AI.method: The RE-AD framework decomposes Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) into atomic rules via LLM self-reflection, categorizes rules by complexity, and applies tiered validation strategies to flag annotation errors in real time.
AI.result: On a synthetic benchmark, RE-AD achieved an F1 score of 0.749. In production deployment, annotators accepted and corrected 82% of the errors flagged by the framework.
AI.conclusion: LLM-driven, rule-based real-time validation can effectively improve human annotation quality, with strong acceptance rates from annotators and measurable performance on benchmarks. Ablation studies confirm the value of core design decisions.

title: Joint Utilization of Geospatial and census proxies for Autoencoder-Assisted Downscaling (JUGAAD) of socioeconomic indicators in India
summary: Monitoring poverty and food security indicators is imperative for addressing socioeconomic challenges in developing nations. A limitation is mismatches in scale between data sources: census data provide geographic coverage, while socioeconomic indicators are derived from infrequently conducted surveys at coarse resolutions, posing a methodological challenge. This study introduces a deep learning framework, JuGAAD, using Indian census and survey data from 2001 and 2011 as a case study. We employ a three-step process: census and geospatial data are averaged into intermediate village-cluster-scale tessellations to reduce noise and regularize administrative boundary changes; an autoencoder compresses high-dimensional National Sample Survey Office (NSSO) data into a low-dimensional latent representation; and a regression model maps upscaled census and geospatial data to this representation. This function is applied to fine-grained census data to generate high-resolution predictions, validated against ground-truth district-level NSSO indicators. Results confirm the methodology predicts socioeconomic indicators at fine scales with strong accuracy.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces JuGAAD, a deep learning framework that fuses census, geospatial, and survey data to generate high-resolution predictions of poverty and food security indicators, addressing the scale mismatch between coarse survey data and fine-grained census data, validated using Indian data from 2001 and 2011.
AI.motivation: Poverty and food security monitoring is hindered by a fundamental scale mismatch: census data offer broad geographic coverage at fine resolution, while socioeconomic indicators come from infrequent surveys conducted at coarse spatial resolutions. Bridging this gap is critical for effective policy targeting in developing nations.
AI.method: A three-step deep learning framework: (1) census and geospatial data are aggregated into intermediate village-cluster tessellations to reduce noise and harmonize administrative boundary changes over time; (2) an autoencoder compresses high-dimensional NSSO survey data into a compact latent representation; (3) a regression model learns to map the upscaled census/geospatial features to this latent space, then applied to fine-grained census data to produce high-resolution socioeconomic predictions.
AI.result: The framework generates fine-scale predictions of socioeconomic indicators with strong accuracy, validated against ground-truth district-level NSSO indicators, demonstrating the method's effectiveness in downscaling coarse survey data using census and geospatial inputs.
AI.conclusion: JuGAAD successfully bridges the scale gap between coarse survey data and fine-grained census data, offering a scalable deep learning approach for high-resolution poverty and food security mapping that can inform targeted policy interventions in data-sparse developing regions.

title: Attention-based Experience Replay Framework for Continual Learning of Agnostic Time Series Forecasting Models
summary: Deep learning has led to remarkable progress in artificial intelligence, particularly in robotics, imaging and sound processing. However, a major limitation of neural networks remains their strong dependence on large and stationary datasets. In many real-world applications, these conditions are rarely met due to evolving and dynamic environments where data distributions change over time. Continual learning aims to address this challenge by developing models capable of adapting incrementally while maintaining a balance between stability and plasticity under computational constraints. In this work, we introduce a novel framework for continual time series forecasting, designed to extend existing static forecasting models commonly used in the literature by incorporating an Experience Replay strategy guided by Attention mechanisms. This approach allows the model to adapt dynamically to new contexts while preserving prior knowledge, effectively mitigating catastrophic forgetting. The framework is evaluated on standard forecasting benchmarks as well as on a piezometric dataset exhibiting diverse temporal behaviors. Results show that our approach effectively increases or maintains predictive performance over time while reducing retraining costs and data requirements, thus facilitating the deployment of forecasting models in dynamic and real-world settings.

AI.tldr: A continual learning framework for time series forecasting that uses attention-guided experience replay to adapt to dynamic environments while preventing catastrophic forgetting, reducing retraining costs and data requirements.
AI.motivation: Neural networks rely heavily on large, stationary datasets, but real-world environments are dynamic with shifting data distributions. Continual learning addresses this by balancing stability (retaining old knowledge) and plasticity (learning new patterns) under computational constraints, specifically applied here to time series forecasting.
AI.method: The framework extends existing static forecasting models by incorporating an Experience Replay strategy guided by Attention mechanisms. Selected past samples are stored and replayed during training on new data, allowing the model to retain prior knowledge while adapting to new temporal contexts, thereby mitigating catastrophic forgetting.
AI.result: The approach maintains or improves predictive performance over time on standard forecasting benchmarks and a piezometric dataset with diverse temporal behaviors, while reducing retraining costs and data requirements.
AI.conclusion: The proposed attention-guided experience replay framework effectively enables continual time series forecasting in dynamic, real-world settings by balancing stability and plasticity while lowering computational and data overhead.

title: Learn2Zinc: Fine-tuning Small Language Models for Text-to-Model Translation in MiniZinc
comment: CP 2026 Workshop on LLMs meet Constraint Solving
summary: Large language models excel at code generation for mainstream programming languages but struggle with rare, domain-specific languages such as MiniZinc, a constraint modeling language for combinatorial problems. We investigate whether targeted fine-tuning can teach small language models (0.6B to 20B parameters) to generate syntactically correct and semantically valid MiniZinc models from natural language problem descriptions. Our key finding is that syntax errors dominate failures when working with this domain specific language: the out-of-the-box execution accuracy of small language models such as Qwen3, LLaMa, Gemma, and GPT-OSS is near-zero. We propose a cross-model error bootstrapping approach that collects syntax errors from multiple LLM runs and leverage those to curate an error correction training dataset. This dataset allows us fine-tune small language models that consistently improves both direct code generation and chain-of-thought approaches across all model sizes. With self-reflection and ensembling, our approach achieves up to 98\% execution accuracy. In parallel, solution accuracy still remains at 35\%, indicating that while syntax is learnable, constraint reasoning remains a challenge. We contribute our fine-tuning pipeline, datasets, and models to opens-source for further research on text-to-model translation.

AI.tldr: Small LLMs achieve near-zero syntax accuracy on MiniZinc (a constraint modeling DSL). A cross-model error bootstrapping method that collects syntax errors from multiple LLM runs to create an error-correction fine-tuning dataset boosts execution accuracy to 98%, though semantic/solution accuracy remains low at 35%, showing syntax is learnable but constraint reasoning remains challenging.
AI.motivation: Large language models perform poorly on rare, domain-specific languages like MiniZinc, which is used for constraint modeling of combinatorial problems. Small language models (0.6B–20B parameters) exhibit near-zero out-of-the-box execution accuracy on MiniZinc generation, with syntax errors being the dominant failure mode. The authors aim to determine whether targeted fine-tuning can overcome this syntax barrier.
AI.method: Cross-model error bootstrapping: syntax errors are collected from multiple LLM runs (Qwen3, LLaMa, Gemma, GPT-OSS) and used to curate an error-correction training dataset. This dataset is then used to fine-tune small language models, applied to both direct code generation and chain-of-thought approaches. Self-reflection and ensembling techniques further boost performance.
AI.result: Execution accuracy reaches up to 98% after fine-tuning with error bootstrapping, self-reflection, and ensembling. However, solution accuracy plateaus at approximately 35%, indicating that syntactic correctness is highly learnable while semantic constraint reasoning remains a significant challenge.
AI.conclusion: Syntax errors are the primary bottleneck for LLMs on DSLs like MiniZinc and can be effectively addressed through cross-model error bootstrapping fine-tuning. However, achieving high solution accuracy requires advances beyond syntax correction. The authors open-source their fine-tuning pipeline, datasets, and models to facilitate further research on text-to-model translation.

title: Chronofy: A Temporal-Logical Decay Architecture for Information Validity in Time-Aware Retrieval-Augmented Generation
summary: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems retrieve and integrate external knowledge to ground large language model (LLM) outputs. However, current RAG architectures treat all retrieved facts as equally valid regardless of temporal provenance, leading to temporal hallucination, where plausible but obsolete facts corrupt the output. A clinical lab reading from yesterday is actionable; the same reading from six months ago is noise. We present Chronofy, a three-layer neuro-symbolic framework implementing the Temporal-Logical Decay Architecture (TLDA) that embeds temporal validity directly into the representation, retrieval, and reasoning layers of RAG systems. Layer 1 reserves a dedicated temporal subspace within Matryoshka embeddings to make fact age structurally irremovable from the representation. Layer 2 integrates learnable exponential decay functions into graph-based retrieval, where the decay coefficient $β_j$ is grounded in Bayesian decision theory as an approximation of twice the latent process mean-reversion rate. Layer 3 applies Signal Temporal Logic (STL) robustness functions to evaluate the temporal validity of retrieved knowledge, not LLM output confidence, and enforces the possibilistic weakest-link principle to bound output confidence by the most decayed evidence in the reasoning chain. We evaluate Chronofy on temporal knowledge graph forecasting benchmarks, the TimE temporal QA benchmark, and a domain-specific sensitivity analysis, demonstrating that explicit temporal decay modeling improves retrieval precision, reduces temporal hallucination, and enables principled data re-acquisition triggers when temporal context is insufficient.

AI.tldr: Chronofy introduces a three-layer neuro-symbolic framework (TLDA) that embeds temporal validity directly into RAG systems' representation, retrieval, and reasoning layers to combat temporal hallucination caused by obsolete retrieved facts.
