AI.motivation: Current RAG systems treat all retrieved facts as equally valid regardless of when they originated, causing temporal hallucination — where plausible but outdated information corrupts LLM outputs. A lab result from yesterday is clinically actionable, but the same result from months ago is noise.
AI.method: Chronofy implements a three-layer Temporal-Logical Decay Architecture: (1) a dedicated temporal subspace within Matryoshka embeddings makes fact age structurally irremovable; (2) learnable exponential decay functions in graph-based retrieval with coefficient βⱼ grounded in Bayesian decision theory as twice the latent process mean-reversion rate; (3) Signal Temporal Logic robustness functions evaluate temporal validity of retrieved knowledge and enforce a possibilistic weakest-link principle to bound output confidence by the most decayed evidence.
AI.result: Chronofy demonstrated improved retrieval precision, reduced temporal hallucination, and enabled principled data re-acquisition triggers when temporal context is insufficient, evaluated on temporal knowledge graph forecasting benchmarks, the TimE temporal QA benchmark, and domain-specific sensitivity analysis.
AI.conclusion: Explicit temporal decay modeling in RAG systems effectively mitigates temporal hallucination, improves retrieval quality, and provides a principled mechanism for triggering data refresh when facts become too stale to be reliable.

title: Dropping the Anchor: Statistical Context Summarization for Distributed Systems via Pulsar Attention
summary: Inference with large language models (LLMs) on long sequences is computationally expensive due to the quadratic complexity of self-attention. Distributed blockwise methods such as Star Attention reduce this cost by sharding context across hosts, but rely on prepending a static, content-blind copy of the first block to every host. We propose Pulsar Attention, which replaces the static anchor with two lightweight, content-aware components: a small attention-sink prefix that stabilizes softmax, and compact cross-block summaries built via a Max-IDF heuristic that selects chunks containing globally rare tokens. This reduces the Phase 1 per-GPU FLOPs by up to 3.3$\times$ over Star Attention while retaining an identical KV cache footprint. On RULER and BABILong with Llama-3.1-8B, Pulsar Attention outperforms both Star Attention and dense attention at sequence lengths up to 128K tokens, with absolute gains of up to 4.7% over the dense baseline.

AI.tldr: Pulsar Attention improves distributed long-sequence LLM inference by replacing Star Attention's static anchor block with content-aware components (a small attention-sink prefix and Max-IDF cross-block summaries), achieving up to 3.3× FLOP reduction while outperforming both Star and dense attention on long-context benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Self-attention's quadratic complexity makes long-sequence LLM inference expensive. While Star Attention reduces cost via distributed blockwise sharding, it relies on a static, content-blind copy of the first block prepended to every host. The authors aim to replace this inefficient static anchor with a content-aware mechanism that preserves or improves accuracy while reducing computation.
AI.method: Pulsar Attention introduces two lightweight components: (1) a small attention-sink prefix that stabilizes the softmax operation, and (2) compact cross-block summaries constructed using a Max-IDF heuristic that selects chunks containing globally rare tokens. These replace Star Attention's static anchor block in the distributed blockwise attention framework.
AI.result: Pulsar Attention reduces Phase 1 per-GPU FLOPs by up to 3.3× compared to Star Attention with an identical KV cache footprint. On RULER and BABILong benchmarks with Llama-3.1-8B, it outperforms both Star Attention and dense attention at sequence lengths up to 128K tokens, achieving absolute gains of up to 4.7% over the dense baseline.
AI.conclusion: Content-aware anchor replacement via attention-sink prefixes and Max-IDF summaries is an effective strategy for distributed long-context inference, offering substantial computational savings without sacrificing—and even improving—model accuracy.

title: CT-Merging: Consensus Directions and Task-Level Scaling for LoRA Adapter Merging
summary: LoRA adapters provide an efficient way to specialize a pretrained model for many downstream tasks, but deploying one adapter per task requires adapter storage and task selection at inference time. Model merging addresses this issue by combining independently trained adapters into one multi-task adapter. Recent SVD-based LoRA merging methods mainly focus on constructing shared or task specific directions, while the coefficients assigned to the final directions are often directly from the original task SVD. On a fixed merged basis, inherited coefficients preserve component order with high rank correlation, yet their magnitudes differ substantially from the coefficients induced by the task updates. To address this mismatch, we propose CT-Merging, a LoRA-aware merging algorithm that estimates consensus directions from average task subspace projectors and assigns task-level RMS coefficient scales in the final update. CT-Merging uses repeated support across task SVD subspaces to construct the common basis, while reducing reliance on rank wise SVD magnitudes after direction construction. On the DC-Merge CLIP adapter benchmark, CT-Merging achieves superior average normalized accuracy compared to state-of-the-art merging methods and further improves over DC-Merge by 2.56 points on ViT-B/32 and 1.51 points on ViT-L/14 KnoTS-trained checkpoints.

AI.tldr: CT-Merging proposes a LoRA-aware model merging method that constructs consensus directions from average task subspace projectors and assigns RMS-scaled coefficients, outperforming SVD-based baselines by 2.56 points on ViT-B/32 and 1.51 points on ViT-L/14.
AI.motivation: Existing SVD-based LoRA merging methods inherit coefficients directly from original task SVDs, which preserve component order but exhibit magnitude mismatch with the coefficients induced by actual task updates on the merged basis. This mismatch degrades multi-task adapter performance.
AI.method: CT-Merging constructs a common basis using repeated support across task SVD subspaces (consensus directions from average subspace projectors), then assigns task-level RMS coefficient scales rather than relying on rank-wise SVD magnitudes. This decouples direction construction from coefficient assignment.
AI.result: On the DC-Merge CLIP adapter benchmark, CT-Merging achieves superior average normalized accuracy over state-of-the-art merging methods, improving upon DC-Merge by 2.56 points on ViT-B/32 and 1.51 points on ViT-L/14 with KnoTS-trained checkpoints.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling direction construction from coefficient assignment—via consensus subspace projectors and RMS scaling—effectively resolves the coefficient mismatch problem in SVD-based LoRA merging, yielding significant gains in multi-task adapter performance.

title: CAMeR: Keyword-Gated Hybrid Activation for Adaptive Memory Retention in LLM Agents
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents operating over extended dialogues accumulate vast amounts of information, yet existing memory systems either retain everything indiscriminately or apply uniform forgetting heuristics that fail to distinguish relevant from irrelevant knowledge. We present CAMeR (Context-Activated Memory Reinforcement), a memory retention framework combining keyword-gated hybrid activation -- a joint symbolic (word-level Jaccard) and sub-symbolic (embedding cosine) gating mechanism -- with adaptive weight dynamics. CAMeR computes a hybrid similarity score for each memory-query pair; memories exceeding a threshold receive reinforcement while all memories undergo controlled decay. We introduce CAMeR-Bench, a 76-memory, 100-round benchmark spanning 8 topic clusters with graded activation frequency, designed to test adaptive retention where existing benchmarks (LoCoMO, LongMemEval) cannot. On CAMeR-Bench, CAMeR's keyword gate achieves a 1.6$\times$ larger retention gap between high-frequency and never-referenced memories compared to embedding-only gating (scissors gap: 0.039 vs. 0.024), while time-driven baselines (Oblivion, SuperLocalMemory) collapse to near-zero weights over 100 rounds. CAMeR's top-5 retrieval saves 83.2\% tokens versus full-context approaches (39k vs. 231k cumulative) while producing weight signals that improve retrieval precision. Through 8 ablation conditions we establish that the keyword gate -- not learnable decay -- is the primary performance driver at this scale. Our findings demonstrate that hybrid symbolic-neural gating provides a simple yet effective mechanism for adaptive memory retention in LLM agents.

AI.tldr: CAMeR introduces a hybrid symbolic-neural gating mechanism (keyword Jaccard + embedding cosine similarity) with adaptive weight dynamics for selective memory retention in LLM agents, demonstrating on a custom benchmark that keyword-gated hybrid activation significantly outperforms embedding-only and time-driven baselines for distinguishing relevant from irrelevant memories.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM agent memory systems either retain all information indiscriminately or apply uniform forgetting heuristics, failing to distinguish relevant from irrelevant knowledge over extended dialogues. There is also a lack of benchmarks that test adaptive, context-dependent memory retention.
AI.method: CAMeR (Context-Activated Memory Reinforcement) uses a hybrid similarity score combining word-level Jaccard similarity (symbolic) and embedding cosine similarity (sub-symbolic) as a gating mechanism. Memories exceeding a similarity threshold receive reinforcement while all memories undergo controlled decay. Authors also introduce CAMeR-Bench: a 76-memory, 100-round benchmark across 8 topic clusters with graded activation frequency.
AI.result: The keyword gate achieves a 1.6× larger retention gap (0.039 vs. 0.024 scissors gap) between high-frequency and never-referenced memories compared to embedding-only gating. Time-driven baselines collapse to near-zero weights. Top-5 retrieval saves 83.2% tokens versus full-context (39k vs. 231k cumulative). Ablation across 8 conditions shows the keyword gate, not learnable decay, is the primary performance driver.
AI.conclusion: Hybrid symbolic-neural gating provides a simple yet effective mechanism for adaptive memory retention in LLM agents, with the keyword component being the critical factor at this scale rather than learnable decay dynamics.

title: AI-Driven Surrogate Models for Predicting Electrode-Scale Discharge Behavior in Lithium-Ion Batteries
summary: Physics-based simulations are essential for understanding the electrode-scale discharge behavior of lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) but suffer from prohibitive computational costs. To address this, we introduce a novel deep learning surrogate pipeline based on the Swin3D Transformer to predict spatiotemporal discharge dynamics directly from volumetric data. Our approach integrates two key innovations: Gaussian Positional Encoding (GPE), which enhances spatial feature representation by adapting to the complex geometry of electrode microstructures, and a specialized Temporal Encoding module to capture non-linear timeseries evolution. Experimental validation on an Electrochemical Simulation (ES) dataset demonstrates that our pipeline significantly outperforms state-of-the-art point cloud baselines in prediction accuracy. Furthermore, the proposed method reduces the computational overhead by orders of magnitude, providing a scalable and efficient framework for high-throughput battery design and optimization.

AI.tldr: A Swin3D Transformer-based deep learning surrogate using Gaussian Positional Encoding and a Temporal Encoding module to predict lithium-ion battery discharge dynamics from volumetric data, achieving orders-of-magnitude speedup over physics-based simulations while surpassing point cloud baselines in accuracy.
AI.motivation: Physics-based electrochemical simulations of electrode-scale LIB discharge are computationally prohibitive, limiting their utility in high-throughput battery design and optimization workflows.
AI.method: A deep learning surrogate pipeline employing a Swin3D Transformer backbone augmented with (1) Gaussian Positional Encoding (GPE) to better represent complex electrode microstructure geometry, and (2) a specialized Temporal Encoding module to capture non-linear spatiotemporal evolution during discharge. The model operates directly on volumetric data and is trained/validated on an Electrochemical Simulation (ES) dataset.
AI.result: The proposed pipeline significantly outperforms state-of-the-art point cloud baselines in prediction accuracy and reduces computational overhead by orders of magnitude compared to conventional physics-based simulations.
AI.conclusion: The Swin3D Transformer surrogate with GPE and temporal encoding provides a scalable, efficient, and accurate alternative to physics-based LIB discharge simulation, enabling practical high-throughput battery design.

title: From Errors to Rules: Iterative Prompt Optimization for Text Classification
summary: Prompt optimization for text classification spans diverse approaches, from demonstration selection to exploration-based search to error-driven diagnosis, each with known but incompletely characterized strengths and limitations. We conduct a comprehensive empirical study across diverse classification benchmarks (2 to 150 classes) comparing these paradigms through both quantitative evaluation and qualitative analysis of optimization traces, revealing that each paradigm excels on structurally different task types and that no single method dominates. Guided by these insights, we propose Error-Guided Optimization (ERGO), an error-driven method that iterates over the full training set in non-overlapping batches, diagnoses classification failures, and generates targeted decision rules through a diagnose-prescribe-rewrite feedback loop. ERGO achieves the best accuracy on tasks where errors concentrate in specific confused label pairs (which we term boundary-learnable tasks): TREC: 90.0%, CLINC150: 94.4%, converges in 3-5 iterations, and produces interpretable decision rules. While ERGO does not achieve the highest overall average, it fills a complementary role: demonstration-based ICL wins on coverage-dependent tasks, exploration-based search wins on many-class intent, and ERGO wins where decision boundaries are learnable from error patterns. We provide a complementarity framework linking task characteristics to optimal paradigm selection, offering practical guidance for practitioners.

AI.tldr: A comprehensive empirical study comparing prompt optimization paradigms (demonstration selection, exploration-based search, error-driven diagnosis) for text classification, revealing task-dependent complementarity. The authors propose ERGO, an error-guided method using a diagnose-prescribe-rewrite loop that excels on "boundary-learnable" tasks where errors cluster in confused label pairs.
AI.motivation: Existing prompt optimization approaches (demonstration selection, exploration-based search, error-driven diagnosis) each have known strengths and limitations, but these are incompletely characterized. No systematic comparison exists to guide practitioners on which paradigm to use for which type of classification task.
AI.method: The authors first conduct a comprehensive empirical study across classification benchmarks (2–150 classes), comparing paradigms quantitatively and qualitatively through optimization trace analysis. Based on insights gained, they design ERGO (Error-Guided Optimization), which iterates over the full training set in non-overlapping batches, diagnoses classification failures, and generates targeted decision rules via a diagnose-prescribe-rewrite feedback loop.
AI.result: Each paradigm excels on structurally different task types; no single method dominates. ERGO achieves top accuracy on boundary-learnable tasks (TREC: 90.0%, CLINC150: 94.4%), converges in 3–5 iterations, and produces interpretable rules. Demonstration-based ICL wins on coverage-dependent tasks, exploration-based search wins on many-class intent tasks.
AI.conclusion: The three paradigms are complementary rather than competing. The authors provide a complementarity framework linking task characteristics (boundary-learnability, coverage-dependence, many-class intent) to optimal paradigm selection, offering practical deployment guidance.

title: THOR: A Theta-Gamma Hierarchical Oscillatory Reasoning Framework for Multi-hop QA
summary: Multi-hop question answering requires retrieving and integrating evidence from multiple contexts. Despite the rapid progress of current research, multi-hop reasoning remains constrained by two persistent limitations: attention decay, where the model's focus on main question degrades as the reasoning chain grows, and error accumulation, where mistakes propagate across hops and compounds into final failure. Inspired by Theta-Gamma hierarchical oscillation which decouples global planning from local retrieval, enabling efficient attention transfer between hops and a verification and repair mechanism that interrupts the accumulation of errors in the wrong paths, we present THOR, a brain-inspired Theta-Gamma hierarchical oscillatory reasoning framework. Extensive comparative experiments and specific validation experiments on multi-hop QA benchmarks demonstrate that THOR improves answer accuracy and robustness while mitigating limitations, showcasing its generalization across different backbones.

AI.tldr: THOR is a brain-inspired multi-hop QA framework that uses Theta-Gamma hierarchical oscillation to decouple global planning from local retrieval, addressing attention decay and error accumulation. It improves accuracy and robustness across benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Current multi-hop QA models suffer from two key limitations: (1) attention decay — the model loses focus on the original question as the reasoning chain lengthens, and (2) error accumulation — mistakes in earlier hops compound into cascading failures. These issues are inspired by the brain's Theta-Gamma oscillation mechanism, which naturally decouples global planning from local retrieval and supports error verification.
AI.method: The authors propose THOR, a Theta-Gamma hierarchical oscillatory reasoning framework. It mimics neural oscillations where Theta rhythms handle global planning (maintaining question focus across hops) and Gamma rhythms manage local evidence retrieval. The framework incorporates a verification-and-repair mechanism that detects and interrupts error propagation along incorrect reasoning paths before they compound.
AI.result: Extensive comparative experiments and validation studies on multi-hop QA benchmarks show that THOR improves answer accuracy and robustness. It effectively mitigates both attention decay and error accumulation, and generalizes well across different backbone models.
AI.conclusion: THOR demonstrates that brain-inspired hierarchical oscillatory reasoning can effectively address core weaknesses in multi-hop QA. By decoupling global and local reasoning and adding error verification, it offers a generalizable framework compatible with various backbones.

title: Fisher Widths: Local Learning Geometry and Anisotropic Recovery
summary:
We study Gaussian-width complexity on statistical manifolds through a pair of functionals: the primal Fisher width $w_G(T) = w(G^{1/2}T)$, induced by the Fisher metric, and the inverse-Fisher width $w_{G^{-1}}(T) = w(G^{-1/2}T)$, induced by the inverse Fisher metric. The two widths play complementary statistical roles.
  On the learning side, the Fisher width measures the size of local parameter fluctuations in the geometry induced by the Fisher information. For Fisher-regular losses, we prove that the scale \(w_G(H_r)/\sqrt n\) is attained on sufficiently small Fisher balls.
  On the recovery side, the inverse-Fisher width captures the effect of anisotropic Gaussian measurements whose covariance is determined by the inverse Fisher information. For sparse recovery, the resulting geometry depends not only on sparsity but also on the position of the active coordinates in the Fisher spectrum. We obtain a two-sided estimate for the corresponding statistical dimension, together with support-sensitive recovery estimates and a natural ordering of supports with different curvature profiles.
  Finally, we establish a sharp relation between the primal and inverse-Fisher widths. On any common compact coordinate set $T$, they satisfy \[ w_G(T)w_{G^{-1}}(T)\geq w(T)^2. \] Thus, Fisher anisotropy may transfer complexity from one geometry to the other, but cannot reduce both widths relative to the Euclidean scale.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces two Gaussian-width functionals on statistical manifolds — the Fisher width (primal) and inverse-Fisher width (dual) — and establishes their complementary roles in learning (local parameter fluctuation bounds) and sparse recovery (anisotropic measurement geometry). A sharp uncertainty-like inequality shows that Fisher anisotropy cannot simultaneously reduce both widths below the Euclidean scale.
AI.motivation: Gaussian width is a fundamental complexity measure in high-dimensional statistics, but its behavior on statistical manifolds — where the Fisher information metric introduces intrinsic geometry — is not well understood. The authors aim to formalize how Fisher geometry interacts with Gaussian complexity, separately for learning (where Fisher metric governs local fluctuations) and recovery (where inverse Fisher governs anisotropic measurements).
AI.method: The authors define two functionals: the primal Fisher width w_G(T) using the Fisher metric G, and the inverse-Fisher width w_{G^{-1}}(T) using the inverse metric. For learning, they analyze Fisher-regular losses and prove scale bounds on small Fisher balls. For sparse recovery, they study anisotropic Gaussian measurements with covariance G^{-1}, deriving two-sided statistical dimension estimates, support-sensitive recovery guarantees, and a curvature-based ordering of supports. They then prove the product inequality w_G(T) w_{G^{-1}}(T) ≥ w(T)^2.
AI.result: (1) For Fisher-regular losses, the scale w_G(H_r)/√n is attained on sufficiently small Fisher balls. (2) For sparse recovery under inverse-Fisher covariance, the statistical dimension admits two-sided estimates depending on both sparsity and the position of active coordinates in the Fisher spectrum; this yields support-sensitive recovery guarantees and a natural ordering of supports by curvature. (3) The sharp product inequality w_G(T) w_{G^{-1}}(T) ≥ w(T)^2 holds on any compact coordinate set T, implying Fisher anisotropy transfers complexity but cannot reduce both widths jointly.
AI.conclusion: The primal and inverse-Fisher widths form a dual pair that cleanly separates learning and recovery geometries on statistical manifolds. Their product is bounded below by the squared Euclidean width, establishing a fundamental trade-off: Fisher anisotropy can shift complexity between the two geometries but cannot evade it entirely.

title: AISE-Bench: A Full-Cycle Curated Benchmark for Information Seeking on Academic Knowledge Graphs
summary: Large language models (LLMs) augmented with tools are emerging as autonomous agents capable of using Web engine, APIs, and code to solve complex, long-horizon tasks. Current tool-using benchmarks for information seeking on academic graphs rely on synthetic templates, simplified solution spaces, or narrow tasks such as paper-centric tasks, leaving key challenges underexplored - realistic user intent, complex multi-step API planning, rich parameter filling for APIs, grounded answers with references, and comprehensive evaluation of both the process and the outcome. We introduce AISE-Bench, a real-world, full-cycle annotated benchmark for information seeking on academic knowledge graphs. AISE-Bench release contains 1,133 QA pairs, including query taxonomies, full API execution trajectories, validated parameters, and source-grounded answers with reference links. To support high-quality annotation, we design a customized agent workflow to enable annotators to plan, execute, and revise complex API workflows efficiently. We develop a comprehensive evaluation protocol measuring answer quality, reference grounding, API-planning correctness, and execution success. Among the 14 evaluated methods, even the strongest model (PLAY2PROMPT with Gemini-3-Pro) achieves only moderate performance and often struggles with API planning and execution. AISE-Bench establishes a challenging new testbed for quantitatively evaluating and improving the stepwise correctness, grounded summarization, and traceable reasoning of multi-step API-using LLM agents. Our code and data are available at https://aise-bench.github.io/.

AI.tldr: AISE-Bench is a new benchmark with 1,133 QA pairs for evaluating LLM agents on realistic, multi-step API-based information seeking over academic knowledge graphs, featuring full execution trajectories, validated parameters, and grounded answers. Even the strongest model achieves only moderate performance, revealing significant challenges in API planning and execution.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks for tool-using LLMs on academic graphs suffer from synthetic templates, simplified solution spaces, narrow paper-centric tasks, and lack of comprehensive evaluation covering realistic user intent, complex multi-step API planning, rich parameter filling, grounded answers with references, and joint process-outcome assessment.
AI.method: The authors construct AISE-Bench with 1,133 QA pairs annotated using a custom agent workflow that lets annotators plan, execute, and revise complex API workflows. The benchmark includes query taxonomies, full API execution trajectories, validated parameters, and source-grounded answers with reference links. They also design a comprehensive evaluation protocol assessing answer quality, reference grounding, API-planning correctness, and execution success across 14 methods.
AI.result: Among 14 evaluated methods, PLAY2PROMPT with Gemini-3-Pro performs best but achieves only moderate performance, with frequent failures in API planning and execution, underscoring the benchmark's difficulty.
AI.conclusion: AISE-Bench establishes a challenging testbed for quantitatively evaluating and improving stepwise correctness, grounded summarization, and traceable reasoning of multi-step API-using LLM agents on academic knowledge graphs.

title: Instruct-FD: Can Your Full-Duplex Speech System Follow Turn-Taking Instructions?
summary: Current full-duplex (FD) spoken dialogue systems can produce fluid interactions, yet it remains unclear whether they can adapt their turn-taking behavior when explicitly instructed. This is critical for real-world deployment, where conversational policies vary across applications (e.g., proactive tutoring vs. passive counseling). We introduce Instruct-FD, an instruction-conditioned benchmark for evaluating controllable turn management in FD systems. To enable this, we develop a human-validated, scalable synthetic pipeline that generates instruction-conditioned conversations, along with a deployment-agnostic multi-turn evaluation protocol and an LLM-based judge. Benchmarking six state-of-the-art full-duplex systems reveals a substantial gap in instruction-following turn management: the best model achieves only 64.4% adherence. Performance is highly uneven across behaviors and scenarios, with proactive behaviors such as model backchanneling and interruption remaining particularly challenging. These findings establish instruction-following turn management as a crucial direction for building adaptable and deployable full-duplex dialogue systems.

AI.tldr: Instruct-FD is a benchmark for evaluating how well full-duplex spoken dialogue systems follow explicit instructions to control turn-taking behaviors. Current systems struggle significantly, with the best model achieving only 64.4% instruction adherence, and proactive behaviors like backchanneling and interruption remain particularly difficult.
AI.motivation: Modern full-duplex spoken dialogue systems produce fluid interactions but lack demonstrated ability to adapt turn-taking behavior based on explicit instructions. This adaptability is essential for real-world deployment where conversational policies differ across applications (e.g., proactive tutoring vs. passive counseling), yet no benchmark exists to evaluate controllable turn management.
AI.method: The authors introduce Instruct-FD, which comprises three components: (1) A human-validated, scalable synthetic pipeline that generates instruction-conditioned conversations; (2) a deployment-agnostic, multi-turn evaluation protocol; and (3) an LLM-based judge for automated assessment. Six state-of-the-art full-duplex systems are benchmarked using this framework.
AI.result: Benchmarking reveals a substantial gap in instruction-following turn management. The best-performing model achieves only 64.4% adherence to turn-taking instructions. Performance is highly uneven across different behaviors and scenarios, with proactive behaviors — specifically model backchanneling and interruption — remaining particularly challenging for all systems tested.
AI.conclusion: Instruction-following turn management represents a critical and under-explored direction for building adaptable, deployable full-duplex dialogue systems. Current state-of-the-art systems are far from reliably controllable in their turn-taking behavior, motivating future research in this area.

title: Exact ReLU realization of affine one-dimensional refinement iterates via residual memory and offset frames
summary:
We study vector-valued affine refinement operators of the form [
(Wγ)(t)=\sum_{j\in\mathbb{Z}} A_jγ(Mt-j)+B(t), ]
with finitely supported matrix mask and compactly supported continuous piecewise linear input and forcing data. Building on the homogeneous realization theorem for (B\equiv 0), we prove that, for (M\ge 3), every finite affine iterate (W^nγ) admits an exact fixed-width ReLU realization whose depth is (O(n)).
  The main new ingredient is a residual memory controller. It replaces the noninvertible residual dynamics by an injective skew-product and permits exact backward replay of the residual states required by a Horner-type evaluation of the affine forcing sum. Offset frames align the forcing atoms away from residual seams, allowing complementary loop readouts to recover their values exactly. The remaining branch-selection ambiguity occurs only where the accumulated affine state has already vanished.
  For (M\ge 3), the result applies to arbitrary compactly supported continuous piecewise linear forcing terms. For (M=2), the same construction applies to ordinary-frame seam-separated forcing. We also prove a stage-dependent extension for forcing terms in a fixed finite-dimensional continuous piecewise linear span and record the resulting linear-depth upgrade for open-curve, finite-state, and Hilbert- and Morton-type recursive constructions.

AI.tldr: The paper proves that for vector-valued affine refinement operators with dilation factor M≥3, every finite iterate admits an exact fixed-width ReLU network realization of depth O(n). The key innovation is a "residual memory controller" that converts noninvertible residual dynamics into an injective skew-product, enabling exact backward replay for Horner-type evaluation of affine forcing sums.
AI.motivation: To establish that iterates of vector-valued affine refinement operators — which blend matrix masks with continuous piecewise linear forcing terms — can be exactly represented by deep ReLU networks of linear depth. Prior work handled the homogeneous case (B≡0); this paper extends to the full affine setting, which is nontrivial because the noninvertible residual dynamics obstruct straightforward reconstruction.
AI.method: The construction uses three main devices: (1) a residual memory controller that replaces noninvertible residual dynamics with an injective skew-product, enabling exact backward replay of residual states; (2) offset frames that align forcing atoms away from residual seams so complementary loop readouts recover values exactly; (3) Horner-type evaluation of the affine forcing sum. Branch-selection ambiguity is benign as it only occurs where the accumulated affine state has already vanished. The result for M≥3 holds for arbitrary compactly supported continuous piecewise linear forcing; for M=2 it requires ordinary-frame seam-separated forcing. A stage-dependent extension covers forcing in a fixed finite-dimensional continuous piecewise linear span.
AI.result: For M≥3, every finite affine iterate W^n γ admits an exact fixed-width ReLU realization with depth O(n), for arbitrary compactly supported continuous piecewise linear input and forcing data. For M=2, the same holds under seam-separation conditions. A stage-dependent extension yields linear-depth upgrades for open-curve, finite-state, and Hilbert- and Morton-type recursive constructions.
AI.conclusion: Vector-valued affine refinement operators with M≥3 can be exactly realized by ReLU networks of linear depth, with the residual memory controller being the central enabling mechanism. This bridges the homogeneous realization theorem to the full affine case and opens linear-depth neural network representations for several recursive construction families.

title: FlowEdit: Information-Theoretic Control of LLM Reasoning Flows for Ill-posed Problems Involving Conflicts
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) perform strongly on well-specified reasoning tasks with a feasible answer. However, problems encountered in the open world can become ill-posed due to inconsistent conditions, conflicting statements, or mutually incompatible requirements, admitting no valid responses. We argue that reasoning of such ill-posed problems involving conflicts require novel LLM capabilities to make hidden conflicts explicit, maintain competing hypotheses via multiple reasoning branches, and generate alternative responses in a single pass, all of which are challenging due to the limitation of the next-token prediction mechanism in LLMs. To this end, we propose FlowEdit, a novel framework that leverages information-theoretic principles to quantify and regulate internal reasoning flows of LLMs, for generating a full set of alternative responses under valid hypotheses. FlowEdit can be viewed as enforcing a branch-aware reasoning process using two dual information-theoretic objectives on the model's internal reasoning representations: maximizing the information flow from each selected hypothesis to the branch outcome, while minimizing the overlap and conditional dependence across sibling branches, to provide a diverse, informative set of responses with broad coverage. We show that this is achieved through tractable variational bounds under boundary embeddings being ε-sufficient, optimizing the underlying conditional mutual information in LLM reasoning process. Extensive experiments demonstrate that FlowEdit outperforms leading proprietary models, improving exact-set-match accuracy by 68%, while boosting overall response informativeness by 24%. We further show that flow regulation surfaces in the token stream as a redistribution of next-token entropy that concentrates inside each branch, amplifies at flow boundaries, and scales with the number of flows the problem requires.

AI.tldr: FlowEdit is a framework that uses information-theoretic principles to regulate LLM internal reasoning flows, enabling the generation of multiple valid responses to ill-posed problems with conflicts. It maximizes information flow per hypothesis branch while minimizing overlap across branches, outperforming proprietary models by 68% in exact-set-match accuracy and 24% in response informativeness.
AI.motivation: Real-world problems are often ill-posed — containing inconsistent conditions, conflicting statements, or mutually incompatible requirements that admit no single valid answer. Current LLMs struggle with such problems because their next-token prediction mechanism constrains them to single-path reasoning, making it difficult to surface hidden conflicts, maintain multiple competing hypotheses, and generate alternative responses in one pass.
AI.method: FlowEdit enforces a branch-aware reasoning process via two dual information-theoretic objectives on internal reasoning representations: (1) maximizing mutual information between each selected hypothesis and its branch outcome, and (2) minimizing conditional dependence and overlap across sibling branches. This is implemented through tractable variational bounds under the assumption of ε-sufficient boundary embeddings, optimizing the conditional mutual information in the LLM reasoning process.
AI.result: FlowEdit outperforms leading proprietary models, improving exact-set-match accuracy by 68% and overall response informativeness by 24%. Additionally, flow regulation manifests in the token stream as a redistribution of next-token entropy that concentrates within each branch, amplifies at flow boundaries, and scales with the number of flows required by the problem.
AI.conclusion: FlowEdit provides a principled, information-theoretic solution for LLM reasoning over ill-posed problems with conflicts, enabling diverse and comprehensive multi-hypothesis generation in a single pass. The entropy redistribution phenomenon offers an interpretable signature of the internal flow regulation mechanism.

title: Evaluating the Effectiveness of Persona Simulation in Opinion Prediction with GPT-4.1
comment: ICDM 2025 Undergraduate and High School Symposium
summary: Persona simulation involves utilizing large language models (LLMs) to anticipate human choices or interactions based on specific characteristic information. To further understand current limitations and future directions, we tested persona simulation in opinion prediction with GPT-4.1 (knowledge cutoff by June 2024). Using personas from nine U.S. states provided by Columbia University's Personas dataset, GPT-4.1 accurately predicted 2024 election outcomes in eight out of the nine states, only failing in one of the swing states. We then focused on opinions related to medicine and healthcare. With the American Trends Panel Wave 123 dataset from Pew Research Center, GPT-4.1 was able to anticipate beliefs about childhood vaccines with an accuracy of up to 0.94. Furthermore, we applied GPT-4.1 to generate conversations among personas and observed that the simulated dialogues and opinions adhered well to personas' personalities and backgrounds, albeit lacking natural human-like flow. Persona simulation proves to be a promising application of artificial intelligence as long as biases are addressed. In the near future, it will be beneficial to apply it to opinion analysis and reaction prediction in diverse fields ranging from public health to lawmaking to economics.

AI.tldr: GPT-4.1 was evaluated on persona simulation for opinion prediction, achieving high accuracy in forecasting 2024 U.S. election outcomes (8/9 states) and beliefs about childhood vaccines (accuracy up to 0.94). Simulated dialogues aligned with persona traits but lacked natural conversational flow.
AI.motivation: To assess the current capabilities and limitations of LLMs in persona simulation — specifically, using demographic/characteristic information to predict human opinions and choices — and to identify future directions for this application.
AI.method: GPT-4.1 was tested on two tasks: (1) predicting 2024 U.S. election outcomes using personas from nine states (Columbia University's Personas dataset), and (2) anticipating beliefs about childhood vaccines using the American Trends Panel Wave 123 dataset from Pew Research Center. Additionally, GPT-4.1 generated simulated conversations among personas to evaluate dialogue coherence and personality alignment.
AI.result: GPT-4.1 correctly predicted election outcomes in 8 of 9 U.S. states, failing only in one swing state. For vaccine beliefs, it achieved prediction accuracy up to 0.94. In dialogue generation, simulated conversations aligned well with persona personalities and backgrounds but lacked natural human-like conversational flow.
AI.conclusion: Persona simulation via LLMs is a promising AI application with strong predictive accuracy, provided biases are addressed. The authors suggest future applications in public health, lawmaking, and economics for opinion analysis and reaction prediction.

title: Detecting Neural Network Failures through Spectral Analysis of Internal Activations
summary:
Neural network misclassifications exhibit characteristic spectral instability in internal activations that is invisible at the output layer. This phenomenon is identified and formalized as Spectral Drift -- the frequency-domain distance between consecutive layer activations -- with empirical validation showing that failures exhibit significantly higher drift than correct predictions (1.9% increase, p<0.001). This spectral signature emerges during internal processing but becomes masked in final outputs, explaining why confidence-based detection methods struggle.
  This work introduces Self-Detecting Neural Networks (SDNN), a framework that monitors spectral dynamics across network depth using Short-Time Fourier Transform, wavelet decomposition, and statistical moments to capture multi-scale spectral features. A lightweight detector network (5% parameter overhead) learns to identify failure-indicative patterns via curriculum learning on progressively challenging distributions: natural misclassifications, distribution shifts, and adversarial perturbations.
  Experiments on CIFAR-10 demonstrate that SDNN achieves 79.0 +/- 25.3% AUROC across three seeds, substantially outperforming confidence-based baselines including MaxSoftmax (50.5%) and Energy Score (52.9%) by approximately 25-30 percentage points. Ablation studies reveal that wavelet decomposition and statistical features make consistent contributions, while STFT's role remains unclear. This work establishes spectral analysis of internal activations as a promising direction for neural network reliability, revealing diagnostic information inaccessible to output-based approaches.

AI.tldr: Neural network failures produce distinct spectral signatures (Spectral Drift) in internal layer activations that are masked at the output. The authors propose Self-Detecting Neural Networks (SDNN), which monitor these spectral dynamics using multi-scale frequency analysis and a lightweight detector network, achieving ~25-30 percentage point AUROC improvements over confidence-based baselines on CIFAR-10.
AI.motivation: Traditional confidence-based failure detection methods (e.g., MaxSoftmax, Energy Score) struggle because the spectral instability characteristic of misclassifications is invisible at the output layer — it emerges during internal processing but becomes masked in final predictions. There is a need for detection mechanisms that operate on internal representations rather than output probabilities.
AI.method: The paper formalizes Spectral Drift as the frequency-domain distance between consecutive layer activations. SDNN monitors spectral dynamics across network depth using Short-Time Fourier Transform (STFT), wavelet decomposition, and statistical moments to capture multi-scale spectral features. A lightweight detector network (5% parameter overhead) is trained via curriculum learning on progressively challenging distributions: natural misclassifications, distribution shifts, and adversarial perturbations.
AI.result: On CIFAR-10, SDNN achieves 79.0 ± 25.3% AUROC across three seeds, substantially outperforming MaxSoftmax (50.5%) and Energy Score (52.9%) baselines. Failures exhibit 1.9% higher Spectral Drift than correct predictions (p<0.001). Ablation studies show wavelet decomposition and statistical features contribute consistently, while STFT's role remains unclear.
AI.conclusion: Spectral analysis of internal activations provides diagnostic information inaccessible to output-based approaches, establishing a promising direction for neural network reliability. The high variance across seeds (25.3%) and unclear STFT contribution suggest further investigation is needed.

title: Frontier Financial Judgement: Can agents tell what might move a stock?
summary: We introduce Frontier Financial Judgement, a challenging new benchmark developed in collaboration with professional equity analysts to assess agents' ability to replicate expert human judgements. Rapidly identifying new information, evaluating its implications and determining its valuation impact is one of the most time-consuming and challenging aspects of real-world equity coverage. This is becoming ever more difficult and important as AI rapidly increases the quantity of new information to process. The strongest agent we evaluate on Frontier Financial Judgement matches all expert labels in only 52.4% of cases. We also find significant divergence in estimated false-positive rates among frontier agents, ranging from ~1% for GPT-5.6 Sol to ~32% for Claude Sonnet 4.6. To construct the benchmark and make it representative of real-world settings, we combine human-designed and labelled synthetic articles with live news articles and historical documents, creating 656 items for assessment. The resulting task requires agents to distinguish genuinely new, valuation-relevant financial information from stale, immaterial or misleading news under realistic conditions. We find substantial trade-offs among agent accuracy, cost, false positives and reliability that continue to hinder the reliable deployment of news-flow filtering in practice.

AI.tldr: Frontier Financial Judgement is a new benchmark for evaluating AI agents on their ability to identify valuation-relevant financial news, developed with equity analysts. Top agents match expert labels only 52.4% of the time, with false-positive rates varying widely (1%–32%). The benchmark uses 656 items combining synthetic and real-world articles, revealing significant accuracy-cost-reliability trade-offs that hinder practical deployment.
AI.motivation: The core motivation is that identifying genuinely new, valuation-relevant information from the flood of daily financial news is one of the most time-consuming and difficult tasks for equity analysts — a problem exacerbated by AI-generated content increasing information volume. There is a need for a rigorous, real-world-representative benchmark to measure how well AI agents can replicate expert human financial judgement in news-flow filtering.
AI.method: The benchmark, Frontier Financial Judgement, was developed in collaboration with professional equity analysts. It combines human-designed and labelled synthetic articles with live news articles and historical documents, yielding 656 assessment items. The task requires agents to distinguish genuinely new, valuation-relevant financial information from stale, immaterial, or misleading news. Multiple frontier agents were evaluated, with metrics focused on accuracy (matching expert labels) and estimated false-positive rates.
AI.result: The strongest agent matched all expert labels in only 52.4% of cases. False-positive rates showed extreme divergence: ~1% for GPT-5.6 Sol versus ~32% for Claude Sonnet 4.6. Substantial trade-offs among accuracy, cost, false positives, and reliability were identified, indicating that no current agent is sufficiently reliable for practical deployment in news-flow filtering.
AI.conclusion: Current frontier AI agents remain inadequate for reliably automating the financial news-filtering task that equity analysts perform. The wide variability in false-positive rates and the sub-60% accuracy ceiling highlight that practical deployment is still hindered by fundamental trade-offs between competing performance dimensions.

title: STeMP: Spatio-Temporal Modelling Protocol
summary:
Spatio-temporal machine-learning modelling is an important tool in environmental research. However, machine-learning models are highly sensitive to both the characteristics of the training data, such as its distribution, and methodological choices, including the cross-validation strategy. Each decision has impact and implications on the model itself as well as the estimation of the model quality and applicability for certain purposes. Taking into account the large role of machine-learning based maps of the environment in science and their transfer into practice, transparent reporting of spatio-temporal models, ideally using standardized model protocols, is essential to enable trust, transparency and comparability. However, such protocols are currently lacking for spatio-temporal modelling.
  We propose STeMP (Spatio-Temporal Modelling Protocol) to fill this gap by serving two purposes: standardized reporting to understand the model functioning as well as providing guidance during the modelling process by pointing at critical decisions and parameters. The protocol is structured in three sections: Overview, Model and Prediction. The Overview section contains metadata, while the Model and Prediction sections go into detail, describing predictors, evaluation and software, and further relevant elements of the modelling workflow.
  The protocol definition is hosted on GitHub and accompanied by an R-package (https://github.com/LOEK-RS/STeMP). The R-package contains a web application that can be used to fill the protocol either manually or in a semi-automated way from provided modelling objects. Warnings are returned from the protocol when common pitfalls are encountered, which may help authors as a guide through the modelling process but also support reviewers in the assessment of modelling studies. Via GitHub, incorporation of contributions and feedback from the community is encouraged.

AI.tldr: STeMP is a standardized spatio-temporal modelling protocol and accompanying R-package that provides structured reporting templates and interactive guidance to improve transparency, comparability, and quality assurance in environmental machine-learning studies.
AI.motivation: Machine-learning models for spatio-temporal environmental mapping are highly sensitive to training data characteristics and methodological choices (e.g., cross-validation strategy). Despite their widespread use in science and practice, no standardized reporting protocol exists for spatio-temporal modelling, undermining trust, transparency, and comparability across studies.
AI.method: The authors developed STeMP, structured into three sections: Overview (metadata), Model (predictors, evaluation, software), and Prediction (workflow details). The protocol is hosted on GitHub and implemented as an R-package with a web application that supports both manual and semi-automated completion from model objects. It includes automated warnings for common pitfalls to guide authors and assist reviewers.
AI.result: The protocol and R-package are publicly available on GitHub (https://github.com/LOEK-RS/STeMP), enabling community contributions and feedback. The web application facilitates protocol completion and flags methodological issues, serving dual roles as an authoring guide and a reviewer assessment tool.
AI.conclusion: STeMP addresses the critical gap of standardized reporting in spatio-temporal machine-learning modelling. By providing structured guidance and automated quality checks, it aims to enhance model transparency, reproducibility, and trustworthiness in environmental research and its practical applications.

title: Inducing Comparability of Factorised Probability Distributions
summary: To allow for principled comparison between two probabilistic graphical models defined over non-identical variable sets, they have to be lifted to a common measurable space. To this end, we propose an extension scheme for any two given models and establish the formal foundation: Unmatched components are completed using conditionally uniform (Laplace) extensions such that the resulting joint distributions differ from the original ones only by multiplicative constants and coincide under projection. This preserves the probabilistic semantics while enabling the application of well-defined distributional discrepancy measures. We establish the invariance of the induced joint under projection and use the extensions to provide a minimal structural extension of two factor graphs to the smalles common measurable space as well as to a common graphical structure by a deterministic algorithm. In addition, we discuss structural and measure-theoretic properties and identify promising criteria for comparison methodologies.

AI.tldr: Proposes a principled extension scheme for comparing probabilistic graphical models defined over different variable sets by lifting them to a common measurable space using conditionally uniform (Laplace) completions.
AI.motivation: Comparing probabilistic graphical models with non-identical variable sets requires a common measurable space, but existing approaches lack a principled, measure-theoretic foundation for such lifting while preserving probabilistic semantics.
AI.method: Unmatched components are completed via conditionally uniform (Laplace) extensions, yielding joint distributions that differ from the originals only by multiplicative constants and coincide under projection. A deterministic algorithm provides minimal structural extension of factor graphs to the smallest common measurable space and common graphical structure.
AI.result: The induced joint distribution is invariant under projection, preserving original semantics. The method yields minimal structural extensions to both a common measurable space and a common graphical structure, with established structural and measure-theoretic properties.
AI.conclusion: The proposed Laplace extension scheme provides a rigorous, principled foundation for comparing PGMs over non-identical variable sets, enabling well-defined distributional discrepancy measures while identifying promising criteria for future comparison methodologies.

title: From Agent Failures to Text Policies: What Works and What Breaks
summary: TextGrad improves language-model systems by revising text from feedback. Its core thesis is that natural-language feedback can act as a gradient for optimizing text components without changing model weights. Applying it to agents is harder because feedback arrives only after a sequence of actions, making it difficult to identify which decision caused failure. We study this problem by separating the ability to follow a useful policy from the ability to learn that policy from experience. Our main finding is a clear gap between these two abilities. Human-written policies improve two frozen 7B agents on TextWorldExpress by 5.0 success points, showing that useful policy text exists. However, policies generated from agent trajectories do not reliably outperform fixed prompting, even with richer traces, counterfactual evidence, or iterative GEPA search. The main challenge for agent-level TextGrad is therefore not executing textual policy updates, but reliably generating and selecting them from experience.

AI.tldr: Textual gradient methods struggle in agent settings not because agents can't follow good policy text, but because reliably generating and selecting policy updates from trajectory experience remains the core bottleneck.
AI.motivation: TextGrad uses natural-language feedback as a "gradient" to optimize text components without weight updates. Prior work shows promise, but applying it to sequential decision-making agents introduces a credit-assignment problem: feedback arrives only after a full action sequence, making it hard to pinpoint which decision caused failure. The authors aim to decompose this into two sub-problems — policy following vs. policy learning from experience — and diagnose where the bottleneck lies.
AI.method: The authors decouple two capabilities: (1) following a useful textual policy and (2) learning/inducing such a policy from trajectory experience. They test human-written policies on frozen 7B agents in TextWorldExpress to establish an upper bound on policy-following ability. They then evaluate whether policies generated from agent trajectories — using richer traces, counterfactual evidence, or iterative GEPA search — can outperform fixed prompting baselines.
AI.result: Human-written policies improve two frozen 7B agents by +5.0 success points on TextWorldExpress, confirming that useful policy text exists and can be followed. However, experience-generated policies do not reliably beat fixed prompting, regardless of trace richness, counterfactual evidence, or iterative GEPA search. This reveals a clear gap between policy-following and policy-learning capabilities.
AI.conclusion: The primary challenge for agent-level TextGrad is not executing textual policy updates (agents can follow good policy text), but rather the reliable generation and selection of effective policy updates from experiential data. This reframes the problem as one of credit assignment and experience-driven policy induction rather than policy expressiveness or adherence.

title: When Does Recurrence Become an Algorithm? Convergence Selection in Weight-Tied Looped Transformers
summary: When does a weight-tied looped transformer -- one block applied T times -- implement an actual algorithm? We answer with four findings from controlled populations on group word problems. (1) The budget law: free training installs a linear computation frontier, a mechanism that solves v positions per loop, whose speed is priced by the training contract: v ~ n_train/T_train (exponent 0.98 +/- 0.04, R^2=0.99), exactly unity under T=n training. SGD selects a frontier matching the minimum the contract demands; granting more test-time loops than ever trained rescues late positions at fixed input length, yielding a principled halting rule T* = ceil(n / v-hat). (2) Architecture prior, not expressivity, picks the algorithm: standard-depth transformers learn parallel scans on this family; weight tying flips the selection to the serial frontier, even when positional addressing for a log-depth scan is supplied. At matched depth and parameters, untied models extrapolate worst and fail to learn A5 at all. (3) The walls are not where circuit complexity says: NC1-completeness costs nothing (A5 generalizes fully), while group order does (S5's 120x120 operator deadlocks joint learning) -- and an operator-first curriculum dissolves the wall in every seed. (4) Mechanisms are portable, not mandatable: warm-starting across budget contracts transfers the algorithm in every seed, re-pricing its speed, while imposing seriality through the input schedule fails where free training succeeds. These results are invisible to standard instruments, which provably saturate at the fixed points trained loops converge to. We introduce a head instrument, the convergence-time scaling tau(n,i), validate it causally via damage cones whose slope reproduces v, and show in-distribution head measurements predict out-of-distribution fate where tail metrics do not. Results replicate on the public easy-to-hard benchmark.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates when weight-tied looped transformers implement actual algorithms, using controlled populations on group word problems. Four key findings emerge: (1) a "budget law" where training establishes a linear computation frontier with speed v ~ n_train/T_train; (2) weight tying flips architecture selection from parallel to serial algorithms; (3) NC1-completeness doesn't hinder learning but group order (e.g., S5's 120×120 operator) does, curable by curriculum; (4) algorithmic mechanisms are portable via warm-starting but cannot be mandated through input scheduling. The authors introduce a new diagnostic, the convergence-time scaling τ(n,i), which predicts out-of-distribution behavior.
AI.motivation: Understanding when and how looped (weight-tied) transformers implement genuine algorithms versus merely pattern-matching. Existing analytical tools saturate at fixed points and fail to reveal the mechanistic structure of learned computations, particularly how training budget, architecture priors, and problem structure interact to determine algorithmic behavior and generalization.
AI.method: Controlled experiments on group word problems (permutation groups including A5, S5) using weight-tied transformers with varying training budgets (n_train, T_train) and test-time loops. Introduction of a new "convergence-time scaling" metric τ(n,i) and damage cone analysis to causally validate learned mechanisms. Ablations compare tied vs. untied architectures, curriculum strategies, and warm-starting across budget contracts.
AI.result: (1) Budget law: v ≈ n_train/T_train with exponent 0.98, R²=0.99; principled halting rule T* = ceil(n/v̂). (2) Weight tying flips algorithm selection from parallel scans to serial frontier; untied models fail A5 entirely. (3) NC1-completeness (A5) generalizes fully; S5's group order creates deadlock solvable by operator-first curriculum. (4) Warm-starting transfers algorithms across budgets; input schedule imposition fails. τ(n,i) and damage cones causally validate speed v and predict OOD fate.
AI.conclusion: Training budget, architecture priors (weight tying), and problem structure (group order, not circuit complexity) jointly determine whether looped transformers learn implementable algorithms. The introduced convergence-time scaling instrument provides mechanistic insight invisible to standard metrics, predicting out-of-distribution behavior from in-distribution measurements.

title: LeanFlow: A Case Study in Workflow-Driven Lean Autoformalization
comment: 14 pages, 3 figures, ICML 2026: AI for Math Workshop
summary: We present and evaluate LeanFlow, an LLM agent system specialized for translating mathematical papers into buildable Lean projects. Recent verifier-in-the-loop systems show that large formal artifacts can be produced, but it remains unclear which runtime mechanisms affect completion, auditability, or efficiency in document-to-project formalization. We study this question through case studies on two previously unformalized mathematical papers in number theory and measure theory, using model, proof-workflow, and toolset ablations with Kimi2.6 and GPT5.5; we report task outcome, API calls, input tokens, and output tokens. With Kimi2.6, the full workflow completes both document-level projects within the 2000-call budget, while no-queue variants reach the budget limit; with GPT5.5, all document-level variants complete, and the full workflow has the lowest or tied-lowest input-token cost on both sources. As complementary calibration, LeanFlow reaches 75.7% BEq+ on the PFR slice of RLM25 and solves all five ICML 2026 AI for Math TCS challenge projects in our GPT5.5 runs.

AI.tldr: LeanFlow is an LLM agent system that translates mathematical papers into buildable Lean projects. Evaluated on number theory and measure theory papers, it achieves full document-level formalization within budget using Kimi2.6, while GPT5.5 yields lowest input-token costs. It also achieves 75.7% BEq+ on RLM25's PFR slice and solves all five ICML 2026 AI for Math TCS challenge projects.
AI.motivation: While verifier-in-the-loop systems can produce large formal artifacts, it remains unclear which runtime mechanisms (queuing strategies, proof workflows, toolset configurations) affect completion, auditability, or efficiency in document-to-project formalization. This gap motivates a systematic ablation study.
AI.method: Case studies on two previously unformalized mathematical papers (number theory and measure theory). Ablation experiments varying model (Kimi2.6 vs. GPT5.5), proof-workflow mechanisms (full workflow vs. no-queue variants), and toolset configurations. Metrics: task outcome, API calls, input tokens, and output tokens, with a 2000-call budget. Complementary calibration on RLM25 (PFR slice, BEq+ metric) and ICML 2026 AI for Math TCS challenge.
AI.result: With Kimi2.6, the full workflow completes both document-level projects within the 2000-call budget; no-queue variants reach the budget limit without finishing. With GPT5.5, all document-level variants complete, and the full workflow achieves lowest or tied-lowest input-token cost on both sources. LeanFlow reaches 75.7% BEq+ on the PFR slice of RLM25 and solves all five ICML 2026 TCS challenge projects.
AI.conclusion: Runtime mechanisms — particularly queuing strategies — significantly affect completion and cost-efficiency in document-to-project formalization. LeanFlow demonstrates that careful workflow design enables budget-constrained, end-to-end formalization of real mathematical papers, with strong complementary performance on standard benchmarks.

title: Learning to Detect UI Principle Violations via Reinforcement Learning
summary:
Small language models and coding agents increasingly generate web front-end code, yet their outputs are typically evaluated primarily for functional correctness. A generated interface may compile, render, and pass unit tests while still violating established interface quality principles, including accessibility barriers, deceptive design patterns, poor visual hierarchy, and excessive decision complexity. Existing auditing approaches face a trade-off between cost, coverage, and scalability: expert human review provides rich judgment but is slow and expensive; frontier vision-language models offer broader reasoning capabilities but remain costly to deploy at scale; and rule-based tools such as axe-core and Lighthouse are inexpensive but primarily capture mechanically checkable accessibility issues.
  We investigate whether a lightweight vision-language model can serve as an effective critic for generated interfaces. We unify 19 interface-quality principles from three complementary sources of HCI knowledge: WCAG 2.2 accessibility standards, deceptive design taxonomies, and established theories of perception, cognition, and interaction. To train this critic, we construct a verified dataset of approximately 10,000 generated web pages by synthetically injecting known violations into clean, LLM-generated Tailwind pages.
  Continued reinforcement learning on a 4B vision-language model improves micro-F1 from 36\% to 84\%, with 13 of 19 principles exceeding 80\% F1. The resulting critic can audit generated interfaces, filter low-quality interface training data, and provide a reward signal for design-aware code generation. We release our data-generation recipe and injection/verification prompts to support reproducible evaluation and future work on scalable interface-quality assessment.

AI.tldr: A 4B vision-language model, trained via continued RL on a synthetically-generated dataset of ~10K web pages with injected quality violations, achieves 84% micro-F1 in auditing interface quality across 19 principles spanning accessibility, deceptive design, and HCI theory — outperforming rule-based tools and rivaling costly frontier models.
AI.motivation: Generated web front-end code is typically evaluated only for functional correctness, overlooking critical interface-quality dimensions such as accessibility, deceptive patterns, visual hierarchy, and decision complexity. Existing solutions present a cost-coverage-scalability trade-off: human review is expensive, frontier VLMs are costly at scale, and rule-based tools like axe-core/Lighthouse only catch mechanically checkable issues. This motivates exploring whether a lightweight VLM can fill the gap as a scalable, comprehensive interface-quality critic.
AI.method: The authors unify 19 interface-quality principles drawn from WCAG 2.2 accessibility standards, deceptive design taxonomies, and HCI theories of perception/cognition/interaction. They construct a verified dataset of ~10,000 generated Tailwind web pages by synthetically injecting known violations into clean LLM-generated pages. Continued reinforcement learning (RL) is then applied to a 4B vision-language model using this dataset to train it as an interface-quality critic.
AI.result: Continued RL on the 4B VLM improves micro-F1 from 36% to 84%. Of the 19 principles, 13 exceed 80% F1. The resulting critic is capable of auditing generated interfaces, filtering low-quality training data, and providing a reward signal for design-aware code generation.
AI.conclusion: A lightweight (4B) VLM can serve as an effective, scalable critic for web interface quality when trained via RL on synthetically-injected violation data. The authors release their data-generation recipe and injection/verification prompts to support reproducible evaluation and future work on scalable interface-quality assessment.

title: Are Single-Token Sparse Autoencoder Features Causally Necessary? Layer-Depth and SAE-Family Effects
summary: Sparse autoencoder (SAE) features are used to interpret and steer large language models, yet whether a feature's causal role is stable across SAE families remains untested. Single-token features that activate on one vocabulary item provide the diagnostic case where ground truth permits direct comparison. We analyze 3.9M features across six models and three SAE families using zero-ablation at full layer depth. Single-token features cluster 4.7x tighter in decoder space and concentrate in early layers (Layer 0 in GPT2-Small; L0-L4 in Gemma). Ablating them yields Benjamini-Hochberg-significant logit reductions in 178 of 208 full-layer conditions, with depth controlling whether damage cascades downstream or shapes the output directly. Cross-family causal differences exceed within-family scale effects: on the same base model, GemmaScope and BatchTopK features remain causally anchored, while LlamaScope features are locally redundant. The target token's rank recovers to within 2x baseline 96-98% of the time after the same ablation, and a controlled activation-function comparison reverses sign within the same model, leaving training recipe as the residual candidate. Cross-family interpretability claims are therefore sensitive to training methodology, not just activation function or scale.

AI.tldr: SAE features exhibit cross-family causal instability: single-token feature ablation effects vary significantly across SAE families trained on the same base model, with training recipe—not activation function or scale—emerging as the key factor undermining consistent interpretability claims.
AI.motivation: SAE features are widely used for interpreting and steering LLMs, but whether a feature's causal role remains stable across different SAE families has never been empirically tested. Single-token features (activating on one vocabulary item) offer a rare ground-truth diagnostic case for direct comparison.
AI.method: The authors analyzed 3.9 million features across six models and three SAE families (GemmaScope, BatchTopK, LlamaScope), applying zero-ablation at full layer depth. They measured: (1) feature clustering in decoder space, (2) layer distribution, (3) logit reduction significance via Benjamini-Hochberg correction, (4) target token rank recovery post-ablation, and (5) controlled activation-function comparisons to isolate training recipe effects.
AI.result: Single-token features cluster 4.7× tighter in decoder space and concentrate in early layers (Layer 0 in GPT2-Small; L0–L4 in Gemma). Ablation produced significant logit reductions in 178/208 full-layer conditions. Cross-family causal differences exceeded within-family scale effects: GemmaScope and BatchTopK remained causally anchored, while LlamaScope features were locally redundant. Target token rank recovered to within 2× baseline 96–98% of the time. A controlled activation-function comparison reversed sign within the same model, isolating training recipe as the residual causal factor.
AI.conclusion: Cross-family interpretability claims are sensitive to training methodology, not just activation function or model scale. This challenges the reliability of SAE-based causal analyses that do not account for the specific SAE family used.

title: Optimizing Hypergraph-Based RAG: Toward Better Fact Extraction and Chunk Retrieval
summary: GraphRAG enables deeper reasoning by structuring knowledge as graphs but struggles with n-ary facts. HyperGraphRAG uses hypergraphs for richer semantics, improving accuracy, yet relies on error-prone LLM extraction and inefficient standard chunk retrieval. We address this by employing self-consistency prompting to improve the extraction, and Personalized PageRank algorithm over hypergraph to enhance chunk retrieval.

AI.tldr: HyperGraphRAG improves retrieval-augmented generation by using hypergraphs to represent n-ary facts, and the proposed enhancements — self-consistency prompting and Personalized PageRank — address LLM extraction errors and inefficient chunk retrieval.
AI.motivation: Standard GraphRAG structures knowledge as binary relational graphs, which cannot natively capture n-ary facts involving more than two entities. HyperGraphRAG addresses this limitation using hypergraphs but suffers from two weaknesses: (1) error-prone LLM-based fact extraction and (2) inefficient retrieval based on standard chunk-level methods. The motivation is to remedy these two specific shortcomings.
AI.method: Two enhancements are proposed: (1) Self-consistency prompting — a technique that samples multiple reasoning paths from the LLM and selects the most consistent extraction, reducing extraction errors; (2) Personalized PageRank algorithm applied over the hypergraph structure — leveraging random-walk-based relevance propagation to improve chunk retrieval quality and efficiency beyond standard retrieval approaches.
AI.result: The abstract does not report quantitative results; it only describes the proposed method and its intended improvements over HyperGraphRAG.
AI.conclusion: The paper argues that combining self-consistency prompting with Personalized PageRank-based retrieval mitigates the key weaknesses of HyperGraphRAG, enabling more accurate extraction of n-ary facts and more effective chunk retrieval within hypergraph-structured knowledge representations.

title: REGARD: Regional Affective Differences in Large Language Models
comment: 17 pages, 11 figures, 3 tables. Includes evaluation of 19 language models, two independent VAD judges, and human validation on 300 items
summary: Large language models trained and aligned within different linguistic and regional ecosystems may frame the same political, cultural, and geopolitical entities in different ways. Such differences are often evaluated through sentiment, favorability, or stance, reducing model attitudes to a single positive-negative axis. We introduce REGARD, a study of what drives affective framing differences across LLMs on post-Soviet entities using target-directed Valence-Arousal-Dominance profiling. We query 19 models on 500 region-specific targets, score their responses with two independent LLM judges, GPT-4o-mini and Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, and validate the measurements on a 300-item human-annotated subset. Post-hoc Ward-linkage clustering of all 19 models by affective and response-behavior profiles yields three behavioral clusters that cut across model origin, family, and parameter count. Generic-answer rate is strongly associated with lower arousal (r = -0.81) and with cluster placement: models that deflect evaluative prompts with templated responses cluster together at low arousal regardless of origin. These findings show that VAD profiling captures emotional intensity, a dimension of affective framing that is largely invisible to conventional sentiment-based evaluation.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces REGARD, a study using Valence-Arousal-Dominance (VAD) profiling to analyze how LLMs differentially frame post-Soviet geopolitical entities, revealing that models cluster by response behavior rather than origin, with generic-answer rates strongly correlating with low arousal — capturing emotional intensity invisible to sentiment-based evaluation.
AI.motivation: Existing methods for evaluating LLM framing differences rely on unidimensional sentiment/favorability/stance axes, which collapse affective nuance into a single positive-negative spectrum. The authors argue this misses emotional intensity and other dimensions of how models construct affective meaning around politically and culturally charged entities, particularly in underrepresented post-Soviet contexts.
AI.method: The authors queried 19 LLMs on 500 region-specific post-Soviet targets. Responses were scored using two independent LLM judges (GPT-4o-mini and Qwen3.6-35B-A3B) on the Valence-Arousal-Dominance affective dimensions. Measurements were validated against a 300-item human-annotated subset. Post-hoc Ward-linkage hierarchical clustering was applied to group models by their VAD profiles and response-behavior patterns.
AI.result: Clustering revealed three behavioral clusters that cut across model origin, family, and parameter count. Generic-answer rate showed a strong negative correlation with arousal (r = -0.81). Models that deflect evaluative prompts with templated, non-committal responses consistently clustered together in the low-arousal region, irrespective of their geographic or organizational origin.
AI.conclusion: VAD profiling effectively captures emotional intensity as a dimension of affective framing that conventional sentiment analysis overlooks. The behavioral convergence of models toward generic, low-arousal responses — regardless of origin — suggests that response style may be a more salient differentiator of LLM affect than developer geography or linguistic ecosystem.

title: One Round Is All You Need: Analytic Federated Learning for Task-Heterogeneous Multi-Label Medical Image Classification
comment: The 14th IEEE International Conference on Healthcare Informatics
summary: Federated learning (FL) enables multiple clinical institutions to collaboratively train a shared disease classifier without centralizing patient data. In practice, however, each institution annotates only the pathologies within its area of expertise, so the federation operates under task heterogeneity: each client holds labels for a strict subset of the target disease categories while the remaining classes are entirely unobserved at that site. Existing gradient-based FL methods fail under this setting because they require hundreds of communication rounds to converge and because missing class labels introduce systematic false-negative bias that the model cannot correct without a principled mechanism. We propose an analytic federated learning framework for multi-label medical image classification under task heterogeneity. The proposed method replaces iterative gradient optimization with three closed-form operations: a balanced label projection that neutralizes class-imbalance bias by normalizing positive and negative contributions to equal total mass; a per-class absolute aggregation law that independently assembles the optimal ridge-regression classifier for each disease category from the sufficient statistics uploaded by its annotating clients; and an optional analytic pseudo-label refinement round that propagates missing-class knowledge from a confidence-filtered teacher classifier to non-annotating clients. The entire procedure requires at most two communication rounds, irrespective of the degree of task heterogeneity or the number of participating clients.
