Experiments on ChestXray14 under four progressively severe missing-class configurations demonstrate that the proposed method consistently outperforms the state-of-the-art federated multi-label method FedMLP by up to 18.44 BACC points and 13.24 AUC points, while reducing the communication.

AI.tldr: A two-round analytic federated learning framework for multi-label medical image classification under task heterogeneity, using closed-form operations (balanced label projection, per-class absolute aggregation, and optional pseudo-label refinement) that outperforms FedMLP by up to 18.44 BACC points while drastically reducing communication rounds.
AI.motivation: In clinical federated learning, task heterogeneity arises because each institution annotates only pathologies within its expertise, leaving many disease classes unobserved at each site. Existing gradient-based FL methods fail here: they require hundreds of communication rounds and suffer from systematic false-negative bias from missing labels, with no principled correction mechanism.
AI.method: The proposed analytic FL framework replaces iterative gradient optimization with three closed-form operations: (1) a balanced label projection that neutralizes class-imbalance bias by normalizing positive and negative contributions to equal total mass; (2) a per-class absolute aggregation law that independently constructs an optimal ridge-regression classifier for each disease from sufficient statistics of annotating clients; and (3) an optional analytic pseudo-label refinement round that propagates missing-class knowledge from a confidence-filtered teacher to non-annotating clients. The entire procedure needs at most two communication rounds.
AI.result: On ChestXray14 under four progressively severe missing-class configurations, the method consistently outperforms the state-of-the-art FedMLP by up to 18.44 BACC points and 13.24 AUC points, with substantially reduced communication cost.
AI.conclusion: The analytic FL framework effectively addresses task heterogeneity in multi-label medical image classification with a communication-efficient, closed-form approach that corrects false-negative bias and achieves superior performance compared to gradient-based federated methods.

title: MiniCache: Reusable Program Caching with Small Model Interfaces for Efficient LLM Inference
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for program-aided reasoning, agentic decision making, and structured task execution, but these applications often incur high inference cost. We present MiniCache, a reusable program caching framework that transforms Program-of-Thought (PoT) programs into parameterized cache objects, enabling reusable computation across structurally similar requests. MiniCache reuses the same small model for semantic variable extraction on cache-hit requests and speculative drafting during target-LLM generation, reducing expensive target-LLM invocations while preserving task quality. Experiments on shopping-style request datasets, WebShop, Formula, and CodeTAT-QA demonstrate that MiniCache improves the trade-off between inference latency, cache reuse, and accuracy, achieving up to 3.1x lower latency and 2.8x higher throughput under parallel serving. These results show that small models are most effective not as replacements for large models, but as lightweight interface models that enable reliable and efficient reusable program caching.

AI.tldr: MiniCache is a reusable program caching framework that transforms Program-of-Thought outputs into parameterized cache objects, using a small model for semantic variable extraction and speculative drafting to reduce expensive LLM calls while maintaining task quality, achieving up to 3.1× lower latency and 2.8× higher throughput.
AI.motivation: LLMs are increasingly deployed for program-aided reasoning and agentic tasks, but these applications incur high inference costs. Many requests are structurally similar, yet current systems recompute from scratch each time, wasting computation and increasing latency.
AI.method: MiniCache introduces a framework with three core mechanisms: (1) transforming PoT programs into parameterized cache objects that capture reusable computation templates; (2) using a small model for semantic variable extraction on cache-hit requests to identify and bind parameters; and (3) employing the same small model for speculative drafting during target-LLM generation, reducing the number of expensive target-LLM forward passes while preserving output quality.
AI.result: Experiments on WebShop, Formula, CodeTAT-QA, and shopping-style request datasets show MiniCache achieves up to 3.1× lower inference latency and 2.8× higher throughput under parallel serving, while maintaining accuracy comparable to uncached baselines.
AI.conclusion: Small models are most effective not as replacements for large models, but as lightweight interface models that enable reliable and efficient reusable program caching, offering a practical path to reducing LLM inference costs in production settings.

title: Rushes: A Human Preference Dataset for Pluralistic Alignment
summary: We introduce Rushes, a dataset and benchmark for studying revealed human engagement preferences in interactive narrative environments. Rushes is collected through a game interface where users interact with AI-generated branching narratives and select one choice from a small, explicit candidate set at each decision point. Each interaction logs the full candidate set, the user's choice, and the evolving narrative context, yielding time-ordered trajectories with persistent user-level identifiers. Rushes contains 44,226 decision events from 8,167 unique users across six games, capturing sequential, personalized engagement behavior rather than static judgments. We show that user choices exhibit structured, non-random patterns, quantified by a low choice entropy relative to a uniform baseline. We position Rushes as a diagnostic benchmark for pluralistic alignment and demonstrate a robust Engagement Gap: state-of-the-art LLMs, including GPT-5, fail to outperform simple baselines. While classical Matrix Factorization (SVD) captures measurable personalized signal (37.7%), frontier LLMs (34.23%) struggle to even match the Popularity Baseline (36.4%) on event-level choice prediction. This gap suggests that single, population-level objectives, like those used in modern RLHF, appear insufficient to capture heterogeneous, context-dependent engagement signals. As a result, even highly capable models default to majority preferences rather than adapting to individual trajectories. We release Rushes to support research into pluralistic alignment and sequential decision-making in generative systems. The full code for the platform and dataset will be available here: https://github.com/microsoft/rushes

AI.tldr: Rushes is a dataset of 44,226 interactive narrative decisions from 8,167 users across six games, designed to benchmark pluralistic alignment. It reveals an "Engagement Gap": even frontier LLMs like GPT-5 fail to beat simple baselines on personalized choice prediction, suggesting current RLHF-style population-level objectives cannot capture heterogeneous user preferences.
AI.motivation: Current alignment methods (e.g., RLHF) optimize for aggregated, population-level preferences, which may fail to capture the heterogeneous, context-dependent, and sequential nature of individual human engagement. There is a lack of benchmarks that reflect revealed preferences in interactive, trajectory-based settings rather than static preference judgments.
AI.method: The authors built a game platform where users make explicit choices among small candidate sets at decision points in AI-generated branching narratives. They logged full candidate sets, user choices, and evolving narrative context, yielding time-ordered trajectories with persistent user IDs. They benchmarked several models — including classical Matrix Factorization (SVD), a Popularity Baseline, and frontier LLMs (including GPT-5) — on event-level choice prediction.
AI.result: User choices show low entropy relative to uniform, confirming structured, non-random patterns. SVD achieved 37.7% accuracy, capturing measurable personalized signal. Frontier LLMs scored only 34.23%, failing to surpass the Popularity Baseline (36.4%). This "Engagement Gap" demonstrates that state-of-the-art models default to majority preferences and cannot adapt to individual trajectories.
AI.conclusion: Population-level objectives used in modern RLHF are insufficient for capturing heterogeneous, context-dependent engagement. The Rushes dataset and benchmark are released to spur research on pluralistic alignment and sequential decision-making in generative systems, pushing beyond one-size-fits-all preference optimization.

title: Scaling Interpretable Transformers with Parity Bottleneck Layers
summary: Language models are thought to exhibit the phenomenon of superposition, representing many more features than dimensions in their residual streams. Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are designed to recover such features post-hoc, but training models that are interpretable by construction has remained impractical, as a per-layer over-complete bottleneck is prohibitively expensive in both memory and compute. To overcome this issue, we introduce the ParityTransformer, a GPT-2-scale architecture whose intermediate representations are efficient and wide / sparse by design. At each layer, a Deep Parity Bottleneck (DPB) replaces a learned over-complete basis with a parameter-free algebraic dictionary, providing a deterministic incoherence guarantee and eliminating the memory requirements that have prevented per-layer interpretable bottlenecks at scale. A DPB is a hierarchically structured sparse bottleneck which efficiently enforces sparsity using a multi-level mixture-of-experts approach: a hardware-aware implementation that closes the cost gap between activation sparse and dense training to a manageable interpretability tax. Empirically, ParityTransformers perform at least as well as post-hoc SAEs on sparse probing tasks, while out-performing on measures of feature absorption, steering effectiveness, and fine-grained causal interventions. Because subsequent computation acts only on features that survive the sparse bottleneck, the ParityTransformer's features are native to the model's forwards pass by construction, addressing the question of whether SAEs probe features the model actually uses during computation. We see this as a step toward training models whose internal representations are interpretable by design rather than recovered post hoc.

AI.tldr: The ParityTransformer introduces Deep Parity Bottlenecks (DPBs)—parameter-free algebraic dictionaries that replace learned over-complete bases—to train GPT-2-scale language models with sparse, interpretable internal representations by construction, eliminating the need for post-hoc sparse autoencoders. The model matches or exceeds SAE-based approaches on interpretability metrics while closing the computational gap between sparse and dense training.
AI.motivation: Language models exhibit superposition, encoding many more features than dimensions. While sparse autoencoders (SAEs) recover these features post-hoc, training models that are interpretable by construction has been impractical because per-layer over-complete bottlenecks are prohibitively expensive in memory and compute. The authors aim to make interpretability native to the forward pass rather than retrofitted.
AI.method: The authors introduce the ParityTransformer with a Deep Parity Bottleneck (DPB) at each layer. The DPB replaces a learned over-complete basis with a parameter-free algebraic dictionary that provides deterministic incoherence guarantees and eliminates memory overhead. It uses a hierarchically structured sparse bottleneck with a multi-level mixture-of-experts approach, implemented in a hardware-aware manner to minimize the cost gap between activation-sparse and dense training (termed the "interpretability tax").
AI.result: ParityTransformers perform at least as well as post-hoc SAEs on sparse probing tasks. They outperform SAEs on feature absorption, steering effectiveness, and fine-grained causal interventions. Because subsequent computation only operates on features that survive the sparse bottleneck, the features are natively part of the model's forward pass, confirming they are genuinely used during computation.
AI.conclusion: Training models with interpretable representations by design (rather than recovering them post-hoc) is feasible at scale. The ParityTransformer demonstrates that parameter-free algebraic bottlenecks can enforce sparsity efficiently, yielding features that are both interpretable and causally relevant to the model's computation, representing a step toward inherently interpretable language models.

title: Telco-GAIA: Bilingual Benchmark for Agents in Telecom Domain
summary: We introduce Telco-GAIA, a bilingual, multi-modal benchmark for evaluating tool-using agents on the data of a real-world telecommunications operator. Telco-GAIA comprises 100 human-verified question-answering tasks, in English and Arabic, that each demand multi-hop reasoning (4.2 hops on average) over three heterogeneous sources: a static website snapshot (HTML, images, and linked PDFs), a synthetic relational SQL database, and external web archives, spanning text, image, and tabular modalities. The benchmark is delivered as a sandboxed Docker environment and scored by normalized exact string matching, making evaluation objective, deterministic, and reproducible over time without any LLM-as-a-Judge. Evaluating a purpose-built reference agent across twelve commercial and open LLMs, we find Telco-GAIA challenging: even the strongest model solves only 71% of tasks; under a moderate cost budget, this falls to about 40%, and the visually grounded categories remain the weakest, where the average backend scores below 30%, leaving substantial headroom in document and image understanding. Telco-GAIA offers a rigorous, reproducible testbed for enterprise agents and a template for constructing closed-domain benchmarks.

AI.tldr: Telco-GAIA is a bilingual (English/Arabic), multi-modal benchmark with 100 human-verified QA tasks for evaluating tool-using agents on real telecom operator data, featuring multi-hop reasoning across heterogeneous sources. Even the strongest LLM achieves only 71% accuracy, with visually grounded tasks scoring below 30%.
AI.motivation: Current agent benchmarks lack (1) real-world enterprise data complexity, (2) multi-modal reasoning across heterogeneous sources, (3) reproducible, objective evaluation without LLM-as-a-Judge, and (4) multilingual support — particularly for underrepresented languages like Arabic in telecom contexts.
AI.method: The authors construct Telco-GAIA: 100 human-verified QA tasks requiring multi-hop reasoning (avg. 4.2 hops) over three heterogeneous sources — a static website snapshot (HTML/images/PDFs), a synthetic relational SQL database, and external web archives — spanning text, image, and tabular modalities. The benchmark is packaged as a sandboxed Docker environment with deterministic scoring via normalized exact string matching. A purpose-built reference agent is evaluated across 12 commercial and open LLMs, including under a moderate cost budget constraint.
AI.result: The strongest model solves only 71% of tasks. Under a moderate cost budget, performance drops to ~40%. Visually grounded categories are the weakest, with average backend scores below 30%, indicating substantial headroom in document and image understanding. Multi-hop reasoning over heterogeneous sources proves highly challenging across all models tested.
AI.conclusion: Telco-GAIA provides a rigorous, deterministic, and reproducible testbed for enterprise-grade tool-using agents and serves as a template for constructing closed-domain, multi-modal, multilingual benchmarks. The significant performance gap — particularly for visually grounded tasks — highlights critical areas for future improvement in document/image understanding for agentic systems.

title: Are Diversity Metrics Measuring Diversity? A Capability-Controlled Audit of Majority-Vote Gain in LLM Ensembles
summary: Majority voting over LLMs is widely assumed to benefit from diversity, and diversity measures are used to choose which models to combine. We ask whether five such measures track diversity or mainly re-express capability, auditing them as predictors of majority-vote gain over the best member across 31,900 subsets of 30 LLMs on MMLU-Pro (29 on TruthfulQA) under explicit capability controls. Three findings emerge. First, latent complementarity is ubiquitous: oracle gain is positive in 100% of subsets, yet simple voting beats the strongest member in only 9.98% of all canonical size-3 subsets (18.71% with held-out best selection); the pooled size-2-4 rate is 1.27%, partly reflecting deterministic even-size voting behavior. Second, a joint-correctness proxy (strict diversity) is nearly collinear with one minus mean accuracy (size-3 Spearman rho = +0.991 / +0.988); raw diversity-gain associations are strongly capability-entangled and, with one exception, unstable under control. Third, three linear contingency-table statistics are algebraically non-separable; after capability control, the empirically stable remainder is a modest residual pairwise co-failure association in which more shared error corresponds to lower gain. This direction is robust, but its magnitude is configuration-dependent. Joint rawspace linear regressions treating strict diversity, disagreement, and double-fault as independent predictors are rank-deficient by construction.

AI.tldr: This paper audits five diversity measures used to select LLMs for majority voting ensembles. Across 31,900 LLM subsets, it finds that apparent diversity-gain correlations are almost entirely driven by capability confounds. After controlling for accuracy, only a residual pairwise co-failure signal remains — more shared errors predict lower gain — but its magnitude is configuration-dependent. Standard linear regressions combining these measures are algebraically rank-deficient.
AI.motivation: The prevailing assumption in LLM ensembling is that diversity among models drives majority-voting gains, and diversity measures are routinely used to select which models to combine. However, it is unclear whether these measures genuinely capture complementarity or merely re-express differences in individual model capability (accuracy). The authors seek to rigorously disentangle diversity from capability to determine what, if anything, diversity measures contribute to predicting ensemble performance beyond what accuracy alone explains.
AI.method: The authors evaluate five diversity measures as predictors of majority-vote gain over the best ensemble member. They construct 31,900 subsets of 30 LLMs on MMLU-Pro (and 29 on TruthfulQA), computing for each subset: individual accuracies, pairwise agreement/disagreement statistics, the diversity measures, and actual majority-vote gain. They then apply explicit capability controls — partialling out mean accuracy and using residualized analyses — to test whether diversity-gain associations survive. They also provide algebraic decompositions showing that three common contingency-table statistics (strict diversity, disagreement, double-fault) are linearly dependent, rendering joint regressions rank-deficient.
AI.result: Three central findings: (1) Oracle (latent complementarity) gain is positive in 100% of subsets, yet simple majority voting beats the strongest member in only 9.98% of size-3 subsets (1.27% pooled for sizes 2–4). (2) A joint-correctness proxy ("strict diversity") is nearly collinear with 1 − mean accuracy (Spearman ρ ≈ +0.99), and raw diversity-gain associations are heavily capability-entangled — only one measure shows any stability under control. (3) Three linear contingency-table statistics (strict diversity, disagreement, double-fault) are algebraically non-separable; after capability control, the only stable residual signal is a modest negative association between pairwise co-failure rate and gain: more shared errors → lower gain. The direction is robust but magnitude varies by configuration.
AI.conclusion: Diversity, as operationalized by standard measures, offers almost no additional predictive value for majority-voting gain beyond what mean accuracy already captures. The seemingly positive diversity-gain relationship is a statistical artifact of capability confounding. The sole robust residual signal — co-failure — is theoretically coherent but too weak and context-dependent to serve as a practical selection criterion. Researchers should treat claims about "diversity" in LLM ensembles with skepticism and recognize that simple accuracy remains the dominant factor.

title: SiGMA: Sign-Guided Merging and Adaptation for Multimodal Continual Instruction Tuning
summary: Multimodal Continual Instruction Tuning (MCIT) is crucial for adapting Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) to evolving a sequence of downstream tasks. Prior methods mostly utilize Mixture of Experts or expansion merge approach, primarily focusing on catastrophic forgetting, yet they still suffer from negative interference during inference, where newly learned updates overwrite useful prior knowledge and degrade overall performance. To address this, we propose SiGMA (Sign Guided Merging and Adaptation), a simple yet effective framework that mitigates negative interference with two components: sign guided adaptive tuning during training and sign guided merging at inference. Sign guided adaptive tuning reduces collisions with past knowledge and learns the current task with minimal drift, mitigating severe forgetting. Sign guided merging further improves consolidation by selectively scaling salient parameters to preserve and amplify useful task specific knowledge. Experiments on UCIT and DCL benchmarks show that SiGMA significantly reduces negative interference and outperforms state of the art MCIT methods. Our code is available at SiGMA.

AI.tldr: SiGMA proposes a sign-guided framework for Multimodal Continual Instruction Tuning that reduces negative interference during both training (via sign-guided adaptive tuning) and inference (via sign-guided merging), outperforming existing MCIT methods on UCIT and DCL benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing MCIT methods (MoE, expansion merge) focus on catastrophic forgetting but still suffer from negative interference at inference, where new updates overwrite useful prior knowledge and degrade overall performance.
AI.method: SiGMA has two components: (1) Sign Guided Adaptive Tuning — during training, it reduces collisions with past knowledge and learns new tasks with minimal drift; (2) Sign Guided Merging — at inference, it selectively scales salient parameters to preserve and amplify useful task-specific knowledge.
AI.result: SiGMA significantly reduces negative interference and achieves state-of-the-art performance on UCIT and DCL benchmarks compared to existing MCIT methods.
AI.conclusion: SiGMA is a simple yet effective solution that addresses both catastrophic forgetting and negative interference in MCIT, demonstrating superior consolidation of multimodal continual instruction tuning.

title: The Geometry of Personality: Activation Steering with Jungian Cognitive Functions
summary:
Activation steering enables control and interpretation of LLMs, yet existing work primarily models personality through static trait frameworks such as the Big Five. We investigate whether personality can instead be represented and controlled as a set of cognitive processes using the eight Jungian Cognitive Functions. To this end, we introduce a framework comprising a Jungian evaluation protocol and a dataset of over 2,100 role-playing character narrations.
  Activation steering vector extraction and evaluation experiments on Llama-3.1-8B demonstrate effective monotonic control over all eight cognitive functions through activation steering. Beyond controllability, our analysis reveals that: 1. personality information is concentrated in middle transformer layers; 2. steering vectors exhibit structured geometric relationships consistent with distinctions between rational and irrational functions; 3. effective multi-dimensional steering directions cannot be recovered as linear combinations of single-function directions. These findings provide new insights into the representation of personality in LLM activation space and establish a framework for studying interpretable, effective, and multi-dimensional personality control.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes representing LLM personality through Jungian Cognitive Functions (eight processes) rather than static trait models like the Big Five. Using a dataset of 2,100+ role-playing narrations and activation steering on Llama-3.1-8B, the authors demonstrate effective monotonic control over all eight functions, find personality concentrated in middle layers, reveal geometric structure aligned with rational/irrational distinctions, and show multi-dimensional steering requires non-linear combinations.
AI.motivation: Existing activation steering work models personality through static trait frameworks (e.g., Big Five), which overlooks the dynamic, process-oriented nature of personality. The authors argue that Jungian Cognitive Functions — eight distinct cognitive processes — offer a richer, more granular representation of how personality manifests in cognition, enabling more interpretable and multidimensional control.
AI.method: The authors introduce a two-component framework: (1) a Jungian evaluation protocol and a dataset of over 2,100 role-playing character narrations annotated with the eight cognitive functions; (2) activation steering vector extraction on Llama-3.1-8B, where vectors are derived to control each function. They evaluate monotonic controllability and analyze vector geometry, layer-wise concentration, and linear combinability for multi-dimensional steering.
AI.result: Activation steering achieves effective monotonic control over all eight Jungian cognitive functions. Key findings: (1) personality-relevant activation information is concentrated in middle transformer layers; (2) steering vectors exhibit structured geometric relationships aligning with the theoretical rational vs. irrational function dichotomy; (3) effective multi-dimensional steering directions cannot be recovered through linear combinations of single-function vectors, indicating non-linear representational structure.
AI.conclusion: Personality in LLMs can be meaningfully represented and controlled through Jungian cognitive processes rather than static traits. The framework enables interpretable, effective, multi-dimensional personality control, and the geometric and layer-wise analyses offer new insights into how personality information is encoded in activation space.

title: Adaptive Multi-Horizon Reinforcement Learning
summary: Effective decision-making in complex and changing environments requires balancing short-term and long-term consequences. In reinforcement learning (RL), this trade-off is typically controlled through a fixed discount factor, which imposes a single exponentially discounted temporal horizon. However, biological agents exhibit flexible and adaptive temporal discounting, suggesting that effective planning requires multiple timescales. Here, we propose a multi-horizon approach that adaptively selects and combines temporal horizons, enabling robust adaptation to changes in reward structure without manual discount-factor tuning. This flexibility makes the method particularly suitable for continual learning scenarios involving task switches and varying environmental configurations. Empirically, we demonstrate that our approach identifies effective discount factors across a range of MiniGrid environments, including continual settings composed of three sequentially changing tasks. These results suggest that adaptive temporal discounting can improve parameter efficiency and enhance adaptability in both artificial and biologically inspired learning systems.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a multi-horizon RL approach that adaptively selects and combines multiple discount factors, enabling flexible temporal discounting without manual tuning, and demonstrates its effectiveness in continual learning scenarios with task switches.
AI.motivation: Fixed discount factors in standard RL impose a single exponentially discounted horizon, which lacks the flexibility seen in biological agents that adaptively balance short-term and long-term consequences. This rigidity is especially problematic in continual learning with changing reward structures and task switches.
AI.method: A multi-horizon approach that adaptively selects and combines multiple temporal horizons (discount factors), allowing the agent to dynamically adjust its effective planning horizon in response to environmental changes without manual tuning.
AI.result: The method successfully identifies effective discount factors across a range of MiniGrid environments and performs well in continual settings with three sequentially changing tasks.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive temporal discounting improves parameter efficiency and adaptability in both artificial and biologically inspired learning systems, offering a promising direction for robust continual RL.

title: Reliability-Aware LLM Alignment from Inconsistent Human Feedback
summary: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) is critical for aligning Large Language Models (LLMs) with human preferences. However, its efficacy is often compromised by the inherent inconsistency and subjectivity of human annotations. Existing preference optimization frameworks, such as Direct Preference Optimization (DPO), typically treat ambiguous pairs with high annotator disagreement identically to those with unanimous consensus, forcing models to overfit to inconsistent supervision signals and leading to suboptimal alignment. In this work, we propose Reliability-Guided Preference Optimization (RGPO), a robust framework designed to mitigate the impact of inconsistent human feedback. RGPO estimates annotator reliability and infers latent ground truth labels from noisy human feedback to identify robust preferences. Furthermore, we introduce a reliability-aware consistency optimization that dynamically modulates the training objective based on the consensus level of annotations, ensuring the model prioritizes high-consensus supervision signals. Extensive experiments on LLM alignment benchmarks demonstrate that RGPO effectively reduces inconsistency and noise in training data and achieves superior performance compared to widely adopted RLHF baselines. Our code and configurations are available at https://github.com/GenieHuang/RGPO.

AI.tldr: RGPO is a framework that addresses inconsistent human annotations in RLHF by estimating annotator reliability, inferring latent ground truth, and dynamically weighting training based on annotation consensus, achieving superior LLM alignment over standard RLHF baselines.
AI.motivation: RLHF relies on human preference annotations, which are inherently noisy, inconsistent, and subjective. Existing methods like DPO treat all preference pairs equally — regardless of annotator agreement — forcing models to overfit conflicting supervision signals, which degrades alignment quality.
AI.method: RGPO introduces two key components: (1) annotator reliability estimation and latent ground truth inference from noisy labels to identify robust preferences; (2) a reliability-aware consistency optimization that dynamically modulates the training objective, emphasizing high-consensus annotations and down-weighting low-consensus ones.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on LLM alignment benchmarks show that RGPO effectively reduces the impact of inconsistency and noise in training data, yielding superior performance over widely adopted RLHF baselines.
AI.conclusion: By explicitly modeling annotator reliability and annotation consensus, RGPO offers a more robust preference optimization framework that mitigates the detrimental effects of inconsistent human feedback, leading to better-aligned LLMs.

title: REFACT: Adaptive Fact Restatement for Compact and Faithful Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
summary: Large language models increasingly rely on long-form reasoning for complex tasks, yet their reasoning traces may drift away from the supplied context when evidence is sparse, noisy, or in conflict with parametric knowledge. Existing grounding methods either attach citations after generation or encourage evidence retrieval inside the trace, but they often do not ensure that cited content is sufficient for the local inference and final answer. We propose REFACT, an adaptive fact-restatement citation framework that trains models to decide when a reasoning step needs contextual grounding and at what granularity source facts should be restated. This design avoids both unsupported inference and indiscriminate fact copying by turning citations into answer-supporting intermediate states. REFACT is optimized with a two-stage SFT-to-RL pipeline in which a citation-utility reward encourages cited facts to be well-formed, source-traceable, and answer-sufficient. Experiments on LongBench, LV-Eval, and ConFiQA show that REFACT improves long-context QA and counterfactual faithfulness while substantially reducing token consumption. Further analysis shows that REFACT preserves more answer-bearing evidence with fewer restated facts, yielding reasoning traces that are denser rather than longer. All code and data are available at https://github.com/NEUIR/REFACT.

AI.tldr: REFACT is an adaptive citation framework that trains LLMs to restate source facts at appropriate granularity during reasoning, using a two-stage SFT-to-RL pipeline with a citation-utility reward, improving QA accuracy and faithfulness while reducing token consumption.
AI.motivation: LLM reasoning traces often drift from context when evidence is sparse, noisy, or conflicts with parametric knowledge. Existing grounding methods either post-hoc attach citations or loosely encourage retrieval during reasoning, but fail to ensure cited content is sufficient for the local inference step and final answer.
AI.method: REFACT trains models to decide when and at what granularity to restate source facts as intermediate reasoning states. It uses a two-stage SFT-to-RL pipeline with a citation-utility reward that optimizes for well-formed, source-traceable, and answer-sufficient cited facts.
AI.result: On LongBench, LV-Eval, and ConFiQA, REFACT improves long-context QA and counterfactual faithfulness while substantially reducing token consumption. It preserves more answer-bearing evidence with fewer restated facts, producing denser reasoning traces.
AI.conclusion: REFACT effectively bridges contextual grounding and efficient reasoning by turning citations into answer-supporting intermediate states, yielding denser rather than longer reasoning traces that maintain faithfulness without indiscriminate copying.

title: End-to-End Learning of Safe Optimal Feedback Control in High Dimensions with Control Barrier Function Layers
summary: We consider the problem of learning high-dimensional semi-global feedback controllers under hard safety constraints enforced by control barrier functions (CBFs). Incorporating CBFs into end-to-end policy training requires embedding a quadratic-program-based safety filter as an optimization layer, but computational and differentiation bottlenecks have largely restricted prior approaches to low-dimensional systems, typically with at most 16 state dimensions. We address this limitation by combining operator splitting with the recently developed Jacobian-Free Backpropagation (JFB) method to enable scalable end-to-end training while preserving hard safety guarantees through the CBF safety filter. We justify this training methodology theoretically using nonsmooth analysis techniques and demonstrate its effectiveness on high-dimensional multi-agent nonlinear control problems with state and control dimensions up to 1200 and 400, respectively.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a scalable method for end-to-end training of high-dimensional control policies with hard safety constraints via CBFs, combining operator splitting with Jacobian-Free Backpropagation to overcome computational bottlenecks. The approach is validated on multi-agent systems with up to 1200 state and 400 control dimensions.
AI.motivation: Existing approaches for learning safety-critical controllers embed CBF-based quadratic program (QP) safety filters as differentiable optimization layers. However, the computational cost and difficulty of differentiating through these QPs have limited prior work to low-dimensional systems (≤16 state dimensions). There is a clear need for scalable training methods that preserve hard safety guarantees for high-dimensional systems.
AI.method: The authors combine operator splitting techniques with Jacobian-Free Backpropagation (JFB) to enable efficient end-to-end training. Operator splitting is used to solve the CBF-QP safety filter efficiently at scale, while JFB avoids explicitly computing Jacobians through the optimization layer during backpropagation. The training methodology is theoretically justified using nonsmooth analysis techniques.
AI.result: The proposed method is demonstrated on high-dimensional multi-agent nonlinear control problems with state dimensions up to 1200 and control dimensions up to 400, successfully enabling end-to-end training with hard safety guarantees at scales far beyond prior approaches.
AI.conclusion: Combining operator splitting with JFB provides a practical and theoretically grounded pathway for scalable end-to-end learning of safety-critical controllers in high-dimensional settings, significantly expanding the applicability of CBF-based safe reinforcement learning.

title: CANN Bench: Benchmarking Agent Generated Kernels against Real NPU and Algorithmic Limits
summary: AI agents are now capable of writing, compiling, and iteratively optimizing low-level operator kernels on different hardware platforms. Existing benchmarks, however, focus almost exclusively on CUDA and Triton, leaving hardware ecosystems with less-exposed programming models without a common evaluation baseline. We present CANN Bench, an open benchmark for AI-generated operator code on Huawei's Ascend NPU. The current release covers 53 operators and 1060 test cases organized into four difficulty tiers -- from simple elementwise primitives to MoE dispatch and FlashAttention kernels -- spanning FP16, BF16, FP32, and INT8 precision formats. Evaluation adopts a \textbf{three-dimensional weighted composite score} that treats compilation, functional correctness, and performance as independent axes, providing a principled reward signal for kernel-generation agents. Performance is graded against an out-of-the-box PyTorch-on-Ascend baseline and an analytical per-case Hardware-Anchored Performance (HAP) limit on real NPU hardware, ensuring scores reflect genuine optimization headroom rather than measurement artifacts. The evaluation harness is designed to resist reward hacking from the ground up. CANN Bench is versioned within the official CANN repository and is designed for long-term community co-construction, providing the Ascend ecosystem with a quantitative, reproducible, and sustainably maintained yardstick for AI operator-authoring capability.

AI.tldr: CANN Bench is an open benchmark for evaluating AI-generated operator kernels on Huawei's Ascend NPU, covering 53 operators across 1060 test cases in four difficulty tiers, using a three-dimensional composite score (compilation, correctness, performance) with hardware-anchored performance limits to resist reward hacking.
AI.motivation: Existing AI kernel-generation benchmarks focus almost exclusively on CUDA and Triton, leaving hardware platforms with less-exposed programming models—such as Huawei's Ascend NPU—without a standardized evaluation baseline. This gap hinders fair comparison and progress in AI-assisted operator development across diverse hardware ecosystems.
AI.method: The authors construct CANN Bench with 53 operators and 1060 test cases across four difficulty tiers (elementwise primitives to FlashAttention/MoE kernels) and four precision formats (FP16, BF16, FP32, INT8). Evaluation uses a three-dimensional weighted composite score measuring compilation success, functional correctness, and performance. Performance is graded against both a PyTorch-on-Ascend baseline and an analytical Hardware-Anchored Performance (HAP) limit computed per case on real NPU hardware. The harness is explicitly designed to prevent reward hacking.
AI.result: The benchmark is released as a versioned artifact within the official CANN repository, providing a reproducible, quantitative yardstick. The three-axis scoring framework yields principled reward signals that reflect genuine optimization headroom rather than measurement artifacts.
AI.conclusion: CANN Bench fills a critical gap in AI code generation evaluation by extending rigorous, reproducible benchmarking to the Ascend NPU ecosystem. Its design—multi-axis scoring, hardware-anchored performance ceilings, and anti-reward-hacking measures—enables sustainable community co-construction and long-term maintenance as a trusted yardstick for operator-authoring capability.

title: CSPF: A Constrained Shared-Private Fusion Method for Non-Verifiable Preference Evaluation
summary: At present, reliable evaluation of non-verifiable tasks remains challenging. Existing approaches often fail to adequately capture the diverse evaluative criteria underlying human preferences in such tasks. To this end, we propose Constrained Shared-Private Fusion (CSPF), a fusion method that treats heterogeneous frozen reward models as complementary evaluators and learns to integrate their hidden-state representations under pairwise human-preference supervision. CSPF decomposes each expert signal into shared and expert-private representations, encouraging cross-expert alignment while preserving complementary viewpoints. Across experiments on LM-Arena target-domain adaptation and PPE out-of-distribution preference evaluation, CSPF achieves the best performance on the primary metrics among the evaluated single-expert reward-model, scalar-score multi-expert, and rubric-judge baselines. Overall, CSPF suggests that fusing hidden-state representations provides a more expressive basis for preference assessment, offering a practical route toward integrated evaluative signals for non-verifiable preference tasks.

AI.tldr: CSPF fuses heterogeneous frozen reward models by decomposing hidden-state representations into shared and private components, learning to integrate them under pairwise human-preference supervision, achieving state-of-the-art on non-verifiable preference evaluation tasks.
AI.motivation: Reliable evaluation of non-verifiable tasks is challenging because existing methods fail to capture the diverse, often complementary evaluative criteria underlying human preferences. Simple scalar-score aggregation or rubric-based judging loses the richness of individual reward models.
AI.method: CSPF takes multiple heterogeneous frozen reward models as complementary evaluators. It decomposes each model's hidden-state representation into a shared component (encouraging cross-expert alignment) and an expert-private component (preserving complementary viewpoints). These fused representations are then learned under pairwise human-preference supervision to produce an integrated preference assessment.
AI.result: CSPF achieves the best performance on primary metrics across LM-Arena target-domain adaptation and PPE out-of-distribution preference evaluation, outperforming single-expert reward models, scalar-score multi-expert baselines, and rubric-judge baselines.
AI.conclusion: Fusing hidden-state representations offers a more expressive basis for preference assessment than aggregating scalar scores or using rubric judges, providing a practical approach for integrating evaluative signals in non-verifiable preference tasks.

title: Explanation-Based Runtime Verification for Trustworthy ML-driven Optical Networks
comment: 6 Pages, 2 Figures. Accepted and presented at the 30th International Conference on Optical Network Design and Modelling (ONDM 2026), Munich, Germany, 12-15 May 2026
summary: Machine learning (ML) models are increasingly integrated into optical network automation frameworks to support tasks such as failure management, performance monitoring and resource allocation. In these environments, ML-driven predictions may be directly coupled with control-plane actions where incorrect decisions can immediately impact service quality, resource efficiency, and network stability. As automation levels increase, ensuring the reliability of individual decisions at deployment time becomes a critical requirement. Explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) techniques have emerged to improve transparency by highlighting the factors influencing ML predictions. In addition to identifying influential features, they provide insights into the underlying reasoning process of the model, revealing how different input variables contribute to the final outcome and how feature interactions shape the decision boundary. In this work, we introduce explanation-based runtime verification, an approach that exploits model explanations to assess the soundness of individual ML decisions before they are executed in the network control loop. The proposed approach evaluates explanation coherence and physics grounding consistency at runtime, enabling the system to defer or reject decisions flagged as uncertain. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on a representative use case of lightpath quality of transmission classification. Experimental results show that explanation-based verification can intercept a significant fraction of erroneous decisions while preserving high automation rate.

AI.tldr: Proposes explanation-based runtime verification for ML-driven optical network automation, using XAI to assess decision soundness before execution, intercepting erroneous predictions while maintaining high automation rates.
AI.motivation: As ML models become tightly coupled with control-plane actions in optical networks, incorrect predictions can directly harm service quality and network stability. Existing XAI methods provide post-hoc transparency but are not leveraged for real-time decision validation before execution.
AI.method: Introduces explanation-based runtime verification that evaluates explanation coherence and physics grounding consistency of ML predictions at runtime. Decisions flagged as uncertain are deferred or rejected before they enter the network control loop. Validated on lightpath QoT classification.
AI.result: The approach intercepts a significant fraction of erroneous decisions while preserving a high automation rate, demonstrating effective trade-off between safety and autonomy.
AI.conclusion: Explanation-based runtime verification provides a practical mechanism for deploying ML safely in optical network control loops, bridging the gap between XAI transparency and operational reliability requirements.

title: LegalCiteTrust: Benchmarking Citation Trustworthiness in Chinese Long-Form Legal Research Reports
comment: 8 pages, 21 pages with appendix, 26 tables, 4 figures
summary: Long-form legal research reports increasingly rely on LLMs and agentic research systems, but their reliability depends not only on answering the task, but also on whether cited legal authorities are trustworthy. A citation can be risky even when it points to a real source: the report may omit limiting conditions, misdescribe the authority, or use it to support a stronger claim than the source allows. We introduce LegalCiteTrust, a benchmark for evaluating citation trustworthiness in Chinese long-form legal research reports. It contains 72 densely annotated report-level tasks and evaluates reports along three dimensions: Coverage, Support, and Citation Trustworthiness. Citation Trustworthiness is operationalized through citation-level Existence, Fidelity, and Applicability (E/F/A). Experiments on general-purpose LLMs, deep-research systems, and legal-specific systems show that task completion, evidence richness, citation density, and citation reliability expose different system behaviors. Retrieval tools can improve evidence support without reliably improving the Trust score, while E/F/A-based revision improves Trust and Final score more clearly than existence-only filtering. These results suggest that trustworthy legal research generation requires citation-aware evidence governance after retrieval: systems must not only retrieve legal authorities, but also select, describe, and apply them reliably.

AI.tldr: LegalCiteTrust is a benchmark for evaluating citation trustworthiness in Chinese long-form legal research reports, measuring three dimensions (Coverage, Support, Citation Trustworthiness) and operationalizing citation reliability through Existence, Fidelity, and Applicability (E/F/A). Experiments reveal that retrieval improves support but not trustworthiness, while E/F/A-based revision outperforms simple existence filtering.
AI.motivation: LLMs and agentic research systems increasingly generate long-form legal reports, but reliability hinges on citation trustworthiness — not just whether cited authorities exist, but whether they are accurately described and correctly applied. Existing evaluation frameworks fail to capture these nuanced failure modes (omitted conditions, mischaracterization, overclaiming).
AI.method: The authors construct LegalCiteTrust, a benchmark of 72 densely annotated Chinese legal research tasks evaluated along three axes: Coverage (issue completeness), Support (evidence-claim alignment), and Citation Trustworthiness (operationalized via citation-level Existence, Fidelity, and Applicability — E/F/A). Multiple system types are tested: general-purpose LLMs, deep-research systems, and legal-specific systems, with ablation studies on retrieval augmentation and E/F/A-based revision vs. existence-only filtering.
AI.result: Task completion, evidence richness, citation density, and citation reliability reveal divergent system behaviors across model types. Retrieval tools improve evidence support but do not reliably improve Trust scores. E/F/A-based revision yields clearer improvements in both Trust and Final scores compared to existence-only filtering, demonstrating that post-retrieval citation governance (selection, description, application) is essential.
AI.conclusion: Trustworthy legal research generation requires citation-aware evidence governance after retrieval: systems must not only retrieve legal authorities but also select, describe, and apply them reliably. The E/F/A framework provides a practical diagnostic for citation trustworthiness beyond binary existence checks.

title: Attribution Markets: A Fisher-Market Formulation for Fractional Credit Assignment Between Planned Tasks and Performed Actions
comment: 35 pages, 3 figures. Companion technical report with extended treatment of dynamic/forward-looking markets and reinforcement-learning extensions available separately
summary: Personal and organizational planning systems maintain two records that drift apart: what was planned (a task's effort budget) and what was done (a logged action's duration and description). Existing systems bridge them with an exclusive, all-or-nothing link that strands genuinely related but unlinked effort and reports false stalls on active goals. We formulate the bridge as a quasi-linear Fisher market: planned tasks are budget-constrained buyers, performed actions are divisible goods, and a fused text/structural/temporal signal sets each buyer's valuation. Two market instruments - a seller reserve price and a buyer cash option - yield conservation, a hard budget cap, and a provable junk filter as theorems. We extend the market with a concave completion utility discounting progress as a task nears its plan; standard convergence theory for the market's algorithm does not transfer here, resolved by a satiation-threshold fixed point with existence (Brouwer) and local uniqueness under an explicit diagonal-dominance condition, validated empirically on random and adversarial instances. A de-circularized, multi-seed benchmark - observed affinity corrupted independently of the scored ground truth - surfaces a genuine weak spot: the market's sharp, zero-entropy equilibrium is more sensitive to affinity noise than entropy-regularized optimal transport's permanently smoothed one. We resolve this with a one-parameter entropy-regularized generalization unifying the two, plus a noise-adaptive rule for its regularization strength. We report full reproducibility parameters, discuss limitations candidly, and relate the result to multi-touch attribution, optimal transport, and online Fisher-market algorithms.

AI.tldr: A quasi-linear Fisher market framework bridges planned task budgets and logged actions, using fused text/structural/temporal signals. The paper proves conservation, hard budget caps, and junk-filter theorems, extends the model with concave completion utility requiring a satiation-threshold fixed-point analysis, identifies sensitivity to affinity noise versus entropy-regularized optimal transport, and resolves this via a unified entropy-regularized generalization with noise-adaptive regularization.
AI.motivation: Existing planning and organizational systems maintain two diverging records — planned effort budgets and logged action durations/descriptions — linked by brittle all-or-nothing connections that either strand genuinely related but unlinked effort or falsely report stalls on active goals. A principled, robust bridging mechanism is needed.
AI.method: The problem is formulated as a quasi-linear Fisher market where planned tasks are budget-constrained buyers and performed actions are divisible goods. A fused text/structural/temporal signal defines buyer valuations. Two market instruments (seller reserve price and buyer cash option) provide theoretical guarantees. The market is extended with a concave completion utility; convergence failure of standard algorithms is addressed via a satiation-threshold fixed point with Brouwer existence and local uniqueness under diagonal dominance. A de-circularized, multi-seed benchmark reveals sensitivity to affinity noise, motivating an entropy-regularized generalization with a noise-adaptive regularization rule, unifying the sharp Fisher equilibrium and entropy-regularized optimal transport.
AI.result: The market yields conservation, a hard budget cap, and a provable junk filter as theorems. The fixed-point analysis is validated empirically on random and adversarial instances. The entropy-regularized generalization successfully addresses noise sensitivity identified in benchmarking, unifying the Fisher market and entropy-regularized optimal transport under one parameter.
AI.conclusion: The Fisher market formulation provides a theoretically grounded, robust bridge between planning and logging systems. The entropy-regularized extension with noise-adaptive regularization resolves real-world noise sensitivity, connecting to multi-touch attribution, optimal transport, and online Fisher-market algorithms.

title: Attention Degradation, Function Token Anchoring, and the Limits of Attention-Based Intervention in Large Language Models
summary: Mean cross-positional attention degradation is widely reported in transformer interpretability, yet whether it causally limits contextual retrieval remains untested. We present six coordinated experiments across GPT-2, LLaMA-3.2-1B/3B, OPT-1.3B, and distilgpt2. We first characterise short-term (5-100 token) attention degradation, finding a universal exponential-then-plateau pattern whose rate is inversely correlated with depth, with distinct layer-wise entropy signatures per architecture. Function token anchoring proves architecture-dependent: OPT-1.3B (absolute positional encoding) shows distance-dependent preposition specificity, GPT-2 shows uniform non-specific dependence, and LLaMA (RoPE) shows reversal at long distances. Strategic comma insertion at clause boundaries causally reduces prediction degradation in the 40-80 token range, with the benefit tied to syntactic boundary alignment rather than token density. We then test the mechanism causally: Relay-Aware Attention (RAA), which biases attention logits toward function token positions, verifiably increases attention mass by 16-24% yet yields null effects on GPT-2 and LLaMA-1B, preliminary harm on LLaMA-3B, and a mixed effect on OPT-1.3B that nets to approximately zero. Multi-fact retrieval probes further show that degradation rate does not predict retrieval accuracy across models. We conclude that mean attention degradation is largely descriptive rather than prescriptive: function tokens contribute through what their hidden states compute, not through the attention they receive -- with implications for interpretability methodology and attention-score-based inference optimisations such as KV-cache eviction.

AI.tldr: Mean cross-positional attention degradation is a widely observed descriptive phenomenon in transformers, but six coordinated experiments across multiple architectures demonstrate it does not causally limit contextual retrieval. Function tokens contribute through their hidden-state computations, not the attention they receive, with implications for interpretability and KV-cache eviction strategies.
AI.motivation: Mean cross-positional attention degradation is extensively documented in transformer interpretability literature, but no prior work has tested whether this phenomenon causally impairs contextual retrieval. The authors seek to distinguish descriptive patterns from prescriptive mechanisms.
AI.method: Six coordinated experiments across GPT-2, LLaMA-3.2-1B/3B, OPT-1.3B, and distilgpt2: (1) characterizing short-term (5–100 token) attention degradation patterns; (2) analyzing function token anchoring across architectures with different positional encodings (absolute, RoPE); (3) causal intervention via strategic comma insertion at clause boundaries; (4) Relay-Aware Attention (RAA), which biases attention logits toward function token positions; (5) multi-fact retrieval probes; and (6) cross-model comparison of degradation rates versus retrieval accuracy.
AI.result: Attention degradation follows a universal exponential-then-plateau pattern inversely correlated with depth, with distinct layer-wise entropy signatures per architecture. Function token anchoring is architecture-dependent: OPT-1.3B shows distance-dependent preposition specificity, GPT-2 shows uniform non-specific dependence, and LLaMA (RoPE) shows reversal at long distances. Strategic comma insertion causally reduces prediction degradation in the 40–80 token range via syntactic boundary alignment. RAA increases attention mass by 16–24% but yields null effects on GPT-2 and LLaMA-1B, preliminary harm on LLaMA-3B, and mixed (~net zero) effects on OPT-1.3B. Degradation rate does not predict multi-fact retrieval accuracy across models.
AI.conclusion: Mean attention degradation is largely descriptive rather than prescriptive. Function tokens contribute to model performance through what their hidden states compute, not through the magnitude of attention they receive. This finding challenges interpretability methodologies that rely on attention scores as faithful explanations and questions the validity of attention-score-based inference optimizations such as KV-cache eviction.

title: CEDAR: Causal Edge Discovery for Autoregressive Processes
summary: We propose CEDAR (Causal Edge Discovery for Autoregressive Processes), a constraint-based method for lagged causal edge discovery in sparse autoregressive time series. CEDAR screens candidate cross-variable lags using AR(1)-residualized, U-centered distance correlation, then applies two targeted conditional-independence tests per significant cross-variable lag candidate and accepts at most one lag per ordered pair. A stable MCI pruning step removes indirect edges, and optional deterministic C-nodes adjust for specified trend-like nonstationarity. In sparse regimes where few lags survive screening, CEDAR requires $O(d^2)$ CI tests after screening while retaining edge-level interpretability. CEDAR is most effective when data are scarce and variables exhibit lag-1 self-dynamics; methods with richer conditioning sets become preferable as $T$ grows or when higher-order autoregressive or simultaneous multi-lag effects are common.

AI.tldr: CEDAR is a constraint-based method for discovering lagged causal edges in sparse autoregressive time series. It screens candidate cross-variable lags using distance correlation, applies targeted conditional-independence tests, selects at most one lag per ordered pair, removes indirect edges via MCI pruning, and optionally adjusts for trend-like nonstationarity. It is particularly effective in sparse, low-T settings with lag-1 self-dynamics.
AI.motivation: Existing causal discovery methods for time series often require large sample sizes or rich conditioning sets, making them inefficient or unreliable when data are scarce and the true causal structure is sparse. There is a need for a method that maintains edge-level interpretability and statistical validity in such regimes, particularly when variables are dominated by lag-1 autoregressive dynamics.
AI.method: CEDAR proceeds in several stages: (1) Screening — uses AR(1)-residualized, U-centered distance correlation to identify candidate cross-variable lags. (2) Targeted CI testing — applies two conditional-independence tests per significant candidate and selects at most one lag per ordered pair. (3) MCI pruning — a stable Momentary Conditional Independence step removes indirect edges. (4) Optional deterministic C-nodes adjust for specified trend-like nonstationarity. The method requires O(d²) CI tests post-screening in sparse regimes.
AI.result: In sparse regimes where few lags survive screening, CEDAR achieves O(d²) complexity after screening while preserving edge-level interpretability. It performs best when data are scarce and variables exhibit lag-1 self-dynamics. As T grows or when higher-order autoregressive or simultaneous multi-lag effects are common, methods with richer conditioning sets become preferable.
AI.conclusion: CEDAR offers a computationally efficient and statistically interpretable approach to lagged causal discovery tailored to sparse, low-sample regimes with dominant lag-1 dynamics. It fills a gap between fully unconstrained methods (which struggle with small T) and overly restrictive assumptions, with clear guidance on when alternative methods should be preferred.

title: Autonomous disproofs of the sum-product conjecture over $\mathbb R$ with GPT-5.5 Pro
summary: OpenAI's recent disproof of the Erdős unit distance conjecture marked a milestone for AI in mathematics. It also inspired another breakthrough: a human disproof of the Erdős--Szemerédi sum-product conjecture over $\mathbb R$. In this paper, we present a simple agent built on GPT-5.5 Pro. Using a problem-agnostic, three-stage prompting pipeline -- proof-plan proposal, proof construction, and review -- the agent autonomously generated correct proofs that the sum-product conjecture is false over $\mathbb R$ in 7 of 8 independent trials; in the remaining trial, it identified an unresolved gap in its argument. The seven proofs are diverse: some are close to existing unit-based constructions, while others avoid units by using $L^p$-type regions of algebraic integers. The system used an average of 132.4k reasoning tokens per trial. We release the code, intermediate outputs, and generated proofs, providing a reproducible, data-contamination-free case study in autonomous proof generation.

AI.tldr: The paper presents an autonomous AI agent (GPT-5.5 Pro) that disproved the Erdős–Szemerédi sum-product conjecture over ℝ in 7/8 trials using a three-stage prompting pipeline, producing diverse proofs with an average of 132.4k reasoning tokens per trial.
AI.motivation: Following OpenAI's AI-driven disproof of the Erdős unit distance conjecture, the authors aim to demonstrate that autonomous proof generation can tackle significant open problems — specifically the Erdős–Szemerédi sum-product conjecture — using a simple, problem-agnostic prompting framework, and to provide a reproducible, contamination-free case study.
AI.method: An agent built on GPT-5.5 Pro employs a three-stage prompting pipeline: (1) proof-plan proposal, (2) proof construction, and (3) review. The pipeline is problem-agnostic. The system was run for 8 independent trials, with full code, intermediate outputs, and generated proofs released for reproducibility.
AI.result: In 7 of 8 independent trials, the agent produced correct proofs that the sum-product conjecture is false over ℝ. The one remaining trial identified an unresolved gap. The generated proofs were diverse: some resembled existing unit-based constructions, while others used L^p-type regions of algebraic integers, avoiding units. Average reasoning token usage was 132.4k per trial.
AI.conclusion: Autonomous proof generation using LLM-based agents with structured prompting pipelines is capable of producing correct, diverse proofs for major open problems. The released code and outputs offer a reproducible benchmark for future work in AI-driven mathematical reasoning.

title: From a Word-Level Dictionary to Sentence-Level Semantics: Multilingual Grievance Labelling with Contextual Models
summary: Grievance is one of the warning signs analysts look for when assessing threats of violence. It is increasingly measured at scale from online text, most often with word-level lexicons like the Grievance Dictionary that score by matching weighted terms. Such matching is a fast and transparent proxy, but it cannot resolve whether a term is asserted, quoted, negated, or condemned. These lexicons are also often evaluated on pools enriched with the very examples they retrieve, so a high score partly reflects agreement with the lexicon's own selection rule. Examining a five-language, 2{,}000-item evaluation pool, we find its halves separated almost perfectly by the lexicon itself: every item labeled ``random'' is in fact lexicon-negative, so the lexicon's apparent macro-AUROC of 0.686 collapses to a 0.500 floor fixed by construction. We keep the dictionary's 22-construct ontology but replace term matching with context-reading models, evaluated on a non-circular benchmark that separates unconditional-random, lexicon-positive, and lexicon-negative strata across five languages. Reading the full post rather than the target sentence alone helps most where the lexicon is silent, raising average precision on lexicon-negative text from 0.14 to 0.20, with the largest gains on quoted, implicit, and cross-sentence grievance. Together, these results show that grievance is measured more faithfully by reading the surrounding context, and more honestly when tested on text the lexicon did not select. We release our code and benchmark at https://github.com/behavioral-ds/multilingual_grievance.

AI.tldr: This paper critiques word-level grievance lexicons for evaluating threats of violence, demonstrating that their apparent performance is artificially inflated by circular evaluation. The authors show that replacing term-matching with context-reading models improves detection, especially on lexicon-negative text, and advocate for non-circular benchmarks stratified by lexicon status across five languages.
AI.motivation: Grievance detection from online text is critical for violence threat assessment, but existing lexicon-based methods (e.g., the Grievance Dictionary) suffer from two key limitations: (1) they cannot resolve linguistic phenomena like assertion, quotation, negation, or condemnation; and (2) their evaluation is circular — evaluation pools are enriched with the very examples the lexicon retrieves, inflating performance metrics. The authors seek to diagnose and correct these flaws.
AI.method: The authors construct a five-language, 2,000-item evaluation pool and demonstrate that the Grievance Dictionary's selection rule cleanly separates the pool into lexicon-positive and lexicon-negative strata, rendering the original macro-AUROC of 0.686 equivalent to a 0.500 floor. They retain the dictionary's 22-construct ontology but replace word-level matching with context-reading models (transformer-based). Crucially, they evaluate on a non-circular benchmark stratified into unconditional-random, lexicon-positive, and lexicon-negative subsets across five languages, and test whether reading the full post (vs. the target sentence alone) improves performance.
AI.result: The lexicon's apparent macro-AUROC of 0.686 collapses to 0.500 once circular evaluation is corrected. Context-reading models improve average precision on lexicon-negative text from 0.14 to 0.20, with the largest gains observed on quoted, implicit, and cross-sentence grievance expressions — cases where the lexicon is silent. Reading the full post context consistently helps most where the lexicon fails.
AI.conclusion: Grievance is measured more faithfully by models that read surrounding context rather than rely on word-level matching, and more honestly when tested on text the lexicon did not select. The authors release their code and stratified benchmark to enable fairer evaluation of grievance detection systems.

title: Perspective Latents as an Architectural Condition for Causal Emergence in Active Inference Agents
summary: A recent line of work measures causal emergence in reinforcement learning agents through Integrated Information Decomposition, reporting that $Φ_r$ grows with training and tracks reward improvement. For active inference, this raises the question of how reward-free predictive organization relates to such information-theoretic signatures. I test this within an active inference agent whose architecture separates a fast perception latent $z$ from a slow global latent $g$, where $g$ is driven by prediction error and structurally decoupled from policy gradients. In a reward-free environmental regime-switching protocol, $Φ_r$ concentrates in $g$; its aggregate magnitude is largely architectural and decreases with training. The substantive effect of learning becomes legible only at the atom-compositional level: decoupling flips sign from negative to positive and becomes regime-invariant under environmental change, while downward causation carries the regime-dependent adjustment. These results identify $g$ as the architectural locus of $Φ_r$-relevant temporal organization in an active inference agent, and argue against reading scalar $Φ_r$ as a direct index of learned integration.

AI.tldr: An active inference agent with decoupled fast (z) and slow (g) latent variables is tested in a reward-free regime-switching protocol. Integrated Information Decomposition reveals that causal emergence (Φ_r) concentrates in g, is largely architectural, and decreases with training. At the atom-compositional level, decoupling sign flips from negative to positive and becomes regime-invariant, while downward causation carries regime-dependent adjustment. The paper argues against interpreting scalar Φ_r as a direct index of learned integration.
AI.motivation: Prior work found that causal emergence (Φ_r) in RL agents grows with training and tracks reward. This paper asks how reward-free predictive organization in active inference agents relates to such information-theoretic signatures, probing whether scalar Φ_r genuinely reflects learned integration or is largely an architectural artifact.
AI.method: An active inference agent is constructed with two latent variables: a fast perception latent z and a slow global latent g, architecturally decoupled from policy gradients and driven by prediction error. The agent is tested in a reward-free environmental regime-switching protocol. Integrated Information Decomposition (ΦID) is applied to measure Φ_r, and its atom-compositional structure (decoupling, downward causation) is analyzed across training and environmental regimes.
AI.result: Φ_r concentrates in g rather than z. Aggregate Φ_r magnitude is largely architectural and decreases with training. The learning effect becomes visible only atom-compositionally: decoupling sign flips from negative to positive and becomes regime-invariant, while downward causation carries regime-dependent adjustment. g is identified as the architectural locus of Φ_r-relevant temporal organization.
AI.conclusion: Scalar Φ_r should not be read as a direct index of learned integration. In active inference agents, temporal-integration signatures are heavily architectural, with g serving as their locus. Genuine learning effects require atom-compositional analysis, not aggregate Φ_r trends.

title: ConfidenceBench: Evaluating Confidence Calibration in Large Language Models
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in settings where fluent but incorrect answers can be costly. In these settings, accuracy alone is insufficient: models must also know when they are likely to be wrong. We present ConfidenceBench, a calibration benchmark that evaluates verbalized confidence estimates in 15 frontier LLMs using the Brier score, a proper scoring rule that incentivises truthful probability reporting. Confidence is elicited via prompting, requiring no access to model logits and making the framework applicable to both closed-source and open-source systems. The benchmark comprises 200 private multiple-choice questions across four categories: spatial reasoning, high-precision mathematics, word lookup, and unknowable questions. Across three independent runs, Claude Opus 4.6 and Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview achieve the lowest Brier scores, both reported as 0.103. Both substantially outperform the calibrated-random baseline of 0.1875, while Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite scores 0.367, indicating severe miscalibration. Accuracy and calibration diverge substantially across model families: the most accurate model is not the best-calibrated, and several models perform worse than the calibrated-random Brier baseline despite reasonable accuracy. These results show that verbalized confidence calibration is a distinct and practically important axis of LLM reliability, complementary to standard accuracy-based evaluation.

AI.tldr: ConfidenceBench evaluates 15 frontier LLMs on verbalized confidence calibration using the Brier score. Claude Opus 4.6 and Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview achieve the best calibration (0.103), while accuracy and calibration diverge across models — the most accurate model is not the best-calibrated.
AI.motivation: LLMs are deployed in high-stakes settings where fluent but incorrect outputs are costly. Models must not only be accurate but also know when they are likely wrong. Standard accuracy benchmarks fail to capture this metacognitive capability, motivating a dedicated calibration benchmark that works for both open-source and closed-source models.
AI.method: ConfidenceBench uses 200 private multiple-choice questions across four categories: spatial reasoning, high-precision mathematics, word lookup, and unknowable questions. Verbalized confidence is elicited via prompting (no logit access required), and calibration is evaluated using the Brier score — a proper scoring rule that incentivizes truthful probability reporting. Three independent runs are conducted per model. A calibrated-random baseline (0.1875) is used for comparison.
AI.result: Claude Opus 4.6 and Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview both achieve a Brier score of 0.103, substantially outperforming the calibrated-random baseline of 0.1875. Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite scores 0.367, indicating severe miscalibration. Accuracy and calibration diverge substantially: the most accurate model is not the best-calibrated, and several models perform worse than the baseline despite reasonable accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Verbalized confidence calibration is a distinct and practically important axis of LLM reliability, complementary to standard accuracy-based evaluation. It should be treated as a separate dimension in model assessment.

title: Where Animacy Lives in Large Language Models: Tracing the Circuits of the Animacy Concept
summary: Distinguishing animate from inanimate concepts in written language requires more than shallow text processing, as it involves recognizing complex selectional constraints and contextual cues, such as verb-argument interactions. Yet, current large language models (LLMs) appear to be capable of doing it. We investigate whether this animacy-sensitive behavior of LLMs can be traced to a localized set of causally relevant components and connections. To do so, we construct a controlled dataset of minimal pairs and perform circuit discovery on four open-weight models. Through in-depth experiments and ablations, we show that a causal mechanism responsible for handling animacy in these models does exist, thus discovering an animacy circuit. At the same time, this circuit appears to be less localized compared to other known ones and generalizes only partially across models and animacy tasks, confirming the distributed, context-dependent, and somewhat graded nature of the animacy concept.

AI.tldr: This paper discovers a causal "animacy circuit" in LLMs that handles distinguishing animate from inanimate concepts. Through circuit discovery on minimal pairs, the authors find the mechanism exists but is less localized than other known circuits, generalizes only partially across models and tasks, confirming animacy's distributed and graded nature.
AI.motivation: Animacy distinction requires complex selectional constraints and contextual cues beyond shallow processing. While LLMs exhibit animacy-sensitive behavior, it's unclear whether this capability stems from a localized, causally relevant set of components—i.e., a distinct neural circuit.
AI.method: The authors construct a controlled dataset of minimal pairs targeting animacy distinctions and perform circuit discovery (including causal tracing and ablation experiments) on four open-weight language models to identify components causally responsible for animacy processing.
AI.result: A causal mechanism (the "animacy circuit") does exist but is less localized than other known circuits (e.g., indirect object identification). It generalizes only partially across different models and animacy-related tasks, exhibiting context-dependent and graded properties.
AI.conclusion: LLMs possess a bona fide but distributed animacy circuit. The distributed, context-dependent, and graded nature of this circuit aligns with the linguistic understanding that animacy is not a rigid binary but a flexible, context-sensitive conceptual distinction.

title: LLMs Get Lost in Evolving User Intent
summary: As LLMs become more capable, they are increasingly deployed as collaborative agents, taking on user-delegated tasks through iterative interaction. Yet genuine interaction is inherently dynamic: users rarely specify their intent upfront, instead disclosing, revising, and reshaping it as the conversation unfolds.
