Despite this, LLMs are still predominantly evaluated or trained in single-turn, fully-specified settings, leaving open a fundamental question: how well do LLMs track and act on user intent as it evolves over the course of a conversation? To study this, we introduce a framework that transforms static, single-turn tasks into dynamic multi-turn conversations in which the user's intent evolves across turns--incrementally revealed, revised, and at times redirected mid-conversation--while preserving each task's original evaluation protocol, enabling existing benchmarks to be reused as controlled testbeds without new annotation. Across multiple tasks, we surface a consistent phenomenon: strong static-setting performance does not transfer to the evolving-intent setting, with substantial drops across model families. Our findings point to a fundamental gap: today's LLMs do not yet faithfully track and act on the user's evolving intent, a capability invisible to static evaluation yet critical for future collaborative agents.

AI.tldr: LLMs perform well on static single-turn tasks but degrade significantly when user intent evolves dynamically across multi-turn conversations, revealing a critical capability gap for collaborative agents.
AI.motivation: Current LLM evaluation and training predominantly assume static, fully-specified, single-turn settings. However, real-world collaborative interaction is dynamic: users reveal, revise, and redirect their intent as conversations unfold. The authors aim to investigate whether LLMs can faithfully track and act on evolving user intent across multi-turn dialogues—a capability invisible to standard benchmarks.
AI.method: The authors propose a framework that converts static single-turn tasks into dynamic multi-turn conversations. In these conversations, user intent evolves across turns—being incrementally revealed, revised, or redirected mid-conversation—while preserving the original evaluation protocol of each task. This allows existing benchmarks to be reused as controlled testbeds without requiring new annotations.
AI.result: Across multiple tasks, the authors find a consistent phenomenon: strong performance in static settings does not transfer to the evolving-intent setting. Substantial performance drops are observed across different model families, indicating a systematic gap in LLMs' ability to track evolving user intent.
AI.conclusion: Today's LLMs do not faithfully track and act on evolving user intent—a fundamental capability gap that is invisible to static evaluation yet critical for future collaborative agents.

title: Evaluating and Guarding Citation Faithfulness in Agentic Scientific Synthesis
comment: 20 pages, 5 figures. Includes supplementary material (Appendices S1-S6). Open single-GPU reproducibility kit included
summary:
Agentic LLM systems such as OpenScholar and PaperQA2 read the scientific literature and return cited answers, and both they and their benchmarks already check whether those citations hold, with a fixed attribution model or human graders. Neither audits the reliability of that check itself. We show it is not reliable, and that this matters. On identical agent outputs the measured unsupported-citation rate ranges from about 3% to about 18% depending only on the verifier's strictness, and although verifiers agree on which citations are supported, they disagree on which to flag (negative-specific agreement 0.27 to 0.30), so no single flag set is trustworthy and cross-paper comparison is invalid without a named verifier and protocol.
  We present a gold-anchored evaluation protocol and a deployable guard that make this behavior measurable and bounded. The protocol validates the verifier, measures re-attribution, and calibrates a guarantee against human gold rather than another model's verdict; the verifier is a swappable instrument chosen on cost (recall 0.94 on the supported class, held out), and re-attribution is a commodity step where a deterministic BM25 matches the best open generator. The guard adds a split-conformal layer placing a distribution-free, finite-sample bound on truly unsupported citations that slip past a chosen flagging rule, a guarantee on catch rate rather than conclusion correctness. The bound holds on held-out gold, and we identify and quantify the condition governing its transfer to deployment, calibration-negative difficulty, with a concrete recalibration recipe, left untested by prior conformal-factuality work.
  Validated across four open 27-35B models and three agentic pipelines on public benchmarks (SciFact, QASA, PubMedQA), with confidence intervals on every headline number, the protocol and guard ship as an open single-GPU kit.

AI.tldr: Agentic LLM systems that cite scientific literature have unreliable citation verification — measured unsupported-citation rates vary dramatically (3% to 18%) depending on verifier strictness, with poor inter-verifier agreement on flagging. The authors present a gold-anchored evaluation protocol and a split-conformal guard that together make verification measurable, bounded, and trustworthy, validated across multiple models and benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Current agentic LLM systems and their benchmarks check whether citations support claims, but no one audits the reliability of that verification itself. The authors demonstrate this verification is unreliable: unsupported-citation rates swing wildly depending on verifier strictness, and verifiers disagree sharply on which citations to flag, rendering cross-paper comparisons invalid and individual flag sets untrustworthy.
AI.method: The authors propose (1) a gold-anchored evaluation protocol that validates the verifier, measures re-attribution, and calibrates guarantees against human-annotated gold data rather than another model's verdict; and (2) a deployable guard that adds a split-conformal layer, producing a distribution-free, finite-sample bound on truly unsupported citations that escape a chosen flagging rule. Re-attribution uses deterministic BM25 as a commodity step. The protocol also identifies "calibration-negative difficulty" as the condition governing bound transfer to deployment, with a recalibration recipe.
AI.result: Validated across four open 27-35B models and three agentic pipelines on SciFact, QASA, and PubMedQA. The protocol and guard ship as an open-source single-GPU kit, with confidence intervals reported on every headline number.
AI.conclusion: Citation verification in agentic scientific LLM systems is currently unreliable and uncalibrated. The proposed protocol and conformal guard make this behavior measurable and bounded, enabling trustworthy attribution checking with formal finite-sample guarantees, and highlighting a previously unexamined condition (calibration-negative difficulty) affecting transfer from calibration to deployment.

title: CultureTalk-ID: A Multi-Task Dialogue Benchmark for Cultural Commonsense in Indonesian Local Languages
summary: Culture is lived through conversation, yet existing Indonesian cultural commonsense benchmarks evaluate LLMs on short and isolated prompts, stripping away the dialogic context in which cultural nuances actually surface. We introduce CultureTalk-ID, the first dialogue-based benchmark for cultural commonsense in Indonesian and its local languages, comprising 4,496 culturally grounded dialogues across 11 languages and 13 culturally salient topics, curated through a multi-stage human pipeline with native speakers to ensure authenticity. CultureTalk-ID introduces three complementary tasks, namely dialogue-based multiple-choice cultural commonsense reasoning, culturally faithful machine translation, and language steering, which jointly probe whether LLMs can understand, transfer, and generate culturally grounded language.

AI.tldr: CultureTalk-ID is a dialogue-based benchmark for Indonesian cultural commonsense spanning 11 languages and 13 topics across 4,496 dialogues, introducing three tasks—cultural reasoning, culturally faithful translation, and language steering—to evaluate LLMs' ability to understand, transfer, and generate culturally grounded language.
AI.motivation: Existing Indonesian cultural commonsense benchmarks use short, isolated prompts that ignore the conversational context where cultural nuances naturally emerge. The authors argue that culture is lived through dialogue, necessitating a benchmark that embeds cultural commonsense within authentic conversational settings across Indonesia's linguistic diversity.
AI.method: The benchmark was curated through a multi-stage human annotation pipeline involving native speakers. It comprises 4,496 culturally grounded dialogues across 11 languages (including Indonesian and local languages) and 13 culturally salient topics. Three complementary evaluation tasks are introduced: (1) dialogue-based multiple-choice cultural commonsense reasoning, (2) culturally faithful machine translation, and (3) language steering, probing understanding, transfer, and generation respectively.
AI.result: The paper presents CultureTalk-ID as a benchmark resource; specific experimental results on LLM performance across the three tasks are not detailed in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: CultureTalk-ID provides a more ecologically valid framework for evaluating whether LLMs can genuinely handle Indonesian cultural commonsense in dialogic contexts, addressing a critical gap in culturally-aware NLP evaluation for under-represented languages.

title: PromptPack: Scaling LLM Annotation Agents for Online Recommendation
summary: Online recommendation platforms increasingly use Large Language Models (LLMs) to extract structured features from ad creatives. While deploying a single-call LLM annotation agent yields significant Click-Through Rate (CTR) improvements in our live production environment, per-creative prompting is prohibitively expensive to scale. The redundant system instructions sent in every request account for 94% of billed input tokens. To break this cost bottleneck, we introduce PromptPack, a scalable, high-throughput LLM annotation agent. PromptPack achieves this scale via in-context batching, combining a shared system prompt, a strict XML structural envelope, and an output correction layer to ensure deterministic, pipeline-ready feature extraction across multiple creatives simultaneously. We evaluate PromptPack via an offline retrieval benchmark using a downstream logistic-regression ranker. To deeply profile the agent's behavior, we measure AUC and introduce Volume-Weighted Absolute Lift (VWAL), a novel metric capturing the signal quality of the generated features. Compared to our live, unbatched production baseline, PromptPack at batch size 20 cuts our LLM costs by 89% and accelerates throughput by 2.5x while fully preserving AUC.

AI.tldr: PromptPack is an LLM-based annotation agent that uses in-context batching with shared prompts, XML structure, and output correction to extract structured features from ad creatives at scale. It reduces LLM costs by 89% and increases throughput by 2.5× at batch size 20 while preserving AUC, solving the prohibitive per-creative prompting costs where 94% of input tokens are redundant system instructions.
AI.motivation: Online recommendation platforms deploy LLMs to extract structured features from ad creatives, improving CTR. However, per-creative single-call prompting is prohibitively expensive to scale because redundant system instructions account for 94% of billed input tokens. A scalable, cost-efficient solution is needed without sacrificing downstream ranking performance.
AI.method: PromptPack employs in-context batching with three key components: (1) a shared system prompt sent once per batch rather than per creative, eliminating token redundancy; (2) a strict XML structural envelope that enforces deterministic, parseable output across multiple simultaneous creatives; and (3) an output correction layer that ensures pipeline-ready feature extraction. Features are then fed into a logistic-regression ranker. Evaluation uses AUC and a novel metric, Volume-Weighted Absolute Lift (VWAL), to measure signal quality of generated features.
AI.result: At batch size 20, PromptPack cuts LLM costs by 89% and accelerates throughput by 2.5× compared to the unbatched production baseline, while fully preserving AUC. The method demonstrates that batched inference with shared prompts can maintain feature quality at dramatically lower cost.
AI.conclusion: In-context batching with shared system prompts, strict structural envelopes, and output correction is an effective strategy for scaling LLM-based feature extraction in recommendation systems. PromptPack demonstrates that significant cost and throughput gains are achievable without degrading downstream ranking performance, making LLM annotation economically viable at production scale.

title: Sample-Efficient Learning from Agent Experience
summary: Real-world agent learning is often constrained by costly environment interactions, such as running time-consuming experiments or obtaining human feedback. In-context learning offers a highly sample-efficient way for agents to learn from their own interaction histories, but its gains disappear once that experience is removed from the context. Separately, context distillation provides a mechanism for internalizing contextual information into model weights. However, applying it to agents' interaction histories without sacrificing environment sample efficiency remains underexplored. We term this problem Experience Distillation and develop an implementation that requires no further environment interaction beyond the collected experience. Experiments on 749 curated software-engineering tasks and six text-adventure games show that it retains at least 64.8\% of the gains from in-context learning across both domains, whereas direct supervised fine-tuning on the collected experience recovers only 3.8\%. Compared with classical reinforcement-learning baselines, in-context learning from trial-and-error experience followed by Experience Distillation matches their performance with at least \(9.6\times\) fewer environment samples.

AI.tldr: Experience Distillation is a method to internalize agents' interaction histories into model weights without requiring additional environment interactions, retaining 64.8% of in-context learning gains compared to only 3.8% for direct supervised fine-tuning, and achieving comparable performance to RL baselines with 9.6× fewer samples.
AI.motivation: Real-world agent learning is limited by costly environment interactions. In-context learning is sample-efficient but transient (gains vanish when experience leaves context). Context distillation can internalize information into weights, but applying it to agent interaction histories without sacrificing sample efficiency remains underexplored.
AI.method: The authors propose Experience Distillation, a method that distills collected interaction histories (trial-and-error experience) into model weights without requiring any further environment interaction beyond what was already collected. This contrasts with direct supervised fine-tuning on the same collected experience.
AI.result: On 749 curated software-engineering tasks and six text-adventure games, Experience Distillation retains at least 64.8% of in-context learning gains, whereas direct supervised fine-tuning recovers only 3.8%. Compared to classical RL baselines, in-context learning followed by Experience Distillation matches their performance with at least 9.6× fewer environment samples.
AI.conclusion: Experience Distillation effectively bridges the gap between transient in-context learning and permanent weight-based learning, enabling agents to retain most of the sample-efficiency benefits of in-context learning in a persistent form while dramatically reducing the number of environment interactions needed compared to traditional RL.

title: Adaptive Confidence-weighted Expansion for Trustworthy Multi-Omics Multimodal Fusion
comment: Accepted for publication in the proceedings of the International Conference on Pattern Recognition (ICPR 2026)
summary: Multimodal learning is a robust approach to improve predictive performance in applications such as medical prognosis. However, the clinical applicability of models that use multimodal learning is hampered by their poor performance under noisy or uninformative data streams. Present fusion approaches often lack robust mechanisms for the dynamic assessment of data quality and for the provision of a trustable confidence score on the final prediction. This dissuades their deployment in safety-critical settings. To address these limitations, we introduce Adaptive Confidence-weighted Expansion (ACE), a novel framework to enhance the trustworthiness of multimodal fusion models. ACE first enhances the multimodal space by generating new, complementary modalities from intra-modality correlations. It then employs a dual-level confidence mechanism that (1) adaptively reweighs all modalities by their reliability before fusion and (2) estimates a global trust score over the fused, final decision. To evaluate ACE, we used four challenging multi-omics datasets (BRCA, KIPAN, LGG, and ROSMAP). ACE significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art algorithms in both classification performance and confidence calibration. Our framework provides a more stable and robust data fusion method that facilitates the use of multimodal learning in addressing high-stakes problems.

AI.tldr: ACE introduces a dual-level confidence mechanism for multimodal fusion that adaptively reweighs modalities by reliability and provides a global trust score, significantly improving both classification performance and confidence calibration on four multi-omics datasets.
AI.motivation: Multimodal learning suffers in safety-critical settings because existing fusion approaches lack mechanisms for dynamic data quality assessment and trustworthy confidence estimation, leading to poor performance under noisy or uninformative data streams.
AI.method: ACE first augments the multimodal space by generating complementary modalities from intra-modality correlations. It then applies a dual-level confidence mechanism: (1) adaptive reweighting of all modalities based on their reliability before fusion, and (2) estimation of a global trust score over the fused final decision.
AI.result: ACE significantly outperforms state-of-the-art algorithms in both classification performance and confidence calibration across four multi-omics datasets (BRCA, KIPAN, LGG, ROSMAP).
AI.conclusion: ACE provides a more stable and robust data fusion framework suitable for high-stakes multimodal learning problems, facilitating safer clinical deployment.

title: DynamicMCPBench: A Trace-Grounded, Effect-Scored Benchmark for LLM Agents over Live MCP Servers
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly deployed over Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, yet the benchmarks used to evaluate them score the final answer or a fixed "ground-truth" list of tools, both of which are fragile once the underlying data is live and stateful. We present DynamicMCPBench, a reusable framework rather than a fixed dataset. A practitioner can run it on their own MCP servers to test models on their own tasks, or let it collect servers automatically to measure a model's general ability to solve agentic tasks. Given the servers and any set of models, it generates realistic goals, pursues each one live to record a successful trajectory, distills that trajectory into path-agnostic effect checkpoints, and scores an agent on whether it reproduces those effects, never on the final answer. To show what the framework reveals, we run it at scale: 24 models over 121 servers and 750 tasks spread evenly over 15 task categories (50 each), where each category targets a distinct tool-use challenge of the generated questions. Each task is scored by pass^3: it counts as solved only if all three independent attempts succeed. Even the strongest agents solve only about half of the tasks, 31% of tasks are solved by no model at all, and accuracy collapses as the required tool chain grows longer (from 39% on the shortest chains to 13% on the longest). A human validation study confirms the automatic scoring is reliable (chance-corrected agreement of 0.76). DynamicMCPBench thus turns benchmark construction into something practitioners can rerun on their own servers and models, while exposing a consistent inability of current agents to handle long, multi-step agentic tasks.

AI.tldr: DynamicMCPBench is a reusable evaluation framework for LLM agents operating over live MCP servers. Instead of scoring final answers against static ground truth, it generates tasks dynamically, records successful trajectories, distills them into effect checkpoints, and scores agents on whether they reproduce those effects. At scale (24 models, 121 servers, 750 tasks), even the strongest agents solve only ~50% of tasks, accuracy collapses with longer tool chains (39%→13%), and 31% of tasks remain unsolved by any model.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks for LLM agents over MCP servers score either the final answer or a fixed list of tools, both of which are fragile when the underlying data is live and stateful. There is a need for a reusable, server-agnostic evaluation framework that tests genuine agentic capabilities on realistic, multi-step tasks without depending on static ground truth.
AI.method: DynamicMCPBench operates as a framework, not a fixed dataset. Given MCP servers and models, it: (1) generates realistic goals across 15 task categories targeting distinct tool-use challenges; (2) pursues each goal live to record a successful trajectory; (3) distills that trajectory into path-agnostic effect checkpoints; and (4) scores agents by whether they reproduce those effects (never by final answer). Scoring uses pass^3: a task is solved only if all three independent attempts succeed. Automatic scoring is validated via a human study (chance-corrected agreement of 0.76).
AI.result: At scale (24 models, 121 servers, 750 tasks, 50 per category): even the strongest agents solve only about half of all tasks; 31% of tasks are solved by no model; accuracy drops sharply with tool-chain length, from 39% (shortest chains) to 13% (longest chains). Human validation confirms reliable automatic scoring.
AI.conclusion: DynamicMCPBench enables practitioners to evaluate LLM agents on their own MCP servers and tasks, moving benchmark construction from fixed datasets to a reusable framework. Results expose a consistent inability of current agents to handle long, multi-step agentic tasks, highlighting a critical area for improvement.

title: GaugeQuant: Online Learning of Quantization-Optimal Bases from LLM Symmetries
summary: Transformers are known to have internal continuous symmetries that leave outputs invariant, while modifying quantization. GaugeQuant leverages this in-training by introducing a LogSumExp term to the loss that breaks the symmetries, thus selecting a basis that minimizes activation outliers. A stop-gradient operator ensures that only rotation matrices are updated, yielding the language modeling objective completely unaltered. Our requires no specific calibration data, no quantization simulation, and adds negligible training overhead. With the LLaMA-2 7B model under W4A4 quantization with group size 128, perplexity drops from 8.22 to 6.73, competing with post-training methods that require frozen models and calibration datasets. Under W4A16, perplexity drops from 11.16 to 5.45. Code is available at https://github.com/MPedraBento/gauge-quant.

AI.tldr: GaugeQuant introduces a training-time loss term (LogSumExp) that breaks internal symmetries in Transformers to select a basis minimizing activation outliers, improving W4A4/W4A16 quantization performance without calibration data or quantization simulation.
AI.motivation: Transformers possess continuous internal symmetries that preserve outputs but alter activation distributions. Post-training quantization methods require frozen models and calibration data. The authors aim to exploit these symmetries during training to naturally produce models with fewer activation outliers, enabling better low-bit quantization without the typical overhead of calibration or simulation.
AI.method: GaugeQuant adds a LogSumExp-based regularization term to the training loss that breaks the internal continuous symmetries of Transformers. This term selects a basis (gauge) that minimizes activation outliers. A stop-gradient operator ensures only rotation matrices are updated, leaving the original language modeling objective completely unaltered. The method requires no calibration data, no quantization simulation, and adds negligible training overhead.
AI.result: On LLaMA-2 7B: W4A4 quantization (group size 128) perplexity drops from 8.22 to 6.73, competitive with post-training methods. Under W4A16, perplexity drops from 11.16 to 5.45.
AI.conclusion: GaugeQuant effectively leverages in-training symmetry breaking to produce quantization-friendly models, matching or approaching post-training quantization methods without requiring frozen models or calibration datasets, while preserving the original LM objective intact.

title: PrefReward: Learning User Preference Matrix for Personalized Text Generation
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable ability in generating personalized content by leveraging user histories and contextual cues. However, most existing personalization approaches rely on implicit representations within model parameters, making it difficult to interpret user-specific preferences or effectively handle long-context dependencies. To address these challenges, we propose PrefReward, a novel preference-aware generative framework that explicitly models user styles through a structured preference matrix and integrates it into the decoding process as a reward signal. PrefReward consists of two stages: (1) extracting a user-specific preference matrix that summarizes individual stylistic tendencies, and (2) using the matrix to guide generation via a KL-divergence-based reward function. Experiments on the LongLaMP dataset show that PrefReward outperforms non-personalized and retrieval-based baselines in both generation quality and personalization interpretability.

AI.tldr: PrefReward is a two-stage personalization framework that extracts explicit user preference matrices and uses them as KL-divergence-based reward signals to guide LLM generation, outperforming baselines on the LongLaMP benchmark in both quality and interpretability.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM personalization methods rely on implicit preference representations within model parameters, which suffer from poor interpretability and difficulty handling long-context dependencies. There is a need for an explicit, interpretable mechanism to model user-specific stylistic preferences.
AI.method: PrefReward operates in two stages: (1) a preference extraction stage that constructs a structured user-specific preference matrix summarizing individual stylistic tendencies from user history, and (2) a decoding-stage integration where this matrix serves as a reward signal via a KL-divergence-based reward function to guide generation toward user-consistent outputs.
AI.result: On the LongLaMP dataset, PrefReward surpasses both non-personalized and retrieval-based baselines in generation quality and personalization interpretability metrics.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly modeling user preferences as a structured matrix and integrating it as a reward signal during decoding is an effective approach for improving both the quality and interpretability of personalized LLM generation.

title: Memory-Computation Tradeoffs in Semi Amortized Parametric Optimization
summary: Learning-enabled decision systems often use offline data or computation to reduce online compute cost. Despite the empirical success of such approaches, there is limited general understanding of how much offline information is needed to achieve a desired accuracy under a fixed online computation budget. We study this question through the lens of amortized parametric optimization: an offline phase stores a finite memory of solved problem instances, and an online phase produces a solution to a new instance by retrieving a warm start and applying $K$ steps of projected gradient descent. We analyze this setup for smooth convex parametric optimization over a compact domain, using a nonparametric predictor built from the stored offline solutions. For $μ$-strongly convex objectives, we establish matching upper and lower bounds on the memory required to guarantee $\varepsilon$-accuracy under a fixed online iteration budget $K$. For convex objectives satisfying a $β$-growth condition ($β>2$), we obtain near-matching bounds and identify a phase transition in $K$ beyond which additional memory provides no benefit. We further provide a general proof framework that (i) explicitly quantifies the memory cost of acceleration---how much offline memory is required to achieve a prescribed speedup over the unaided online optimizer---and (ii) identifies two key quantities driving this cost: the convergence rate of the online optimizer and the Lipschitz sensitivity of the solution map to the problem parameter. Experiments on parameterized ridge regression confirm the predicted memory--computation--accuracy tradeoffs.

AI.tldr: This paper theoretically analyzes the tradeoff between offline memory (stored problem instances), online computation budget (gradient descent steps), and solution accuracy in amortized parametric optimization. For strongly convex and growth-conditioned convex objectives, it establishes matching/near-matching upper and lower bounds on memory required for ε-accuracy, revealing a phase transition beyond which additional memory yields no benefit. A general proof framework quantifies the memory cost of acceleration and identifies convergence rate and solution-map sensitivity as key drivers.
AI.motivation: Despite empirical success of learning-enabled decision systems that use offline data/computation to reduce online cost, there is limited theoretical understanding of the fundamental tradeoff between offline memory, online computation, and accuracy. The paper aims to formally characterize how much offline information is necessary and sufficient to achieve a target accuracy under a fixed online computation budget.
AI.method: The authors formulate the problem as amortized parametric optimization with a two-phase setup: (1) an offline phase stores a finite memory of solved problem instances, and (2) an online phase retrieves a warm start and applies K steps of projected gradient descent. They analyze smooth convex parametric optimization over compact domains using a nonparametric predictor (nearest-neighbor retrieval from stored solutions). For μ-strongly convex objectives, they derive matching upper and lower bounds via covering number arguments and oracle complexity analysis. For β-growth convex objectives, they extend the analysis using a general proof framework that relates memory cost to the optimizer's convergence rate and the Lipschitz sensitivity of the solution map.
AI.result: For μ-strongly convex objectives, matching upper and lower bounds on memory are established as a function of ε and K. For convex objectives under a β-growth condition (β>2), near-matching bounds are obtained, and a phase transition in K is identified: beyond a threshold, additional memory provides no benefit—the online optimizer alone suffices. The general framework explicitly quantifies the memory cost of achieving a prescribed speedup and shows that the convergence rate and Lipschitz sensitivity of the parameter-to-solution map are the two determining quantities.
AI.conclusion: The paper provides a theoretical foundation for amortized parametric optimization by formally characterizing the memory–computation–accuracy tradeoff. It demonstrates that offline memory can effectively substitute for online computation only within certain regimes, and that beyond a critical K, memory ceases to help. The framework offers practical guidance for designing systems that balance offline storage against online iteration budgets, validated by experiments on parameterized ridge regression.

title: One More Turn, Less Regret: A Regret-Based Multi-Turn Benchmark for LLMs' Clarification Policies
summary: Ambiguous user requests make clarification a sequential decision problem for conversational LLM assistants: they must decide whether to ask, what to ask, when to stop, and when to answer. We introduce RegretBench, a multi-turn benchmark that evaluates clarification as policy behavior rather than isolated question quality. RegretBench provides a hidden-intent formulation of ambiguity, supports free-form interaction grounded in semantic-state tracking, and introduces a regret-based objective that measures how much value a model loses relative to a reference clarification policy. Experiments on open-domain QA and product recommendation scenarios show that final success alone is insufficient, as models with similar accuracy can differ substantially in efficiency, robustness to user behaviors, and stopping decisions. By jointly measuring intent resolution, interaction cost, ineffective clarification, and regret, RegretBench reveals whether models clarify usefully and efficiently. Our results show that effective clarification requires more than plausible questions: models must ask the right question at the right time and stop once the user's intended meaning is clear.

AI.tldr: RegretBench is a multi-turn benchmark that evaluates conversational LLMs' clarification strategies as sequential decision-making policies, using a hidden-intent framework and regret-based metrics to measure whether models ask the right questions at the right time and stop appropriately.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluations treat clarification as isolated question quality, ignoring the sequential nature of the decision problem: when to ask, what to ask, when to stop clarifying, and when to answer. Final accuracy alone masks critical differences in efficiency, robustness, and stopping behavior.
AI.method: RegretBench uses a hidden-intent formulation where the user's true intent is known to the simulator but hidden from the model. It supports free-form interaction grounded in semantic-state tracking and introduces a regret-based objective that quantifies the value lost relative to an optimal reference clarification policy. The framework jointly measures intent resolution, interaction cost, ineffective clarification, and regret across open-domain QA and product recommendation scenarios.
AI.result: Models with similar final accuracy exhibit substantial differences in efficiency, robustness to diverse user behaviors, and stopping decisions. Final success alone is insufficient as an evaluation metric; regret-based measurement reveals whether models clarify usefully and efficiently.
AI.conclusion: Effective clarification requires more than generating plausible questions — models must ask the right question at the right time and stop once the user's intended meaning is clear. RegretBench provides a rigorous framework for evaluating this capability as a policy-learning problem.

title: Toward Mechanistic Interpretability of an AI Foundation Model Fine-Tuned for Atmospheric Chemistry
summary: Weather forecasting foundation models (FMs) are increasingly fine-tuned to predict air quality, offering fast global pollution forecasts at lower computational cost than conventional chemical transport models. These FMs are typically trained on reanalysis data and generate forecasts through autoregressive rollout. They do not explicitly represent governing physical or chemical processes. Therefore, high forecast skill does not reveal whether a model has learned physical mechanisms or exploits statistical regularities in its training data. Here, we present the first study of what a FM fine-tuned for atmospheric chemistry has learned by examining Microsoft's Aurora model. We impose controlled chemical perturbations on its forecasts and test them against known photochemical relationships. We then examine the internal representations that generate these forecasts. We find that Aurora captures a first-order ozone response to reactive nitrogen but does not enforce the chemical constraints that a process-based model encodes. It generates chemically inconsistent combinations of related species and relaxes localized emission features such as wildfire plumes toward background. Internally, its representations remain largely organized around the meteorology inherited during pretraining, with little structure specific to chemistry. Using sparse autoencoders, we identify internal components that causally control the chemical forecast but do not map cleanly onto individual atmospheric processes. This work provides a framework for testing whether AI forecasting systems learn atmospheric chemistry from reanalysis data. As these models are increasingly positioned to inform environmental policy decisions, we argue that composition forecasts should also be judged by their internal mechanisms rather than by benchmark skill alone.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates what the fine-tuned Aurora weather foundation model has actually learned about atmospheric chemistry. By imposing chemical perturbations and probing internal representations, the authors find Aurora captures some first-order ozone-NOx relationships but produces chemically inconsistent species combinations, relaxes emission features, and lacks chemically structured internal representations. They argue AI-based composition forecasts should be evaluated on mechanistic fidelity, not predictive accuracy alone.
AI.motivation: Foundation models fine-tuned for air quality forecasting achieve high skill without explicit physical/chemical process representation. This raises a critical question: does high benchmark performance indicate that the model has learned genuine photochemical mechanisms, or merely statistical regularities in reanalysis data? Without answering this, there is risk in deploying such models for environmental policy decisions.
AI.method: The authors perform three classes of analysis on Aurora: (1) controlled chemical perturbation experiments (e.g., perturbing NOx and testing ozone response against known photochemical relationships); (2) examination of internal representations via dimensionality reduction and probing to assess whether latent features organize around chemistry or remain dominated by pretrained meteorology; (3) use of sparse autoencoders to identify causally influential internal components, evaluating whether these map onto interpretable atmospheric processes.
AI.result: Aurora captures the qualitative, first-order ozone response to reactive nitrogen perturbations but fails to enforce chemical consistency constraints (e.g., producing physically implausible combinations of chemically coupled species). It relaxes localized emission features like wildfire plumes toward background levels. Internal representations remain predominantly organized around meteorological features inherited from pretraining, with minimal chemistry-specific structure. Sparse autoencoder-identified components causally control chemical outputs but do not cleanly correspond to individual atmospheric processes.
AI.conclusion: Forecast skill benchmarks are insufficient for evaluating AI atmospheric chemistry models. Mechanistic interpretability analyses reveal that these models can achieve high accuracy without learning robust chemical constraints. The authors advocate that composition forecasts intended for policy applications must be judged by internal mechanisms, not predictive skill alone, and offer a framework for conducting such evaluations.

title: CMI-Mem: Toward Generalizable Long-Term Memory Management via CMI-Augmented Reinforcement Learning
summary: Memory Manager models are pivotal in agent systems. Existing methods rely predominantly on LLM-judged synthetic question-answer (QA) pairs, making memory valuation dependent on sampled queries and the downstream reader. To address this limitation, we propose \textbf{CMI-Mem}, a reinforcement learning(RL)-based lightweight memory manager model with a hybrid reward that combines downstream QA correctness and intrinsic Conditional Mutual Information (CMI). CMI evaluates the information contributed by new conversational inputs relative to the current memory state without conditioning on a sampled QA query, thereby complementing rather than replacing QA grounding. Our codes are available at: https://github.com/Wyb0627/CMIMem , and the CMI-Mem-4B model checkpoint is available at: https://www.modelscope.cn/models/wyb0627/CMIMem-4B

AI.tldr: CMI-Mem is a lightweight RL-based memory manager for agent systems that uses a hybrid reward combining downstream QA correctness with Conditional Mutual Information (CMI), which evaluates informational contribution of new inputs independently of sampled QA queries, thereby reducing dependence on synthetic QA pairs.
AI.motivation: Existing memory manager models for agent systems rely on LLM-judged synthetic QA pairs to assess memory value, creating unwanted dependence on both the sampled queries and the downstream reader model. This makes memory valuation brittle and query-conditioned. The authors aim to introduce a query-independent intrinsic reward that complements QA-based signals.
AI.method: The authors propose CMI-Mem, a lightweight memory manager trained via reinforcement learning with a hybrid reward function. The reward combines two components: (1) downstream QA correctness (extrinsic reward), and (2) Conditional Mutual Information (CMI) as an intrinsic reward that quantifies the information gain of new conversational inputs relative to the current memory state, without conditioning on any sampled QA query. The CMI complements rather than replaces QA grounding.
AI.result: A 4B-parameter model checkpoint (CMI-Mem-4B) is released, with code available on GitHub. The paper demonstrates that CMI-based intrinsic rewards can effectively augment QA-based memory valuation.
AI.conclusion: CMI provides a principled, query-independent signal for memory valuation in agent systems, complementing traditional QA-based approaches. The hybrid reward strategy enables more robust memory management without fully relying on synthetic QA pair quality or downstream reader variability.

title: Progressive Cramming: Reliable Token Compression and What It Reveals
summary: Token cramming compresses sequences into learned embeddings with near-perfect reconstruction, but fixed token budgets and 99\% accuracy thresholds leave it unclear whether residual errors reflect optimization failures or fundamental limits. We introduce progressive cramming, which grows the target prefix token-by-token, stopping only when reconstruction is no longer achievable within a fixed optimization budget. Progressive trajectories occupy low-dimensional structure in embedding space. Prepending a crammed embedding causes a moderate but consistent accuracy drop on multiple-choice benchmarks even with the original prefix in context, and collapses capability almost entirely under generative evaluation. Causal attention-knockout interventions trace this degradation to the embedding's interactions in the model's early layers. These results position progressive cramming as a tool for studying compression limits and show that perfect reconstruction - achievable through brittle steering rather than transferable semantics - is insufficient for meaningful compression.

AI.tldr: Progressive cramming grows compressed token sequences until reconstruction fails, revealing that near-perfect reconstruction does not preserve downstream model capabilities. The degradation is traced to early-layer causal attention interactions, showing that brittle steering achieves reconstruction without transferable semantics.
AI.motivation: Previous token cramming work showed near-perfect reconstruction within fixed token budgets at 99% accuracy thresholds, but left open whether residual errors are optimization failures or fundamental limits. The authors aim to distinguish between these and assess whether reconstruction fidelity translates to preserved model utility.
AI.method: The authors introduce progressive cramming — incrementally growing a target prefix token-by-token until reconstruction can no longer be achieved within a fixed optimization budget. They analyze the low-dimensional structure of resulting embedding trajectories, evaluate downstream performance on multiple-choice and generative benchmarks, and use causal attention-knockout interventions to isolate which model layers degrade capability.
AI.result: Progressive trajectories exhibit low-dimensional structure in embedding space. Prepending crammed embeddings causes moderate accuracy drops on multiple-choice benchmarks (even with the original prefix present) and near-total collapse under generative evaluation. Causal attention-knockout interventions trace this degradation specifically to the embedding's interactions in the model's early layers.
AI.conclusion: Perfect reconstruction is achievable via brittle steering rather than transferable semantics, and is therefore insufficient for meaningful compression. Progressive cramming serves as a tool for probing the fundamental limits of token-level compression in language models.

title: Synthetic minority data is redundant or invalid: a data-dependent validity theory and a de-biased test
comment: 45 pages, 7 figures; Supplementary Information included as appendix
summary: For two decades, the standard remedy for class-imbalanced learning has been to fabricate synthetic minority examples, and the standard evidence of their validity has been a check that cannot fail: synthetic points are scored against the very data that generated them. We de-bias the check. Validity becomes a population quantity -- the probability that a synthetic point truly belongs to the minority class -- with a consistent estimator that scores synthetic points against withheld real data. Where held-out ground truth is available, the classical test underestimates true invalidity in 96-99% of method-by-imbalance-ratio cells, while the de-biased estimator tracks it closely. We prove validity is a property of the data, not the method: class overlap sets an invalidity floor no faithful generator escapes, making oversampling redundant where classes separate and invalid where they overlap. Across 91 methods, three classifiers, and datasets spanning medicine and finance -- including a generator engineered to pass the classical check -- none clears both bars: gains over the best trivial baseline are noise-thin (median below 0.01 F1, a decision threshold's reach), and most damage calibration. We release the audit as a pip-installable test and flip the burden of proof: synthetic minority data must now demonstrate, on the data at hand, both validity and information gain.

AI.tldr: The paper challenges two decades of class-imbalanced learning practice by debiasing the standard validity check for synthetic minority data. It introduces a population-level validity estimator scored against withheld real data, proves that validity is fundamentally limited by class overlap (a property of the data, not the generator), and demonstrates through an extensive audit of 91 methods that no synthetic oversampling approach provides meaningful gains over trivial baselines while most damage calibration.
AI.motivation: For 20 years, synthetic minority oversampling methods have been validated using a circular check: synthetic points are evaluated against the same real data used to generate them, making the test unfalsifiable. The authors aim to de-bias this evaluation, establish a rigorous notion of validity as a population quantity, and determine whether any oversampling method actually provides genuine information gain beyond trivial baselines.
AI.method: The authors define validity as the probability that a synthetic point truly belongs to the minority class and propose a consistent estimator that scores synthetic points against withheld real data (not the data that generated them). They derive theoretical results showing class overlap sets an invalidity floor. They then conduct a large-scale empirical audit across 91 oversampling methods, three classifiers, and multiple real-world datasets (medicine, finance), measuring both validity and F1 gain over the best trivial baseline, as well as calibration impact.
AI.result: The classical test underestimates true invalidity in 96–99% of method-by-imbalance-ratio cells; the de-biased estimator closely tracks held-out ground truth. No method clears both bars: median F1 gain over the best trivial baseline is below 0.01, and most methods damage calibration. Even a generator deliberately engineered to pass the classical check fails the de-biased audit. Class overlap alone dictates the invalidity floor, making oversampling redundant where classes separate and invalid where they overlap.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that the burden of proof must shift: synthetic minority data must demonstrate both validity and information gain on the data at hand. The authors release their audit as a pip-installable package and argue that oversampling's presumed benefits are largely illusory, driven by a flawed evaluation paradigm.

title: AI-Driven Multi-Hop Relay Selection for Smart Urban NR-V2X Networks via Learning-to-Optimize Graph Neural Networks
summary:
Reliable and low-latency NR-V2X communications are essential for smart mobility in dense urban environments. However, limited Road-Side Unit (RSU) density, frequent non-line-of-sight conditions, and highly dynamic vehicular topologies often prevent many Connected and Automated Vehicles (CAVs) from maintaining stable single-hop connectivity. Although multi-hop relay-assisted communication can extend infrastructure coverage, selecting relay links in real time under practical flow, capacity, and connectivity constraints remains challenging.
  Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (MILP) yields optimal multi-hop relay decisions, but its computational complexity scales sharply with network density, limiting real-time applicability. To address this, we propose a Learning-to-Optimise (L2O) framework based on Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) for real-time NR-V2X relay selection. Vehicular communication states are modeled as attributed graphs, where CAVs and RSUs are nodes and candidate radio links are enriched with propagation-aware features. An offline MILP oracle provides optimal supervision, while an edge-aware Graph Isomorphism Network (GINE) approximates oracle decisions with near-constant inference latency. Experiments on large-scale urban datasets generated by an integrated SUMO--GEMV2 simulation pipeline show that the proposed approach achieves connectivity comparable to that of the MILP oracle while reducing execution time by orders of magnitude. The framework enables cost-effective enhancement of urban V2X connectivity by leveraging existing vehicular assets and supporting scalable, real-time NR-V2X operation in smart city environments.

AI.tldr: A GNN-based Learning-to-Optimise framework is proposed for real-time NR-V2X multi-hop relay selection, trained via MILP oracle supervision. It achieves near-optimal connectivity with dramatically reduced inference latency compared to MILP, enabling scalable real-time V2X operation in dense urban environments.
AI.motivation: In dense urban NR-V2X scenarios, limited RSU density, frequent NLOS conditions, and dynamic topologies prevent CAVs from maintaining stable single-hop connectivity. While multi-hop relaying can extend coverage, real-time relay selection under practical constraints is computationally prohibitive using optimal MILP approaches, which scale poorly with network density.
AI.method: The authors propose a Learning-to-Optimise (L2O) framework using Graph Neural Networks. Vehicular communication states are modeled as attributed graphs (nodes: CAVs and RSUs; edges: candidate radio links with propagation-aware features). An offline MILP oracle generates optimal relay decisions as training labels, and an edge-aware Graph Isomorphism Network (GINE) is trained to approximate those decisions. Experiments use an integrated SUMO–GEMV2 simulation pipeline for large-scale urban data.
AI.result: The GINE-based approach achieves connectivity performance comparable to the MILP oracle while reducing execution time by orders of magnitude, delivering near-constant inference latency regardless of network density.
AI.conclusion: The framework enables cost-effective, scalable, real-time NR-V2X relay selection by leveraging existing vehicular assets. It supports reliable smart mobility in smart city environments without the computational burden of traditional optimisation.

title: slang.gr as a Large-Scale Crowdsourced Resource for Non-Standard Greek
comment: Preprint of a paper accepted for publication in the Proceedings of the 14th EETN Conference on Artificial Intelligence (SETN 2026)
summary: Slang is a central component of everyday language, reflecting linguistic creativity, social identity, and cultural change, yet its dy- namic and non-standard nature makes it difficult to model computationally. We present the first large-scale computational study of slang.gr, a crowdsourced lexicon of Greek non-standard language, combining lexical content, user-generated tags, and interaction data. To enable the systematic analysis, we map noisy folksonomic tags to a structured multi-layer taxonomy capturing both semantic categories and sociolinguistic metadata. Using this representation, we analyze the linguistic structure of Greek slang and the behavior of its contributor community. We find that slang is strongly centered on person-related and evaluative language, exhibits high morphological creativity, and is shaped by highly skewed participation with short user lifespans and overlapping communities. Building on these signals, we introduce a community-based confidence score for definitions that integrates user roles, interaction patterns, and moderation signals. Our results show that taxonomy-based representations improve interpretability while retaining meaningful aspects of behavioral structure, enabling a more structured and interpretable analysis of confidence signals. Overall, this work establishes slang.gr as a computational resource for non-standard Greek and provides a foundation for sociolinguistic NLP, bias analysis, and the study of informal language in LLMs.

AI.tldr: A large-scale computational analysis of slang.gr, a crowdsourced Greek slang lexicon, using a structured taxonomy to map folksonomic tags. The study reveals slang's focus on person-related/evaluative language and high morphological creativity, characterizes contributor community dynamics (skewed participation, short lifespans), and introduces a community-based confidence scoring mechanism that improves interpretability of definitions.
AI.motivation: Slang is pervasive in everyday language and encodes rich sociolinguistic signals (identity, cultural change), yet its dynamic, non-standard nature poses significant challenges for computational modeling. Prior work lacks large-scale, structured resources for analyzing non-standard Greek, motivating this first computational study of slang.gr.
AI.method: The authors (1) collect lexical entries, user-generated tags, and interaction data from slang.gr; (2) map noisy folksonomic tags to a structured, multi-layer taxonomy capturing both semantic categories and sociolinguistic metadata; (3) analyze linguistic structure and contributor community behavior using this taxonomy; (4) develop a community-based confidence score integrating user roles, interaction patterns, and moderation signals.
AI.result: Greek slang is strongly centered on person-related and evaluative language with high morphological creativity. The contributor community exhibits highly skewed participation, short user lifespans, and overlapping subcommunities. Taxonomy-based representations improve interpretability while preserving behavioral structure, and the community-based confidence score enables more structured analysis of definition reliability.
AI.conclusion: Slang.gr is established as a computational resource for non-standard Greek, providing a foundation for sociolinguistic NLP, bias analysis, and the study of informal language in LLMs.

title: Memoir: Should a Model Write to Its Memory While It Thinks?
comment: 9 pages, 4 figures, 4 tables, 1 algorithm. Code: https://github.com/RightNow-AI/Memoir
summary: Memoir combines per-sample fast memory, shared slow parameters, variable-depth latent recurrence, and a future-latent energy objective. We test its riskiest coupling: each pondering iteration may rewrite the fast tier that the same iteration reads. On procedural associative recall with key interference, we compare a coupled arm against an otherwise identical read-only pondering arm. Both arms contain 81,738 parameters, including 76,362 trainable parameters, and use matched declared forward multiply-accumulate counts, data, optimizer, schedule, and seeds. After 240 training steps across 12 seeds, coupled recall is 0.5203 with a 95 percent interval of [0.4522, 0.5883], while read-only recall is 0.6557 with [0.5953, 0.7160]. The arms are paired per seed, and the read-only lead of 0.1354 gives a paired t of 3.23 on 11 degrees of freedom with a 95 percent interval of [0.0431, 0.2277] on the difference, winning on 10 of 12 seeds. After 960 steps across 8 seeds, both arms reach 1.0000, so the measured effect is a learning-speed penalty at a fixed budget, not a demonstrated capability penalty. That longer control is ceiling limited, leaving convergence on a non-saturating task unmeasured. A predicted failure in which memory rewriting corrupts the energy signal did not occur: the energy margin grew and held. Kernel restructuring also reduced delta-rule forward time from 0.907 ms to 0.351 ms on the stated device. Code and evidence are available at https://github.com/RightNow-AI/Memoir

AI.tldr: Memoir introduces a coupled architecture where each pondering iteration can rewrite the fast memory it simultaneously reads. Testing this coupling on associative recall with key interference shows a learning-speed penalty (lower recall at 240 steps) compared to a read-only variant, but both converge to perfect recall by 960 steps, indicating no ultimate capability loss.
AI.motivation: To test the riskiest design choice in the Memoir architecture: allowing each recurrent pondering iteration to rewrite the same fast memory tier that it reads during that iteration. This coupling could theoretically corrupt the learning signal.
AI.method: A controlled experiment comparing two arms — "coupled" (read-write pondering) vs. "read-only" (pondering without in-iteration writes) — both with 81,738 parameters (76,362 trainable), matched forward MAC counts, identical data, optimizer, schedule, and seeds. Task: procedural associative recall with key interference. Measured at 240 steps (12 seeds) and 960 steps (8 seeds). Paired t-test across seeds. Also reports kernel optimization reducing delta-rule forward time.
AI.result: At 240 steps: coupled recall = 0.5203 [0.4522, 0.5883]; read-only = 0.6557 [0.5953, 0.7160]; paired difference = 0.1354 (t=3.23, df=11, p<0.01), read-only won 10/12 seeds. At 960 steps: both arms reach 1.0000 recall. The feared energy signal corruption did not occur — the energy margin grew and held. Kernel restructuring reduced delta-rule forward time from 0.907ms to 0.351ms.
AI.conclusion: The coupling imposes a statistically significant learning-speed penalty at a fixed compute budget but does not prevent eventual convergence. Whether convergence rate differs on non-saturating tasks remains unmeasured due to ceiling effects. The predicted failure mode (memory rewriting corrupting the energy signal) was not observed.

title: KeySI: An Interaction Framework for Tuning Text Embeddings Based on Human Feedback
summary: In large-scale text analysis tasks, pre-trained language models are often used to embed text corpora for downstream analysis. However, such models may struggle to capture domain-specific semantics and adapting them typically requires large amounts of labeled data and technical expertise to implement training pipelines. Recent approaches have demonstrated how visual interactions in document projections can capture human feedback as training signals for model tuning. However, these methods operate on document-level feedback, which requires users to open and assess individual documents in order to provide effective feedback. In this paper, we propose KeySI, an interaction framework that enables feature-level feedback through keyword-based concept specification. Users specify feedback by organizing extracted keywords into groups representing concepts, which KeySI translates into document-level supervision for subsequent tuning. By operating on keywords as the primary interaction medium, KeySI reduces the need for manual document inspection and labeling and lowers the barrier to adapting embedding models. We present a prototype implementation that, given a corpus, curates representative keywords, visualizes keywords and document embeddings via dimensionality reduction, allows interactive specification of keyword groups, and supports iterative refinement through system feedback. We evaluate KeySI through a user study, usage scenarios, and quantitative experiments demonstrating its effectiveness in capturing user intent and improving embedding alignment.

AI.tldr: KeySI is an interaction framework that enables users to tune pre-trained language model embeddings through keyword-based concept specification, reducing the need for manual document inspection. Users organize extracted keywords into semantic groups, which the system translates into document-level supervision for model adaptation.
AI.motivation: Pre-trained language models often fail to capture domain-specific semantics. Existing visual interaction methods for embedding adaptation require document-level feedback, forcing users to open and assess individual documents — a labor-intensive process. There is a need for a more efficient, lower-barrier approach to adapting embeddings to user intent.
AI.method: KeySI introduces feature-level feedback via keyword-based concept specification. The system (1) curates representative keywords from a corpus, (2) visualizes both keywords and document embeddings using dimensionality reduction, (3) allows users to interactively organize keywords into concept groups as feedback, and (4) translates these keyword groupings into document-level supervision signals for iterative model tuning. A prototype implements this pipeline with support for iterative refinement through system feedback.
AI.result: The authors evaluate KeySI through a user study, usage scenarios, and quantitative experiments. Results demonstrate that KeySI effectively captures user intent and improves embedding alignment compared to baseline approaches.
AI.conclusion: Operating on keywords as the primary interaction medium lowers the barrier to adapting embedding models by reducing manual document inspection and labeling requirements. KeySI demonstrates that feature-level concept feedback is a viable and effective paradigm for interactive embedding model tuning.

title: A Comparative Evaluation of Embeddings and LLMs in a Greek Book Publisher Setting - The CUP Dataset
comment: Preprint of a manuscript submitted to the 14th EETN Conference on Artificial Intelligence (SETN 2026)
summary: We present CUP, a Greek book retrieval benchmark consisting of 868 catalog records and 104 expert-annotated queries with graded relevance judgments. We evaluate sparse (BM25), dense (sentence-transformers), hybrid, and LLM-assisted retrieval methods in this book-search setting. Multilingual embeddings outperform Greek-specific models, while hybrid retrieval performs best overall. A query-level analysis shows that BM25 excels at named-entity queries, while dense and hybrid methods improve natural-language, noisy, cross-lingual, and concept queries. Field-aware prompting has model-specific effects, while LLM TOC summarization improves TOC-only retrieval and LLM post-filtering improves early-stage retrieval at a high cost. Overall, CUP enables real-world evaluation of Greek retrieval across lexical, semantic, noisy, and cross-lingual queries.

AI.tldr: CUP is a Greek book retrieval benchmark with 868 records and 104 annotated queries, used to evaluate sparse, dense, hybrid, and LLM-assisted retrieval methods. Hybrid retrieval performs best overall, with multilingual embeddings surpassing Greek-specific models. BM25 excels at named-entity queries, while dense/hybrid methods handle natural-language, noisy, cross-lingual, and concept queries better.
AI.motivation: There is a lack of real-world retrieval benchmarks for Greek-language book search, particularly ones with graded relevance judgments that can assess lexical, semantic, noisy, and cross-lingual query scenarios. The authors aim to fill this gap and systematically compare modern retrieval paradigms in a low-resource language setting.
AI.method: The authors construct CUP, a benchmark of 868 Greek book catalog records and 104 expert-annotated queries with graded relevance. They evaluate four retrieval paradigms: (1) sparse retrieval (BM25), (2) dense retrieval using sentence-transformers (both multilingual and Greek-specific), (3) hybrid retrieval combining sparse and dense scores, and (4) LLM-assisted retrieval including field-aware prompting, TOC summarization via LLMs, and LLM-based post-filtering. A query-level analysis categorizes performance by query type (named-entity, natural-language, noisy, cross-lingual, concept).
AI.result: Multilingual embeddings consistently outperform Greek-specific models. Hybrid retrieval achieves the best overall performance. BM25 is strongest on named-entity queries. Dense and hybrid methods significantly improve over BM25 on natural-language, noisy, cross-lingual, and concept queries. Field-aware prompting yields model-specific effects. LLM-based TOC summarization enhances TOC-only retrieval. LLM post-filtering improves early-stage retrieval but incurs high computational cost.
AI.conclusion: CUP provides a realistic testbed for Greek book retrieval across diverse query types. The findings demonstrate that hybrid retrieval is the most robust approach, multilingual models are preferable to monolingual Greek models for this task, and LLM-assisted techniques offer targeted improvements but come with trade-offs in cost and model sensitivity.

title: External Clustering Validation by the Homogeneity-Parsimony Trade-off
summary: Scalar metrics are often used to evaluate clusterings against known classes, but they can obscure a fundamental trade-off: clusterings should be informative about class labels while avoiding unnecessary fragmentation. Here we describe normalized scores of cluster homogeneity and parsimony that quantify this trade-off. These scores build on the information bottleneck principle, modified to not reward lossy compression. We show by example and mathematical proof that our definitions of these scores have the intuitive property of varying monotonically under cluster refinement in contrast to related proposals. Extending the information-theoretic framework beyond Shannon entropies, we furthermore derive set-matching and pair-based counterparts of the homogeneity and parsimony scores. These unify commonly used evaluation criteria and show that, in the pair-based setting, the homogeneity-parsimony trade-off recovers the receiver operating characteristic of binary classifiers. We demonstrate the framework's utility for feature selection and algorithm comparison, illustrating how considering scores jointly can clarify clustering operating points and identify Pareto-optimal solutions.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces normalized homogeneity and parsimony scores for clustering evaluation based on the information bottleneck principle, modified to avoid rewarding lossy compression. These scores vary monotonically under cluster refinement, unify existing evaluation criteria, and reveal that the homogeneity-parsimony trade-off recovers the ROC of binary classifiers in pair-based settings.
AI.motivation: Scalar clustering metrics obscure a fundamental trade-off: clusterings should be informative about class labels (homogeneity) while avoiding unnecessary fragmentation (parsimony). Existing metrics fail to capture this trade-off in a principled, monotonic manner under cluster refinement.
AI.method: The authors build on the information bottleneck principle, modifying it to not reward lossy compression. They define normalized homogeneity and parsimony scores with proven monotonicity under cluster refinement. The framework is extended beyond Shannon entropy to derive set-matching and pair-based counterparts, unifying common evaluation criteria and connecting to ROC analysis.
AI.result: The proposed scores provably vary monotonically under cluster refinement, unlike related proposals. In the pair-based setting, the homogeneity-parsimony trade-off recovers the ROC of binary classifiers. The framework is demonstrated for feature selection and algorithm comparison, enabling identification of Pareto-optimal clustering solutions.
AI.conclusion: Jointly considering homogeneity and parsimony scores clarifies clustering operating points and identifies Pareto-optimal solutions, offering a more principled and unified framework for clustering evaluation than traditional scalar metrics.

title: WaveformQA: Benchmarking LLM Temporal Reasoning on Digital Waveforms
comment: 10 pages; abridged version published in IEEE International Conference on LLM-Aided Design (ICLAD), 2026
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong capabilities in code generation and reasoning, yet their ability to perform temporal reasoning over digital waveform data remains largely unexplored. Although reasoning over digital waveforms is a critical bottleneck in design verification, existing benchmarks primarily evaluate hardware description language (HDL) code generation and use waveforms only as supplementary context. This paper presents WaveformQA, an open-source question-answering benchmark for evaluating LLM temporal reasoning over digital waveforms. The benchmark comprises 360 questions with programmatically generated ground truths across eight categories of varying difficulty, including questions targeting multi-signal correlation and event ordering. Waveforms are generated from open-source design implementations, ensuring reproducibility and grounding the benchmark in real hardware behavior. Evaluation of frontier LLMs reveals that while models achieve reasonable accuracy on simple queries, performance degrades due to context window limitations and reasoning difficulties on complex temporal and multi-step questions. In addition, we show that an event-time JSON representation of waveforms improves LLM reasoning accuracy versus the standardized value change dump (VCD) format. The open-source framework supports extending to new question categories and importing new waveform sources, enabling researchers to rapidly prototype temporal reasoning experiments.

AI.tldr: WaveformQA is a benchmark of 360 question-answer pairs for evaluating LLM temporal reasoning over digital waveforms. Frontier LLMs perform well on simple queries but struggle with complex multi-signal and multi-step temporal questions. An event-time JSON format outperforms the standard VCD format for LLM reasoning.
AI.motivation: LLM temporal reasoning over digital waveform data is unexplored yet critical for hardware design verification. Existing benchmarks focus on HDL code generation with waveforms only as supplementary context, lacking dedicated evaluation of temporal reasoning on waveforms themselves.
AI.method: The authors introduce WaveformQA, an open-source QA benchmark with 360 questions across 8 difficulty categories. Waveforms are sourced from real open-source hardware designs with programmatically generated ground truths. Questions target multi-signal correlation, event ordering, and other temporal reasoning tasks. Two input representations are compared: standard VCD format and a proposed event-time JSON format.
AI.result: Frontier LLMs show reasonable accuracy on simple waveform queries but performance degrades significantly on complex temporal and multi-step questions due to context window limitations and reasoning difficulties. The event-time JSON representation consistently improves LLM accuracy over the VCD format.
AI.conclusion: WaveformQA exposes key weaknesses in LLM temporal reasoning over digital waveforms and demonstrates that representation format (JSON vs. VCD) significantly impacts performance. The extensible open-source framework enables further research on temporal reasoning in hardware verification contexts.

title: A Unified Moral-Value Dataset for Instruction Tuning
comment: Accepted at the 4th International Workshop on Value Engineering in AI (VALE 2026), co-located with IJCAI-ECAI 2026
summary: Large language models (LLMs) have developed rapidly and become valuable tools in everyday life. However, how to align LLMs to a particular set of human values is still an open problem. Recent studies show that instruction tuning has strong potential for zero-shot tasks and may serve as an effective approach to addressing value alignment. Nevertheless, although many datasets for instruction tuning already exist, they are not specifically designed around moral scenarios and behaviors. We construct a unified moral-value dataset that can be directly used for instruction tuning. This dataset is built upon existing moral-value datasets by merging them into a unified corpus and converting them into an instruction-response format. We show that training on a mixed dataset combining general task datasets with our dataset preserves general-task performance, and we report preliminary observations on how the mixing ratio affects value-oriented task performance. Our work provides a moral-value dataset for instruction tuning and offers a useful resource for further alignment research. The dataset is available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/teohzzh/value-for-instruction-tuning.

AI.tldr: The authors construct a unified moral-value dataset in instruction-response format by merging and converting existing moral datasets, and demonstrate that mixing this dataset with general task data during instruction tuning preserves general performance while enabling value alignment.
AI.motivation: Aligning LLMs with human values remains an open problem. While instruction tuning shows promise for zero-shot generalization, existing instruction-tuning datasets lack specific focus on moral scenarios and behaviors. A dedicated moral-value dataset for instruction tuning is needed.
AI.method: The authors aggregate existing moral-value datasets, merge them into a unified corpus, and convert them into an instruction-response format suitable for instruction tuning. They then evaluate training on a mixed dataset combining general task data with their moral-value dataset.
AI.result: Training on the mixed dataset preserves general-task performance. Preliminary observations indicate that the mixing ratio between general and moral-value data affects performance on value-oriented tasks.
AI.conclusion: The unified moral-value dataset serves as a practical resource for instruction-tuning-based value alignment research, enabling future work on balancing general capabilities with moral alignment.

title: New Complexity-Theoretic Frontiers of Tractability for Neural Network Training
comment: Appeared in the proceedings of NeurIPS 2023
summary: In spite of the fundamental role of neural networks in contemporary machine learning research, our understanding of the computational complexity of optimally training neural networks remains incomplete even when dealing with the simplest kinds of activation functions. Indeed, while there has been a number of very recent results that establish ever-tighter lower bounds for the problem under linear and ReLU activation functions, less progress has been made towards the identification of novel polynomial-time tractable network architectures. In this article we obtain novel algorithmic upper bounds for training linear- and ReLU-activated neural networks to optimality which push the boundaries of tractability for these problems beyond the previous state of the art. In particular, for ReLU networks we establish the polynomial-time tractability of all architectures where hidden neurons have an out-degree of $1$, improving upon the previous algorithm of Arora, Basu, Mianjy and Mukherjee. On the other hand, for networks with linear activation functions we identify the first non-trivial polynomial-time solvable class of networks by obtaining an algorithm that can optimally train network architectures satisfying a novel data throughput condition.

AI.tldr: The paper establishes new polynomial-time algorithmic upper bounds for optimally training neural networks with linear and ReLU activations. For ReLU networks, it proves tractability when hidden neurons have out-degree 1. For linear networks, it identifies the first non-trivial polynomially solvable class via a novel data throughput condition.
AI.motivation: Despite neural networks' central role in ML, the computational complexity of optimal training remains poorly understood. Recent work has focused on lower bounds, but progress on identifying tractable architectures has lagged. This paper aims to close that gap by pushing the boundaries of polynomial-time solvability.
AI.method: The paper develops novel algorithmic techniques to derive upper bounds. For ReLU networks, it leverages the out-degree-1 constraint on hidden neurons to design a polynomial-time optimal training algorithm, improving on prior work by Arora et al. For linear networks, it introduces a data throughput condition that characterizes a new tractable class and constructs an algorithm exploiting this structural property.
AI.result: For ReLU-activated networks, all architectures with hidden neuron out-degree of 1 are polynomially tractable for optimal training. For linear-activated networks, architectures satisfying the data throughput condition are polynomially solvable — the first non-trivial tractable class identified for this setting.
AI.conclusion: The paper successfully expands the known frontier of tractable neural network training, both for ReLU networks (out-degree-1 architectures) and linear networks (data throughput condition), establishing new algorithmic upper bounds that surpass the previous state of the art.

title: NVIDIA-labs OO Agents: Native Python Object-Oriented Agents
summary:
Traditional agent development is split across prompt templates, tool schemas, callback code, and workflow graphs. We present NVIDIA Object-Oriented Agents (NOOA), a model-agnostic Python framework for building reliable AI agents. NOOA takes a simpler approach: an agent is a Python object. Its methods are the actions the model can take, fields are its state, docstrings are its prompts, and its type annotations are contracts. A method whose code body consists of "..." is completed at runtime by an LLM-driven agent loop, while methods with normal bodies remain standard deterministic Python.
