This gives developers and agents the same interface, so agent behavior can be tested, traced, refactored, and improved just like other software.
  This paper makes three contributions. (1) We present the agent-as-a-Python-object programming model and the design principles behind it. Where Python has existing abstractions, we adopt them directly. Agent-specific capabilities--context, events, state rendering, long-term memory, and validated LLM loops--are exposed through simple Pythonic APIs, so both developers and agents share one familiar programming model. (2) We identify six model-facing ideas that NOOA is, to our knowledge, the first to combine on a single surface: typed input/output, pass-by-reference over live objects, code as action, programmable loop engineering, explicit object state, and model-callable harness APIs for context and events. We find the community already converging on several of these ideas--often as experimental or partial features--and present the comparison to encourage further adoption. (3) We demonstrate that current models use this interface effectively, both in targeted capability tests and on agentic and reasoning benchmarks such as SWE-bench Verified and Terminal-Bench 2.0 and ARC-AGI-3.

AI.tldr: NOOA is a Python framework where agents are just Python objects — methods are actions, docstrings are prompts, type annotations are contracts. Empty-bodied methods ("...") are filled at runtime by an LLM agent loop, while normal methods remain deterministic code. The paper introduces this object-oriented agent model, identifies six novel model-facing design ideas combined for the first time, and demonstrates strong performance on benchmarks like SWE-bench Verified, Terminal-Bench 2.0, and ARC-AGI-3.
AI.motivation: Traditional agent development fragments agent logic across disparate artifacts: prompt templates, tool schemas, callback code, and workflow graphs. This fragmentation makes agents hard to test, trace, refactor, and improve using standard software engineering practices. NOOA aims to unify agent development into a single, familiar Python object-oriented programming model that both developers and AI agents share.
AI.method: NOOA treats an agent as a Python object with: (1) methods as actions the model can invoke; (2) fields as persistent state; (3) docstrings as prompts; (4) type annotations as input/output contracts. A method body set to "..." triggers LLM-driven runtime completion via an agent loop, while methods with regular code bodies execute deterministically. Agent-specific capabilities — context management, events, state rendering, long-term memory, validated LLM loops — are exposed through Pythonic APIs. The six model-facing design ideas combined are: typed input/output, pass-by-reference over live objects, code as action, programmable loop engineering, explicit object state, and model-callable harness APIs for context and events.
AI.result: Current LLMs use the NOOA interface effectively. The framework demonstrates capability on targeted tests and achieves strong results on agentic and reasoning benchmarks: SWE-bench Verified, Terminal-Bench 2.0, and ARC-AGI-3. The paper also observes that the community is independently converging on several of the six design ideas, though typically as experimental or partial features.
AI.conclusion: NOOA demonstrates that collapsing agent development into a single Python object-oriented abstraction is both feasible and effective. By leveraging Python's native constructs (methods, fields, docstrings, type annotations), the framework eliminates the fragmentation of traditional agent stacks. The convergence of the community toward similar ideas validates the approach, and NOOA provides the first unified implementation combining all six model-facing design principles.

title: news-crawler-LM: A Small Long-Context Model For High-Quality News Crawling
summary: Extracting structured content from news pages remains challenging due to heterogeneous HTML layouts, inconsistent markup, and substantial boilerplate such as navigation elements and advertisements. Rule-based news crawlers can achieve high extraction accuracy by encoding site-specific structure, but require manual configuration in order to generalize to new publishers. Large language models provide a more flexible alternative by reducing the need for handcrafted rules, but their high computational cost limits practical deployment. In this paper, we introduce news-crawler-LM, a small long-context language model fine-tuned on high-quality, human-validated extractions from the Fundus news-crawling library. Our model converts raw HTML into plaintext and structured JSON, including fields such as headline, author, publication date, and article body. In our experiments, news-crawler-LM outperforms strong baselines in HTML-to-Markdown and HTML-to-JSON extraction, improving performance by +4.8 BLEU and +6.1 METEOR in the HTML-to-Markdown task, and by +2.2 BLEU and +4.1 METEOR in the HTML-to-JSON task. However, we also observe that our model only slightly better compared to other rule-based parsing libraries on the HTML-to-plaintext task in evaluations on previously unseen publishers. We release all models and artifacts to the research community.

AI.tldr: The paper presents news-crawler-LM, a small long-context language model fine-tuned on human-validated extractions to convert raw HTML news pages into structured plaintext and JSON. It outperforms strong baselines on HTML-to-Markdown and HTML-to-JSON tasks but shows only marginal improvement over rule-based parsers on plaintext extraction for unseen publishers.
AI.motivation: News content extraction is hindered by heterogeneous HTML layouts, inconsistent markup, and boilerplate. Rule-based crawlers require costly manual configuration per publisher, while large language models offer flexibility but are computationally expensive for practical deployment. A small, efficient LM fine-tuned for this task could bridge the gap.
AI.method: The authors fine-tune a small long-context language model on high-quality, human-validated extractions sourced from the Fundus news-crawling library. The model takes raw HTML as input and outputs plaintext or structured JSON containing headline, author, publication date, and article body fields.
AI.result: On HTML-to-Markdown, news-crawler-LM achieves +4.8 BLEU and +6.1 METEOR over baselines. On HTML-to-JSON, it improves by +2.2 BLEU and +4.1 METEOR. However, on HTML-to-plaintext for unseen publishers, it only slightly outperforms rule-based parsing libraries.
AI.conclusion: The fine-tuned small LM effectively combines the flexibility of LLMs with practical efficiency, yielding strong structured extraction performance. The marginal gains on plaintext for unseen publishers suggest that rule-based methods remain competitive for simpler extraction tasks, while the model excels at structured output generation.

title: Robust Asynchronous Q-Learning under Reward and State Corruption via Batching
comment: To appear at the 65th IEEE Conference on Decision and Control (CDC) 2026
summary: Motivated by reinforcement learning in harsh environments, we consider the problem of learning an optimal policy subject to adversarially corrupted feedback. Specifically, at each time-step, an adversary can perturb both the reward and state observations of the learner following the Huber contamination model. To defend against such data corruption, we propose {\texttt{BR-Async-Q}}: a novel, epoch-based, robust \(Q\)-learning algorithm built upon two key ideas: (i) partitioning the online data stream into batches to reduce variance, and (ii) constructing robust estimates of the Bellman optimality operator using such batched data. We prove a high-probability $\ell_\infty$ error bound for {\texttt{BR-Async-Q}} that matches that for vanilla \(Q\)-learning, up to a small additive term that scales with the fraction of corrupted samples. To our knowledge, this provides the first robustness guarantee for asynchronous \(Q\)-learning subject to both reward and state corruption. Furthermore, when only rewards are corrupted, the dependence of our algorithm's bound on the corruption fraction is minimax optimal.

AI.tldr: Proposes BR-Async-Q, the first robust asynchronous Q-learning algorithm with guarantees under both reward and state corruption (Huber contamination), achieving near-optimal error bounds matching vanilla Q-learning up to an additive corruption-dependent term.
AI.motivation: Reinforcement learning deployed in harsh/adversarial environments where both reward and state observations can be corrupted. Existing robust RL methods lack guarantees for the asynchronous Q-learning setting with simultaneous reward and state corruption.
AI.method: BR-Async-Q: an epoch-based robust Q-learning algorithm that (i) partitions the online data stream into batches to reduce variance, and (ii) constructs robust estimates of the Bellman optimality operator using batched data under the Huber contamination model.
AI.result: Proves a high-probability ℓ∞ error bound matching vanilla Q-learning up to a small additive term scaling with the corruption fraction. When only rewards are corrupted, the dependence on corruption fraction is minimax optimal. First robustness guarantee for asynchronous Q-learning under both reward and state corruption.
AI.conclusion: BR-Async-Q provides the first provably robust asynchronous Q-learning framework against joint reward and state corruption, with statistically optimal guarantees in the reward-only corruption setting.

title: ArbiGraph: Arbitrarily Scalable Verifiable Task Graphs for Evaluating Context Management
summary: We introduce ARBIGRAPH, a benchmark generator for evaluating whether tool-assisted language agents can retain, update, compose, and discard task-relevant context across extended reasoning workflows. ARBIGRAPH represents each task as a natural-language problem with an executable Python solver, and composes tasks through typed intermediate states, instantiated here as scalar and list values. This design enables controllable task graphs whose length, dependency structure, distractor count, and value type can be varied while preserving exact automatic verification. We instantiate ARBIGRAPH with math, GSM-style word-problems, and Python-tracing task categories, and evaluate a Qwen3.5-27B tool-assisted agent across four topologies. The results show high accuracy on isolated tasks but substantial degradation on more complex dependent tasks: accuracy drops by up to 33.3% on branching chains of dependent math tasks. This shows that ARBIGRAPH exposes failures that are not visible from single-task evaluation alone. Our code, generated datasets, and evaluation results are available at https://github.com/pavelgolikov/ArbiGraph.git

AI.tldr: ARBIGRAPH is a benchmark generator that evaluates tool-assisted language agents on their ability to manage context across multi-step reasoning workflows. It creates task graphs with controllable complexity (length, dependencies, distractors) and shows that agents degrade significantly on dependent tasks despite performing well on isolated ones.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks evaluate language agents on isolated tasks, failing to capture failures in context retention, updating, composition, and discarding that emerge in extended reasoning workflows. There is a need for controllable, automatically verifiable benchmarks that test these capabilities.
AI.method: ARBIGRAPH generates tasks as natural-language problems paired with executable Python solvers. Tasks are composed through typed intermediate states (scalar and list values), forming task graphs where length, dependency structure, distractor count, and value types are systematically varied. Tasks span math, GSM-style word problems, and Python-tracing categories. Evaluation uses a Qwen3.5-27B tool-assisted agent across four topology types.
AI.result: The Qwen3.5-27B agent achieves high accuracy on isolated tasks but suffers up to 33.3% accuracy degradation on more complex dependent tasks, particularly on branching chains of dependent math tasks. Failures emerge that single-task evaluation cannot reveal.
AI.conclusion: ARBIGRAPH effectively exposes context-management failures in tool-assisted language agents that are invisible under standard single-task evaluation, highlighting the need for multi-step, dependency-aware benchmarks in assessing agent capabilities.

title: Adaptive Depth Sparse Framework: Similarity-Driven Resource Allocation for Pre-Trained LLMs
comment: Accepted by ICIC 2026. 12 pages, 2 figures, 4 tables
summary: Large language models (LLMs) achieve strong generation and reasoning performance, but the Transformer architecture incurs high inference cost. Existing acceleration methods often rely on task-specific fine-tuning or training from scratch, increasing adaptation cost and limiting cross-task usability. We present an Adaptive Depth Sparse Framework (AdaDSF) that converts off-the-shelf pre-trained LLMs into depth-sparse models without full retraining. Our key insight is that layers contribute unequally to representation transformation, characterized by the cosine similarity between layer input and output hidden states. Based on this, AdaDSF assigns layer-wise token retention ratios from similarity statistics, uses a lightweight router to select informative tokens at each layer, and introduces a feature-preserving alignment objective to match intermediate and final representations between sparse and dense models. On GPT-NeoX and Qwen2.5 over language modeling and commonsense reasoning, AdaDSF substantially reduces inference FLOPs while preserving performance close to dense counterparts. Under comparable sparsity, AdaDSF consistently yields smaller accuracy degradation than strong baselines including MoD, D-LLM, and DLO.

AI.tldr: AdaDSF converts pre-trained LLMs into depth-sparse models without retraining by using cosine similarity between layer inputs/outputs to guide token retention, a lightweight router for token selection, and a feature-preserving alignment objective. It reduces inference FLOPs while maintaining performance close to dense models, outperforming MoD, D-LLM, and DLO.
AI.motivation: LLMs suffer from high inference costs due to the Transformer architecture. Existing acceleration methods require task-specific fine-tuning or training from scratch, increasing adaptation cost and limiting cross-task usability. The authors aim to convert off-the-shelf pre-trained LLMs into sparse models without full retraining.
AI.method: AdaDSF (Adaptive Depth Sparse Framework) uses three components: (1) layer-wise token retention ratios derived from cosine similarity statistics between layer input and output hidden states, based on the insight that layers contribute unequally to representation transformation; (2) a lightweight router that selects informative tokens at each layer; (3) a feature-preserving alignment objective that matches intermediate and final representations between the sparse and dense models.
AI.result: Evaluated on GPT-NeoX and Qwen2.5 across language modeling and commonsense reasoning tasks, AdaDSF substantially reduces inference FLOPs while preserving near-dense performance. Under comparable sparsity, it consistently yields smaller accuracy degradation than MoD, D-LLM, and DLO.
AI.conclusion: AdaDSF provides an effective method for post-hoc depth sparsification of pre-trained LLMs, achieving inference acceleration with minimal performance loss and outperforming existing sparse inference baselines.

title: The Human-AI Substitution Principle: When will you be replaced by AI in your organization?
summary: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming organizations, raising a fundamental organizational and economic question: when will a human employee be replaced by AI? We present an analytical model for studying Human--AI Task Allocation (HAT) in hierarchical organizations. A central feature of the HAT model is that it formally encodes the economic asymmetry between human skill acquisition and AI capability scaling. The HAT model allows us to derive how risk-adjusted costs, skills, organizational depth, deployment scale, strategic adaptation, and risk jointly determine when, where, why, and under what structural conditions human--AI replacement occurs. A key result is the Human--AI Substitution Principle, which provides a precise condition --- grounded in the formal asymmetry assumption --- under which AI replaces human labor. Building on this result, we show that AI adoption can produce abrupt workforce transitions, hybrid human--AI organizations, including cases where risk heterogeneity sustains human and AI roles without requiring a minimum-human-fraction constraint, and flatter managerial hierarchies with wider spans of control. The HAT model identifies structural conditions under which middle-management roles exhibit elevated vulnerability to automation, and shows that the vulnerability of highly skilled workers depends on a skill threshold shaped by organizational depth, baseline costs, and risk differentials. More broadly, the paper connects automation economics, organizational design, AI governance, and workforce planning into a unified theory of AI-driven organizational transformation.

AI.tldr: The paper presents the Human-AI Task Allocation (HAT) model, a formal analytical framework for determining when, where, and why AI replaces human labor in hierarchical organizations. The model encodes the economic asymmetry between human skill acquisition and AI capability scaling, yielding the Human-AI Substitution Principle — a precise condition for replacement — and reveals structural implications including abrupt workforce transitions, flatter hierarchies, and elevated automation vulnerability in middle management.
AI.motivation: AI is rapidly transforming organizations, but there is no formal, unified analytical framework for determining under what structural and economic conditions human employees will be replaced by AI. The authors aim to fill this gap by modeling the fundamental economic asymmetry between how humans acquire skills and how AI capabilities scale.
AI.method: The authors develop the Human-AI Task Allocation (HAT) model, an analytical model of hierarchical organizations that formally encodes the asymmetry between human skill acquisition (costly, time-intensive) and AI capability scaling (capital-intensive, rapidly scalable). The model incorporates risk-adjusted costs, skills, organizational depth, deployment scale, strategic adaptation, and risk heterogeneity to derive equilibrium conditions for task allocation between humans and AI.
AI.result: Key results include: (1) the Human-AI Substitution Principle — a precise condition for when AI replaces human labor grounded in the formal asymmetry assumption; (2) AI adoption can cause abrupt workforce transitions; (3) risk heterogeneity can sustain hybrid human-AI organizations without requiring minimum-human-fraction constraints; (4) AI adoption leads to flatter managerial hierarchies with wider spans of control; (5) middle-management roles face elevated automation vulnerability; and (6) highly skilled worker vulnerability depends on a skill threshold shaped by organizational depth, baseline costs, and risk differentials.
AI.conclusion: The HAT model provides a unified theory connecting automation economics, organizational design, AI governance, and workforce planning. It demonstrates that AI-driven organizational transformation is governed by identifiable structural conditions, not merely technological capability, and offers a formal toolkit for analyzing workforce transitions, hierarchy reshaping, and strategic adaptation to AI deployment.

title: GRADRAG: Cross-Component Prompt Adaptation for Coordinated Multi-Agent RAG
summary: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems increasingly employ multiple LLM agents. Yet, most prior work optimizes components in isolation rather than coordinating improvements across the pipeline. We introduce GRADRAG, a framework for cross-component prompt adaptation that models the RAG pipeline as a computational graph and propagates structured evaluation feedback to update upstream agents. An Evaluator critiques downstream answers and supporting evidence, producing actionable feedback that a Prompt Optimizer uses to iteratively update adaptive agents, such as retrievers, graph constructors, and answerers. The Evaluator also triggers early stopping when the output is deemed satisfactory. We evaluate GRADRAG on the SQUALITY and QMSUM benchmarks under two retrieval paradigms: flat chunk-based retrieval using IRCoT-style query refinement (Trivedi et al., 2023), and graph-based retrieval that constructs and iteratively enriches an entity-relation graph from the document. Across both settings, GRADRAG consistently outperforms one-step refinement baselines that update only the final generator, achieving a 12-15 percentage point net preference margin in LLM-judged pairwise comparisons, with most gains realized within two refinement iterations.

AI.tldr: GRADRAG introduces a cross-component prompt optimization framework for multi-agent RAG systems that models the pipeline as a computational graph and propagates evaluation feedback upstream, achieving 12-15 pp gains over single-component baselines within two iterations.
AI.motivation: Most prior work on RAG systems optimizes individual components (retrievers, graph constructors, answer generators) in isolation, missing opportunities for coordinated, cross-component improvements driven by downstream answer quality.
AI.method: GRADRAG models the RAG pipeline as a computational graph. An Evaluator critiques downstream answers and supporting evidence, producing structured feedback. A Prompt Optimizer then iteratively updates upstream adaptive agents (retrievers, graph constructors, answerers) based on this feedback. The Evaluator also implements early stopping when outputs are satisfactory.
AI.result: On SQUALITY and QMSUM benchmarks, GRADRAG consistently outperforms one-step refinement baselines (which update only the final generator) across both flat chunk-based (IRCoT-style) and graph-based retrieval paradigms, achieving a 12-15 percentage point net preference margin in LLM-judged pairwise comparisons. Most gains are realized within two refinement iterations.
AI.conclusion: Cross-component feedback propagation via structured prompt adaptation significantly improves multi-agent RAG performance over isolated component optimization, and the approach converges quickly (within ~2 iterations).

title: Offline RL with Hierarchical Action Chunking
summary: Offline goal-conditioned reinforcement learning (RL) holds the promise of learning general-purpose policies from static datasets. However, scaling these methods to long-horizon tasks remains a challenge due to the curse of horizon, where value estimation errors can compound through long chains of bootstrapped Bellman backups. Existing hierarchical approaches mitigate this by decomposing tasks into subgoals, yet they often rely on low-level controllers that suffer from myopic execution and biased value estimates. In this work, we propose Hierarchical Implicit Q-Chunking (HiQC), an offline goal-conditioned RL algorithm that combines high-level latent planning with low-level action chunking. By conditioning the low-level critic on temporally extended action sequences, HiQC enables unbiased k-step value backups, compressing the horizon at both the planning and execution levels. We theoretically demonstrate that this dual decomposition results in a tighter bound on value error under a bounded per-backup error model compared to standard hierarchy or flat chunking alone. Empirically, HiQC achieves the highest aggregate performance among the compared methods on the OGBench suite, with its largest gains on long-horizon navigation tasks such as humanoid-giant.

AI.tldr: HiQC combines hierarchical latent planning with action chunking for offline goal-conditioned RL, using k-step unbiased value backups to reduce horizon-induced compounding errors, achieving SOTA on long-horizon navigation benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Scaling offline goal-conditioned RL to long-horizon tasks is hindered by the curse of horizon: bootstrapped Bellman backups compound value estimation errors. Existing hierarchical methods decompose tasks into subgoals but low-level controllers remain myopic with biased value estimates. Flat action chunking alone is insufficient.
AI.method: HiQC integrates two levels: (1) a high-level latent planner that generates subgoals, and (2) a low-level action chunking mechanism where the critic conditions on temporally extended action sequences, enabling unbiased k-step value backups. This dual decomposition compresses the effective horizon at both planning and execution levels.
AI.result: Theoretically, HiQC provably yields a tighter bound on value error under bounded per-backup error compared to standard hierarchy or flat chunking alone. Empirically, HiQC achieves the highest aggregate performance on the OGBench suite, with largest gains on long-horizon tasks like humanoid-giant.
AI.conclusion: HiQC demonstrates that jointly decomposing the horizon at planning and execution levels via hierarchical subgoal planning and action chunking effectively mitigates compounding value errors in offline goal-conditioned RL, enabling robust scaling to long-horizon tasks.

title: Refusal-Gated Decoding: Preserving Refusal Behavior Under High-Temperature Sampling
summary: High-temperature sampling is one of the primary mechanisms for increasing diversity in LLMs. Recent advances in truncation-based sampling techniques have helped mitigate drawbacks of high-temperature sampling such as neural text degeneration, thereby enabling greater diversity in LLM outputs without sacrificing coherence. However, increasing the entropy of the token probability distribution via high temperatures has also been shown to weaken model guardrails by reducing the model's refusal response in the presence of harmful prompts. Despite the potential benefits of high-temperature sampling and the importance of maintaining model safety, there is a lack of existing solutions for maintaining the refusal behavior of LLMs under a higher entropy regime. To address this gap, we systematically study how temperature influences refusal behavior in LLMs and propose an efficient sequential decoding approach which preserves a model's greedy decoding refusal response at high temperatures while incurring minimal additional latency. Through extensive experiments, we show that our approach preserves 91-99% of the greedy decoding refusal behavior across three benchmark datasets without compromising the model's high-temperature response for safe prompts. Our work demonstrates how refusal behavior can be maintained in an efficient manner for applications which require high-temperature sampling.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses the problem that high-temperature sampling in LLMs, while increasing output diversity, undermines safety guardrails by reducing refusal responses to harmful prompts. The authors propose a sequential decoding method that preserves greedy-decoding refusal behavior at high temperatures with minimal latency overhead, achieving 91-99% refusal preservation across benchmarks without degrading safe-prompt responses.
AI.motivation: High-temperature sampling increases LLM output diversity but simultaneously weakens model guardrails by reducing refusal rates on harmful prompts. Existing truncation-based methods mitigate text degeneration but do not address this safety degradation. There is a critical gap: no prior work maintains refusal behavior under high-entropy decoding regimes, which is essential for applications requiring both diversity and safety.
AI.method: The authors systematically study how temperature affects refusal behavior and propose a sequential decoding approach that operates efficiently at inference time. The method preserves the model's greedy-decoding refusal response when sampling at high temperatures, adding only minimal latency overhead.
AI.result: The proposed approach preserves 91-99% of greedy-decoding refusal behavior across three benchmark datasets while maintaining high-temperature response quality for safe prompts.
AI.conclusion: Refusal behavior can be efficiently maintained under high-temperature sampling regimes, enabling applications that require both output diversity and robust safety guardrails without sacrificing performance on safe prompts.

title: Phonetic forced alignment for low-resource language varieties: Model training and evaluation on Chengdu Mandarin
summary: Phonetic forced alignment is a key technique in phonetic research, yet existing alignment systems lack specialized models for low-resource language varieties. We address this by training text-dependent and text-independent aligners for Chengdu Mandarin using a 17-hour corpus and a custom G2P dictionary. We trained a text-dependent GMM-HMM model (Chengdu-MFA) and fine-tuned a pretrained audio encoder on frame classification with Chengdu-MFA's pseudo label for text-independent alignment (Chengdu-FC). Evaluation on an expert-annotated test set show that both methods significantly outperform Standard Mandarin baselines. Chengdu-MFA reduced average phone boundary differences by 31.8%, while Chengdu-FC achieved a 61.2% reduction. This work establishes a practical bootstrapping pipeline for developing accurate aligners for under-resourced varieties without labor- and time-intensive manual annotation.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a bootstrapping pipeline for phonetic forced alignment in low-resource language varieties, using Chengdu Mandarin as a case study. A text-dependent GMM-HMM model and a text-independent fine-tuned encoder both significantly outperform Standard Mandarin baselines, with the text-independent approach achieving a 61.2% reduction in phone boundary errors.
AI.motivation: Existing phonetic forced alignment systems lack specialized models for low-resource language varieties, forcing researchers to rely on mismatched models (e.g., Standard Mandarin models for dialectal speech). Manual annotation of training data is labor- and time-intensive, creating a need for automated bootstrapping approaches.
AI.method: The authors used a 17-hour corpus of Chengdu Mandarin and a custom G2P dictionary. They trained a text-dependent GMM-HMM Montreal Forced Aligner model (Chengdu-MFA). They then used Chengdu-MFA's pseudo labels to fine-tune a pretrained audio encoder on frame classification, yielding a text-independent aligner (Chengdu-FC). Both were evaluated against expert-annotated ground truth and compared to Standard Mandarin baselines.
AI.result: Both Chengdu-MFA and Chengdu-FC significantly outperformed Standard Mandarin baselines. Chengdu-MFA reduced average phone boundary differences by 31.8%, while Chengdu-FC achieved a 61.2% reduction — more than doubling the improvement of the text-dependent approach.
AI.conclusion: The proposed bootstrapping pipeline enables the development of accurate phonetic aligners for under-resourced language varieties without requiring costly manual annotation. The text-independent fine-tuning approach (Chengdu-FC) proved particularly effective, offering a practical pathway for extending forced alignment to low-resource dialects and languages.

title: Multilevel Graph Wavelet Compressed Sensing with Scale-Aware Neural Recovery
summary: Scientific machine learning methods such as neural operators and physics-informed neural networks have advanced engineering applications and inverse problems, but their training typically requires large volumes of simulated data. This makes data preparation and model training expensive. We propose Graph Wavelet Compressed Sensing (GWCS), a learning-based framework for offline compression of graph signals by representing them as sparse, interpretable wavelet-domain representations using the spectral graph wavelet transform. The framework combines a nonparametric multilevel importance sampler, which retains high-energy wavelet coefficients within each scale for a given compression ratio, with a scale-aware graph neural network that reconstructs the signal from the sparse coefficients. We evaluate the proposed framework on synthetic approximately band-limited graph signals over random graphs and four PDE simulation datasets over meshes, which include Turbulent Radiative Layer, Viscoelastic Instability, Kolmogorov Flow, and Dynamic Stall. We compare against graph signal sampling methods and graph autoencoder baselines. Results demonstrate that the framework achieves high reconstruction fidelity and substantial data compression compared to existing benchmarks.

AI.tldr: GWCS is a learning-based framework that compresses graph signals offline by representing them sparsely in the spectral graph wavelet domain, using a multilevel importance sampler and a scale-aware GNN for reconstruction, achieving high fidelity and substantial compression on PDE simulation data.
AI.motivation: Training neural operators and physics-informed neural networks requires large volumes of simulated data, making data preparation and model training expensive. There is a need for effective offline compression of graph-structured simulation data to reduce storage and training costs.
AI.method: GWCS combines two key components: (1) a nonparametric multilevel importance sampler that retains high-energy wavelet coefficients within each scale for a given compression ratio, leveraging the spectral graph wavelet transform; and (2) a scale-aware graph neural network that reconstructs the original signal from the sparse wavelet coefficients.
AI.result: On synthetic approximately band-limited graph signals and four PDE simulation datasets (Turbulent Radiative Layer, Viscoelastic Instability, Kolmogorov Flow, Dynamic Stall), GWCS outperforms graph signal sampling methods and graph autoencoder baselines in reconstruction fidelity at substantial compression ratios.
AI.conclusion: GWCS provides an effective offline compression framework for graph signals, combining interpretability of wavelet-domain sparsity with learned reconstruction, and demonstrates strong empirical performance across diverse PDE simulation scenarios.

title: Capital Markets LLM Reliability Score (CM-LRS): From Plausible to Bankable
comment: 23 pages. Rubrics, prompts, and demonstration tasks are publicly available.
summary:
In capital-markets workflows the question is rarely whether a large language model can produce a fluent draft, but whether the draft is bankable: defensible in front of a counter-party or a regulator, with the documents in hand. Existing methods address parts of that gap: open-domain QA benchmarks reward surface accuracy, and finance benchmarks (FinanceBench, FinQA, ConvFinQA) advance document-grounded and numerical QA but evaluate at the question-answer layer rather than the workflow outputs practitioners defend.
  We introduce CM-LRS, a Capital Markets LLM Reliability Score, evaluating outputs at the workflow-output layer across seven dimensions: factual accuracy, evidence traceability, numerical consistency, workflow completeness, source discipline, decision usefulness, and reviewability/auditability. Each is scored 0-5 against a rubric anchored on signals reviewers in regulated settings use; the aggregate is tunable to the workflow.
  We demonstrate CM-LRS on five workflows (DCM transaction-terms extraction, precedent retrieval, issuer profile synthesis, M&A transaction-comparable reasoning, ECM transaction-terms extraction) over public SEC EDGAR filings, a public UK takeover release, and fictional synthetic supplements, scoring four models against four independent LLM judges spanning three model families.
  Three findings. First, the frontier closed-source models cluster within 0.22 points on four-judge averaged CM-LRS (Sonnet 4.6 = 4.31, Opus 4.7 = 4.30, GPT-5.5 = 4.09); all four judges place the open-weights baseline (Llama 3.3 70B = 3.15) last. Second, that gap concentrates on retrieval (2.23) and synthesis (2.15), not extraction (0.84). Third, Decision Usefulness shows the widest cross-model dispersion of any dimension (4.0 points on issuer profiling) and top-tier inter-judge agreement (mean r = 0.52).
  Plausibility is cheap. Bankability is the bar.

AI.tldr: CM-LRS introduces a seven-dimension reliability framework for evaluating LLM outputs in capital markets workflows, moving beyond surface accuracy to assess "bankability." Testing across five workflows with four models and four judges reveals frontier models cluster closely while an open-weights baseline lags, with the largest gaps in retrieval and synthesis tasks, and Decision Usefulness showing the widest model dispersion.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM evaluation benchmarks (open-domain QA, FinanceBench, FinQA, ConvFinQA) assess surface accuracy or document-grounded QA, but they fail to evaluate at the workflow-output layer — the actual deliverables that capital markets practitioners must defend before counterparties and regulators. The critical gap is measuring whether a generated draft is "bankable" (legally and regulatorily defensible), not merely plausible or fluent.
AI.method: CM-LRS evaluates LLM outputs across seven rubric-scored dimensions (0–5 scale): factual accuracy, evidence traceability, numerical consistency, workflow completeness, source discipline, decision usefulness, and reviewability/auditability. These rubrics are anchored on signals used by reviewers in regulated settings, with an aggregate score tunable per workflow. The framework was demonstrated on five capital markets workflows (DCM terms extraction, precedent retrieval, issuer profile synthesis, M&A comparable reasoning, ECM terms extraction) using public SEC EDGAR filings, a UK takeover release, and synthetic supplements. Four models were scored by four independent LLM judges from three model families.
AI.result: (1) Frontier closed-source models cluster within 0.22 points on four-judge averaged CM-LRS (Sonnet 4.6: 4.31, Opus 4.7: 4.30, GPT-5.5: 4.09), while Llama 3.3 70B trails at 3.15. (2) The performance gap concentrates in retrieval (2.23 point difference) and synthesis (2.15), with extraction showing a smaller gap (0.84). (3) Decision Usefulness exhibits the widest cross-model dispersion (4.0 points on issuer profiling) and the highest inter-judge agreement (mean r = 0.52).
AI.conclusion: Plausibility is cheap; bankability is the bar. CM-LRS demonstrates that meaningful evaluation of LLMs in regulated financial workflows requires assessing outputs at the deliverable layer, not the QA layer. The framework reveals that frontier models have converged on reliability but still struggle with retrieval and synthesis tasks, and that Decision Usefulness is both the most discriminating and most reliably judged dimension.

title: Position Bias is Hidden Behind Ceiling Effects: A Permutation Diagnostic for LLM Benchmarks
comment: 25 pages, 4 figures, 2 appendices. Code, data, and preregistration verification at https://github.com/TambaClan/inspect_permute. Companion paper: arXiv:2606.26185
summary: Position bias in multiple-choice LLM evaluation is widely cited as a confound in capability comparisons, but published measurements rely on single answer-order shuffles whose results confound the bias signal with content-level noise and sampling stochasticity. I introduce inspect_permute, an open-source extension to the inspect_ai evaluation framework that runs exhaustive answer-order permutations per question and reports the chi-squared / Cramer V signature of position bias with bootstrap confidence intervals. I apply the tool across four vendors (gpt-4o-mini, claude-haiku-4-5, gemini-2.5-flash, grok-3) on five MMLU subjects, 24,000 API calls under temperature-0 generation, with falsifier predictions pre-registered via a public SHA-256 hash before half the data was observed. Position bias turns out to be statistically detectable only within a roughly 60-95% base-accuracy Goldilocks zone. Below it, processing-load dominance swamps subject-specific signal; above it, ceiling effects compress the variance below the chi-squared test resolution. Detectable cells separate into two mechanism types: monotone A-to-D decrease (processing_load, in low-tier models) and non-monotone D-drop (content_ambiguity, in a narrow capability band). Standard MMLU places every frontier-tier model above the detection band, so absence of signal there should be read as not measurable, not unbiased. Together with the ceiling-effect characterisation in arXiv:2606.26185, this work brackets the detectable region of position-bias measurement and makes the field central question askable in a verifiable form. Package, data, preregistration under MIT.

AI.tldr: Position bias in LLM multiple-choice evaluation is only statistically detectable within a "Goldilocks zone" (~60-95% base accuracy). The author introduces inspect_permute, a tool using exhaustive answer-order permutations and chi-squared/Cramér's V tests with bootstrap confidence intervals, revealing two distinct bias mechanisms: monotone A-to-D decrease (processing load) and non-monotone D-drop (content ambiguity). Frontier models sit above the detection band, meaning absence of signal reflects non-measurability, not unbiasedness.
AI.motivation: Existing position-bias measurements in LLM evaluation rely on single answer-order shuffles, which confound the bias signal with content-level noise and sampling stochasticity. This makes published comparisons unreliable and the central question of position bias unfalsifiable. The work aims to provide a rigorous, statistically principled framework for detecting and characterizing position bias.
AI.method: The author introduces inspect_permute, an open-source extension to the inspect_ai evaluation framework. It runs exhaustive answer-order permutations per question and computes chi-squared statistics and Cramér's V effect sizes with bootstrap confidence intervals. The tool was applied across four vendors (gpt-4o-mini, claude-haiku-4-5, gemini-2.5-flash, grok-3) on five MMLU subjects, totaling 24,000 API calls under temperature-0 generation. Falsifier predictions were pre-registered via a public SHA-256 hash before half the data was observed.
AI.result: Position bias is statistically detectable only within a ~60-95% base-accuracy "Goldilocks zone." Below this zone, processing-load dominance swamps subject-specific signal; above it, ceiling effects compress variance below chi-squared test resolution. Detectable cells reveal two mechanism types: (1) monotone A-to-D decrease attributed to processing load (in low-tier models), and (2) non-monotone D-drop attributed to content ambiguity (in a narrow capability band). Standard MMLU places every frontier-tier model above the detection band.
AI.conclusion: Absence of position-bias signal in frontier models on MMLU should be interpreted as "not measurable" rather than "unbiased." Together with the ceiling-effect characterization in arXiv:2606.26185, this work brackets the detectable region of position-bias measurement, making the central question askable in a verifiable, falsifiable form.

title: Profiling Lightweight Large Language Models
summary: Lightweight large language models (LLMs) are increasingly being deployed locally on personal computers and are expected to play a growing role in resource-constrained edge and mobile environments. In such settings, energy consumption, execution time, and memory usage directly affect practical usability, yet existing evaluations of LLM efficiency largely rely on proxy descriptors such as parameter count or FLOPs, often decoupled from task precision. This paper introduces a PTME-based experimental framework for the precision-aware profiling of lightweight LLM inference, jointly measuring Precision, execution Time, peak Memory usage, and Energy consumption through direct hardware-level measurements. The methodology is applied to a representative set of lightweight LLMs executed locally under edge-class resource envelopes on a controlled desktop platform, using benchmarks spanning code generation, mathematical reasoning, and multi-task understanding. We find that static proxy descriptors approximate inference cost well but fail to predict precision. Tightening the resource envelope increases cost without affecting precision, amplifying execution time more strongly than energy and penalizing larger models the most. Moreover, no single model dominates across all PTME dimensions, and a Pareto analysis reveals non-dominated configurations that would be hidden by accuracy-only or efficiency-only assessments, providing practical guidance for selecting models under different resource envelopes. These results show that selecting lightweight LLMs by size, FLOPs, latency, or accuracy alone can select the wrong deployment candidate; PTME profiling exposes configurations that preserve useful accuracy at lower physical cost.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a PTME (Precision, Time, Memory, Energy) experimental framework for hardware-level profiling of lightweight LLM inference. Applied to local edge deployments, it reveals that static proxies (parameter count, FLOPs) predict cost but not accuracy, and that Pareto-optimal configurations hidden by single-metric evaluations offer superior precision-efficiency trade-offs.
AI.motivation: Lightweight LLMs are increasingly deployed on resource-constrained edge and mobile devices where energy, time, and memory directly impact usability. Existing efficiency evaluations rely on proxy metrics (parameter count, FLOPs) decoupled from actual task precision, risking suboptimal deployment decisions.
AI.method: A PTME-based experimental framework that jointly measures Precision, execution Time, peak Memory usage, and Energy consumption via direct hardware-level measurements. Applied to representative lightweight LLMs on a controlled desktop platform under edge-class resource envelopes, using benchmarks for code generation, mathematical reasoning, and multi-task understanding. Pareto analysis identifies non-dominated configurations.
AI.result: Static proxies approximate inference cost well but fail to predict precision. Tightening resource envelopes increases cost without affecting precision, amplifies execution time more than energy, and penalizes larger models most. No single model dominates all PTME dimensions. Pareto analysis reveals non-dominated configurations hidden by accuracy-only or efficiency-only assessments.
AI.conclusion: Selecting lightweight LLMs by size, FLOPs, latency, or accuracy alone can lead to wrong deployment candidates. PTME profiling exposes configurations that preserve useful accuracy at lower physical cost, providing practical guidance for model selection under diverse resource constraints.

title: Word meaning co-determines vowel-inherent spectral change. A corpus-based investigation of conversational Mandarin
summary: This study investigates vowel-inherent spectral change (VISC) in spontaneous conversational Mandarin. Using the generalized additive model and word embeddings from distributional semantics, we show that, when controlling for variables such as vowel duration, gender, speaker identity, co-articulation, vowel identity, and utterance position, vowel formant trajectory dynamics have word-specific components that are tied to their meaning in context: The F1 and F2 trajectories of words can be predicted from their contextualized embeddings with an accuracy that substantially exceeds a permutation baseline. Challenging modular cognitive models of speech production, these results indicate that, words' semantics co-determine the fine details of their articulation.

AI.tldr: This study demonstrates that vowel formant trajectories (F1, F2) in spontaneous Mandarin speech carry word-specific information predictable from contextualized word embeddings, suggesting that semantic content co-determines fine-grained articulatory detail.
AI.motivation: To challenge modular cognitive models of speech production by testing whether vowel-inherent spectral change (VISC) in spontaneous speech is influenced by word-level semantics, beyond traditional phonetic and phonological factors.
AI.method: The authors analyzed spontaneous conversational Mandarin using Generalized Additive Models (GAMs) to control for vowel duration, gender, speaker identity, co-articulation, vowel identity, and utterance position. They then tested whether contextualized word embeddings (from distributional semantics) could predict F1 and F2 formant trajectory dynamics, comparing prediction accuracy against a permutation baseline.
AI.result: Word-specific components of vowel formant trajectories were predictable from contextualized embeddings with accuracy substantially exceeding the permutation baseline, indicating that F1 and F2 trajectories carry word-meaning-dependent information beyond what is accounted for by controlled phonetic variables.
AI.conclusion: The findings argue against strictly modular models of speech production, instead supporting the view that lexical semantics co-determine the fine articulatory details of vowel production in spontaneous speech.

title: TwistedMerge: Certified Higher-Order Diagnostics and Abstention for Model Merging
summary: Model merging combines independently trained or fine-tuned models, but pairwise alignability does not imply globally consistent alignment. We formulate merging as a finite descent problem in which checkpoints are local objects, alignment maps are transitions, and cycle products are residuals. TwistedMerge is a conservative certification pipeline that separates fixed-chart averaging, synchronization-removable gauge inconsistency, a certified central obstruction on a specified comparison complex, and nonabelian holonomy. A residual is promoted to a cohomology class only after inverse-consistency, coefficient-identification, centrality, and closure tests; otherwise the method abstains and returns an ordinary or synchronized fallback. We prove a constant-edge no-go result, frozen-complex three-way and predeclared-family error-control theorems, and a refinement test for comparison-complex sensitivity. A planted neural alignment defect is removed by cycle-consistent synchronization, showing that a nonzero cycle score alone is not a higher obstruction. Controlled central systems recover the predicted non-coboundary and projective-rank behavior, while noisy estimates move from certification to abstention without false lifts on the tested controls. A trained low-rank-adapter audit shows that naive factor averaging depends on the chosen GLr representative, whereas global factor synchronization and dense-delta SVD are stable. On natural checkpoint collections, cycle residuals do not predict merge degradation and no natural central or period-index class is certified. The results position descent theory as a falsifiable certification and abstention framework.

AI.tldr: TwistedMerge proposes a conservative certification pipeline for model merging based on descent theory. It treats checkpoints as local objects, alignment maps as transitions, and cycle products as residuals. The framework applies rigorous tests (inverse-consistency, coefficient-identification, centrality, closure) before promoting residuals to cohomology classes, abstaining otherwise. The authors prove error-control theorems and demonstrate that cycle residuals do not predict merge degradation in natural checkpoints, positioning descent theory as a falsifiable certification framework.
AI.motivation: Existing model merging methods assume pairwise alignability implies global consistency, which is false. This motivates a rigorous, falsifiable certification framework grounded in descent theory that can detect genuine obstructions, abstain when tests fail, and avoid false positives from noisy estimates.
AI.method: The method formulates model merging as a finite descent problem using the language of cohomology and gauge theory. TwistedMerge consists of: (1) fixed-chart averaging, (2) synchronization-removable gauge inconsistency removal, (3) a certified central obstruction test on a specified comparison complex, and (4) nonabelian holonomy analysis. A residual advances through four tests (inverse-consistency, coefficient-identification, centrality, closure) before being promoted to a cohomology class; failure triggers abstention with a fallback. Theoretical results include a constant-edge no-go theorem, frozen-complex error-control theorems, and a refinement test for comparison-complex sensitivity.
AI.result: Key findings: (1) A planted neural alignment defect is removed by cycle-consistent synchronization, proving nonzero cycle scores alone are not higher obstructions. (2) Controlled central systems recover predicted non-coboundary and projective-rank behavior. (3) Noisy estimates move from certification to abstention without false lifts on controls. (4) Low-rank adapter audit shows naive factor averaging depends on the chosen GLr representative, while global factor synchronization and dense-delta SVD are stable. (5) On natural checkpoints, cycle residuals do not predict merge degradation and no natural central or period-index class is certified.
AI.conclusion: The authors establish descent theory as a viable falsifiable certification and abstention framework for model merging. The work provides rigorous theoretical guarantees (no-go results, error-control theorems) and empirical validation showing that genuine obstructions can be certified while noisy estimates are correctly filtered through abstention, avoiding false positives.

title: Enhancing Explainable Cardiac Diagnosis with Guide-Grounded Multimodal LLMs
summary: The electrocardiogram (ECG) is a cornerstone of cardiac as- sessment, yet clinical deployment of deep learning models remains con- strained by limited interpretability and the hallucination risk of large language models (LLMs). Existing CNN+Grad-CAM+multimodal LLM frameworks can generate ECG reports, but their explanations are often only weakly grounded in established diagnostic criteria, reducing trust- worthiness and reproducibility. We propose a guide-grounded multimodal framework that explicitly anchors report generation in curated clinical knowledge. A convolutional neural network (CNN) and Grad-CAM first produce class probabilities and class-specific heatmaps from 12-lead ECG images. In parallel, authoritative ECG textbooks and guideline materials are distilled offline into a structured ECG Interpretation Guide, which is injected as a fixed knowledge block for every sample. Conditioned on the ECG image, Grad-CAM overlay, CNN-derived fact pack, and the in- jected guide, a multimodal LLM generates structured diagnostic reports with guideline-consistent terminology and criteria usage. Experiments on the full PTB-XL test set demonstrate that guide grounding improves se- mantic quality and perceived consistency of generated reports while pre- serving competitive classification performance. In particular, our method increases the average BERTScore of generated impressions from 0.818 to 0.953 relative to a strong CNN+Grad-CAM+MLLM baseline, indicat- ing closer alignment with reference reports. These findings suggest that injecting a distilled interpretation guide into the multimodal prompting pipeline offers a practical pathway to reduce hallucinations and enhance the clinical plausibility of LLM-based ECG explanations, bringing ex- plainable cardiac diagnosis closer to real-world deployment.

AI.tldr: A guide-grounded multimodal framework that injects distilled clinical ECG interpretation guidelines into a CNN+Grad-CAM+LLM pipeline, improving report generation quality (BERTScore from 0.818 to 0.953) and reducing hallucinations while maintaining classification performance.
AI.motivation: Deep learning models for ECG analysis suffer from limited interpretability and LLM hallucination risks. Existing CNN+Grad-CAM+multimodal LLM frameworks produce reports with explanations only weakly grounded in established diagnostic criteria, undermining trustworthiness and reproducibility in clinical settings.
AI.method: A two-stage framework: (1) CNN and Grad-CAM extract class probabilities and class-specific heatmaps from 12-lead ECG images; (2) Authoritative ECG textbooks and guidelines are distilled offline into a structured ECG Interpretation Guide, injected as a fixed knowledge block per sample. A multimodal LLM then generates diagnostic reports conditioned on the ECG image, Grad-CAM overlay, CNN-derived fact pack, and the injected guide, ensuring guideline-consistent terminology and criteria usage.
AI.result: On the full PTB-XL test set, guide grounding improved semantic quality and perceived consistency of generated reports. Average BERTScore of generated impressions increased from 0.818 to 0.953 relative to a CNN+Grad-CAM+MLLM baseline, indicating significantly closer alignment with reference reports, while preserving competitive classification performance.
AI.conclusion: Injecting a distilled clinical interpretation guide into the multimodal prompting pipeline offers a practical pathway to reduce LLM hallucinations and enhance the clinical plausibility of automated ECG explanations, advancing explainable cardiac diagnosis toward real-world deployment.

title: MemTools: A Unified Research Framework for Interoperable Agent Memory
summary: While memory systems are essential for agent architectures, pervasive architectural fragmentation restricts systematic research. Existing implementations typically couple different stages of the memory lifecycle, entangle evaluation logic with specific datasets, and provide limited support for the management of heterogeneous memory types. We introduce MemTools, an interoperability research framework that decouples memory system components from their underlying deployment environments. MemTools standardizes the memory lifecycle through declarative data contracts, enabling the interchangeable assembly of components across different systems. It orthogonally separates benchmark datasets from execution protocols to facilitate controlled assessments. Furthermore, MemTools provides a unified computational interface for coordinating symbolic, neural, and multimodal memory representations within a shared runtime. Empirical evaluations on cross-system component integration, evaluation protocol reconfiguration, and heterogeneous memory coordination demonstrate that MemTools enables systematic isolation and analysis of memory design variables. These findings suggest that MemTools provides a practical and extensible infrastructure for advancing principled research on agent memory.

AI.tldr: MemTools is an interoperability research framework that decouples memory system components, standardizes the memory lifecycle via declarative data contracts, separates benchmarks from execution protocols, and unifies symbolic, neural, and multimodal memory representations, enabling systematic isolation and analysis of memory design variables in agent architectures.
AI.motivation: Pervasive architectural fragmentation in agent memory systems restricts systematic research. Existing implementations couple different stages of the memory lifecycle, entangle evaluation logic with specific datasets, and offer limited support for managing heterogeneous memory types, making controlled experimentation difficult.
AI.method: MemTools introduces three key design principles: (1) declarative data contracts to standardize the memory lifecycle and enable interchangeable component assembly; (2) orthogonal separation of benchmark datasets from execution protocols for controlled assessments; (3) a unified computational interface that coordinates symbolic, neural, and multimodal memory representations within a shared runtime.
AI.result: Empirical evaluations demonstrate that MemTools enables systematic isolation and analysis of memory design variables across three dimensions: cross-system component integration, evaluation protocol reconfiguration, and heterogeneous memory coordination.
AI.conclusion: MemTools provides a practical and extensible infrastructure for advancing principled research on agent memory, addressing fragmentation by enabling modular, interoperable experimentation.

title: Information-Theoretically Secure Aggregation for Lightweight Federated Learning: Resilient to Dropouts and Adversaries
summary: On-device federated learning (FL) enables privacy-preserving and personalized model training on resource-constrained devices such as smartphones and IoT nodes. To reduce communication cost, sign-based methods (e.g., signSGD) transmit one-bit gradients. However, exposing gradient signs makes them vulnerable to inference attacks, while existing secure aggregation schemes are often incompatible with such methods or incur significant computational and communication overhead. We propose a lightweight and information-theoretically secure aggregation framework tailored for sign-based FL. The framework securely computes the majority vote (MV) polynomial through single-round secure multiplication, ensuring end-to-end information-theoretic security under the honest-majority assumption while revealing only the final aggregated sign to the server. To enhance efficiency and scalability, we introduce two key techniques. First, inverse-form exponent reduction halves the effective MV polynomial degree, reducing both communication and computation costs. Second, we propose single-round secure multiplication, achieving linear offline complexity and storage with only a single online communication. Together, these techniques reduce online communication by up to 99.5% and latency by up to 85.7% compared to conventional approaches. Also, by leveraging inherent MDS-code-based decoding, the framework achieves robustness against both dropouts and adversarial behaviors, yielding accuracy gains of up to 20.65% and 10.74%, respectively. Overall, the proposed framework establishes a practical foundation for large-scale, low-latency, and information-theoretically secure aggregation in sign-based FL.

AI.tldr: A lightweight, information-theoretically secure aggregation framework for sign-based federated learning that uses majority-vote polynomials, inverse-form exponent reduction, and single-round secure multiplication to drastically cut communication and latency while remaining robust to dropouts and adversarial behaviors.
AI.motivation: Sign-based FL (e.g., signSGD) reduces communication by transmitting 1-bit gradients, but exposing gradient signs invites inference attacks. Existing secure aggregation schemes are either incompatible with sign-based methods or impose heavy computational/communication burdens. A lightweight, provably secure aggregation framework tailored for sign-based FL is needed.
AI.method: The authors propose an information-theoretically secure framework under the honest-majority assumption that securely computes a majority-vote (MV) polynomial via single-round secure multiplication. Two key innovations: (1) inverse-form exponent reduction that halves the effective degree of the MV polynomial, cutting both communication and computation; (2) single-round secure multiplication with linear offline complexity/storage and only one online communication round. Robustness is achieved through MDS-code-based decoding, handling both client dropouts and adversarial behaviors.
AI.result: Compared to conventional approaches, online communication is reduced by up to 99.5% and latency by up to 85.7%. The MDS-code-based robustness mechanism yields accuracy gains of up to 20.65% under dropout conditions and 10.74% under adversarial settings.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides a practical foundation for large-scale, low-latency, information-theoretically secure aggregation in sign-based FL, effectively bridging the gap between communication-efficient sign-based training and strong privacy guarantees.

title: Efficient and Interpretable Body-Based Emotion Recognition with Lightweight Temporal Convolutional Networks
comment: Accepted at the 14th International Conference on Affective Computing and Intelligent Interaction (ACII 2026)
summary: Body-based emotion recognition is important for real-time affective systems, but graph-based skeleton models can be computationally expensive. This paper studies whether lightweight temporal convolutional networks (TCNs) can provide an efficient and interpretable alternative for body-based emotion classification. We evaluate a family of TCN models on DIEM-A and compare them with a graph-based time-series graph (G-TSG) baseline using accuracy, macro-F1, parameter count, and inference latency. Although G-TSG achieves the highest mean performance, TCN-Base remains within $1.58$ accuracy points and $1.25$ macro-F1 points while using $79.18\%$ fewer parameters and reducing classifier latency by approximately $12.5\times$. We also analyze body-region contributions using region-specific TCN models, zero-based occlusion, and G-TSG gradient saliency. The results show that upper-body motion provides the strongest standalone regional cue, that the usefulness of body regions varies across emotions, and that different interpretability methods capture distinct aspects of model behavior. These findings suggest that lightweight TCNs can support efficient body-based emotion recognition while also providing practical insight into how motion cues contribute to classification.

AI.tldr: Lightweight TCNs approach graph-based skeleton models in body-based emotion recognition while using ~79% fewer parameters and achieving ~12.5× faster inference, with upper-body motion emerging as the strongest regional cue.
AI.motivation: Graph-based skeleton models for body-based emotion recognition are computationally expensive, limiting their deployment in real-time affective systems. The authors investigate whether lightweight temporal convolutional networks (TCNs) can serve as an efficient and interpretable alternative.
AI.method: A family of TCN models is evaluated on the DIEM-A dataset and compared against a graph-based time-series graph (G-TSG) baseline. Metrics include accuracy, macro-F1, parameter count, and inference latency. Interpretability is assessed through region-specific TCN models, zero-based occlusion, and G-TSG gradient saliency.
AI.result: G-TSG achieves the highest mean accuracy and macro-F1, but TCN-Base trails by only 1.58 accuracy points and 1.25 macro-F1 points while using 79.18% fewer parameters and reducing classifier latency by ~12.5×. Upper-body motion is the strongest standalone regional cue; the usefulness of body regions varies across emotions; and different interpretability methods capture distinct aspects of model behavior.
AI.conclusion: Lightweight TCNs offer a viable, efficient alternative for body-based emotion recognition with practical interpretability benefits, revealing that emotion-relevant motion cues are regionally distributed in distinct ways.

title: Anti-Periodic Positional Encoding: Möbius Boundary Conditions Make In-Context Retrieval Reliable
summary: Möbius RoPE is a rotary positional encoding built on the anti-periodic frequency ladder $θ_i=π(2i+1)/N$: every rotation plane advances by an odd multiple of $π$ across the training context, so the positional holonomy is $-1$ and the two ends of the sequence are deterministically coupled through a closed-form Dirichlet "dipole"; to our knowledge this is the first anti-periodic boundary condition in positional encoding. We verify the theory numerically to $\sim 10^{-6}$ and pretrain 48 models spanning six 160M-class and three 410M-class arms (2B FineWeb-Edu tokens each; the hybrid arm puts Möbius frequencies on 25% of heads). Hybrid perplexity is unchanged (29.66 vs. 29.72), but needle-in-a-haystack retrieval becomes reliable: $90.3\pm5.7\%$ versus $63.3\pm31.4\%$ at context 512 ($n=6$ seeds), observed worst seed 86% versus 14%, robust variance tests $p=0.013$-$0.029$ (unadjusted), recurring at 410M (Levene $p=0.040$). Matched controls isolate the mechanism: an aperiodic ladder in the same frequency band reproduces none of the effect, and a periodic (holonomy $+1$) ladder only a fraction. Swapping trained models' frequency table back to standard RoPE (weights frozen) collapses retrieval, with damage concentrated on far needles: trained models depend on this long-range geometry. A NoPE arm is even more reliable at short context but pays a 13% perplexity tax and extrapolates worst; only the anti-periodic hybrid pairs baseline perplexity with a high reliability floor. The effect is scoped to single-needle retrieval within the training window; a one-line frequency swap thus provides zero-cost insurance against the retrieval seed lottery.

AI.tldr: Möbius RoPE introduces anti-periodic rotary positional encoding with holonomy −1, deterministically coupling sequence ends via odd-π frequency ladders. A hybrid variant achieves baseline-level perplexity while dramatically improving needle-in-a-haystack retrieval reliability (90% vs 63% at context 512), eliminating the "seed lottery" with a one-line frequency swap.
AI.motivation: Standard RoPE suffers from unreliable long-range retrieval due to high variance across random seeds (the "retrieval seed lottery"). The authors aim to provide deterministic coupling between sequence endpoints to improve retrieval robustness without sacrificing perplexity, exploring anti-periodic boundary conditions as a novel design dimension in positional encoding.
AI.method: The authors propose Möbius RoPE, using frequency ladders θᵢ = π(2i+1)/N where each rotation plane advances by odd multiples of π, yielding holonomy −1 (anti-periodic boundary). This creates a closed-form Dirichlet "dipole" coupling sequence ends. The hybrid variant applies Möbius frequencies to only 25% of attention heads, with the rest using standard RoPE. Experiments pretrain 48 models (160M and 410M parameters) on 2B FineWeb-Edu tokens each, with ablations including aperiodic ladders (same band), periodic ladders (holonomy +1), standard RoPE, and NoPE baselines.
AI.result: Hybrid Möbius RoPE matches baseline perplexity (29.66 vs 29.72) while dramatically improving needle-in-a-haystack retrieval: 90.3±5.7% vs 63.3±31.4% at context 512 (n=6 seeds), with worst-seed performance 86% vs 14%. Robust variance tests yield p=0.013-0.029 (unadjusted), replicated at 410M scale (Levene p=0.040). Ablations confirm the anti-periodic mechanism: aperiodic ladders reproduce no effect; periodic ladders yield only partial improvement. Swapping frequencies back to standard RoPE post-training collapses retrieval, confirming dependence on the learned geometry. NoPE achieves excellent short-context retrieval but suffers a 13% perplexity penalty and poor extrapolation.
AI.conclusion: The anti-periodic hybrid provides "zero-cost insurance" against the retrieval seed lottery — baseline perplexity with a high reliability floor — scoped to single-needle retrieval within the training window. The work introduces a new design axis (boundary conditions / holonomy) for positional encodings and demonstrates that a one-line frequency swap suffices for robust gains.

title: HierarchicalDAEW: Domain-Aware Edge-Weighted Graph Convolution with Evidential Uncertainty for Multi-Section Spatial Gene Expression Prediction from H&E Histology
summary: Spatial transcriptomics assays remain costly and technically demanding, restricting transcriptome-wide profiling to specialist settings and preventing routine clinical deployment. Predicting spatially resolved gene expression from H&E histology could close this gap, yet current methods largely ignore the underlying tissue architecture and rarely quantify how their predictions can be trusted. We introduce HierarchicalDAEW, a dual-graph architecture that addresses both gaps. On the spot graph, a Domain-Aware Edge-Weighted convolutional operator learns separate projections for inter-domain, intra-domain, and boundary edges derived from Leiden clustering, allowing the model to treat tissue heterogeneity as an explicit structural signal rather than an implicit one. A second gene-level graph then fuses protein-protein interaction priors from STRING-DB with tissue-specific co-expression through learned attention gating, propagating predictions from a landmark gene set to a broader gene panel. Reliability is handled through evidential uncertainty estimation, which produces far better calibrated confidence intervals than Monte Carlo dropout under identical conditions. Across six human Visium sections spanning breast, colorectal, prostate, and cerebellar tissue, and against thirteen published baselines, HierarchicalDAEW achieves the strongest correlation with ground-truth expression, with gains that hold up under multi-seed reproducibility checks and negative controls that rule out positional shortcuts. Ablations further confirm that both the domain-aware edge typing and the hierarchical depth are necessary to this improvement, and calibrated uncertainty estimates identify low-confidence predictions for pathologist review before clinical action.

AI.tldr: HierarchicalDAEW introduces a dual-graph architecture for predicting spatial gene expression from H&E histology, explicitly modeling tissue heterogeneity via domain-aware edge-weighted convolutions and fusing PPI priors with tissue-specific co-expression via a gene-level graph, while providing calibrated uncertainty estimates through evidential deep learning. It outperforms 13 baselines across six human tissue sections.
AI.motivation: Spatial transcriptomics is costly and technically demanding, limiting its clinical deployment. Predicting gene expression from routine H&E histology could bridge this gap, but existing methods (1) ignore underlying tissue architecture as an explicit signal and (2) rarely quantify prediction reliability, which is essential for clinical decision-making.
AI.method: HierarchicalDAEW employs a dual-graph design: (1) a spot graph with a Domain-Aware Edge-Weighted (DAEW) convolutional operator that learns separate projections for inter-domain, intra-domain, and boundary edges derived from Leiden clustering, treating tissue heterogeneity as structural signal; (2) a gene-level graph that fuses STRING-DB protein-protein interaction priors with tissue-specific co-expression via learned attention gating, propagating from landmark genes to a broader panel. Reliability is quantified via evidential uncertainty estimation, yielding well-calibrated confidence intervals superior to Monte Carlo dropout.
AI.result: Across six human Visium sections (breast, colorectal, prostate, cerebellar tissue) and against thirteen published baselines, HierarchicalDAEW achieved the strongest correlation with ground-truth expression. Gains persisted under multi-seed reproducibility checks and negative controls ruling out positional shortcuts. Calibrated uncertainty estimates successfully flagged low-confidence predictions.
AI.conclusion: Both domain-aware edge typing and hierarchical depth are necessary for the observed performance gains. The calibrated uncertainty framework enables pathologist review of low-confidence predictions before clinical action, making the approach a step toward clinically deployable gene expression prediction from routine histology.

title: Auditing Provenance Sensitivity in LLM Agent Action Selection
summary: LLM agents choose tools and arguments from context that mixes user requests, tool outputs, retrieved records, memory, and untrusted text. Evidence can be relevant without being authorized to determine a decision, so a correct action need not be grounded only in permitted evidence. We introduce a target-specific authorization audit that labels context factors separately for each tool and argument target. Its primary test holds the task, proposition, position, and policy fixed while changing only the proposition's source authority. We then test behavior when valid evidence is weakened and use context-subset interactions as a secondary localization diagnostic. Across 450 controlled next-action tasks and multiple open-weight LLM families, trusted and untrusted variants produce different actions in 5.4 percent of competing cases versus 1.7 percent of supporting cases. Under controlled degradation, unauthorized competition is retained in a full-correct, mixed-error, clean-correct pattern in 2.4 percent of comparisons, with a 95 percent confidence interval from 2.1 to 3.0 percent. These are controlled stress-set rates, not deployment prevalence. The models respond to textual source-authority cues, but this does not prevent untrusted evidence from influencing their actions.

AI.tldr: LLM agents can be influenced by untrusted evidence even when source-authority cues are present. The paper introduces a target-specific authorization audit that isolates source authority by holding task, proposition, position, and policy fixed. Across 450 controlled tasks, trusted vs. untrusted evidence variants produce different actions in 5.4% of competing cases, and unauthorized competition persists under degradation.
AI.motivation: LLM agents select tools and arguments from contexts that mix authorized and unauthorized evidence. A correct action need not be grounded solely in permitted evidence, meaning unauthorized sources can influence decisions. There is a need to audit whether LLMs respect source authorization when choosing actions, beyond just checking if the action is correct.
AI.method: The authors propose a target-specific authorization audit that labels context factors separately for each tool and argument target. The primary test holds the task, proposition, position, and policy fixed while varying only the proposition's source authority. They also test behavior when valid evidence is weakened and use context-subset interactions as a secondary localization diagnostic. Experiments span 450 controlled next-action tasks across multiple open-weight LLM families.
AI.result: Trusted and untrusted variants produce different actions in 5.4% of competing cases versus 1.7% of supporting cases. Under controlled degradation, unauthorized competition persists in a full-correct, mixed-error, clean-correct pattern in 2.4% of comparisons (95% CI: 2.1–3.0%). The models respond to textual source-authority cues, but this does not prevent untrusted evidence from influencing their actions.
AI.conclusion: LLMs are sensitive to textual source-authority cues but remain susceptible to influence from untrusted evidence. The authorization audit framework demonstrates that unauthorized competition is a measurable, reproducible phenomenon across model families, highlighting a security-relevant failure mode in LLM agent architectures.

title: An Evaluation Framework for Structured Audio Captions Validated by Controlled Perturbations
summary: Recent advancements in automated audio captioning (AAC) have shifted from monolithic sentence generation toward structured formats that explicitly disentangle distinct acoustic and semantic properties. However, evaluating this heterogeneous data remains a significant challenge. Existing caption metrics focus on flat textual outputs and fail to reliably assess multimodal attributes. To bridge this gap, we propose a multi-axis evaluation framework tailored for structured audio descriptions. Building on the AudioCards dataset, we evaluate outputs across five orthogonal axes: tag-sets, descriptions, logical reasoning, numeric measurements, and spectral profiles.
