Our approach combines Large Language Model (LLM) judges to capture semantic nuance with deterministic computational metrics to precisely measure acoustic deviations. To rigorously validate the reliability of this framework, we introduce a controlled perturbation testing protocol that injects typed, graded errors into groundtruth annotations. Our results demonstrate that this framework successfully distinguishes meaning-preserving paraphrases from genuine semantic and acoustic corruptions.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a multi-axis evaluation framework for structured audio captioning, combining LLM judges with deterministic metrics to assess five orthogonal dimensions (tags, descriptions, reasoning, numeric measurements, spectral profiles). A perturbation testing protocol validates the framework's ability to distinguish paraphrases from genuine errors.
AI.motivation: Existing caption metrics only evaluate flat textual outputs and cannot reliably assess heterogeneous structured audio descriptions that disentangle distinct acoustic and semantic properties. There is a critical gap in multi-attribute evaluation for the new generation of structured AAC outputs.
AI.method: The authors propose a multi-axis evaluation framework operating across five orthogonal axes: tag-sets, descriptions, logical reasoning, numeric measurements, and spectral profiles. The framework hybridizes LLM-based judges (for semantic nuance) with deterministic computational metrics (for precise acoustic deviation measurement). A controlled perturbation testing protocol is introduced that injects typed, graded errors into ground-truth annotations to rigorously validate reliability.
AI.result: The framework successfully distinguishes meaning-preserving paraphrases from genuine semantic and acoustic corruptions, as demonstrated through the perturbation testing protocol with typed, graded error injection.
AI.conclusion: The proposed multi-axis evaluation framework effectively bridges the gap in assessing structured audio captions by combining semantic LLM judging with acoustic-precision metrics, enabling reliable differentiation between benign paraphrasing and true errors across multiple orthogonal dimensions.

title: Multi-turn RL with Structural and Performance Aware Rewards for CUDA Kernel Generation
summary: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) has emerged as a powerful technique to enhance the reasoning capacity of LLMs for optimized code generation. However, existing RLVR approaches primarily rely on outcome-based signals such as correctness and speedup, overlooking performance-critical structural properties of programs that are essential for generating optimized code. In this work, we propose CudaPerf, a reflective RL framework that incorporates both verifiable execution rewards and structural code-aware rewards derived from parallelization features (e.g., memory coalescing, occupancy, Arithmatic Intensity, and synchronization patterns). CudaPerf operates in two stages: (1) an offline pairwise ranking module that learns to distinguish strong and weak program candidates via contrastive comparisons, and (2) an online RL training phase that jointly optimizes for correctness, performance, and structural efficiency through a unified reward signal. To further enhance learning, CudaPerf utilizes iterative refinement using execution feedback enabling progressive improvement of generated candidates. We also introduce a dataset comprising 2.9k C to CUDA and 1k PyTorch to CUDA programs, each paired with diverse input configurations and multiple CUDA implementations encompassing diverse optimization strategies. CudaPerf is evaluated across multiple benchmarks comprising both C to CUDA and PyTorch to CUDA transformations. Empirical findings suggest that CudaPerf significantly outperforms strong baselines, including Qwen-3-32B (for C to CUDA) and CUDA Agent (for PyTorch to CUDA) by achieving up to 5X & 3.32X improvements in speedup, and 17% & 7% improvements in correctness, respectively.

AI.tldr: CudaPerf is a reflective RL framework for CUDA code generation that combines execution-based rewards with structural code-aware rewards (memory coalescing, occupancy, arithmetic intensity, synchronization) via a two-stage process: offline pairwise ranking + online RL, achieving up to 5× speedup and 17% correctness gains over baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing RLVR methods for code generation rely solely on outcome-based signals (correctness, speedup), ignoring performance-critical structural properties of parallel programs (e.g., memory coalescing, occupancy). This gap limits the ability to generate truly optimized CUDA code.
AI.method: CudaPerf uses a two-stage reflective RL framework: (1) an offline pairwise ranking module that learns to contrast strong vs. weak program candidates using structural features like memory coalescing, occupancy, arithmetic intensity, and synchronization patterns; (2) an online RL phase that jointly optimizes a unified reward combining correctness, performance, and structural efficiency. Iterative refinement with execution feedback enables progressive improvement. A new dataset of 2.9k C→CUDA and 1k PyTorch→CUDA programs with diverse implementations is introduced.
AI.result: CudaPerf significantly outperforms Qwen-3-32B (C→CUDA) and CUDA Agent (PyTorch→CUDA), achieving up to 5× and 3.32× speedup improvements, and 17% and 7% correctness improvements, respectively.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating structural code-aware rewards into RLVR substantially improves both correctness and performance of LLM-generated CUDA code. The two-stage reflective framework with iterative execution feedback is an effective paradigm for optimizing code generation.

title: Auditing Evidence Use in Medical LLM Diagnosis
summary: Medical LLMs are often evaluated by whether they select the correct diagnosis, but diagnostic accuracy alone does not show whether the model used the case evidence appropriately. We present a behavioral audit of evidence use in medical diagnosis. For each case, we decompose patient information into evidence units, score candidate diagnoses under controlled evidence subsets, and mine low-order interactions in diagnostic margins. Because medical evidence is diagnosis-relative, the audit separates interaction discovery from failure assignment: large or negative interactions can reflect plausible differential diagnosis, while suspicious interactions require robustness checks and clinical review. We evaluate five open-weight LLMs on DDXPlus, CupCase, and MedCase. Across datasets, faithful support and differential conflict or cancellation account for most interaction strength, showing that many evidence interactions are clinically plausible rather than failures. In a DDXPlus-focused blinded five-reviewer 130-item enriched review sample, invalid or shortcut-like cases concentrate in negated or absent findings and clinically local evidence. These results show that accuracy can hide candidate evidence-use failures and motivate role-aware audits for medical LLM evaluation.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a behavioral audit framework for evaluating how medical LLMs use clinical evidence during diagnosis, decomposing case information into evidence units and analyzing interaction patterns. Testing five open-weight LLMs across three datasets reveals that most evidence interactions are clinically plausible, but accuracy metrics can mask evidence-use failures, particularly with negated/absent findings.
AI.motivation: Diagnostic accuracy alone is insufficient to evaluate medical LLMs because it fails to reveal whether models appropriately use case evidence. A model can select the correct diagnosis while relying on spurious patterns or ignoring key clinical information, necessitating a more granular behavioral audit of evidence use.
AI.method: The authors propose a behavioral audit framework with three components: (1) decomposing patient information into discrete evidence units, (2) scoring candidate diagnoses under systematically controlled evidence subsets to measure marginal contributions, and (3) mining low-order interactions (up to second-order) in diagnostic margins. The framework distinguishes between plausible differential diagnosis interactions and suspicious patterns via robustness checks and clinical review. A blinded five-reviewer enriched review (130 items, DDXPlus) validates discovered interaction types.
AI.result: Across DDXPlus, CupCase, and MedCase datasets with five open-weight LLMs, faithful support and differential conflict/cancellation accounted for most interaction strength, indicating clinical plausibility rather than model failure. Invalid or shortcut-like cases concentrated in negated/absent findings and clinically local evidence. The enriched review confirmed that accuracy can hide candidate evidence-use failures.
AI.conclusion: Accuracy-based evaluation of medical LLMs conceals important evidence-use failures. The paper advocates for role-aware behavioral audits that examine how models integrate clinical evidence, with particular attention to negated findings and local evidence, as a necessary complement to diagnostic accuracy metrics in medical AI evaluation.

title: Token Budget Saturation and Mechanistic Early Detection of Reasoning Non-Convergence in Chain-of-Thought Models
summary: Chain-of-thought reasoning models such as DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B exhibit a bimodal convergence pattern: generations either terminate within a token budget (converged) or exhaust it without reaching a conclusion (non-converged). We characterize this phenomenon empirically, showing that converged generations achieve 90.3% accuracy on AIME 1983-2024 while non-converged ones achieve only 6.6%, with an overall convergence rate of 62.0%. We then ask whether this outcome is detectable early in the thinking chain using internal model representations. Training linear probes on hidden-state activations at token positions 50-300, we find that layer-20 activations at token 150 achieve AUC 0.608 (+-0.080, 5-fold CV), reliably above chance even at token 50. Activation probes consistently outperform behavioral baselines derived from token entropy and repetition statistics. A sweep-level permutation test yields p=0.063 (100,000 permutations), consistent with a modest signal that our sample size cannot confirm at conventional thresholds. These findings suggest that convergence fate is partially encoded in intermediate representations well before the generation ends, opening a path toward early-exit inference and adaptive compute allocation.

AI.tldr: Chain-of-thought reasoning models exhibit bimodal behavior — generations either converge or don't. The authors find this convergence fate is partially detectable early in the thinking process (token 150, layer 20) using linear probes on hidden states (AUC ~0.608), outperforming behavioral baselines, enabling potential early-exit strategies.
AI.motivation: Chain-of-thought reasoning models like DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B waste compute on non-converged generations (38% of cases) that achieve only 6.6% accuracy. The authors aim to determine whether this convergence outcome can be predicted early in the thinking chain, enabling early termination and adaptive compute allocation to save inference costs.
AI.method: The authors first empirically characterize the bimodal convergence phenomenon on AIME 1983-2024, measuring accuracy stratified by convergence status. They then train linear probes on hidden-state activations from the model's intermediate layers at token positions 50–300, evaluating via 5-fold cross-validated AUC. They compare these activation probes against behavioral baselines (token entropy, repetition statistics) and validate statistical significance using a sweep-level permutation test with 100,000 permutations.
AI.result: Converged generations achieve 90.3% accuracy vs. 6.6% for non-converged, with 62.0% overall convergence rate. Linear probes on layer-20 activations at token 150 yield AUC 0.608 (±0.080, 5-fold CV), reliably above chance even at token 50. Activation probes consistently outperform behavioral baselines. The permutation test yields p=0.063, suggesting a modest signal not confirmed at conventional thresholds.
AI.conclusion: Convergence fate is partially encoded in intermediate model representations well before generation ends. This opens a path toward early-exit inference and adaptive compute allocation, though the signal is modest and requires larger samples for conventional statistical confirmation.

title: Three-Pronged Spectral Control for Federated Parameter Efficient Fine Tuning
summary: Federated parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) enables communication-efficient adaptation of large pretrained models on decentralized edge data, but it remains fragile under non-IID client heterogeneity. In low-rank adaptation (LoRA), different clients may learn locally useful but spectrally misaligned update subspaces, causing high-variance aggregation and poor global transfer. We propose TRISHUL, a spectral-control framework for robust federated PEFT. TRISHUL follows the FL no-raw-data-sharing setting but does not itself provide formal privacy guarantees. TRISHUL uses shared frozen multi-head low-rank bases to obtain algebraically exact aggregation of compact core updates, applies nuclear norm proximal shrinkage to suppress client-specific high-rank spectral components before upload, and allocates adaptation heads non-uniformly across layers using a concave water filling budget rule derived from pretrained layer capacity. Because shrinkage is performed only on small core matrices, TRISHUL adds negligible computation and no extra per-round communication over the underlying multi-head PEFT protocol. Across vision and language benchmarks, including CIFAR-100, SVHN, 20 Newsgroups, MRQA, and GLUE with LLaMA3.2-1B, TRISHUL improves convergence, stability, and final performance over federated LoRA baselines, with greater gains under stronger heterogeneity.

AI.tldr: TRISHUL proposes a spectral-control framework for federated parameter-efficient fine-tuning that uses shared multi-head low-rank bases, nuclear norm proximal shrinkage to suppress high-rank noise, and a concave water-filling budget allocation across layers, achieving improved convergence and stability over standard federated LoRA under non-IID data heterogeneity without adding extra communication cost.
AI.motivation: Federated LoRA suffers under non-IID client data because locally learned low-rank update subspaces become spectrally misaligned across clients, leading to high-variance aggregation and poor global model transfer. Existing solutions lack mechanisms to control the spectral properties of client updates.
AI.method: TRISHUL introduces three key components: (1) shared frozen multi-head low-rank bases across clients to enable algebraically exact aggregation of compact core updates; (2) nuclear norm proximal shrinkage applied to the small core matrices before upload to suppress client-specific high-rank spectral components; and (3) a concave water-filling budget rule derived from pretrained layer capacity to non-uniformly allocate adaptation heads across layers. Shrinkage operates solely on small core matrices, adding negligible computation and zero extra per-round communication.
AI.result: Evaluated on vision benchmarks (CIFAR-100, SVHN) and language benchmarks (20 Newsgroups, MRQA, GLUE with LLaMA3.2-1B), TRISHUL achieves improved convergence speed, stability, and final performance over federated LoRA baselines, with performance gains increasing under stronger data heterogeneity.
AI.conclusion: TRISHUL demonstrates that spectral control via shared bases and nuclear norm shrinkage is an effective, lightweight strategy for robustifying federated PEFT under heterogeneous client data distributions, without compromising communication efficiency.

title: Code Monitor Red Teaming for Public-Test-Passing Code
summary: Visible tests are a common gate for LLM-generated code, but passing them does not certify specification correctness. We study a deployment-like monitoring problem: after code has passed public tests, can a weaker LLM verifier identify the residual hidden bugs? We introduce Code Monitor Red Teaming, a monitor-red-teaming protocol that fixes a public-check information boundary while varying generator pressure, verifier scaffolding, and weak-to-strong capability. We instantiate it as CodeMonitorBench, spanning function-level, data-science, and workflow code. Across 71,000 generated candidates, 43,677 pass public tests and 23,081 of those fail hidden tests. Weak verifiers improve with scaffolding and model family, but still miss most hidden bugs at 5% false-positive rate. As a robustness stress test, adversarial public-test-overfit pressure lowers verifier AUROC and raises low-FPR miss rates in most cells. A GLM-5.1 verifier recovers part of the gap under the same evidence boundary; an inferability audit shows that remaining misses mix verifier failures with M1 evidence limits.

AI.tldr: Code Monitor Red Teaming reveals that weaker LLM verifiers miss most hidden bugs in LLM-generated code that passes public tests, even with scaffolding improvements; adversarial overfitting to public tests further degrades verifier performance, and an inferability audit shows remaining misses stem from both verifier limitations and inherent evidence insufficiency.
AI.motivation: LLM-generated code is commonly gated by visible (public) tests, but passing these tests does not guarantee correctness against hidden specification requirements. The authors investigate whether a weaker LLM can serve as a monitor to detect residual bugs after code has passed public tests—a deployment-relevant monitoring scenario where the verifier has access only to the same public-test information boundary.
AI.method: The paper introduces Code Monitor Red Teaming, a structured protocol that fixes a public-check information boundary while systematically varying three axes: (1) generator pressure (including adversarial public-test overfitting), (2) verifier scaffolding strategies, and (3) weak-to-strong model capability gaps. This is instantiated as CodeMonitorBench, a benchmark spanning function-level code, data-science notebooks, and workflow code. Across 71,000 generated candidates, 43,677 pass public tests, of which 23,081 fail hidden tests. Evaluation uses AUROC and low-FPR miss rates, plus an inferability audit to distinguish verifier failures from evidence limits.
AI.result: Weak verifiers improve with better scaffolding and stronger model families but still miss most hidden bugs at a 5% false-positive rate. Adversarial public-test overfitting reduces verifier AUROC and increases low-FPR miss rates in most experimental cells. A GLM-5.1 verifier partially recovers performance under the same evidence boundary. The inferability audit indicates that remaining misses are a mixture of genuine verifier failures and cases where the public-test evidence is fundamentally insufficient (M1 evidence limits) to infer the hidden bug.
AI.conclusion: Passing public tests is insufficient evidence for code correctness, and current weaker LLM verifiers cannot reliably close this gap even with scaffolding enhancements. The dual challenge involves both improving verifier capability and acknowledging inherent information-boundary limits. Code Monitor Red Teaming provides a systematic framework for stress-testing code verification pipelines under realistic deployment constraints.

title: When Trivia Is Not Trivial: Everyday Knowledge Failures in Multilingual LLMs
summary: Quiz rooms, trivia nights, and quiz shows challenge human knowledge across a wide range of topics, from canonical facts to everyday culture. In this paper, we examine whether large language models (LLMs) can perform competitively in such settings, using quiz-style questions to test them on both common and niche topics. We introduce TriviaRoomQA, a multilingual benchmark designed to evaluate everyday, culturally grounded, and long-tail knowledge across 288 topics. The benchmark contains 3,300 parallel multiple-choice questions in six European languages and additional 5,340 French-only questions for a more fine-grained case study. We evaluate 30 open-weight LLMs from European, Asian, and North American providers, covering models from 7 to 70B parameters. We find that models are strong on knowledge-intensive topics such as history, geography, and mathematics, but substantially weaker on everyday popular-culture topics such as celebrities, music, movies, and news. Moreover, model performance varies across languages even for the same underlying questions, suggesting that access to factual knowledge is not always language-independent. In sum, our dataset and experiments demonstrate an important knowledge gap which is not captured by existing academic-based saturated benchmarks.

AI.tldr: TriviaRoomQA is a multilingual benchmark of 8,640 quiz-style questions spanning 288 topics, revealing that LLMs excel at academic knowledge (history, geography, math) but significantly underperform on everyday pop culture (celebrities, music, movies), with performance varying across languages even for identical questions.
AI.motivation: Existing QA benchmarks are academically saturated and fail to capture everyday, culturally-grounded, and long-tail knowledge. The authors aim to test whether LLMs can perform competitively in real-world trivia settings that span both canonical facts and popular culture across multiple languages.
AI.method: The authors introduce TriviaRoomQA, a multilingual multiple-choice QA benchmark with 3,300 parallel questions across six European languages plus 5,340 French-only questions, covering 288 topics. They evaluate 30 open-weight LLMs (7–70B parameters) from European, Asian, and North American providers on this benchmark.
AI.result: Models perform well on knowledge-intensive topics (history, geography, mathematics) but substantially worse on popular-culture topics (celebrities, music, movies, news). Performance varies significantly across languages for the same underlying questions, indicating that factual knowledge access is not language-independent.
AI.conclusion: TriviaRoomQA exposes a critical knowledge gap in LLMs — weak everyday and culturally-grounded knowledge — that existing academic-saturated benchmarks fail to reveal. The language-dependent performance further suggests that multilinguality introduces uneven access to factual knowledge.

title: Best-of-Evidence: Best-of-N Selection under Partial Verification
summary: BoN improves model outputs by sampling several candidates and selecting one with a proxy score, but it assumes that complete candidates can be evaluated reliably. Many vision-language tasks instead provide only partial verification: a finding, span, value, region, or relation may be checkable even when no dependable whole-response verifier exists. Moreover, the same claim may recur across candidates with opposing stances, allowing one observation to support part of the pool and contradict another. We introduce Best-of-Evidence (BoE), an inference-time selection framework that keeps the BoN candidate pool fixed, represents reusable claims with a signed candidate--factor graph, and allocates a limited budget to evidence actions that can change the final choice. BoE formalizes selection under partial verification and provides a practical score-based controller, with the zero-budget case recovering the underlying BoN decision. Theoretically, we show that residual evidence capacity limits any evidence-driven improvement and that shared factor queries can achieve an O(log K) versus Θ(K) query separation in a factor-code model. Common-ledger experiments on four medical VQA settings show that BoE can improve fixed-pool selection and rescue some BoN failures when evidence is reliable, contrastive, and decision-relevant, while also revealing the channel-quality and candidate-generation limits that prevent universal gains.

AI.tldr: BoE extends Best-of-N by replacing holistic candidate scoring with partial verification through reusable signed claims in a candidate-factor graph, allocating a limited evidence budget to improve selection when only fragmentary verification is available.
AI.motivation: Best-of-N (BoN) assumes complete, reliable candidate evaluation, but many vision-language tasks offer only partial verification (e.g., a specific span, value, region, or relation can be checked, not the whole response). Additionally, the same claim may appear across candidates with opposing stances, enabling one piece of evidence to simultaneously support some candidates and contradict others. No existing framework addresses inference-time selection under these partial-verification constraints.
AI.method: BoE keeps the BoN candidate pool fixed and constructs a signed candidate–factor graph where nodes are candidates and factors are verifiable claims with positive/negative stances. A limited budget is allocated to "evidence actions" — queries that verify individual claim factors. A score-based controller decides which factors to verify, and the final candidate is selected by aggregating verified claim scores. The zero-budget case recovers standard BoN. Theoretical analysis bounds improvement via residual evidence capacity and demonstrates an O(log K) vs. Θ(K) query separation using shared factor queries in a factor-code model.
AI.result: Experiments on four medical VQA settings show BoE can improve fixed-pool selection and rescue some BoN failures when evidence is reliable, contrastive, and decision-relevant. However, results also reveal limits: channel quality and candidate-generation quality constrain universal gains, indicating BoE is not a panacea.
AI.conclusion: BoE provides a principled framework for inference-time selection under partial verification, leveraging shared, reusable claims across candidates. While effective under favorable evidence conditions, its performance is bounded by the quality of both the underlying candidate pool and the verification channel.

title: Is Deep Research Reliable? Misleading Knowledge Induces False Conclusions
summary: Deep Research agents extend LLM-based assistants into long-horizon workflows involving planning, retrieval, evidence synthesis, and report generation, yet their reliability in open information environments remains underexplored. A key concern is whether apparently credible but factually misleading knowledge encountered in such environments can propagate through these workflows and be adopted as false conclusions in final reports. To study this failure mode, we introduce MisKnow-Agent, a framework for constructing and validating misleading knowledge for Deep Research tasks. MisKnow-Agent generates misleading instances with controllable authority levels and styles, yielding 5,933 quality-controlled instances built on DeepResearch Benchmark tasks. Extensive experiments across open-source and closed-source Deep Research agents show that even limited exposure to misleading knowledge can induce false-conclusion adoption in final reports, revealing a broad reliability vulnerability in current Deep Research agents. Although search-enabled verifier models consistently identify the retained instances as misleading during focused corpus validation, the same instances can still be adopted during long-horizon research, revealing a disconnect between focused verification and workflow-level evidence use. Finally, we evaluate pre- and post-research defenses, both individually and in combination, finding that all three configurations mitigate but do not fully prevent false-conclusion adoption. Our findings suggest that reliable Deep Research requires evidence verification and correction capabilities at both the model and framework levels, beyond improvements in planning, retrieval, evidence integration, or report-generation abilities.

AI.tldr: Introduces MisKnow-Agent, a framework generating 5,933 controlled misleading knowledge instances to test Deep Research agents. Finds that even limited exposure to misleading knowledge induces false conclusions in final reports, and that existing defenses mitigate but do not fully prevent this vulnerability, revealing a disconnect between focused verification and workflow-level evidence use.
AI.motivation: Deep Research agents are increasingly deployed for long-horizon information synthesis tasks, but their susceptibility to misleading knowledge encountered in open information environments is underexplored. The authors aim to investigate whether apparently credible but factually incorrect information can propagate through multi-step agent workflows and become adopted as false conclusions in final reports.
AI.method: The authors introduce MisKnow-Agent, a framework that constructs misleading knowledge instances with controllable authority levels and styles. They generate 5,933 quality-controlled instances grounded in DeepResearch Benchmark tasks. Extensive experiments are conducted across both open-source and closed-source Deep Research agents, evaluating false-conclusion adoption rates under varying exposure conditions. They also test pre- and post-research defenses (individually and combined) and compare focused verifier model performance against workflow-level evidence use.
AI.result: Even limited exposure to misleading knowledge induces false-conclusion adoption in final reports across all tested agents. Search-enabled verifier models consistently identify misleading instances during focused corpus validation, yet the same instances are adopted during long-horizon research, revealing a disconnect between focused verification and workflow-level reasoning. All three defense configurations (pre-research, post-research, and combined) mitigate but do not fully prevent false-conclusion adoption.
AI.conclusion: Reliable Deep Research requires evidence verification and correction capabilities at both the model and framework levels, beyond improvements in planning, retrieval, evidence integration, or report-generation abilities alone. The vulnerability is systemic and not fully addressed by current defense strategies.

title: RUMBA: Russian User Memory Benchmark
summary: The ability to handle long-term memory in LLMs is becoming increasingly critical, yet existing benchmarks remain English-centric and rely on aggregate retrieval metrics, failing to capture interactions between long-range context, temporal information, and reasoning. To address this, we introduce RUMBA (Russian User Memory BenchmArk) - a new benchmark for long-term conversational memory that provides a fine-grained taxonomy of memory-centric question types and a unified methodology accounting for semantic type, session scope, temporal reasoning, and the explicitness of temporal expressions. RUMBA consists of timestamped user-assistant dialogues with QA pairs requiring retrieval, combination, and reasoning across sessions. While designed for Russian, we also provide an aligned English subset under the same methodology. We evaluate contemporary memory systems and long-context models, and show how RUMBA serves as a diagnostic tool to analyze model behavior across benchmark slices and identify strengths and failure modes of different memory mechanisms.

AI.tldr: RUMBA is a Russian long-term conversational memory benchmark (with an English subset) that introduces a fine-grained taxonomy of memory-centric question types, accounting for semantic type, session scope, temporal reasoning, and temporal expression explicitness, enabling diagnostic analysis of LLM memory mechanisms beyond aggregate retrieval metrics.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks for long-term memory in LLMs are English-centric and rely solely on aggregate retrieval metrics, failing to capture the nuanced interplay between long-range context, temporal information, and reasoning. There is a need for a diagnostically rich, multilingual benchmark that dissects model performance across fine-grained dimensions of conversational memory.
AI.method: The authors introduce RUMBA, a benchmark composed of timestamped user-assistant dialogues with QA pairs. It employs a unified taxonomy categorizing questions by semantic type, session scope (within/across sessions), temporal reasoning requirements, and explicitness of temporal expressions. The benchmark is primarily in Russian, with an aligned English subset following the same methodology. Contemporary memory systems and long-context models are evaluated and compared across benchmark slices.
AI.result: RUMBA serves as an effective diagnostic tool, revealing distinct strengths and failure modes of different memory mechanisms across fine-grained benchmark slices. The evaluation demonstrates that model performance varies significantly depending on question type, session scope, and temporal reasoning demands, which aggregate metrics would obscure.
AI.conclusion: RUMBA fills a critical gap by providing a fine-grained, multilingual framework for evaluating long-term conversational memory. It enables precise diagnosis of model capabilities and limitations, moving beyond coarse retrieval metrics to capture the multi-dimensional nature of memory-centric reasoning in LLMs.

title: The Weight of Silence: A Causal Case for Weights Over the Scratchpad in Latent Chess Reasoning
comment: 28 pages, 5 figures, preprint also available at Zenodo: https://zenodo.org/records/21454434
summary: Latent, or silent, reasoning lets language models carry out intermediate computation in continuous vector space instead of words, and is widely assumed to function as an internal scratchpad the model actively consults during inference. Whether that assumption survives reinforcement learning has not been tested directly: existing causal analyses of latent reasoning are confined to math and logic tasks, and compare a model's reliance on its thoughts within a single checkpoint, never before and after an RL stage. We train a chess-playing model through a staged latent-reasoning curriculum followed by reinforcement learning, and find legality climbs monotonically to 61% (from a 48% pre-RL baseline) while checkmate confabulation is eliminated entirely. To locate this gain, we run a six-condition causal intervention suite on the same model before and after RL: substituting or adding matched noise to the latent thought vectors leaves performance unchanged, ablating them causes only mild degradation, and only exact-zero vectors cause collapse. This robustness gap is itself the finding: under exact-zero corruption, legality collapses to 1% pre-RL versus 9% post-RL, a gap that survives correction for testing across the full battery; milder conditions trend similarly without independently reaching significance. RL appears to add robustness to disruption, not reliance on thought content. These results push back against the field's default assumption that latent thoughts function as an actively consulted inference-time scratchpad, and instead indicate latent reasoning's principal effect here is shaping the model's parameters during training. We also demonstrate a working RL gain in chess, a domain outside the math and logic settings where multiple groups report the same latent-reasoning-plus-RL recipe failing to improve accuracy over SFT.

AI.tldr: This paper challenges the assumption that latent reasoning serves as an actively consulted scratchpad during inference. By training a chess model with RL and running causal interventions before and after, the authors find RL adds robustness to disruption rather than increasing reliance on thought content, suggesting latent reasoning primarily shapes parameters during training.
AI.motivation: The field widely assumes latent (silent) reasoning in language models functions as an internal scratchpad actively consulted during inference. However, existing causal analyses are limited to math/logic tasks and compare models at a single checkpoint. No prior work tests whether this assumption holds after reinforcement learning, nor across a broader task domain like chess.
AI.method: The authors train a chess-playing model using a staged latent-reasoning curriculum followed by RL. They then apply a six-condition causal intervention suite to the same model before and after RL: (1) substituting noise, (2) adding matched noise to latent thought vectors, (3) ablating them, and (4) corrupting with exact-zero vectors. Legality and checkmate confabulation rates are measured across conditions, with statistical correction for multiple comparisons.
AI.result: Legality improves from 48% (pre-RL) to 61% (post-RL), and checkmate confabulation is eliminated. Causal interventions reveal a robustness gap: under exact-zero corruption, legality collapses to 1% pre-RL vs. 9% post-RL. Substituting/adding noise or ablating latent thoughts causes only mild degradation. The gap survives full-battery correction; milder conditions trend similarly but do not reach independent significance.
AI.conclusion: RL adds robustness to disruption rather than reliance on thought content, pushing back against the default assumption that latent thoughts are an actively consulted inference-time scratchpad. Instead, latent reasoning's principal effect appears to be shaping model parameters during training. The paper also demonstrates a working RL gain in chess, a domain where prior latent-reasoning-plus-RL recipes have failed to improve over SFT.

title: Source-Prior-Driven Selective Adaptation for Efficient Diffusion Model Finetuning
summary: Fine-tuning large diffusion models for new domains or styles involves a trade-off: improving target-specific generation often degrades the pretrained model's broad generative capability. Existing full and parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods typically handle this trade-off only implicitly. In this work, we propose a novel source-prior-driven selective adaptation method to efficiently fine-tune diffusion models, achieving a favorable trade-off. Our method relies on two key observations: (1) the loss of general generative capability is highly inconsistent across pretrained parameters, and (2) parameters that have a relatively small impact on the model's general generative capability remain structurally inconsistent across layers and parameter types. Motivated by these observations, we first learn a static mask to explicitly identify parameters better suited for downstream adaptation, and then construct structured update strategies for the selected subset. Experiments show that our method achieves a better adaptation-retention trade-off than existing strong baselines.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a source-prior-driven selective adaptation method for fine-tuning diffusion models. It learns a static mask to identify parameters with minimal impact on general generative capability and applies structured updates only to those parameters, achieving a better trade-off between target-specific generation and retention of pretrained capabilities.
AI.motivation: Fine-tuning large diffusion models for new domains creates a trade-off: target-specific improvements often come at the cost of degrading the model's broad generative capability. Existing full and parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods address this trade-off only implicitly, motivating a more explicit, principled approach.
AI.method: Based on two observations — (1) the loss of general generative capability varies significantly across pretrained parameters, and (2) parameters with low impact on general capability are structurally inconsistent across layers and types — the method first learns a static mask to explicitly identify parameters suitable for downstream adaptation, then constructs structured update strategies applied only to the selected subset.
AI.result: Experiments demonstrate that the proposed method achieves a superior adaptation-retention trade-off compared to existing strong baselines.
AI.conclusion: A source-prior-driven selective adaptation approach, using explicit parameter masking and structured updates, effectively balances domain adaptation and preservation of pretrained generative capabilities in diffusion models.

title: What, Where, and How: Disentangling the Roles of Task, Language, and Model in Code Model Representations
comment: 16 pages, 11 figures, 6 tables. Code: https://github.com/piotrwilam/Atlas2x2 ; dataset: https://huggingface.co/datasets/piotrwilam/Atlas2x2
summary:
Do independently trained language models come to represent the same thing in the same way? We answer for code, extending a recently introduced concept-circuit extraction method to a 2x2 design -- Python and Rust crossed with Qwen2.5-Coder-7B and DeepSeek-Coder-V1-6.7B -- and measuring a complete inventory of grammatical concepts (58 Python, 57 Rust) identically in all four cells: the smallest design that separates what depends on the task, the language, and the model.
  The answer splits into three parts. What earns dedicated circuitry is set by the task: the models agree on which concepts receive circuits (Spearman $ρ$ = 0.638 for Python, 0.673 for Rust, both p < $10^{-7}$). Where those circuits sit is set by the model: Qwen processes concepts in a late band (~L17-19), DeepSeek at L6-7, for both languages. How circuits grow across layers is also set by the model: Qwen gives its atomic concepts an early spike that DeepSeek does not. "Are circuits universal?" thus has no single answer: yes for What, no for Where and How -- universality is a property of representational content, not of computational organisation.
  None of this structure was fixed in advance. The agreement could have landed anywhere between independence and identity; it lands at $ρ\approx 0.65$. Rust constructs receive 2-3x more concept-specific circuitry than their Python equivalents, in both models. Both models share neurons between the languages (6/7 and 7/7 paired constructs), DeepSeek 1.94x more than Qwen -- a direction no prior result predicts. And Qwen binds nine keywords of Rust's type-and-trait machinery into one tight neuron cluster (Jaccard 0.535 vs null 0.112, p < 0.001), a semantic dimension invisible in surface syntax. Ablation and linear probes confirm the circuits are functional.
  All claims are scoped to this 2x2; whether the per-model profile predicts a third model is the designed next test.

AI.tldr: A 2×2 cross-factorial study (Python/Rust × Qwen2.5-Coder-7B/DeepSeek-Coder-V1-6.7B) finds that whether independently trained language models represent code concepts "universally" has a three-part answer: *what* gets circuitry is task-driven (models agree, ρ≈0.65), but *where* circuits sit and *how* they grow are model-specific. This reveals universality as a property of representational content, not computational organization.
AI.motivation: To determine whether independently trained language models converge on the same internal representations for the same concepts, and to disentangle what aspects of circuit structure depend on the task, the programming language, or the specific model architecture/training.
AI.method: A 2×2 factorial design crossing two programming languages (Python, Rust) with two code-focused LLMs (Qwen2.5-Coder-7B, DeepSeek-Coder-V1-6.7B). The authors extend concept-circuit extraction to map a complete inventory of grammatical concepts (58 Python, 57 Rust) identically across all four cells. Circuit agreement is measured via Spearman correlation; neuron sharing across languages quantified; cluster analysis (Jaccard) identifies cross-lingual semantic groupings. Ablation and linear probes validate circuit functionality.
AI.result: Three findings: (1) *What* earns dedicated circuitry is task-driven — models agree on which concepts get circuits (Python ρ=0.638, Rust ρ=0.673, both p<10⁻⁷). (2) *Where* circuits sit is model-specific — Qwen uses a late band (~L17-19), DeepSeek at L6-7, for both languages. (3) *How* circuits grow is also model-specific — Qwen shows an early spike for atomic concepts absent in DeepSeek. Additionally: Rust constructs receive 2-3× more concept-specific circuitry; both models share neurons across languages (6/7 and 7/7 paired constructs), with DeepSeek sharing 1.94× more than Qwen; Qwen binds nine Rust type-and-trait keywords into a tight neuron cluster (Jaccard 0.535 vs null 0.112, p<0.001), revealing a semantic dimension invisible in surface syntax.
AI.conclusion: Universality in neural representations is not monolithic: it holds for *what* content is represented but breaks for *where* and *how* that content is organized — universality is a property of representational content, not computational organization. The next designed test is whether a model's circuit profile predicts that of a third model.

title: ADABORD: a novel AdaBoost approach for ordinal classification
comment: 42 pages, 6 figures, 7 tables. Submitted to CS top tier journal
summary: Ordinal Classification (OC) deals with classification tasks where the classes follow a natural order. Despite the progress in OC, many existing approaches fail to fully leverage the ordinal information, treating the problem as nominal classification and thereby losing performance potential. In this work, ADABORD, an AdaBoost framework specifically designed for ordinal classification problems, is introduced. The ordinal nature of the classes is incorporated into two key components of the well-known AdaBoost algorithm: 1) the base estimator, where decision trees with the ordinal Gini splitting criterion are proposed; 2) the error function used to update sample weights at each stage and the weights of the classifier in the final ensemble model, given by the absolute ranked probability score, a measure that accounts for both the ordering and the distance between classes. ADABORD is extensively compared against seven state-of-the-art methods on the TOC-UCO repository, the largest benchmark collection for OC to date. The experimental results, supported by statistical analysis, show that ADABORD significantly outperforms competing methods, particularly on datasets with five or more classes, where the ordinal structure becomes more pronounced. Source code, along with all experimental protocols, is publicly available to ensure reproducibility and facilitate future research in OC.

AI.tldr: ADABORD is an AdaBoost framework tailored for ordinal classification, introducing ordinal Gini splitting in decision trees and an absolute ranked probability score-based error function. It significantly outperforms seven state-of-the-art methods, especially on datasets with five or more classes.
AI.motivation: Existing ordinal classification methods often treat the problem as nominal classification, failing to fully exploit the natural ordering among classes, which leaves performance potential untapped.
AI.method: ADABORD extends AdaBoost with two ordinal-aware components: (1) decision tree base estimators using an ordinal Gini splitting criterion, and (2) an error function based on the absolute ranked probability score that accounts for both class ordering and inter-class distances when updating sample weights and classifier ensemble weights.
AI.result: Extensive evaluation on the TOC-UCO repository (the largest OC benchmark) with statistical analysis shows ADABORD significantly outperforms seven state-of-the-art methods, with gains particularly pronounced on datasets with five or more classes.
AI.conclusion: ADABORD effectively integrates ordinal information into the boosting framework, yielding superior performance over competing approaches. Code and protocols are publicly released for reproducibility.

title: Traceable Scholarship: Page Anchors and Ariadne's Thread for Humanistic Inquiry in the Age of Generative AI
comment: 33 pages, 8 tables. This paper proposes a normative and infrastructural framework for traceable, AI-assisted humanistic research and presents an auditable Kant case study
summary: Generative AI lets large language models produce scholarly-looking text within seconds, yet fluency does not equal valid explanation. The deepest risk is not factual error alone but the appearance that an explanation is already established without clear sources, page numbers, editions, or evidence. We liken the page anchor to Ariadne's thread: within the labyrinth of generative fluency, it is the thread that leads the scholar back to the source. This paper proposes Traceable Scholarship as the minimum normative condition for AI-assisted humanistic research, situating it across the three revolutions of knowledge infrastructure: print, digital, and generative AI. We introduce page anchors, dual page numbers, citation-first generation, NO_EVIDENCE, human verification, four-level compliance, and Scope Contract, and present AIH-Infra as a three-layer reference implementation: Contexture (document structuring), Open WebUI AIH-Infra (traceable knowledge base), and AIH-Infra MCP Server (agent gateway). A case study on a 29-volume Kant Akademie-Ausgabe knowledge base illustrates how traceability supports retrieval correction, evidence grading, and judgment downgrading. Traceability is not a software feature; it is the condition under which humanistic research can remain public and refutable in the age of generative AI.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes "Traceable Scholarship" as a normative framework for AI-assisted humanities research, introducing page anchors and a three-layer reference architecture (AIH-Infra) to ensure scholarly work remains verifiable, source-linked, and refutable in the generative AI era.
AI.motivation: Generative AI produces fluent scholarly-looking text but lacks verifiable grounding — no sources, page numbers, editions, or evidence. The core risk is the illusion of established explanation without traceability, threatening the public and refutable nature of humanistic research.
AI.method: The authors propose a framework centered on page anchors (likened to Ariadne's thread) as the minimal unit of traceability, supported by dual page numbers, citation-first generation, NO_EVIDENCE markers, human verification protocols, four-level compliance grading, and a Scope Contract. They implement AIH-Infra, a three-layer reference architecture: Contexture for document structuring, Open WebUI AIH-Infra for traceable knowledge bases, and an MCP Server as agent gateway. Validation uses a 29-volume Kant Akademie-Ausgabe corpus.
AI.result: The Kant case study demonstrates that page-anchor-based traceability enables retrieval correction, evidence grading, and judgment downgrading — allowing scholars to identify unsupported claims and downgrade confidence when sources are absent. The system shows feasibility of enforcing citation-first generation workflows.
AI.conclusion: Traceability is not a software feature but a necessary normative condition for humanistic scholarship to remain public, accountable, and refutable under generative AI. Traceable Scholarship is presented as the minimum standard for AI-assisted research.

title: Artificial Epanorthosis: Why large language models overuse a classical rhetorical figure, and how to mitigate it
summary: A rhetorical figure that Cicero and Quintilian catalogued two thousand years ago reappears, systematically, in the text of large language models: epanorthosis, the self-correction of the specimen «This is not a course. It is a journey of transformation». This essay argues that the overuse is a trained disposition, driven mainly by a training distribution rich in promotional prose and by preference tuning (RLHF) that rewards confident, emphatic phrasing; the left-to-right nature of generation is an amplifier rather than the root cause. Building on evidence that models diverge from human rhetorical style, and on Fontanier's classification of epanorthosis as a figure of thought, it sets out a programme that scores the figure against genre-specific human baselines through an Epanorthosis Index (density relative to the human rate). A first measurement, on three sizes of one instruction-tuned model family, finds mis-calibration by register in both directions: the models overshoot in oratory (about twofold, near threefold in Italian, concentrated in the larger tiers) and undershoot in informal question-and-answer writing, while matching humans in argument, journalism, and encyclopedic prose. Three constructive contributions follow: a survey of mitigation techniques centred on lightweight LoRA adapters; a demonstration, in Italian, that a one-line instruction cuts the figure by half to nearly three-quarters and that a supervised-fine-tuning adapter removes it almost entirely, with a scaling coefficient that dials the reduction back onto the human rate; and the argument that the target is calibration to the human rate for each genre, not elimination. It closes on the stakes: the real risk is that we begin to write like the machines.

AI.tldr: LLMs systematically overuse the rhetorical figure of epanorthosis (self-correction), driven by promotional training data and RLHF. The paper introduces an Epanorthosis Index, finds genre-specific miscalibration (overshoot in oratory, undershoot in informal Q&A), and demonstrates mitigation via instruction-based and LoRA adapter methods, arguing the goal is calibration to human baselines, not elimination.
AI.motivation: LLMs exhibit a distinct, systematic overuse of epanorthosis — a rhetorical figure of self-correction (e.g., "This is not an X. It is a Y.") — that diverges from human rhetorical patterns. The paper seeks to understand the root cause (training distribution and RLHF, rather than left-to-right generation), quantify the phenomenon across genres and model sizes, and develop mitigation strategies calibrated to human baselines rather than outright elimination.
AI.method: The paper introduces an Epanorthosis Index measuring figure density relative to genre-specific human rates. It applies this metric across three sizes of an instruction-tuned model family, comparing model output to human baselines in five genres: oratory, informal Q&A, argument, journalism, and encyclopedic prose. Mitigation experiments include (1) a survey of lightweight LoRA adapters, and (2) a demonstration in Italian showing that a one-line instruction and supervised fine-tuning adapters can reduce epanorthosis, with scaling coefficients to dial reduction back to the human rate.
AI.result: Models show genre-dependent miscalibration: roughly twofold overshoot in oratory (nearly threefold in Italian, concentrated in larger model tiers), undershoot in informal Q&A writing, but match human rates in argument, journalism, and encyclopedic prose. A one-line instruction reduces the figure by 50–75%, and a supervised-fine-tuning adapter removes it almost entirely. A scaling coefficient can tune the reduction to the human baseline for each genre.
AI.conclusion: The systematic overuse of epanorthosis in LLMs stems from training data and preference tuning, not generation architecture. Calibration to genre-specific human rates — not elimination — is the appropriate target. The broader stakes are cultural: without intervention, we risk adopting machine-like rhetorical patterns in our own writing.

title: Weight-norm Criticality: A Mechanism for Loss Spikes Induced by the Normalization and Weight Decay
summary: Most explanations of training instability focus on \emph{learning-rate criticality}, typically characterized by the Edge of Stability, beyond which optimization becomes unstable. We argue that, in practical deep neural network training, there is an additional and often overlooked \emph{weight-norm criticality}. This criticality is induced by the interaction between normalization (which introduces scale-invariant components) and weight decay (which persistently shrinks parameter norms). As the weight decay coefficient increases, the norms of scale-invariant weights are progressively driven toward zero. Meanwhile, the sharpness of the loss landscape increases rapidly, destabilizing the optimization dynamics and resulting in abrupt loss spikes. This perspective provides a rationale for why weight penalties can improve generalization yet cannot be made arbitrarily strong: excessive decay drives scale-invariant weight norms past a critical boundary and destabilizes training. Our work provides a new mechanistic understanding of loss spikes through the lens of \emph{weight-norm criticality}. Moreover, \emph{weight-norm criticality} yields testable predictions that we validate empirically in networks with scale-invariant components, providing empirical support for the proposed mechanism.

AI.tldr: Beyond the Edge of Stability, training instability can arise from weight-norm criticality — an interaction between normalization layers and weight decay that progressively shrinks scale-invariant weight norms, rapidly increasing loss landscape sharpness and causing abrupt loss spikes.
AI.motivation: Existing explanations of training instability focus predominantly on learning-rate criticality (the Edge of Stability). The authors identify an overlooked, complementary instability mechanism arising from the interplay of normalization and weight decay, which limits how strongly weight decay can be applied despite its generalization benefits.
AI.method: The authors propose a theoretical framework centered on weight-norm criticality, analyzing how weight decay interacts with scale-invariant components introduced by normalization layers. They derive testable predictions from this mechanism and validate them empirically in networks containing scale-invariant components.
AI.result: As the weight decay coefficient increases, scale-invariant weight norms are driven toward zero, causing a rapid increase in loss landscape sharpness. Beyond a critical boundary, this destabilizes optimization dynamics and produces abrupt loss spikes. The empirical results support the proposed weight-norm criticality mechanism.
AI.conclusion: Weight-norm criticality provides a new mechanistic understanding of training instability: weight decay improves generalization but cannot be made arbitrarily strong without crossing a critical norm boundary that destabilizes training. This complements the Edge of Stability perspective.

title: OPOD: On-Policy Omni Distillation
summary: Omni-modal models can handle text, images, and audio in one system, but improving all of these abilities together remains difficult. Training a single model on pooled multimodal data often fails to match models specialized for individual modalities. On-policy distillation (OPD) offers a way to combine such specialists: the student generates a response, and a teacher evaluates that same response, so the student learns directly from behaviors it actually produces. Yet using several teachers can introduce competing guidance and improve one modality at the expense of another. We present On-Policy Omni Distillation (OPOD), which routes each student response to the matching text, image, or audio teacher. OPOD keeps teacher guidance only on tokens where the teacher assigns a higher probability than the student, adjusts the influence of each modality teacher independently during training, and asks the routed teacher to assess both the final answer and whether the reasoning supports the correct answer. Across twelve benchmarks and three backbone sizes, OPOD achieves the best average score at every scale, reaching 70.8, 51.7, and 46.2 and exceeding the strongest comparator by 2.1, 1.8, and 1.7 points. On the 30B model, it outperforms both the base model and a counterpart post-trained jointly on pooled multimodal data on all twelve benchmarks, and ranks first or second on eleven even when the individual specialists are included. The specialists are discarded after training, leaving one deployable omni-modal model. These results show that coordinating modality-specific teachers is an effective way to improve a shared model while maintaining cross-modal balance.

AI.tldr: OPOD routes student responses to modality-specific teachers during on-policy distillation, using token-level probability gating and independent modality weighting to improve omni-modal models without cross-modal interference. The method achieves SOTA across 12 benchmarks at three scales, with specialists discarded post-training.
AI.motivation: Training a single omni-modal model on pooled multimodal data typically underperforms modality-specific specialists. On-policy distillation can combine specialists, but multiple teachers introduce competing guidance that may improve one modality at the expense of another. There is a need for a coordination mechanism that preserves cross-modal balance.
AI.method: OPOD introduces three key mechanisms: (1) routing each student response to the matching modality teacher (text, image, or audio); (2) applying teacher guidance only on tokens where the teacher assigns higher probability than the student; (3) independently adjusting each modality teacher's influence during training. The routed teacher evaluates both the final answer and whether the reasoning supports it. Specialists are discarded after training.
AI.result: OPOD achieves best average scores at every backbone scale: 70.8, 51.7, and 46.2, exceeding the strongest comparator by 2.1, 1.8, and 1.7 points respectively. On the 30B model, it outperforms both the base model and a jointly post-trained counterpart on all 12 benchmarks, ranking first or second on 11 benchmarks even against individual specialists.
AI.conclusion: Coordinating modality-specific teachers via OPOD is an effective strategy for improving shared omni-modal models while maintaining cross-modal balance, yielding a single deployable model that surpasses jointly-trained counterparts and approaches or exceeds specialist-level performance.

title: DONDO: Open w2v-BERT Speech-Recognition Base Models for African Languages
summary: We present DONDO, a family of open, permissively licensed automatic speech recognition (ASR) base models for African languages, built on the w2v-BERT 2.0 self-supervised speech encoder. DONDO comprises twenty-one monolingual models and five multilingual models spanning twenty-seven language varieties across Ghana, Sierra Leone, Nigeria, Senegal, Kenya and Zimbabwe. Models are fine-tuned primarily on read speech drawn from religious texts, which offer broad, license-clear and orthographically consistent coverage for languages that otherwise lack transcribed audio. We describe a two-step (and, for one family, three-step) learning-rate-annealed fine-tuning procedure that first adapts a shared multilingual model at a high learning rate and then anneals it to recover, and in several cases surpass, strong monolingual baselines. We further describe a lightweight language-conditioning mechanism that injects a one-hot language identity as a sequence of prefix frames prepended to the acoustic features, allowing a single multilingual checkpoint to be steered to a target language at inference. Across the five multilingual families the annealed models reach average word error rates (WER) of 10-13%, closing most of the gap to monolingual models while covering many languages in a single checkpoint. All models are released on the Hugging Face KhayaAI organisation under the Apache-2.0 license (attribution only) so that others may fine-tune them freely, including for commercial use. We provide a conservative estimate that the languages covered are spoken by on the order of one hundred million first-language speakers, and by substantially more when second-language use is included.

AI.tldr: DONDO is a family of open-source ASR base models for 27 African language varieties, built on w2v-BERT 2.0, fine-tuned on religious read speech with a novel annealed fine-tuning procedure and lightweight language conditioning, achieving 10–13% WER while covering ~100M+ first-language speakers.
AI.motivation: African languages suffer from a severe lack of transcribed audio data for ASR development. Religious texts provide broad, license-clear, orthographically consistent coverage for languages otherwise lacking resources. The authors aim to democratize ASR for underserved African languages through fully open, permissively licensed (Apache-2.0) models suitable for both research and commercial use.
AI.method: DONDO uses w2v-BERT 2.0 as the self-supervised speech encoder. Fine-tuning employs religious read speech corpora spanning 27 language varieties across six African countries. A two-step (and in one case three-step) learning-rate-annealed fine-tuning procedure first adapts a shared multilingual model at a high learning rate, then anneals to recover or surpass monolingual baselines. A lightweight language-conditioning mechanism injects a one-hot language identity as prefix frames prepended to acoustic features, enabling a single multilingual checkpoint to be steered to a target language at inference time.
AI.result: The five multilingual families achieve average WERs of 10–13%, substantially closing the gap to monolingual models while serving many languages in a single checkpoint. Annealed fine-tuning recovers and in several cases surpasses strong monolingual baselines.
AI.conclusion: DONDO demonstrates that license-clear religious read speech combined with careful fine-tuning strategies can yield competitive ASR models for massively underserved languages. All 21 monolingual and 5 multilingual models are released on Hugging Face under Apache-2.0, covering languages spoken by approximately 100 million first-language speakers and many more second-language users.

title: Regularized Optimization on Grassmann Manifold: Theory, Algorithm and Applications
summary: Spectral methods are among the most widely used techniques for community detection, clustering, and graph learning. Their performance, however, critically depends on the accurate estimation of the underlying spectral subspace and can deteriorate substantially in the presence of noise, outliers, or model perturbations. To address this limitation, we propose a Regularized Projection Matrix Approximation (RPMA) framework for robust estimation of rank-$K$ projection matrices. RPMA extends classical spectral projection by incorporating a regularization term, producing projection estimates that are more robust, sparse, and interpretable. We formulate the proposed model as an optimization problem on the manifold of rank-$K$ projection matrices and exploit its geometric equivalence to the Grassmann manifold. Based on this manifold characterization, we derive the first- and second-order optimality conditions, establish the local stability of the regularized leading eigenspace, and characterize the stability of the critical-point landscape under sufficiently small regularization. To efficiently solve the resulting nonconvex optimization problem, we develop a Riemannian gradient projection algorithm with backtracking line search, together with a more efficient Cayley--Sherman--Morrison--Woodbury (Cayley--SMW) gradient method that avoids repeated eigendecompositions. Extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that RPMA substantially improves the recovery accuracy of projection matrices and consistently outperforms conventional spectral projection methods for community detection and clustering under noisy environments.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes RPMA, a Regularized Projection Matrix Approximation framework that adds regularization to classical spectral methods for robust rank-K projection matrix estimation. It formulates the problem on the Grassmann manifold, derives optimality conditions and stability results, and develops efficient Riemannian optimization algorithms (including a Cayley-SMW variant). Experiments show RPMA significantly outperforms conventional spectral methods for community detection and clustering under noise.
AI.motivation: Spectral methods for community detection, clustering, and graph learning depend critically on accurate spectral subspace estimation, but their performance degrades substantially under noise, outliers, or model perturbations. There is a need for robust projection matrix estimators that maintain accuracy in adverse conditions.
AI.method: RPMA extends classical spectral projection by incorporating a regularization term into the projection matrix approximation objective. The optimization is formulated on the manifold of rank-K projection matrices, leveraging its geometric equivalence to the Grassmann manifold. First- and second-order optimality conditions are derived, along with local stability analysis of the regularized leading eigenspace and critical-point landscape. Two Riemannian algorithms are developed: (1) a gradient projection method with backtracking line search, and (2) a more efficient Cayley–Sherman–Morrison–Woodbury (Cayley-SMW) gradient method that avoids repeated eigendecompositions.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that RPMA substantially improves projection matrix recovery accuracy and consistently outperforms conventional spectral projection methods for community detection and clustering under noisy environments.
AI.conclusion: The RPMA framework provides a principled, geometrically grounded approach to robust spectral subspace estimation. By regularizing projection matrix approximation on the Grassmann manifold and solving it with efficient Riemannian optimization, RPMA achieves superior robustness to noise, sparsity, and interpretability compared to classical spectral methods.

title: Representing Entity Importance in AI Knowledge Systems: A Dual-Signal Framework of Audience Evaluation and Structural Authority
summary:
AI knowledge systems require representations of entity importance for retrieval, recommendation, evidence selection, and knowledge-intensive reasoning. Yet importance is often reduced to a single score derived from either human response or graph structure. Such compression may discard distinctions that matter when an AI system must choose among entities for different tasks. This study introduces an interpretable dual-signal representation in which each entity is characterized by an audience-evaluation dimension and a structural-authority dimension.
  The framework is evaluated using movie entities as an empirical validation domain. IMDb non-commercial datasets provide a rating-based audience ranking, Wikidata supports entity alignment, and English Wikipedia hyperlinks form the knowledge network on which PageRank estimates structural authority. Experiments on 482 entities and 13,690 directed relationships reveal a statistically significant but weak association between the two dimensions (Spearman rho = 0.2275, p < 0.001). Their overlap is only 10% in the top 10 and 34% in the top 100, while entity-level divergence occurs in both directions.
  The results show that audience evaluation and structural authority are non-redundant signals and should not automatically be collapsed into a single scalar notion of importance. The contribution is not a new ranking algorithm or learned embedding, but a minimal knowledge-representation framework and an empirical test of its dimensional necessity. The findings support task-aware AI knowledge systems that preserve distinct importance signals before applying context-specific selection or aggregation.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a dual-signal importance representation for AI knowledge systems, distinguishing audience evaluation from structural authority, and demonstrates empirically using movie/IMDb/Wikipedia data that these two dimensions are statistically weakly correlated and substantially non-overlapping, arguing they should not be collapsed into a single scalar.
AI.motivation: Current AI knowledge systems typically reduce entity importance to a single score (from human judgments or graph structure), which discards meaningful distinctions. When AI systems must select entities for different tasks, different notions of importance may be required, yet no formal framework exists to preserve these distinct signals.
AI.method: The authors construct an interpretable dual-signal framework with two dimensions: (1) audience-evaluation, operationalized via IMDb ratings, and (2) structural-authority, operationalized via PageRank on a Wikipedia hyperlink network aligned through Wikidata. They evaluate 482 movie entities with 13,690 directed relationships, measuring correlation (Spearman's rho) and overlap between top-k rankings from both dimensions.
AI.result: Spearman correlation between audience evaluation and structural authority is statistically significant but weak (rho = 0.2275, p < 0.001). Overlap is only 10% in the top 10 entities and 34% in the top 100. Entity-level divergence occurs in both directions, confirming the two dimensions are non-redundant.
AI.conclusion: Audience evaluation and structural authority are distinct, non-redundant importance signals that should not be collapsed into a single scalar. The contribution is a minimal knowledge-representation framework with empirical validation supporting task-aware AI systems that preserve multiple importance dimensions before context-specific aggregation.

title: Counterfactual Explainability Framework With CycleGAN And Counterfactual-Classifier Alignnment Score for Retinal Disease Classification
summary: Automated detection of vision impairing retina-based ocular conditions from fundus images is important for early screening, timely referral and reducing dependency on specialist-only assessment, for which neural network-based deep learning (DL) models have been widely utilized. However, explainability of the DL frameworks remains a major bottleneck for clinical adoption, particularly when model decisions are not linked to retinal regions that are clinically meaningful. To address this issue, this study presents CounterFundus, a novel CycleGAN-driven counterfactual explainability framework, integrating EfficientNet-B5-based retinal disease detection with visually interpretable disease-to-normal fundus image translation. For each pathological image, the counterfactual yielded by the CycleGAN generator represents an estimated healthy counterpart and the resultant difference map is utilized to localize disease-associated retinal changes. Unlike conventional post-hoc saliency methods, CounterFundus provides counterfactual explanations through visually plausible disease-to-normal retinal translation. Thereafter, to quantify the spatial agreement between counterfactual difference maps and classifier saliency, the Counterfactual-Classifier Alignment Score (CCAS) is introduced, embedding Spearman correlation, binary IoU and pointing accuracy into a single assessment protocol. To this end, EigenCAM-aligned evaluation demonstrates that the generated counterfactual explanations remain spatially consistent with classifier-relevant retinal evidence across all CCAS dimensions. Along with that, ablation studies further confirm that CCAS-filtered counterfactual augmentation improves the downstream classification performance in fundus images, establishing CounterFundus as a clinically-grounded, explainable artificially intelligence (XAI) framework for retinal disease detection.

AI.tldr: CounterFundus is a CycleGAN-based explainability framework that generates counterfactual healthy versions of pathological fundus images, localizes disease-associated retinal changes via difference maps, and introduces the CCAS metric to validate spatial alignment between counterfactual explanations and classifier saliency, with ablation-confirmed downstream classification improvements.
AI.motivation: Deep learning models for retinal disease detection lack explainability that links decisions to clinically meaningful retinal regions, hindering clinical adoption. Existing post-hoc saliency methods are insufficient for providing intuitive, visually interpretable explanations.
AI.method: CounterFundus integrates (1) EfficientNet-B5 for retinal disease classification, (2) a CycleGAN for disease-to-normal fundus image translation that produces counterfactual healthy counterparts, (3) difference maps derived from original vs. counterfactual images to localize disease-associated changes, and (4) the Counterfactual-Classifier Alignment Score (CCAS), which combines Spearman correlation, binary IoU, and pointing accuracy to assess spatial agreement between counterfactual difference maps and EigenCAM classifier saliency maps. Ablation studies using CCAS-filtered counterfactual augmentation are conducted to evaluate downstream classification improvements.
AI.result: EigenCAM-aligned evaluation showed that counterfactual explanations remain spatially consistent with classifier-relevant retinal evidence across all CCAS dimensions. Ablation studies confirmed that CCAS-filtered counterfactual augmentation improves downstream classification performance.
AI.conclusion: CounterFundus establishes a clinically-grounded, explainable AI framework for retinal disease detection, offering visually plausible counterfactual explanations with validated spatial alignment to classifier-relevant regions, thereby addressing a key barrier to clinical adoption.

title: SciExplore: Evaluating Autonomous Agents from Scientific Navigation to Information Integration
summary: Scientific research involves complex information-seeking and reasoning workflows across heterogeneous sources. However, existing benchmarks primarily emphasize general-domain retrieval or static scientific question answering, and therefore fail to assess key capabilities required in realistic scientific research workflows. We introduce SciExplore, a benchmark designed to evaluate scientific information-seeking and reasoning capabilities of LLMs and agents. SciExplore comprises four task types covering 103 expert-curated tasks across more than ten scientific disciplines: scientific database navigation, ambiguous literature retrieval, missing reference completion, and cross-source structured knowledge synthesis, which probe progressively higher-level abilities from entity-level reasoning and document-level identification to evidence-level grounding and domain-level synthesis. We evaluate over ten state-of-the-art LLMs and autonomous agents on SciExplore, revealing substantial performance gaps with performance degrading sharply as task complexity increases and extremely low accuracy on the most challenging structured synthesis tasks. These results highlight significant limitations of current models and agents in realistic scientific information-seeking scenarios.

AI.tldr: SciExplore is a benchmark with 103 expert-curated tasks across four task types and 10+ scientific disciplines, designed to evaluate LLMs and agents on realistic scientific information-seeking and reasoning. Evaluation of 10+ state-of-the-art models reveals steep performance degradation as task complexity increases, with near-zero accuracy on the hardest structured synthesis tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks focus on general-domain retrieval or static scientific QA and fail to capture the complex, heterogeneous, multi-step information-seeking and reasoning workflows inherent to real scientific research. A benchmark is needed to assess capabilities like database navigation, ambiguous retrieval, evidence grounding, and cross-source synthesis.
AI.method: The authors construct SciExplore, a benchmark comprising four task types of increasing complexity: (1) scientific database navigation (entity-level reasoning), (2) ambiguous literature retrieval (document-level identification), (3) missing reference completion (evidence-level grounding), and (4) cross-source structured knowledge synthesis (domain-level synthesis).
