Tasks span 10+ scientific disciplines and are expert-curated. Over ten state-of-the-art LLMs and autonomous agents are evaluated on these tasks.
AI.result: Performance degrades sharply as task complexity increases across all evaluated models and agents. The most challenging cross-source structured knowledge synthesis tasks yield extremely low accuracy, exposing substantial limitations of current systems in realistic scientific information-seeking scenarios.
AI.conclusion: Current LLMs and autonomous agents are ill-equipped for realistic scientific information-seeking workflows, particularly those requiring multi-step reasoning across heterogeneous sources and structured knowledge synthesis. SciExplore provides a rigorous evaluation framework to guide future improvements in this domain.

title: Surprisal Theory is Tautological (without Rational Grounding)
summary: Surprisal theory holds that the human processing difficulty of a linguistic unit in context is an affine function of its surprisal under some language model. I argue this claim is a tautology without further constraint: for any non-negative difficulty measure over units in context, there exists a language model whose surprisal is an affine function of it under mild technical conditions. Therefore, because any pattern of difficulty is consistent with some language model, without an additional constraint on the language model, surprisal theory makes no falsifiable predictions. The tautology was long obscured by an assumption implicit in two decades of psycholinguistic work---that the relevant language model is the distribution that generated the training corpus, so that improving corpus fit improves predictions of human behavior. Recent empirical work has undermined this assumption, demonstrating that better corpus models can be worse predictors of processing difficulty. I conclude that breaking the tautology requires a rationalist intervention, i.e., the relevant language model must be derived from a non-empirically motivated model of the comprehender, which could be based on, for instance, memory constraints or processing goals, and that, thus, does not depend on the behavioral data surprisal theory is meant to explain.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that surprisal theory is unfalsifiable because for any difficulty measure, a language model exists whose surprisal is an affine function of it. Breaking this tautology requires constraining the language model with non-empirical, rationalist principles like memory constraints or processing goals, rather than relying on corpus-fitting models.
AI.motivation: To expose a fundamental logical flaw in surprisal theory: without independent constraints on what language model is relevant, the theory is a tautology and makes no falsifiable predictions. Recent empirical findings showing better corpus models can be worse predictors of human processing difficulty underscore the urgency of this critique.
AI.method: The author constructs a formal proof demonstrating that for any non-negative difficulty measure over linguistic units, there exists a language model (under mild technical conditions) whose surprisal values are an affine function of that difficulty. This reveals surprisal theory's unfalsifiability absent additional constraints. The argument is supported by a critical review of two decades of psycholinguistic assumptions and recent empirical counter-evidence.
AI.result: The proof shows surprisal theory is a tautology: any pattern of processing difficulty can be accommodated by some language model. The implicit assumption that the relevant model is the corpus-generating distribution has been empirically undermined, as demonstrated by recent work where better corpus-fitting models yield worse human predictions.
AI.conclusion: To render surprisal theory falsifiable, the field must adopt a rationalist approach: the language model must be derived from independently motivated principles (e.g., memory constraints, processing goals) rather than optimized solely for corpus fit. This decouples the model from the behavioral data surprisal theory aims to explain.

title: From Evaluation to Optimisation: Hierarchy-Aware Training Signals for CWE Prediction in Python
summary: The original ALPHA benchmark introduced a taxonomy-aware penalty for evaluating CWE-level vulnerability prediction in Python and proposed that the penalty could theoretically also serve as a training signal. This paper provides that validation. We compare three delivery mechanisms: supervised fine-tuning, a dual-head classification loss, and reinforcement learning with a dense reward derived from the normalised penalty. We find that supervised approaches consistently regress below the zero-shot baseline under distribution shift, while GRPO succeeds. Our best policy reduces the cumulative ALPHA penalty of Qwen2.5-Coder-7B on Security Hardening and Adversarial Testing (SVEN) dataset by 27.9% under greedy decoding, and by 25.5% under sampled decoding(p = 0.005, Welch's t-test), reaching statistical parity with its 4.5x larger zero-shot teacher. We conclude that the value of a hierarchical penalty as a training signal depends largely on the directness of its delivery.

AI.tldr: Validates ALPHA's taxonomy-aware penalty as a training signal for CWE-level vulnerability prediction. Supervised fine-tuning and dual-head loss regress under distribution shift, while GRPO with dense normalized penalty reward succeeds, reducing cumulative penalty by 27.9% and matching a 4.5× larger teacher model.
AI.motivation: The original ALPHA benchmark proposed that its hierarchical, taxonomy-aware penalty for CWE-level vulnerability prediction could theoretically serve as a training signal, but this hypothesis was never empirically validated. This paper aims to test whether the penalty can effectively guide model training and, if so, determine which delivery mechanism works best.
AI.method: Three training delivery mechanisms are compared: (1) supervised fine-tuning (SFT), (2) a dual-head classification loss, and (3) reinforcement learning using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with a dense reward derived from the normalized ALPHA penalty. Experiments use Qwen2.5-Coder-7B as the base model, evaluated on the Security Hardening and Adversarial Testing (SVEN) dataset under both greedy and sampled decoding.
AI.result: Supervised approaches consistently regress below the zero-shot baseline under distribution shift. GRPO succeeds: the best policy achieves a 27.9% reduction in cumulative ALPHA penalty under greedy decoding and 25.5% under sampled decoding (p = 0.005, Welch's t-test), reaching statistical parity with its 4.5× larger zero-shot teacher.
AI.conclusion: The value of a hierarchical penalty as a training signal depends largely on the directness of its delivery. Indirect methods like SFT fail under distribution shift, while directly optimizing the penalty via RL (GRPO) yields robust improvements.

title: Clustered Edge Intelligence: Beyond Just Convergence of Edge Computing and AI
comment: This is not survey or position paper. 28 Pages, 10 figures, 4 Tables, 108 references, Under review, submitted to Information Fusion
summary: We are moving from an information age to the age of intelligence. A decade, or possibly less than that, data will not be the gold anymore rather the derived intelligence out of the data and the information we posses from the edge of the network. Existing Edge Intelligence research focuses mainly on two directions: using AI for edge resource management and deploying lightweight AI models on edge devices. However, existing edge computing research lacks an intelligence-centric framework in which derived intelligence is treated as a first-class, independently manageable entity that can be described, discovered, observed, shared, reused, and dynamically clustered across heterogeneous edge devices and applications. To address these research gaps, we introduced Clustered Edge Intelligence, a visionary intelligence-centric approach. The aim of CEI is to make intelligence a shareable and reusable first-class entity that can be independently represented, discovered, observed, exchanged, and managed across the distributed edge-cloud continuum. We present a three layer CEI architecture and examine enabling technologies and research dimensions, including intelligence inventories, semantic knowledge representation, communication, discoverability, observability, lifecycle automation, clustering mechanisms, marketplaces, interoperability, and standardization.

AI.tldr: Proposes Clustered Edge Intelligence (CEI), an intelligence-centric framework where derived intelligence becomes a first-class, shareable, and reusable entity across the edge-cloud continuum, with a three-layer architecture and supporting ecosystem.
AI.motivation: Current Edge Intelligence research focuses narrowly on AI for resource management or lightweight on-device AI, but lacks a framework where derived intelligence itself is treated as an independent, first-class entity that can be described, discovered, shared, reused, and dynamically clustered across heterogeneous edge environments.
AI.method: Introduces the CEI paradigm with a three-layer architecture. Examines enabling technologies and key research dimensions including intelligence inventories, semantic knowledge representation, communication protocols, discoverability, observability, lifecycle automation, clustering mechanisms, marketplaces, interoperability, and standardization.
AI.result: The paper presents a conceptual framework and research agenda, identifying gaps in current edge computing and outlining the foundational pillars required to realize intelligence as a first-class, manageable entity across the edge-cloud continuum.
AI.conclusion: CEI represents a paradigm shift from data-centric to intelligence-centric edge computing, enabling intelligence to be independently represented, discovered, observed, exchanged, and managed. The framework opens new research directions toward an interoperable, standardized intelligence-sharing ecosystem at the edge.

title: Spectral Transformation for Layer-wise Global Rank Discovery in Federated LoRA for Vision Transformers
comment: Accepted at ECML-PKDD 2026 (Research Track). This is the submitted version, prior to peer review. Code: https://github.com/DASS-Lab-Group/SpecTraL
summary: Fine-tuning Vision Transformers (ViTs) with low-rank adapters (LoRA) promises better communication efficiency under federated setup, yet existing aggregation strategies face fundamental limitations. Independently averaging these LoRA factors is mathematically inconsistent, introducing cross-term aggregation error. In contrast, approaches that preserve heterogeneous client ranks by concatenating local adapters on the server substantially increase download cost and often require merging global LoRA updates into pretrained weights on the clients, causing reinitialization lag and unstable convergence. Other approaches further increase server-side overhead by reconstructing dense weight updates or training auxiliary models to refine aggregation error. In this work, we propose SpecTraL, spectral transformation for layer-wise global rank discovery, that resolves these challenges within a unified design. SpecTraL stacks local LoRA modules from clients and performs orthonormal Householder Transformation of the stacked adapters directly in the low-rank latent space, eliminating dense reconstruction of the global update and any auxiliary refinement on the server. By leveraging the Spiked Covariance Model from Random Matrix Theory, SpecTraL analytically separates the global consensus signal from non-IID noise, discovering optimal layer-wise global ranks without manual hyperparameter tuning. To match local ranks in subsequent rounds, we introduce a padding-aware initialization framework that lets clients incorporate residual LoRA dimensions without re-merging them into the pre-trained base model. Experiments on federated fine-tuning of ViT-B/16 and ViT-L/16 over DomainNet and NICO++ demonstrate improved accuracy-communication trade-offs, reduced server computation, and elimination of hyperparameter search for rank selection. Our code is available at https://github.com/DASS-Lab-Group/SpecTraL

AI.tldr: SpecTraL is a federated fine-tuning method for Vision Transformers that uses spectral transformation (Householder) on stacked client LoRA adapters in low-rank space, leveraging Random Matrix Theory (Spiked Covariance Model) to automatically discover optimal layer-wise global ranks, eliminating aggregation error, dense reconstruction, and manual hyperparameter tuning.
AI.motivation: Existing federated LoRA aggregation strategies suffer from three core issues: (1) independent averaging of LoRA factors introduces cross-term aggregation error due to mathematical inconsistency, (2) concatenation-based approaches that preserve heterogeneous ranks increase download costs and cause reinitialization lag from merging into pretrained weights, and (3) other methods incur heavy server overhead via dense weight reconstruction or auxiliary model training. A unified solution addressing all these limitations is needed.
AI.method: SpecTraL stacks local LoRA modules from clients on the server and applies orthonormal Householder Transformation directly in the low-rank latent space, avoiding dense global update reconstruction. It uses the Spiked Covariance Model from Random Matrix Theory to analytically separate the global consensus signal from non-IID noise, automatically discovering optimal layer-wise global ranks without hyperparameter tuning. A padding-aware initialization framework allows clients to incorporate residual LoRA dimensions in subsequent rounds without re-merging into pretrained weights.
AI.result: Experiments on federated fine-tuning of ViT-B/16 and ViT-L/16 over DomainNet and NICO++ demonstrate improved accuracy-communication trade-offs, reduced server computation, and elimination of hyperparameter search for rank selection.
AI.conclusion: SpecTraL unifies low-rank federated aggregation within a spectral transformation framework that mathematically resolves cross-term errors, automatically discovers optimal ranks via random matrix theory, and maintains communication efficiency, outperforming existing approaches on ViT benchmarks.

title: From Scalars to Time Series: Rethinking Implicit Neural Representations for Time-Varying Volumetric Data
summary: Implicit neural representations (INRs) for time-varying volumetric data are typically trained using dense sampling over spatiotemporal coordinates, where each observation corresponds to a single point in space and time. This coordinate-wise formulation requires extensive sampling during optimization, leading to high computational cost and inefficient use of temporal structure. In this work, we revisit this design choice and show that dense spatiotemporal sampling is not necessary for learning time-varying fields. Instead, we represent the data as a collection of spatially indexed time series and train INRs using sequence-level supervision over each spatial location, rather than coordinate-wise scalar samples. This reformulation eliminates the need for dense spatiotemporal sampling and instead learns each spatial location from its full temporal evolution in a structured manner. We demonstrate that this representation is compatible with a range of existing INR architectures and consistently improves reconstruction quality, while significantly reducing training cost. Furthermore, we show that this formulation can be combined with mixture-of-experts architectures, and that our MoE instantiation further improves reconstruction quality compared to both the base reformulation and existing MoE-based INR methods, providing a stronger capacity allocation under heterogeneous temporal dynamics.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a reformulation of implicit neural representations (INRs) for time-varying volumetric data, replacing dense spatiotemporal point-wise sampling with spatially indexed time series and sequence-level supervision. This eliminates redundant sampling, reduces training cost, and improves reconstruction quality, with further gains achieved via a mixture-of-experts (MoE) architecture.
AI.motivation: Standard INRs for time-varying volumetric data use coordinate-wise training with dense spatiotemporal sampling, which is computationally expensive and fails to leverage temporal structure efficiently. The authors aim to eliminate this inefficiency by exploiting the natural temporal coherence present at each spatial location.
AI.method: The authors reformulate the training paradigm: instead of sampling individual (x,y,z,t) scalar points, the data is represented as spatially indexed time series. INRs are trained with sequence-level supervision over the full temporal evolution at each spatial location. This is compatible with existing INR architectures and is further extended with a mixture-of-experts (MoE) design that allocates capacity according to heterogeneous temporal dynamics across spatial regions.
AI.result: The sequence-level reformulation consistently improves reconstruction quality and significantly reduces training cost across multiple existing INR architectures. The MoE instantiation further outperforms both the base reformulation and prior MoE-based INR methods, demonstrating stronger capacity allocation under heterogeneous temporal dynamics.
AI.conclusion: Dense spatiotemporal sampling is unnecessary for learning time-varying fields. Representing data as spatially indexed time series with sequence-level supervision is a more efficient and effective paradigm, and combining it with MoE architectures yields additional improvements.

title: Nipping the Butterfly Effect in the Bud: Self-Output Fine-Tuning for Autoregressive Weather Prediction
summary: Long-horizon weather forecasting is a fundamental challenge in atmospheric science, for which autoregressive Deep Learning Weather Prediction (DLWP) has emerged as the primary paradigm. Although the autoregressive pipeline is highly scalable and flexible, its prediction errors grow rapidly over long forecasting horizons. In this work, we study this error growth phenomenon from both theoretical and empirical perspectives. Our analysis reveals that the growth is driven by a feedback loop between output errors and input distribution shifts. Specifically, the autoregressive process amplifies small initial output errors, which progressively corrupt subsequent input distributions, echoing the butterfly effect in atmospheric science and ultimately deteriorating forecasting accuracy over longer horizons. Furthermore, we show that this distributional shift originates at the earliest stage of inference, with out-of-distribution signatures detectable as early as the first autoregressive step. To mitigate this issue, we propose \textbf{Self-Output Fine-Tuning (SOFT)}, a plug-and-play strategy that leverages the model's own one-step predictions to calibrate the biased input distribution encountered at the first step. Extensive experiments demonstrate that, despite its simplicity, SOFT achieves state-of-the-art performance on long-horizon forecasting tasks and substantially reduces both prediction errors and distributional discrepancy. The success of SOFT highlights the importance of reexamining the fundamental pipeline of deep learning weather prediction, representing a critical pipeline advance for atmospheric science.

AI.tldr: Autoregressive deep learning weather prediction suffers from error growth over long horizons due to a feedback loop between output errors and input distribution shifts. The authors propose Self-Output Fine-Tuning (SOFT), which uses the model's own one-step predictions to calibrate the biased input distribution at the first inference step, achieving SOTA long-horizon forecasting performance.
AI.motivation: Autoregressive DLWP models experience rapidly growing prediction errors over long forecasting horizons. The authors aim to understand the root cause of this error growth phenomenon and develop a practical mitigation strategy.
AI.method: The authors first provide a theoretical and empirical analysis showing that error growth stems from a feedback loop: small initial output errors amplify through autoregressive steps, progressively corrupting input distributions (akin to the butterfly effect). They detect out-of-distribution signatures as early as the first autoregressive step. To address this, they propose Self-Output Fine-Tuning (SOFT), a plug-and-play strategy that fine-tunes the model using its own one-step predictions to calibrate the biased input distribution encountered at the first inference step.
AI.result: SOFT achieves state-of-the-art performance on long-horizon weather forecasting tasks, substantially reducing both prediction errors and distributional discrepancy, despite its simplicity.
AI.conclusion: The success of SOFT underscores the importance of reexamining the fundamental autoregressive pipeline in deep learning weather prediction and represents a critical pipeline advance for atmospheric science.

title: CASC: Causal Adversarial Subspace Clustering for Multivariate Spatiotemporal Data
summary: Deep subspace clustering plays a critical role in applications involving multivariate spatiotemporal data, such as sea ice monitoring, disease spread analysis, and tracking neuro-degeneration over time. Despite recent advances, existing methods primarily rely on geometric self-expressiveness, assume static subspace structures, and often fail to capture causal dependencies, local spatial interactions, and long-range temporal dynamics inherent in complex spatiotemporal systems. To address these limitations, we propose a novel Causal Adversarial Subspace Clustering (CASC) framework for discovering evolving latent regimes in high-dimensional spatiotemporal data. CASC integrates a U-Net-inspired deep adversarial clustering architecture with stacked FAConvLSTM layers to preserve spatial and temporal structure while learning robust latent representations. A graph attention transformer-based self-expressive network is introduced to jointly model local spatial relationships, global dependencies, and long-range temporal interactions. Furthermore, we propose two new learning objectives: (1) a Causal Subspace Preservation Loss that aligns self-expression coefficients with latent causal relationships, encouraging clusters to reflect underlying causal processes rather than simple feature similarity, and (2) a Dynamic Temporal Subspace Evolution Loss that captures evolving subspace structures and temporal regime transitions in nonstationary environments. Together, these components transform deep subspace clustering from a correlation-driven paradigm into a causal-temporal regime discovery framework.

AI.tldr: Proposes CASC, a causal adversarial subspace clustering framework that integrates U-Net architecture, FAConvLSTM, and graph attention transformers with two novel losses—Causal Subspace Preservation Loss and Dynamic Temporal Subspace Evolution Loss—to discover evolving latent regimes in spatiotemporal data by shifting from correlation-based to causal-temporal clustering.
AI.motivation: Existing deep subspace clustering methods rely on geometric self-expressiveness, assume static subspace structures, and fail to capture causal dependencies, local spatial interactions, and long-range temporal dynamics inherent in complex spatiotemporal systems such as sea ice monitoring and disease spread analysis.
AI.method: The CASC framework combines: (1) a U-Net-inspired deep adversarial clustering architecture with stacked FAConvLSTM layers for spatial-temporal structure preservation; (2) a graph attention transformer-based self-expressive network for joint modeling of local, global, and long-range dependencies; (3) a Causal Subspace Preservation Loss aligning self-expression coefficients with latent causal relationships; and (4) a Dynamic Temporal Subspace Evolution Loss capturing evolving subspace structures and regime transitions in nonstationary environments.
AI.result: Not explicitly stated in the provided abstract.
AI.conclusion: The proposed components collectively transform deep subspace clustering from a correlation-driven paradigm into a causal-temporal regime discovery framework capable of handling nonstationary spatiotemporal data.

title: Beyond Independent Optimization: Compression, MoE Routing, and Quantization Interactions in Multimodal Edge Intelligence
summary: Efficient multimodal inference is increasingly constrained not only by model quality or FLOP count, but also by the cost of preserving, moving, routing, caching, and quantizing multimodal representations under latency, memory, and energy constraints. This paper reviews recent advances in efficient vision-language and multimodal large language models, covering visual token compression, video token management, KV-cache optimization, Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) routing, low-bit quantization, edge deployment, and hardware-aware benchmarking. We argue that these techniques cannot be treated as independent optimizations. Visual token compression alters downstream feature distributions and MoE routing decisions, routing behavior affects expert utilization and quantization sensitivity, quantized router logits influence expert assignment, KV-cache policies determine retained multimodal evidence, and hardware constraints often transform computational savings into memory and communication bottlenecks. We organize the literature around these interactions and identify key design trade-offs, including accuracy versus token budget, static versus adaptive compression, sparse routing efficiency versus expert collapse, and low-bit inference versus modality-specific degradation. Finally, we introduce Temporal Routing Consistency as a diagnostic for video MoE models and highlight open research directions in routing-aware compression, cross-modal cache management, hardware-aware co-design, and unified benchmarking for multimodal edge intelligence.

AI.tldr: This paper surveys recent advances in efficient multimodal inference, arguing that techniques like visual token compression, MoE routing, KV-cache optimization, and quantization are deeply interdependent. It organizes the literature around these interactions, identifies key design trade-offs, introduces Temporal Routing Consistency as a diagnostic for video MoE models, and highlights open directions in routing-aware compression, cross-modal cache management, and hardware-aware co-design.
AI.motivation: Efficient multimodal inference faces constraints beyond model quality and FLOP count—namely the costs of preserving, moving, routing, caching, and quantizing multimodal representations under latency, memory, and energy budgets. Current approaches treat compression, routing, caching, and quantization as independent optimizations, ignoring their significant interactions and emergent bottlenecks.
AI.method: This is a survey/review paper that synthesizes and organizes recent literature across six core areas: visual token compression, video token management, KV-cache optimization, Mixture-of-Experts routing, low-bit quantization, and edge deployment with hardware-aware benchmarking. The authors analyze cross-technique interactions and trade-offs rather than proposing a novel algorithm. They also introduce Temporal Routing Consistency as a diagnostic metric for evaluating routing stability in video MoE models.
AI.result: Key findings include: (1) visual token compression alters MoE routing decisions and downstream feature distributions; (2) routing behavior affects expert utilization and quantization sensitivity; (3) quantized router logits influence expert assignment quality; (4) KV-cache policies determine which multimodal evidence is retained; (5) hardware constraints often convert computational gains into memory/communication bottlenecks. The paper maps design trade-offs: accuracy vs. token budget, static vs. adaptive compression, sparse routing efficiency vs. expert collapse, and low-bit inference vs. modality-specific degradation.
AI.conclusion: Efficient multimodal inference requires holistic co-design rather than isolated optimization of individual components. The interactions among compression, routing, caching, and quantization create compounding effects that must be jointly modeled. Open research directions include routing-aware compression, cross-modal cache management, hardware-aware co-design, and unified benchmarking for multimodal edge intelligence. Temporal Routing Consistency offers a principled way to diagnose routing instability in video MoE systems.

title: Training Large Language Models for Self-Explanation Faithfulness
comment: To appear at the ICLR 2026 Workshop on Representational Alignment (Re-Align), 10 pages (long paper)
summary: We propose a Reinforcement Learning (RL) method to directly optimize the faithfulness of self-explanations - the extent to which a model's generated reasoning accurately reflects its internal decision-making process. While existing work focuses on evaluating faithfulness or using inference-time prompting frameworks to improve an LLM's self-explanation's tractability, these approaches do not provide a mechanism to directly optimize a model's parameters to generate faithful self-explanations. We bridge this gap by modifying existing faithfulness metrics into an RL training objective. We investigate (1) if models can be trained to accurately detect factors that affect their decisions, and (2) whether RL can directly optimize for the disclosure of these factors thereby improving LLM self-explanations' faithfulness. We experiment with two intervention types: random-word insertions and user-bias insertions, using a per-sample reward derived from the Phi-CCT correlation metric. RL fine-tuned Llama3.1-8B and Qwen3-8B show substantial improvements on the Phi-CCT faithfulness metric, with in-distribution scores rising from near-zero to as high as 0.664, and out-of-distribution scores reaching up to 0.691 on held-out tasks such as StrategyQA. Cross-intervention generalization is weaker but more interesting: a priori we would not expect a model trained only on random word insertions to generalize to user-bias phrases, yet Llama3.1-8B shows non-zero transfer in this direction. The reverse direction and Qwen3-8B do not replicate this, indicating model-dependent and setup-dependent effects we cannot yet explain. Lastly we analyze model behavior to rule out reward gaming behaviors that often plague RL training. Ultimately, we show that models can be trained to implicitly identify influential factors and disclose them, offering a scalable path toward reducing unfaithful reasoning in LLMs.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes using Reinforcement Learning to directly optimize the faithfulness of LLM self-explanations, training models to disclose factors influencing their decisions. RL fine-tuning yields substantial faithfulness gains (near-zero to ~0.66-0.69) on Llama3.1-8B and Qwen3-8B, with limited cross-intervention generalization. The approach offers a scalable path to reduce unfaithful reasoning.
AI.motivation: Existing work either passively evaluates faithfulness or uses inference-time prompting to improve tractability of self-explanations, but none provides a mechanism to directly optimize model parameters for generating faithful explanations. The authors aim to bridge this gap by recasting faithfulness metrics into an RL training objective.
AI.method: The authors convert the Phi-CCT correlation metric into a per-sample RL reward. They train Llama3.1-8B and Qwen3-8B using RL fine-tuning under two intervention types: random-word insertions and user-bias insertions. The reward signal encourages the model to disclose factors that influenced its decisions. Both in-distribution and out-of-distribution (e.g., StrategyQA) evaluations are conducted, along with cross-intervention generalization tests and reward gaming analysis.
AI.result: RL fine-tuning dramatically improves Phi-CCT faithfulness: in-distribution scores rise from near-zero to 0.664, out-of-distribution up to 0.691 on StrategyQA. Cross-intervention generalization is limited but notable: Llama3.1-8B shows non-zero transfer from random-word to user-bias interventions, though the reverse and Qwen3-8B fail to replicate this, suggesting model- and setup-dependent effects. Analysis rules out reward gaming behaviors.
AI.conclusion: Models can be trained via RL to implicitly identify and disclose influential factors in their decision-making, substantially improving self-explanation faithfulness. This represents a scalable approach to reducing unfaithful reasoning in LLMs, though cross-intervention generalization remains incomplete and partially unexplained.

title: GuardianAgentBench: Where Agents Fail and How to Guard Them
summary: As large language model agents increasingly operate autonomously with access to tools and external environments, ensuring their safe and reliable behavior becomes critical. We present GuardianAgentBench (GABench), a benchmark of 580 scenarios across six domains evaluated on three production-ready frameworks: LangChain, LlamaIndex, and Vectara. The benchmark incorporates rigorous multi-stage validation and five adversarial attack modes. Experiments with six state-of-the-art models reveal that even the strongest configuration achieves only 74.8% overall accuracy and expose two distinct failure regimes: stronger models under-call required tools, while weaker models mis-select and over-call tools. Performance degrades monotonically with both tool-set size and sequential turn depth, with long-horizon planning proving the steeper bottleneck. Our guardrail implementation consistently outperforms system-prompt-based defenses across all models, recovering 19.9% of failures at a false positive rate of just 0.5%. These results demonstrate that execution-time structural intervention improves safety without disrupting correct agent behavior.

AI.tldr: GABench is a benchmark of 580 scenarios across 6 domains for evaluating LLM agent safety. Testing on LangChain, LlamaIndex, and Vectara with 6 SOTA models shows max 74.8% accuracy. Two failure regimes emerge: stronger models under-call tools, weaker models over-call/mis-select. Performance degrades with tool-set size and turn depth. A guardrail implementation recovers 19.9% of failures at 0.5% FPR, outperforming system-prompt defenses.
AI.motivation: As LLM agents gain autonomy with tool access and external environment interaction, safety and reliability become critical concerns. Existing evaluations lack comprehensive benchmarks that test agent safety across diverse scenarios, frameworks, and adversarial conditions, motivating a systematic assessment of failure modes and defense mechanisms.
AI.method: The authors construct GuardianAgentBench (GABench), a benchmark comprising 580 scenarios spanning 6 domains, evaluated on three production-ready agent frameworks (LangChain, LlamaIndex, Vectara). The benchmark employs rigorous multi-stage validation and 5 adversarial attack modes. Six state-of-the-art models are tested. A structural guardrail mechanism is implemented and compared against system-prompt-based defenses, measuring failure recovery rates and false positive rates.
AI.result: The strongest model configuration achieves only 74.8% overall accuracy. Two distinct failure regimes are identified: stronger models tend to under-call required tools, while weaker models mis-select and over-call tools. Performance degrades monotonically with increasing tool-set size and sequential turn depth, with long-horizon planning being the steeper bottleneck. The guardrail implementation consistently outperforms system-prompt defenses, recovering 19.9% of failures at a 0.5% false positive rate.
AI.conclusion: Execution-time structural intervention (guardrails) improves agent safety without disrupting correct behavior, consistently outperforming system-prompt-based defenses. The findings highlight that current LLM agents remain far from reliable autonomous operation and that architectural safety mechanisms are necessary complements to prompt engineering.

title: A Polynomial Architecture-Attribution Co-Design Framework for Exact Aumann-Shapley Attribution in GNNs
summary: We study feature-level and node-level explanations for graph neural networks (GNNs) through the lens of Aumann-Shapley attribution. Path-integral methods such as Integrated Gradients provide an axiomatic formulation of attribution, but their practical use in deep GNNs typically relies on finite-sample numerical approximations to the path integral, requiring a trade-off between quadrature error and computational cost. This paper proposes APEX, a model-attribution co-design framework that makes the attribution integral exactly computable under a polynomial GNN architecture. The key component is PolyGIN, a GIN-style graph network whose message-passing, normalization, and transformation operations preserve a bounded multivariate polynomial form for scalar model scores, such as pre-softmax logits. We show that, for a PolyGIN with $L$ polynomial transformation blocks, the derivative along the attribution path has degree at most $2^L-1$. Therefore, Gauss--Legendre quadrature can evaluate the Aumann--Shapley path integral exactly, up to floating-point precision, with $2^{L-1}$ deterministic evaluation points. The resulting attributions can be computed at the feature level and then aggregated into node-level scores while preserving completeness. Experiments on synthetic and real-world graph benchmarks show that PolyGIN maintains competitive predictive performance, while the complete APEX framework achieves higher attribution fidelity than the compared baselines and substantially reduces the number of evaluations required for path integration.

AI.tldr: APEX proposes a co-designed polynomial GNN architecture (PolyGIN) that enables exact, closed-form computation of Aumann-Shapley attributions via Gauss-Legendre quadrature, eliminating the approximation error inherent in standard Integrated Gradients for GNNs.
AI.motivation: Existing path-integral attribution methods (e.g., Integrated Gradients) for GNNs rely on finite-sample numerical approximations of the Aumann-Shapley integral, introducing a trade-off between quadrature accuracy and computational cost. The authors aim to eliminate this trade-off by making the integral exactly computable.
AI.method: The authors introduce PolyGIN, a GIN-style GNN where message-passing, normalization, and transformation layers preserve a bounded multivariate polynomial form for scalar outputs. In this architecture, the derivative along the attribution path has degree at most 2^L−1 (L = number of polynomial blocks), allowing Gauss-Legendre quadrature with 2^{L−1} points to evaluate the Aumann-Shapley integral exactly (to floating-point precision). Attributions are computed at the feature level and aggregated to node-level while preserving the completeness axiom.
AI.result: PolyGIN maintains competitive predictive performance on synthetic and real-world graph benchmarks. The full APEX framework achieves higher attribution fidelity than baselines and substantially reduces the number of evaluations needed for path integration.
AI.conclusion: Co-designing the model architecture to constrain its functional form enables exact, efficient Aumann-Shapley attribution for GNNs, resolving the accuracy-efficiency trade-off in path-integral explainability methods without sacrificing model performance.

title: Workflow-Localized Mechanism Learning: Attribution-Guided Repair and Knowledge Reuse for Structured Agent Skills
summary: Agent Skills package reusable procedural knowledge as external artifacts for frozen language-model agents, yet existing optimizers do not jointly resolve where a failure occurs in a workflow, which mechanism caused it, and how relevant knowledge from third-party Skills should be reused locally. We introduce Workflow-Localized Mechanism Learning (WML). Its Node--Mechanism Attribution identifies the failed workflow node, implicated mechanisms, and smallest valid edit target, routing single-mechanism defects to L3 resources and relational defects across mechanisms to L2 composition protocols. A six-module Workflow-Guided Skill Optimization (WGSO) loop then selects provenance- and scope-aware third-party knowledge, applies bounded patches, evaluates candidates, and stores verified outcomes in optimizer-side memory. On SpreadsheetBench, WML reaches 90.33 +/- 1.53 and 74.67 +/- 3.51 Hard Accuracy with DeepSeek and Qwen3.6-Flash, respectively; without additional optimization, the learned Skills transfer to WikiTableQuestions with 84.00 +/- 2.00 and 83.00 +/- 2.00 Denotation Accuracy. On Compiler-Supported50, WML attains both the highest hard-PASS rate and the lowest cost per successful task; compiled execution sharply reduces tokens and calls relative to a direct SkillAgent while retaining most of its successful tasks. Code and artifacts are available at https://github.com/xiaolin9595/workflow-localized-mechanism-learning.

AI.tldr: WML introduces a two-stage framework that first pinpoints where and why agent workflows fail (Node-Mechanism Attribution), then applies a Workflow-Guided Skill Optimization loop (WGSO) to selectively reuse third-party knowledge, apply localized patches, and store verified outcomes. It achieves strong performance on SpreadsheetBench and transfers effectively to WikiTableQuestions, while also excelling on Compiler-Supported50 with high accuracy and low cost.
AI.motivation: Existing optimizers for frozen LM agents treat Skills as reusable procedural knowledge but fail to jointly address three critical questions: (1) where in the workflow a failure occurred, (2) which mechanism caused it, and (3) how to locally reuse relevant knowledge from third-party Skills. Without this joint resolution, optimization is imprecise and inefficient.
AI.method: WML consists of two core components: (1) Node-Mechanism Attribution, which identifies the failed workflow node, the implicated failure mechanisms, and the smallest valid edit target — routing single-mechanism defects to L3 (skill-level) resources and relational cross-mechanism defects to L2 (composition-protocol) resources; (2) a six-module Workflow-Guided Skill Optimization (WGSO) loop that selects provenance- and scope-aware third-party knowledge, applies bounded patches, evaluates candidate patches, and stores verified outcomes in optimizer-side memory for future reuse.
AI.result: On SpreadsheetBench, WML achieves 90.33±1.53 Hard Accuracy with DeepSeek and 74.67±3.51 with Qwen3.6-Flash. Without additional optimization, Skills learned on SpreadsheetBench transfer to WikiTableQuestions with 84.00±2.00 and 83.00±2.00 Denotation Accuracy, respectively. On Compiler-Supported50, WML achieves both the highest hard-PASS rate and the lowest cost per successful task; compiled execution sharply reduces token usage and API calls relative to a direct SkillAgent baseline while retaining most successful tasks.
AI.conclusion: WML demonstrates that joint localization of workflow failures and their underlying mechanisms enables precise, efficient skill optimization for frozen LM agents. The learned Skills exhibit strong cross-benchmark transferability, and compiled execution offers substantial cost savings without sacrificing task success.

title: Smooth Neural Point Processes via B-Splines
summary: Temporal point processes (TPPs) provide a general and flexible framework for modeling sequences of events in continuous time. Neural networks have been successfully employed to model TPPs in a highly expressive and data-driven way. Neural TPPs are typically trained via Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE) by minimizing the negative log-likelihood (NLL), which depends on both the conditional intensity function (CIF) and its integral over time, the compensator. Recent neural TPP approaches enable exact evaluation of the NLL without numerical integration. However, these methods typically model the compensator rather than the CIF directly, impose constraints on the neural network architecture, and are computationally expensive during training, as event contributions to the NLL are evaluated sequentially rather than in parallel. In this work, we propose a novel neural TPP model that directly parametrizes the CIF as a non-negative combination of B-spline basis functions, whose coefficients are predicted by a neural network. This formulation enables exact evaluation of the NLL, preserves full flexibility in the neural architecture, allows efficient parallelization during training, and naturally supports CIF smoothness regularization through the integrated squared second derivative. Experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets show improved computational efficiency and predictive accuracy compared to the reference neural TPP baseline.

AI.tldr: Proposes a neural temporal point process (TPP) model that directly parameterizes the conditional intensity function (CIF) using a non-negative combination of B-spline basis functions with neural network-predicted coefficients, enabling exact NLL evaluation, architectural flexibility, parallelizable training, and smoothness regularization.
AI.motivation: Existing neural TPP methods either model the compensator rather than the CIF directly, impose architectural constraints, or require sequential evaluation of event contributions during training, making them computationally expensive. The authors seek a model that allows direct CIF parameterization with exact likelihood computation, unrestricted neural architectures, and efficient parallel training.
AI.method: The CIF is parameterized as a non-negative linear combination of B-spline basis functions over time. A neural network predicts the coefficients of these basis functions. This formulation yields a closed-form compensator (integral of the CIF), enabling exact NLL evaluation without numerical integration. Training is parallelizable across events, and smoothness regularization is applied via the integrated squared second derivative of the CIF.
AI.result: Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate improved computational efficiency and predictive accuracy compared to the reference neural TPP baseline.
AI.conclusion: Direct B-spline-based CIF parameterization offers a practical and principled approach to neural TPP modeling, combining exact likelihood evaluation, architectural flexibility, parallel training efficiency, and natural smoothness regularization.

title: Naju: A Native Discrete State-Space Model with Independent Retention and Writing for Long-Sequence Memory
summary: Long-sequence memory tracking places two opposing demands on a recurrent state: near-lossless retention of stored bindings over long horizons, and active overwriting of stale ones. In our diagnostic suite, the strongest efficient baselines tend to solve only one side well. Continuous-time-parameterized state-space models (SSMs) such as Mamba obtain their discrete recurrence by zero-order-hold discretization of a continuous-time system; we argue that this detour is unnecessary for memory tracking and parameterize the discrete transition directly. Naju (Native Adaptive Junction Unit) factorizes the recurrent update, schematically $x_n = f_n\odot x_{n-1} + i_n\odot(B_n u_n)$, into an explicit discrete pole (a learned forget gate $f_n$), an independent write gain $i_n$, and input-dependent write/read maps. Since the sigmoid pole satisfies $0<f_n<1$, each frozen local coordinate is Schur-stable by construction, and the full time-varying recurrence satisfies a fading-memory/BIBO bound under uniform boundedness assumptions, with no stability regularizer. We formalize the key structural limitation of coupled designs: any non-expansive complementary single-gate recurrence ties the effective retention $r$ and write gain $w$ through $|r|+w\le 1$, so near-complete retention forces weak writing; decoupling $f_n$ from $i_n$ removes this constraint. Empirically, Naju is the only evaluated model that remains strong on both retention and overwriting at 4x the training length. Beyond the diagnostic suite, we evaluate Naju on WikiText-103 language modeling, Long Range Arena, and multi-query associative recall. Across these settings, Naju consistently combines strong long-range memory with competitive or superior performance, outperforming the Mamba baselines in the principal comparisons while remaining competitive with the Transformer and preserving linear-time, linear-memory scaling.

AI.tldr: Naju proposes a discrete-time recurrent architecture that decouples the forget gate from the write gate, overcoming a fundamental trade-off in coupled single-gate designs (like Mamba) that forces a compromise between long-term memory retention and active overwriting. By factorizing the update into independent forget ($f_n$) and write gain ($i_n$) terms, Naju achieves Schur-stability by construction and outperforms baselines on both retention and overwriting tasks, while scaling linearly in time and memory.
AI.motivation: Long-sequence memory tracking requires simultaneously retaining old bindings near-losslessly and overwriting stale ones — two opposing demands. Existing efficient baselines (including Mamba-style SSMs) tend to excel at only one side. The authors identify that Mamba's zero-order-hold discretization couples the retention and write gain through a non-expansive constraint ($|r| + w \le 1$), meaning near-perfect retention forces weak writing. This structural limitation motivates a decoupled design.
AI.method: Naju factorizes the recurrent update as $x_n = f_n \odot x_{n-1} + i_n \odot (B_n u_n)$, with three decoupled components: (1) an explicit discrete pole via a learned sigmoid forget gate $f_n \in (0,1)$, ensuring per-coordinate Schur-stability without regularization; (2) an independent write gain $i_n$; and (3) input-dependent write/read maps $B_n$. This removes the coupled constraint $|r| + w \le 1$. The time-varying recurrence satisfies a fading-memory/BIBO bound under uniform boundedness assumptions. The design operates in discrete time directly, bypassing continuous-time parameterization and zero-order-hold discretization.
AI.result: In diagnostic tests, Naju is the only model that remains strong on both retention and overwriting at 4× the training sequence length. On WikiText-103 language modeling, Long Range Arena, and multi-query associative recall, Naju consistently achieves strong long-range memory with competitive or superior performance, outperforming Mamba baselines in principal comparisons while matching Transformer competitiveness and preserving linear-time, linear-memory scaling.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling the forget and write gates eliminates a fundamental limitation of coupled single-gate recurrent designs. Naju demonstrates that a discrete-time parameterized recurrence with independent forget and write gains can simultaneously achieve stable long-range retention and effective overwriting, offering a principled and performant alternative to continuous-time-derived SSMs.

title: TOUR: A Trajectory-Level Unlearning Benchmark for Offline Reinforcement Learning
summary: Offline Reinforcement Learning (RL) agents are trained on fixed behavioral trajectories, which makes trajectory-level deletion important when selected data must be removed after training. Evaluating such deletion is difficult because a lower membership score can reflect trajectory removal, residual memorization visible to another attack, or policy collapse that destroys useful behavior. We introduce Trajectory-level memOrization and Unlearning in offline RL (TOUR), a benchmark that combines trajectory-level partitioning, matched non-member controls, retraining references, retained-performance anchors, and multi-attack privacy auditing. Across D4RL locomotion experiments and an exploratory AntMaze extension, TOUR shows that common deletion baselines have environment-dependent privacy-utility behavior. Retraining and fine-tuning often provide stronger retained-utility references than uniform GA+Refit, while TrajDeleter remains a useful comparator but is not uniformly stronger under the same audit. Reference-model, threshold, deviation, equivalence, action-error, representation-based, and query-limited attacks further show that a single likelihood-based membership score can overstate deletion quality. In the evaluated settings, conclusions about offline RL unlearning are therefore not stable under single-score auditing. They depend on matched non-member construction, retraining-relative calibration, attack family, retained utility, and explicit scope for diagnostic architecture or component-level evidence.

AI.tldr: TOUR is a benchmark for evaluating trajectory-level unlearning in offline RL, revealing that deletion quality conclusions are unstable under single-score auditing and depend on matched controls, retraining references, attack family, and retained utility.
AI.motivation: Offline RL agents train on fixed behavioral trajectories, necessitating trajectory-level deletion when data must be removed post-training. Existing evaluation is unreliable because low membership scores can arise from genuine removal, residual memorization visible to other attacks, or catastrophic policy collapse — making it unclear whether deletion actually succeeded.
AI.method: TOUR combines: (1) trajectory-level partitioning with matched non-member controls, (2) retraining-from-scratch references, (3) retained-performance anchors to detect policy collapse, and (4) multi-attack privacy auditing including reference-model, threshold, deviation, equivalence, action-error, representation-based, and query-limited attacks. Experiments span D4RL locomotion tasks and an exploratory AntMaze extension.
AI.result: Common deletion baselines exhibit environment-dependent privacy-utility behavior. Retraining and fine-tuning generally provide stronger retained-utility references than uniform GA+Refit. TrajDeleter is a useful comparator but not uniformly stronger under identical auditing. A single likelihood-based membership score systematically overstates deletion quality. Unlearning conclusions are not stable under single-score auditing.
AI.conclusion: Reliable offline RL unlearning evaluation requires matched non-member construction, retraining-relative calibration, diverse attack families, retained-utility verification, and explicit scope for diagnostic architecture or component-level evidence — single-score auditing is insufficient.

title: Reexamining zero-shot summarization: Empirical investigation of trustworthiness of LLM-summarizers
comment: 28 pages, Under review in a journal
summary:
Zero-shot summarization using Large Language Models (LLMs) has significantly advanced the abstractive summarization task by producing coherent and fluent summaries. However, underlying stochasticity of the large language models raises concerns about the stability and trustworthiness of the LLM-generated summaries. This issue has become increasingly important due to proliferation of LLM-generated summaries in educational settings, where students and researchers summarize complex academic materials in zero-shot manner.
  We propose a novel two-level diagnostic protocol for benchmarking LLM-summarizers based on the stability of the generated summaries. At the lower level, document-level stability analysis is performed over multiple LLM-summaries generated under controlled environment, and the stability coefficient is computed. Each generated summary is scored for semantic and factual alignment with the original document, enabling estimation of stability along more than one dimensions. At the next level, observations from a stratified sample of documents drawn from the corpus are consolidated to estimate the stability index of the LLM-summarizer, which is the proxy for its trustworthiness.
  Our empirical investigation of three LLM-summarizers across three genres of documents reveals statistically significant differences in the generation-level variability among LLMs across summary evaluation metrics. This study advances the LLM-summarization research by evidential recognition of the stability problem in LLM-summaries and motivates further research towards development of robust, reliable and trustworthy LLM-summarizers.

AI.tldr: Proposes a two-level diagnostic protocol to benchmark LLM summarizers by measuring summary stability across multiple generations, revealing significant variability among LLMs and advocating for more robust, trustworthy summarization systems.
AI.motivation: LLMs produce coherent summaries in zero-shot settings, but their inherent stochasticity raises concerns about stability and trustworthiness. This is especially critical in educational contexts where unreliable summaries of academic materials can have serious consequences. Existing work lacks systematic methods to quantify and benchmark this stability problem.
AI.method: A two-level diagnostic protocol: (1) At the document level, multiple summaries are generated under controlled conditions; a stability coefficient is computed by scoring each summary for semantic and factual alignment with the source document across multiple dimensions. (2) At the corpus level, observations from a stratified document sample are consolidated to estimate a stability index for the LLM summarizer, which serves as a proxy for trustworthiness. The framework is applied to three LLM summarizers across three document genres.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation reveals statistically significant differences in generation-level variability among the three LLM summarizers across various summary evaluation metrics, confirming that stability is not uniform across models.
AI.conclusion: The study provides evidential recognition of the stability problem in LLM-generated summaries and calls for further research into developing robust, reliable, and trustworthy LLM summarizers.

title: GlucoTune: A Unified Framework for Blood Glucose Preprocessing, Forecasting, and Benchmarking in Diabetes
summary: Preprocessing blood glucose time-series data is a critical yet often overlooked step in developing data-driven methods for diabetes management, particularly for type 1 diabetes. The lack of standardized preprocessing workflows and evaluation protocols hinders reproducibility and complicates fair comparison across studies. These challenges are further exacerbated by data-sharing restrictions, as privacy and licensing constraints often prevent the redistribution of preprocessed medical datasets. To address these limitations, we present GlucoTune, a comprehensive and extensible framework for reproducible experimentation with blood glucose time-series data. The framework standardizes the entire experimental workflow, from preprocessing to model evaluation, enabling reproducible experiments directly from the original datasets. Reproducible preprocessing is achieved through configurable pipelines defined in portable YAML configuration files, ensuring consistent data handling without distributing sensitive preprocessed data. Beyond preprocessing, GlucoTune provides a unified interface for implementing, training, and evaluating blood glucose prediction models. The framework integrates public datasets through standardized wrappers and provides a curated collection of state-of-the-art blood glucose prediction and general time-series forecasting methods, while remaining readily extensible to additional datasets, preprocessing strategies, and forecasting models. To promote transparent and consistent evaluation, GlucoTune includes a benchmarking leaderboard that reports results across datasets, preprocessing configurations, and forecasting methods, enabling systematic comparison of experimental settings. We demonstrate the effectiveness of GlucoTune through comprehensive experiments and assess its usability in a user study.

AI.tldr: GlucoTune is a standardized, extensible framework for reproducible blood glucose time-series experimentation that provides configurable preprocessing pipelines, unified model interfaces, and a benchmarking leaderboard, addressing the lack of standardization and data-sharing restrictions in diabetes management research.
AI.motivation: Blood glucose data preprocessing lacks standardized workflows, hindering reproducibility and fair comparison across studies. This problem is compounded by privacy and licensing constraints that prevent redistribution of preprocessed datasets, making it difficult for researchers to replicate and benchmark methods on consistent data.
AI.method: The authors propose GlucoTune, a framework that (1) defines preprocessing via portable YAML configuration files—without distributing sensitive data, (2) provides standardized dataset wrappers for public datasets, (3) offers a unified interface for implementing, training, and evaluating prediction models, (4) includes a curated collection of state-of-the-art glucose prediction and time-series forecasting methods, and (5) features a benchmarking leaderboard for transparent comparison across datasets, preprocessing configurations, and models.
AI.result: The effectiveness of GlucoTune was demonstrated through comprehensive experiments, and its usability was validated in a user study.
AI.conclusion: GlucoTune successfully addresses the reproducibility crisis in blood glucose time-series research by standardizing the full experimental workflow while respecting data-sharing restrictions, thereby enabling fair, transparent, and systematic benchmarking in diabetes management research.

title: EmoAgent-R1: Towards Multimodal Emotion Understanding with Reinforcement Learning-based Dynamic Agent Specialization
summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have achieved impressive performance in multimodal emotion recognition (MER) tasks and lifted MER to a new level that is complex emotion understanding with advanced video understanding abilities and natural language description. However, existing MLLM-based methods often use a fixed prompt to perceive the emotions, ignoring the dynamicity and complexity of the emotion source in the multimodal inputs. To address these issues, we propose a novel Reinforcement Learning-based Dynamic Agent Specialization framework (\textbf{EmoAgent-R1}) to optimize the emotion recognition, reasoning, and generalization abilities of an MLLM with dynamic agent specialization based on reinforcement learning. Specifically, we first adopt a cold start strategy to endow an MLLM with preliminary emotion recognition, reasoning, and agent routing ability by training with synthetic answer-conditioned chain-of-thought data and agent routing data. Then, we further train the MLLM with reinforcement learning to perceive emotions in a two-step agentic workflow with agent selection and agent specialization. To effectively train EmoAgent-R1, we propose a novel Progressive Group-Relative Policy Optimization (P-GRPO) to combine group-based relative advantages with a PMI-inspired progressive token-level modulation to transform sparse rewards into fine-grained learning signals, mitigating the coarse-grained uniform credit assignment issue in GRPO. Extensive experiments on MER benchmarks demonstrate the superiority of our EmoAgent-R1 in stronger emotion reasoning performance and improved optimization stability.

AI.tldr: EmoAgent-R1 proposes a reinforcement learning framework with dynamic agent specialization for multimodal emotion recognition, using a novel P-GRPO algorithm to improve emotion reasoning in MLLMs by replacing fixed prompts with adaptive agent selection and specialization.
AI.motivation: Existing MLLM-based methods for multimodal emotion recognition rely on fixed prompts to perceive emotions, which fails to capture the dynamic and complex nature of emotional sources in multimodal inputs. This limitation hinders robust emotion recognition, reasoning, and generalization.
AI.method: The framework, EmoAgent-R1, operates in three stages: (1) cold-start training with synthetic answer-conditioned chain-of-thought and agent routing data to equip the MLLM with preliminary emotion recognition, reasoning, and routing abilities; (2) a two-step reinforcement learning workflow involving agent selection and agent specialization; and (3) a novel Progressive Group-Relative Policy Optimization (P-GRPO) that combines group-based relative advantages with PMI-inspired progressive token-level modulation, converting sparse rewards into fine-grained learning signals to address the coarse-grained credit assignment problem in standard GRPO.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on MER benchmarks show that EmoAgent-R1 achieves superior emotion reasoning performance and improved optimization stability compared to existing methods.
AI.conclusion: Dynamic agent specialization via reinforcement learning, enabled by P-GRPO, effectively addresses the limitations of fixed-prompt MLLM-based emotion recognition, yielding stronger reasoning and more stable training.

title: Relative Value Learning
comment: Published as a conference paper at ICLR 2026
summary: In reinforcement learning, critics typically estimate absolute state values $V(s)$, estimating how good a particular situation is in isolation. However, it turns out that only differences in value are relevant for control. Motivated by this, we propose Relative Value Learning (RV), a framework that learns value differences directly via an antisymmetric function $Δ(s_i, s_j) = V(s_i) - V(s_j)$. We introduce a pairwise Bellman operator and prove it is a $γ$-contraction with a unique fixed point equal to the true value differences, derive well-posed $1$-step, $n$-step and $λ$-return targets and reconstruct generalized advantage estimation from pairwise differences to obtain an unbiased policy-gradient estimator (R-GAE). Beyond theoretical results, we integrate RV with PPO and achieve competitive performance on the Atari benchmark (49 ALE games) compared to standard PPO, indicating that relative value estimation is an effective alternative to absolute critics.

AI.tldr: Proposes Relative Value Learning (RVL), a framework that learns value differences between state pairs via an antisymmetric function Δ(s_i, s_j) = V(s_i) - V(s_j), rather than absolute state values. Introduces a pairwise Bellman operator (γ-contraction), derives multi-step targets, reconstructs GAE as R-GAE for unbiased policy gradients, and demonstrates competitive PPO performance on Atari.
AI.motivation: Standard critics in RL estimate absolute state values V(s), but only value differences matter for control. Learning differences directly could be more natural and efficient, avoiding the redundancy of estimating absolute quantities when only relative comparisons drive action selection and policy improvement.
AI.method: Defines an antisymmetric function Δ(s_i, s_j) = V(s_i) - V(s_j) and a pairwise Bellman operator proved to be a γ-contraction with unique fixed point equal to true value differences. Derives well-posed 1-step, n-step, and λ-return targets for relative values. Reconstructs generalized advantage estimation (GAE) from pairwise differences to yield an unbiased policy-gradient estimator (R-GAE). Integrates RV into the PPO algorithm.
AI.result: RVL integrated with PPO achieves competitive performance against standard PPO on the Atari benchmark across 49 ALE games, demonstrating that relative value estimation is a viable alternative to absolute critics.
AI.conclusion: Relative Value Learning provides a theoretically sound and empirically effective alternative to absolute value function approximation in RL, suggesting that directly modeling value differences is sufficient — and potentially advantageous — for control tasks.

title: Demographically-Informed Heat-Mortality Risk Curves via Risk Graph Neural Networks
summary: Estimating heat-related mortality risk is a core task in environmental epidemiology, typically addressed with Distributed Lag Non-linear Models (DLNMs); interpretable exposure-response surfaces fitted to temperature-mortality time series. DLNMs are effective but ignore demographic and geographic context, despite well-established relevance to heat vulnerability. We propose Risk Graph Neural Networks (RGNNs), a hierarchical GNN encoder that uses granular census features to optimise DLNM coefficient vectors, preserving interpretable risk curve outputs while substantially improving predictive calibration. Evaluated across 10 regions of England and Wales on two unprecedented heat years, RGNN variants maintain both lower point-errors and near-nominal uncertainty coverage during the 2022 heatwave where baselines collapse.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Risk Graph Neural Networks (RGNNs), a hierarchical GNN encoder that enriches Distributed Lag Non-linear Models (DLNMs) with granular census-based demographic and geographic context, preserving interpretable exposure-response curves while improving predictive calibration, particularly during extreme heat events where standard DLNMs fail.
AI.motivation: Standard DLNMs for heat-related mortality risk estimation are effective but disregard demographic and geographic context (e.g., age, socioeconomic status, urban/rural setting), despite these factors being well-established determinants of heat vulnerability. This omission limits predictive calibration, especially during extreme heatwaves.
AI.method: RGNNs employ a hierarchical Graph Neural Network encoder that ingests granular census features (demographic and geographic covariates) to optimize DLNM coefficient vectors. The architecture preserves the interpretable exposure-response surface structure of DLNMs while conditioning predictions on local population characteristics.
AI.result: Evaluated across 10 regions of England and Wales on two historically unprecedented heat years, RGNN variants achieved both lower point-prediction errors and near-nominal uncertainty coverage during the 2022 heatwave, where baseline DLNMs collapsed in calibration.
AI.conclusion: Infusing DLNMs with spatially-resolved demographic context via GNNs yields substantial gains in heat-mortality risk estimation, particularly under extreme, out-of-distribution heat conditions, without sacrificing the interpretability of the dose-response curves.

title: Faster IndexTTS-2: Accelerating and Streaming Autoregressive Zero-Shot Text-to-Speech Synthesis on GPUs
summary: Autoregressive text-to-speech models achieve strong naturalness but suffer from slow inference due to sequential token generation, limiting their deployment in production applications that require low latency. IndexTTS-2 is a state-of-the-art autoregressive TTS model consisting of a GPT, a flow-matching Diffusion Transformer, and a vocoder. Despite its high synthesis quality, its inference speed barely reaches real-time without streaming or batching support. We present Faster IndexTTS-2, which accelerates all neural network components of IndexTTS-2 for production deployment on GPUs using NVIDIA TensorRT and TensorRT-LLM. Faster IndexTTS-2 also enables streaming synthesis for latency-sensitive interactive applications, and batched inference across all components to maximize GPU utilization. Experiments on the Seed-TTS benchmark for both English and Chinese demonstrate up to 5.0$\times$ speedup on the autoregressive GPT and 3.6$\times$ end-to-end, with minimal degradation in word error rate, speaker similarity, and naturalness. Our methodology provides a practical reference for efficiently accelerating similar autoregressive speech models on GPUs.

AI.tldr: Faster IndexTTS-2 accelerates the autoregressive TTS model IndexTTS-2 using TensorRT and TensorRT-LLM, achieving up to 5.0× speedup on the GPT component and 3.6× end-to-end, while enabling streaming and batched inference with minimal quality degradation.
AI.motivation: Autoregressive TTS models like IndexTTS-2 produce high-quality speech but suffer from slow sequential inference, making them impractical for production environments requiring low latency. The goal is to accelerate all components for real-world GPU deployment without sacrificing synthesis quality.
AI.method: The authors apply NVIDIA TensorRT and TensorRT-LLM to accelerate all three neural network components of IndexTTS-2 (GPT, flow-matching Diffusion Transformer, and vocoder). They further introduce streaming synthesis for interactive scenarios and batched inference across all components to improve GPU utilization.
AI.result: On the Seed-TTS benchmark for both English and Chinese, Faster IndexTTS-2 achieves up to 5.0× speedup on the autoregressive GPT and 3.6× end-to-end speedup, with minimal degradation in word error rate (WER), speaker similarity, and naturalness.
AI.conclusion: The proposed acceleration methodology offers a practical blueprint for efficiently deploying similar autoregressive speech models on GPUs in production settings, balancing speed and quality.

title: Can Generative Recommendation Reach Cold Items? A Temporal Perspective on Semantic-ID Generation
summary: Semantic-ID-based generative recommendation represents items as sequences of shared semantic tokens, enabling token recombination beyond isolated item IDs. However, closed-world recombination does not necessarily imply temporal open-token cold-start induction, where new items enter the item catalog with unseen atomic tokens or weakly supported SID paths. In this work, we revisit SID-based generative recommendation under an absolute-time temporal protocol that separates seen and unseen targets and diagnoses the cold item reachability at the token level. Through seen/unseen-hit analysis, coldness taxonomy, and oracle-prefix probing, we show that current SID-based models can occasionally reach future items supported by observed tokens and prefixes, but struggle with unseen atomic tokens and unsupported SID paths. We further explain this boundary by interpreting SID generation as hierarchical semantic bucketing: early tokens select coarse semantic regions, while later tokens refine item-specific paths. These findings show that SID generation is compositional but not fully open-ended, and suggest future directions in more independent SID spaces, scoring-based interfaces, and dynamic textual context.

AI.tldr: This paper diagnoses the cold-start limitations of Semantic ID (SID)-based generative recommendation, revealing that while SID generation is compositional, it fails on unseen atomic tokens and unsupported paths. The authors interpret SID generation as hierarchical semantic bucketing and suggest future directions toward more open-ended SID spaces.
AI.motivation: Existing SID-based generative recommenders assume closed-world recombination of shared semantic tokens, but this does not guarantee open-token cold-start induction — the ability to generate recommendations for new items introduced with unseen atomic tokens or weakly supported SID paths. The paper aims to systematically diagnose this boundary.
AI.method: The authors establish an absolute-time temporal protocol that cleanly separates seen and unseen targets. They then perform three diagnostic analyses: (1) seen/unseen-hit analysis measuring cold item reachability at the token level, (2) a coldness taxonomy categorizing failure modes, and (3) oracle-prefix probing to test whether models can reach future items when given partial SID prefixes. They further interpret SID generation through the lens of hierarchical semantic bucketing.
AI.result: Current SID-based models can occasionally reach future items supported by observed tokens and prefixes but consistently struggle with unseen atomic tokens and unsupported SID paths. The hierarchical semantic bucketing interpretation explains this: early tokens select coarse semantic regions, while later tokens refine item-specific paths, making the generation compositional but not fully open-ended.
AI.conclusion: SID generation exhibits compositional generalization but is not truly open-ended. The findings point to future research directions including more independent SID spaces, scoring-based interfaces instead of generative decoding, and integration of dynamic textual context to improve cold-start induction.

title: Automated Synthesis and Adversarial Validation of Executable Causal Research Pipelines
summary: While automated research systems promise to accelerate empirical analysis, they are prone to silent failures: instances in which analysis code executes successfully yet relies on invalid causal assumptions. We present the Artificial Intelligence (AI)-based Epidemiology Research Assistant (ARA), a framework that makes these failures visible by explicitly encoding causal design principles, study-specific assumptions, and methodological constraints. ARA integrates protocol construction, synthetic data generation, and adversarial validation into a unified pipeline. The framework translates natural language research questions into structured causal protocols and executable analysis code by first constructing a protocol and then generating synthetic datasets using Structural Causal Models (SCMs) with known ground-truth effects. This synthetic-data step can also support pipeline development when access to confidential data, such as medical data, is restricted. The generated analysis is then evaluated under controlled violations of identification assumptions. We evaluate ARA on the Automated Causal Reasoning Benchmark, assessing recovery of identification strategies, causal quantities, treatment and outcome variables, and consistency between generated code and approved protocol. Protocol construction and adversarial validation did not consistently improve numerical agreement with benchmark estimates compared with standard LLM-based generation. However, they changed the failure mode: instead of silently returning causal estimates, ARA often surfaced protocol concerns, diagnostic failures, incomplete inference, or downgraded non-causal interpretations. These findings suggest that validity-first automated science systems should be evaluated not only by answer accuracy, but also by whether they indicate when causal claims are unwarranted.

AI.tldr: ARA is a framework that makes silent causal failures in automated research visible by encoding causal design principles, generating synthetic data with known ground truth via SCMs, and applying adversarial validation. While it did not improve numerical accuracy over standard LLM generation, it changed failure modes from silently returning invalid causal estimates to surfacing diagnostic concerns and downgrading non-causal interpretations.
AI.motivation: Automated research systems risk silent failures where analysis code runs successfully but rests on invalid causal assumptions. The authors aim to make these failures visible rather than letting them go undetected.
AI.method: ARA integrates three components into a unified pipeline: (1) protocol construction that translates natural language research questions into structured causal protocols, (2) synthetic data generation using Structural Causal Models (SCMs) with known ground-truth effects, and (3) adversarial validation evaluating the analysis under controlled violations of identification assumptions. Evaluation uses the Automated Causal Reasoning Benchmark.
AI.result: Protocol construction and adversarial validation did not consistently improve numerical agreement with benchmark estimates compared to standard LLM-based generation.
