The results demonstrate the feasibility of using structured large-language-model-based code generation to construct executable control-design workflows, while also highlighting the need for broader validation on larger plantwide-control benchmarks.

AI.tldr: A structured LLM-driven workflow automates multi-variable control design from process models, generating decentralized PI control with Bayesian optimization tuning that improves closed-loop performance by ~26.5% on a nonlinear gas-preheater benchmark.
AI.motivation: Automating the multi-variable control design workflow for dynamic process models remains challenging due to the need for coordinated code generation, validation, and repair across multiple engineering steps. The authors aim to leverage structured large-language-model (LLM) code generation to construct an end-to-end, executable control-design pipeline.
AI.method: The proposed workflow decomposes control design into constrained code-generation steps: plant-interface construction, normalization, MV-CV pairing, controller specification, closed-loop simulation, scenario generation, performance evaluation, and Bayesian optimization (BO)-based tuning. Each step generates artifacts that are executed and validated before downstream steps proceed; failed artifacts are repaired using validation feedback. The approach is demonstrated on a nonlinear gas-preheater benchmark with coupled pressure and temperature dynamics, producing a decentralized PI feedback-feedforward control structure.
AI.result: The workflow successfully produces a physically consistent decentralized PI feedback-feedforward controller and an executable tuning environment. Bayesian optimization reduces the closed-loop performance objective (aggregating set-point tracking and disturbance-rejection errors) by approximately 26.5% relative to the initial controller, primarily through improved pressure-loop transient performance.
AI.conclusion: Structured LLM-based code generation is feasible for constructing executable control-design workflows. However, the authors highlight the need for broader validation on larger plantwide-control benchmarks to establish generalizability.

title: Error Certificates for KV-Cache Eviction via Randomized Design
summary: Deterministic KV-cache eviction keeps the top-$k$ tokens under an importance score and deletes the rest. We prove that this design cannot know what it destroyed: evicted values can be altered so that everything the serving system retains is unchanged while the true attention-output error grows arbitrarily, so no serving-time estimator of that error is consistent. Randomized eviction restores identifiability. With a Poisson-sampled tail at known inclusion probabilities, one logit offset performs the Hájek correction inside the softmax, and a survey-sampling variance estimator over the retained set becomes a per-step error certificate with 0.97 empirical coverage at no accuracy cost. On real workloads we pre-registered seven claims and lost three: question-aware eviction at 25--50\% budgets is nearly free; output log-probability predicts failure better than the certificate; certificate-gated budget escalation adds nothing. What survives is attribution: the certificate separates cache-induced from inherent failures (AUC 0.73--0.75, against 0.47--0.54 for output confidence) and schedules recomputation better than random or confidence gating. Randomization buys attribution, not prediction.

AI.tldr: The paper proves deterministic KV-cache eviction suffers from a fundamental identifiability problem—evicted values can be adversarially altered without changing retained outputs, making error estimation impossible. Randomized eviction with Poisson sampling and Hájek correction restores identifiability, enabling a variance-based error certificate. Empirical results show the certificate excels at attribution (separating cache-induced vs. inherent failures) rather than prediction, and question-aware eviction at modest budgets is nearly lossless.
AI.motivation: Deterministic top-k KV-cache eviction is widely used for efficient LLM inference, but lacks principled ways to estimate the resulting attention-output error at serving time. The authors investigate whether such error estimation is even theoretically possible, and if not, what mechanism can restore it.
AI.method: First, a theoretical proof demonstrating that under deterministic top-k eviction, an adversary can perturb evicted values arbitrarily while keeping all retained KV pairs and attention weights identical—making the true attention-output error unidentifiable from retained information alone. Second, a randomized eviction scheme using Poisson sampling with known inclusion probabilities, applying a Hájek correction (one logit offset inside the softmax) to unbias the attention computation, and a Horvitz-Thompson-style survey-sampling variance estimator to produce per-step error certificates. Third, extensive empirical evaluation on real workloads testing seven pre-registered claims about prediction, attribution, budget escalation, and question-aware eviction.
AI.result: The error certificate achieves 0.97 empirical coverage (i.e., the true error falls within bounds 97% of the time) at no accuracy cost. However, three of seven pre-registered claims failed: output log-probability predicts failure better than the certificate; certificate-gated budget escalation adds no benefit; and randomization does not improve prediction. The key success is attribution: the certificate separates cache-induced from inherent failures with AUC 0.73–0.75 vs. 0.47–0.54 for output confidence, and schedules recomputation better than random or confidence-based gating.
AI.conclusion: Randomization in KV-cache eviction buys attribution, not prediction. The error certificate reliably identifies whether a failure is due to cache eviction, enabling principled recomputation scheduling. Question-aware eviction at 25–50% budgets is nearly free, suggesting practical deployment can use modest budgets without significant quality degradation.

title: KroQuant: Kronecker-Structured Block Transforms for Efficient Post-Training Quantization of Diffusion Transformers
summary:
Post-training quantization (PTQ) of diffusion transformers (DiTs) to W4A4 severely degrades output quality, because activations entering each linear layer contain outliers that 4-bit formats cannot represent. The standard fix applies an invertible linear transform to the activations and its inverse to the weights before quantizing both. Normalization layers between blocks force this transform to run online at every denoising step, making its inference computation cost the binding design constraint. Existing options trade quantization quality for inference cost: per-channel scaling (SmoothQuant) is computationally cheap but impacts the magnitude of the channels, which can harm quantization accuracy; fixed Hadamard transforms yield better quantization accuracy but require large block sizes that incur a high online cost; learned full-$d$ invertible transforms calibrate best but entail a prohibitive dense $d \times d$ matrix multiplication (GEMM) per layer per step.
  We propose KroQuant, a PTQ method that applies a learned Kronecker-structured invertible transform to each 32-element block of the activation, storing less than half the parameters of per-channel scaling. The block-local structure runs as small tensor-core GEMMs, and on an MI350 GPU the KroQuant quantizer kernel is up to $14\%$ faster than the SmoothQuant kernel. Offline LoRaQ weight calibration then absorbs the residual per-weight quantization error. On PixArt-$Σ$, SANA, and FLUX.1-schnell at W4A4 (MXFP4e2), KroQuant produces outputs closer to the FP reference than SVDQuant and LoRaQ on MJHQ-30K and SDCI, while preserving or improving image quality.

AI.tldr: KroQuant introduces a Kronecker-structured learned invertible transform for block-wise activation smoothing and LoRaQ-based weight calibration, achieving W4A4 PTQ for DiTs that outperforms SVDQuant and LoRaQ while being faster than SmoothQuant.
AI.motivation: PTQ of DiTs to W4A4 severely degrades quality due to activation outliers. Existing smoothing transforms face a trade-off: per-channel scaling (SmoothQuant) is cheap but harms accuracy; fixed Hadamard transforms need large block sizes with high online cost; learned full-d transforms are optimal but require prohibitive per-step dense matrix multiplications. The goal is to achieve high quantization quality without the inference-time overhead of full-d transforms.
AI.method: KroQuant uses two components: (1) a learned Kronecker-structured invertible transform applied to 32-element blocks of activations, parameterized as a Kronecker product of smaller matrices, stored with fewer parameters than per-channel scaling, and executed as small tensor-core GEMMs; (2) offline LoRaQ weight calibration that absorbs residual per-weight quantization error after the activation transform.
AI.result: On an MI350 GPU, the KroQuant quantizer kernel runs up to 14% faster than SmoothQuant. On PixArt-Σ, SANA, and FLUX.1-schnell at W4A4 (MXFP4e2), KroQuant produces outputs closer to FP reference than SVDQuant and LoRaQ on MJHQ-30K and SDCI benchmarks while preserving or improving image quality.
AI.conclusion: KroQuant effectively resolves the activation-outlier quantization problem in DiTs by combining a computationally efficient Kronecker-structured transform with offline weight calibration, achieving state-of-the-art W4A4 PTQ results without the prohibitive cost of full-d learned transforms.

title: Expert Behavior Prior Reinforcement Learning
summary: Behavior prior reinforcement learning (BPRL) has emerged as a promising paradigm to improve sample efficiency in online reinforcement learning (RL) by leveraging policy priors derived from offline demonstrations. However, most existing BPRL methods rely on static offline datasets, which often suffer from low data diversity and suboptimal trajectory quality. This reliance restricts the effectiveness of policy priors, hindering both policy exploitation and stability during online training. Consequently, agents are prone to inefficient exploration and unstable learning dynamics. To address these limitations, we deviate from existing offline pre-training methods and propose an Expert Behavior Prior (EBP) algorithm. Specifically, we introduce a Q-guided conditional variational autoencoder (Q-CVAE) that learns to generate expert policy priors directly from the online replay buffer. This enables the generation of high-value actions for guiding policy updates without relying on pre-collected expert trajectories. To further enhance policy exploitation, we propose an expert policy guidance (EPG) mechanism that selects expert actions from a generative support set, and we integrate a policy gradient correction (PGC) module to harmonize Q-guidance with expert supervision, promoting stable and consistent policy improvement. Extensive experiments conducted on robotic control (Gym, PyBullet) and industrial control (DMControl) benchmarks demonstrate that EBP significantly outperforms state-of-the-art online RL algorithms, achieving higher sample efficiency and more stable convergence.

AI.tldr: EBP introduces a Q-guided conditional VAE that generates expert-level actions directly from the online replay buffer, combined with expert policy guidance and policy gradient correction, achieving superior sample efficiency and stability in online RL without relying on static offline datasets.
AI.motivation: Existing BPRL methods depend on static offline datasets with low diversity and suboptimal trajectories, which limits policy prior effectiveness and causes inefficient exploration and unstable learning. The authors aim to eliminate this dependency by generating expert priors online.
AI.method: EBP consists of three components: (1) Q-CVAE, a Q-guided conditional variational autoencoder that generates high-value actions from the online replay buffer; (2) EPG, an expert policy guidance mechanism that selects expert actions from a generative support set; and (3) PGC, a policy gradient correction module that balances Q-guidance with expert supervision for stable policy improvement.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on Gym, PyBullet, and DMControl benchmarks show EBP significantly outperforms state-of-the-art online RL algorithms in both sample efficiency and convergence stability.
AI.conclusion: By generating expert behavior priors online rather than relying on static offline data, EBP overcomes key limitations of existing BPRL methods, enabling more efficient exploration and stable policy learning in continuous control tasks.

title: Agentic coding without the cloud: evaluating open-weight large language models on longitudinal data preparation tasks
summary: Large language models (LLMs) and agents are now widely used tools in code development, with data typically sent to third-party cloud-based models. Their adoption in research using personal data is constrained by governance requirements that typically prohibit data transmission to external services. Locally deployable open-weight models offer an alternative since sensitive data never leave the local environment. We introduce an open-source framework for evaluating the efficacy of AI agents powered by open-weight LLMs on one of the most persistent bottlenecks in research on longitudinal population studies: data preparation. The framework comprises: a curated ground-truth dataset (cleaning scripts preparing six sweeps of data from a British cohort study), task definitions encompassing tasks such as category harmonization and multi-wave merging, and automated routines for evaluating the LLM-produced R code and outputted data. We benchmark LLMs across the (consumer grade) deployment spectrum to assess their efficacy in 20 data preparation tasks (creation of 102 variables). Current state-of-the-art, 31-35B parameter models almost saturated our benchmark ("average task completion" up to 87.9%). The performance of open-weight LLMs running on consumer-grade hardware shows promise of a viable path toward AI-assisted data preparation in governance-restricted research settings. Our framework is publicly available at: https://github.com/UCL-ARC/RRBench.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces RRBench, an open-source framework for evaluating open-weight LLMs on data preparation tasks for longitudinal population studies. It benchmarks models (up to 35B parameters) across 20 data preparation tasks involving 102 variables from a British cohort study, finding that current models nearly saturate the benchmark (up to 87.9% task completion) even on consumer-grade hardware, demonstrating a viable path for AI-assisted data preparation in governance-restricted settings.
AI.motivation: Research using personal/longitudinal data is constrained by governance requirements that prohibit transmitting sensitive data to external cloud-based LLM services. Locally deployable open-weight models could solve this, but their efficacy on complex data preparation tasks (a persistent bottleneck in longitudinal studies) has not been systematically evaluated.
AI.method: The authors built an open-source evaluation framework (RRBench) with: (1) a curated ground-truth dataset from six sweeps of a British cohort study, (2) task definitions covering category harmonization, multi-wave merging, etc., and (3) automated routines for evaluating LLM-generated R code and output data. They benchmarked open-weight LLMs across the consumer-grade deployment spectrum on 20 data preparation tasks (102 variables).
AI.result: Current 31-35B parameter open-weight models nearly saturated the benchmark, achieving up to 87.9% average task completion. Performance on consumer-grade hardware was promising, indicating feasibility for governance-compliant, local AI-assisted data preparation workflows.
AI.conclusion: Open-weight LLMs running locally on consumer-grade hardware represent a viable path toward AI-assisted data preparation in governance-restricted research settings, enabling sensitive personal data to be processed without ever leaving the local environment.

title: Test-Time Scaling via Error Localization
summary: Scaling inference-time computation has emerged as a reliable method to improve the performance of large language models on complex reasoning and programming tasks. However, standard approaches such as independent sampling and sequential multi-turn refinement operate without token-level credit assignment, resulting in computational inefficiency, since valid reasoning prefixes are frequently discarded. In this work, we introduce Test-Time Scaling via Error Localization (TTEL), an inference-time algorithm that utilizes fixed or environment feedback to perform token-level error localization. By comparing conditional probabilities under informed feedback against a null-context baseline, TTEL isolates the step at which an error occurred. The algorithm then truncates the trajectory and branches a new generation, maximally reusing the valid prefix. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that TTEL establishes strictly dominating Pareto frontiers across sequential reasoning domains, measured by pass-at-k vs. generated-token cost. With Qwen3-8B on LiveCodeBench, TTEL attains a pass@64 of 71.0% while generating approximately half as many tokens as independent sampling (360.4k vs. 735.0k). Generalizing to math benchmarks AIME-2025 and HMMT-2025, TTEL cleanly outperforms competing test-time baselines across both Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-4B-Thinking-2507.

AI.tldr: TTEL introduces token-level error localization at inference time by comparing conditional probabilities under informed feedback vs. a null-context baseline. It truncates erroneous trajectories at the localized error step and branches new generations, maximizing reuse of valid prefixes. This yields Pareto-dominant pass@k vs. token-cost tradeoffs on coding and math benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Standard inference-time scaling methods (independent sampling, sequential multi-turn refinement) lack token-level credit assignment, causing valid reasoning prefixes to be repeatedly discarded and wasting computation. The authors aim to improve computational efficiency by pinpointing exactly where errors occur in a reasoning trajectory and reusing everything before that point.
AI.method: TTEL uses environment or fixed feedback to compute conditional probabilities of each token under both an informed-feedback context and a null-context baseline. By comparing these probabilities, it localizes the error step — the point where the model deviates from a correct reasoning path. The trajectory is then truncated at that step, and a new generation is branched from the validated prefix, maximally preserving correct reasoning.
AI.result: On LiveCodeBench with Qwen3-8B, TTEL achieves pass@64 of 71.0% while generating ~360.4k tokens, roughly half the token cost of independent sampling (735.0k). TTEL establishes strictly dominating Pareto frontiers across sequential reasoning domains. On AIME-2025 and HMMT-2025 math benchmarks, TTEL outperforms competing test-time baselines with both Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-4B-Thinking-2507.
AI.conclusion: Token-level error localization via TTEL enables significantly more compute-efficient inference-time scaling by preserving valid reasoning prefixes and only re-generating from identified error points, yielding superior pass@k per generated token across both code and math reasoning tasks.

title: Regulating autonomous and agentic AI
summary: Regulating activities where regulatees use autonomous and agentic AI is challenging. Regulatory assumptions about regulatee knowledge and control no longer hold true; much of that lies elsewhere in the AI supply chain which thus needs to be brought within the scope of regulation. Governance systems for autonomous AI cannot replicate existing governance models, but need a fresh approach. Retrospective supervisory oversight becomes ineffective as a risk management tool, and AI autonomy generates new systemic risks which require new solutions. This paper investigate four regulatory systems: UK regulation of content platforms, data protection, UK financial services, and the EU AI Act\'92s cross-sectoral regime. It analyses the challenges posed by autonomous and agentic AI and proposes potential solutions which regulators might adopt. These will transform regulation from a reactive process to an active one, and assist it in adapting to the challenges of AI autonomy.

AI.tldr: Regulating autonomous/agentic AI is fundamentally challenging because traditional regulatory assumptions about regulatee knowledge and control break down. This paper examines four regulatory regimes, identifies the challenges AI autonomy poses, and proposes solutions that shift regulation from reactive to active governance.
AI.motivation: Autonomous and agentic AI systems undermine core regulatory assumptions: that regulatees possess sufficient knowledge of their systems and maintain meaningful control over them. As knowledge and control disperse across the AI supply chain, existing retrospective supervisory models become ineffective, and new systemic risks emerge that current governance frameworks cannot address. A fresh regulatory approach is needed.
AI.method: Comparative legal and regulatory analysis of four governance systems: UK online content platform regulation, data protection law, UK financial services regulation, and the EU AI Act's cross-sectoral regime. The paper analyzes how each regime confronts the challenges of autonomous/agentic AI and synthesizes potential regulatory solutions.
AI.result: The analysis reveals that retrospective oversight fails as a risk management tool for autonomous AI. Regulatory scope must expand to encompass the broader AI supply chain where knowledge and control actually reside. New systemic risks specific to AI autonomy require novel governance mechanisms distinct from existing models.
AI.conclusion: Regulation must transform from a reactive process to an active one. Regulators need to adopt proactive, supply-chain-spanning approaches that account for dispersed knowledge and control, address emergent systemic risks, and move beyond traditional retrospective supervision to remain effective in the face of increasing AI autonomy.

title: Windowed-MTP: Removing the Full-Context Draft-KV Tax at Million-Token Context
summary: Speculative decoding accelerates autoregressive generation by having a cheap draft propose tokens that a target verifies in parallel. Frontier models increasingly ship a built-in Multi-Token-Prediction (MTP/NEXTN) draft head under the assumption that the draft is negligibly cheap. At million-token context this breaks: an MTP draft head typically runs full attention over the entire KV cache at every draft step, so its read grows linearly with context and comes to dominate the draft cost -- precisely where speculation is most valuable. The effect compounds with draft length (a deep native draft can turn net-negative, slower than no speculation) and sharpens under hybrid/linear-attention targets, where cheaper verification leaves the draft's full-attention read exposed. We apply a StreamingLLM-style sliding window plus attention sink to the draft's attention only (Windowed-MTP), leaving full-attention verification intact. It is training-free, drop-in, and lossless by construction: the full-attention target still decides every accepted token, so windowing changes only which tokens are proposed, never which are accepted. It bounds the draft's KV working set to a constant, dropping ~99% of KV entries at 1M. Across three architecture families (Qwen GDN-MoE 35B/122B and a Mamba2-hybrid NoPE 120B) at 1M context on a single GPU in SGLang, windowing cuts the per-decode-step cost over the shipping native MTP draft by +28% to +44%, an input-invariant margin that widens with context. Since per-token latency is this cost divided by acceptance length, at matched acceptance end-to-end decode latency improves by the same amount, and more where windowing also lifts acceptance, while preserving the target's verified output distribution. Finally, the unread draft KV -- 7.7-11% of total KV at 1M -- is reclaimed via a compact ring buffer at no acceptance or quality cost.

AI.tldr: Multi-Token-Prediction (MTP) draft heads become prohibitively expensive at million-token contexts due to full-attention KV cache reads dominating draft cost. The authors propose Windowed-MTP, a training-free, drop-in fix that applies a StreamingLLM-style sliding window + attention sink to the draft's attention only, bounding draft KV to a constant size and cutting per-step cost by 28–44% at 1M context without altering the target model's verified output distribution.
AI.motivation: Frontier LLMs increasingly ship with built-in MTP draft heads for speculative decoding, assuming draft cost is negligible. At million-token contexts, this assumption breaks: the draft's full attention over the entire KV cache causes linear growth in read cost, which compounds with draft length and becomes especially problematic with hybrid/linear-attention targets where cheap verification exposes the draft's cost. The draft can become net-negative (slower than no speculation).
AI.method: Windowed-MTP applies a StreamingLLM-style sliding window plus attention sink exclusively to the draft head's attention, leaving the target model's full-attention verification intact (lossless by construction). The draft's KV working set is bounded to a constant size, dropping ~99% of KV entries at 1M context. Additionally, unread draft KV memory (7.7–11% of total KV at 1M) is reclaimed via a compact ring buffer with no quality cost.
AI.result: Across three architecture families (Qwen GDN-MoE 35B/122B and a Mamba2-hybrid NoPE 120B) at 1M context on a single GPU in SGLang, Windowed-MTP cuts per-decode-step cost by +28% to +44% over the shipping native MTP draft. End-to-end decode latency improves by the same margin, and in some cases windowing also lifts acceptance rates. The method preserves the target's verified output distribution exactly.
AI.conclusion: Windowed-MTP is a simple, training-free, drop-in solution that restores the practicality of native MTP speculative decoding at long contexts. By windowing the draft only, it eliminates the context-length dependence of draft cost while guaranteeing losslessness, making speculation viable and net-positive even at million-token scales.

title: SPORD: A Simulation-Propose-then-OR-Dispose Approach for Supply Chain Planning
summary: For years, supply chain planning at e-commerce firms has operated as a collection of isolated projects. Each planning task from static network planning to dynamic warehouse assortment planning requires analysts to spend weeks building models from scratch, calibrating and persuading executives to act on outputs they cannot verify. Three barriers drive this: bespoke models proliferate because standardization is difficult (operational fragmentation); once unified, the combinatorial scale of millions of SKUs, thousands of nodes, and intricate routing logic exceeds what solvers can handle within a tight window (computational intractability); and a mathematically optimal solution still fails to be implemented if the executives do not trust it (implementation hurdle). To bridge this gap, we propose and implement the Simulation-Propose-then-OR-Dispose method, deployed as JD.com's NetSim platform. The central insight is decoupling: simulation proposes by generating and evaluating the full set of operationally valid candidate paths-absorbing all idiosyncratic business logic, while an integer program disposes by selecting the globally optimal subset. Computationally, matrix-vectorized CPU/GPU accelerated simulation achieves a 10-100 times speedup over serial methods, and a list scheduling algorithm reduces coupled-order processing from hours to minutes. Operationally, we establish a closed loop via an intelligent diagnosis engine. Since 2025, NetSim has optimized end to-end services for over 20,000 suppliers, the cross-regional fulfillment rate dropped from 6.1% to 4.9%, and the average monthly carbon reduction is approximately 5,745 tCO2e. SPORD moves simulation from monitoring to active planning. The transparent outputs turn skeptical executives into engaged collaborators, and the modular architecture ensures that the next planning requires just configuration, not reconstruction.

AI.tldr: JD.com's NetSim platform introduces the Simulation-Propose-then-OR-Dispose (SPORD) method to unify supply chain planning. It decouples simulation (which generates operationally valid candidate paths) from integer programming (which selects the globally optimal subset), overcoming fragmentation, computational intractability, and executive distrust. GPU-accelerated simulation yields 10–100× speedups, and real-world deployment since 2025 has reduced cross-regional fulfillment rates from 6.1% to 4.9% and cut ~5,745 tCO₂e monthly.
AI.motivation: Supply chain planning at e-commerce firms suffers from three chronic barriers: (1) operational fragmentation — bespoke models are rebuilt from scratch for each planning task due to lack of standardization; (2) computational intractability — millions of SKUs, thousands of nodes, and complex routing logic exceed solver capacity within tight time windows; (3) implementation hurdle — even mathematically optimal solutions fail when executives distrust unverifiable outputs. These barriers prevent unified, scalable, and trusted supply chain planning.
AI.method: The SPORD (Simulation-Propose-then-OR-Dispose) method decouples the planning problem: a simulation engine proposes and evaluates all operationally valid candidate paths, absorbing idiosyncratic business logic, while an integer program disposes by selecting the globally optimal subset. Computational accelerations include matrix-vectorized CPU/GPU simulation achieving 10–100× speedup over serial methods and a list scheduling algorithm reducing coupled-order processing from hours to minutes. An intelligent diagnosis engine establishes a closed operational loop. The system is deployed as JD.com's NetSim platform with a modular, configuration-driven architecture.
AI.result: Since deployment in 2025, NetSim has optimized end-to-end services for over 20,000 suppliers. The cross-regional fulfillment rate dropped from 6.1% to 4.9%, and average monthly carbon reduction reached approximately 5,745 tCO₂e. The transparent outputs converted skeptical executives into engaged collaborators, and the modular architecture ensures new planning tasks require only configuration rather than reconstruction.
AI.conclusion: SPORD shifts simulation from a passive monitoring role to active planning, successfully bridging the gap between optimization theory and practical supply chain execution. The decoupled architecture, computational acceleration, and closed-loop diagnosis engine together overcome the three barriers of fragmentation, intractability, and distrust, providing a replicable framework for large-scale e-commerce supply chain planning.

title: Finite-Sample Coverage Audits for High-Recall Candidate Generation: Certification and Learning-Theoretic Design
summary: An initial high-recall stage in an empirical pipeline decides which items pass to later review, labelling, or modelling, and relevant items it misses are lost to every subsequent stage. We study how many audit labels are needed to certify, with finite-sample validity, that this missed relevant mass is small, and our main results characterise the label complexity of this problem. We first show that no procedure using only labels from inside the candidate set can certify any non-trivial bound on the missed mass: the audit must sample the excluded pool, the only region where unrecovered relevant items can lie. We then prove a matching finite-corpus lower bound. Any valid audit that certifies fewer than $m$ missed relevant items with high probability when none are present, even if adaptive and permitted to label the entire included pool, must inspect on the order of $N_0/m$ excluded-pool labels. Excluded-pool auditing is therefore minimax rate-optimal, not merely convenient, for missed-mass certification in the zero-miss regime. Building on this characterisation, we develop an exact finite-sample toolkit, using binomial and hypergeometric inversion rather than asymptotic approximation, that certifies missed mass, converts it to recall through a two-pool design, certifies pre-specified families of nested candidate generators simultaneously, and produces stress-test certificates against declared perturbation mechanisms. These certificates can be paired with observable review burden to select the least burdensome pre-specified candidate generator meeting a missed-mass target. Every guarantee holds under one discipline: the candidate generator, or the pre-specified family from which it is selected, and the audit rule are fixed before the certification labels are examined.

AI.tldr: The paper studies the label complexity of certifying that a high-recall screening stage misses few relevant items. It proves that auditing the excluded pool is necessary and minimax rate-optimal, and provides exact finite-sample certification tools using binomial/hypergeometric inversion.
AI.motivation: High-recall filtering stages in empirical pipelines (e.g., document screening for systematic reviews) inevitably miss some relevant items. Practitioners need finite-sample valid guarantees that the missed relevant mass is small, but the statistical properties of auditing this missed mass were not well understood.
AI.method: The authors prove lower bounds showing that excluded-pool auditing is necessary (no procedure using only candidate-set labels can certify non-trivial bounds) and minimax rate-optimal (requiring order N₀/m labels). They then develop exact finite-sample certification procedures using binomial and hypergeometric inversion, supporting simultaneous certification of nested candidate generators and stress-testing against perturbation mechanisms.
AI.result: Two main theoretical results: (1) impossibility of certification using only in-candidate labels; (2) a matching lower bound proving excluded-pool auditing is minimax rate-optimal. The practical toolkit provides exact finite-sample certificates for missed mass, recall, nested generator families, and perturbation robustness.
AI.conclusion: Excluded-pool auditing is not merely convenient but statistically necessary and optimal for missed-mass certification. The finite-sample toolkit enables rigorous, distribution-free quality guarantees for high-recall screening pipelines under the discipline of pre-specifying generators and audit rules.

title: Towards Faithful Graph Explanations with Synergistic Edge Effects via Granular Balls
summary: Instance-level explanations aim to reveal the rationale behind a model's decisions for a specific graph. Previous methods explain graph neural networks (GNNs) by selecting important edges to induce subgraphs, where edge importance is assessed by perturbing each edge and observing changes in the model predictions. However, they often neglect the synergistic effects among edges, which are crucial for accurately characterizing edge importance. To address this issue, we propose SeeExplainer, a parameter-free explainer to interpret GNNs. Specifically, we first introduce a granular-ball graph refinement mechanism that decomposes a graph into several disjoint granular-balls with no fixed size, and utilize them as nodes to construct a structural graph. This process can better capture the synergistic effects among edges. Then, we perturb nodes and edges in the structural graph to generate explanatory subgraphs based on their respective contributions. Experiments on several graph classification datasets of different networks show that SeeExplainer outperforms state-of-the-art baselines.

AI.tldr: SeeExplainer is a parameter-free GNN explainer that uses granular-ball graph refinement to capture synergistic edge effects, then perturbs structural graph nodes/edges to generate explanatory subgraphs, outperforming existing baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing instance-level GNN explanation methods assess edge importance via individual edge perturbation but neglect synergistic effects among edges, leading to inaccurate edge importance characterization. Capturing these synergies is crucial for faithful explanations.
AI.method: SeeExplainer introduces a granular-ball graph refinement mechanism that decomposes the input graph into disjoint, variable-sized granular-balls used as nodes to construct a structural graph, better capturing edge synergies. It then perturbs nodes and edges in this structural graph based on their contributions to generate explanatory subgraphs. The method is parameter-free.
AI.result: Experiments on multiple graph classification datasets with different network architectures show SeeExplainer outperforms state-of-the-art baselines.
AI.conclusion: Accounting for synergistic effects among edges via granular-ball refinement significantly improves the quality of GNN explanations, as demonstrated by SeeExplainer's superior performance.

title: OpenForgeRL: Train Harness-native Agents in Any Environment
summary: Modern AI agents rely on elaborate inference harnesses such as Claude Code, Codex, and OpenClaw to drive multi-turn reasoning, tool use, and access to external systems. While powerful, these complex harnesses also make agents hard to train end-to-end with open infrastructure, whose SFT/RL stacks cannot natively express stateful, multi-process harness inference. To address this, we present OpenForgeRL, an open-source framework for training harness-based agents end-to-end in diverse environments. OpenForgeRL achieves this with a lightweight proxy that serves the harness's model calls while recording them as training data for a standard RL codebase (e.g., veRL), and a Kubernetes orchestrator that runs each rollout in its own remote container, together enabling training on any harness in any environment at scale. By decoupling training and inference, OpenForgeRL allows researchers to easily train, study, and improve agents directly in the real harnesses and environments they are deployed with. We validate our framework across diverse, complex harnesses and environments, spanning tool/claw-based agents and multimodal GUI browser- and computer-use agents. Using only hundreds to a few thousand tasks, OpenForgeClaw reaches 31.7 pass^3 and 55.9 pass@3 on ClawEval and 33.7 on QwenClawBench. OpenForgeGUI reaches 37.7 on OSWorld-Verified, 63.0 on Online-Mind2Web, and 72.3 on WebVoyager. Both outperform open baselines of similar size on nearly all benchmarks, and in the GUI setting match or surpass models several times larger. Beyond benchmarks, we analyze how harness choice (e.g., ZeroClaw, OpenClaw, Codex) and RL shape agent behavior. We find that some harnesses are substantially harder to learn than others, and that RL improves agentic reliability, such as self-verification, tool coverage, and completing multi-step plans, though critical abilities such as error recovery remain weak.

AI.tldr: OpenForgeRL is an open-source framework enabling end-to-end RL training of harness-based agents (Claude Code, Codex, OpenClaw) at scale by decoupling training from inference via a lightweight proxy and Kubernetes orchestration. It achieves strong results on tool-use and GUI benchmarks, often surpassing larger models, and reveals that harness choice significantly impacts learnability and that RL improves agentic reliability.
AI.motivation: Modern AI agents depend on complex, stateful, multi-process inference harnesses (e.g., Claude Code, Codex, OpenClaw) that are incompatible with standard open-source SFT/RL stacks, which cannot natively handle multi-turn, tool-calling inference. This prevents end-to-end training of agents in their actual deployment harnesses, limiting research on improving agent behavior in realistic settings.
AI.method: OpenForgeRL introduces two key components: (1) a lightweight proxy that intercepts and serves the harness's model calls while simultaneously recording them as training data for standard RL codebases (e.g., veRL), and (2) a Kubernetes orchestrator that executes each rollout in an isolated remote container, enabling scalable training on any harness in any environment. This architecture decouples training from inference, allowing researchers to train agents directly in their real deployment harnesses and environments.
AI.result: OpenForgeClaw achieves 31.7 pass^3 and 55.9 pass@3 on ClawEval, and 33.7 on QwenClawBench. OpenForgeGUI reaches 37.7 on OSWorld-Verified, 63.0 on Online-Mind2Web, and 72.3 on WebVoyager. Both outperform open baselines of similar size on nearly all benchmarks; GUI agents match or surpass models several times larger. Analysis shows harness choice significantly affects learnability and that RL improves self-verification, tool coverage, and multi-step plan completion, though error recovery remains weak.
AI.conclusion: OpenForgeRL successfully bridges the gap between complex agent harnesses and standard RL infrastructure, enabling scalable end-to-end training. The framework demonstrates that RL training within real harnesses yields substantial performance gains, but also highlights that harness design critically impacts trainability and that key capabilities like error recovery remain challenging frontiers for agent research.

title: Multimodal Pretraining for Generalizable EEG Representation Learning
summary: Electroencephalography (EEG) models used for epilepsy are often limited to specific datasets and tasks. This limited approach can make it challenging to apply these models across different datasets or in various situations. However, recent studies in foundation models and self-supervised learning suggest that an adaptable EEG backbone could support a range of EEG related tasks. In this study, we have developed a multimodal EEG foundation model that combines a raw signal encoder based on the Mamba architecture, a Vision Transformer (ViT)-style encoder for time-frequency data, and a lightweight encoder for text, all within a shared embedding space. The pretraining process relies on several innovative techniques, such as masked modeling, cross-view contrastive alignment, and temporal consistency losses. These methods are designed to create rich, seizure-relevant representations without requiring labeled data. To assess the efficacy and generalization of our pretrained model, we fine-tuned it on the canonical CHB-MIT seizure detection benchmark and additional seizure detection datasets, and conducted extensive experiments comparing different model variants. On the standard CHB-MIT split, our best single model achieved an AUROC of 0.874, and an ensemble variant reached 0.878 AUROC, representing state-of-the-art performance on this benchmark. In addition to standard train-test splits, we evaluated performance under a leave-one-subject-out (LOSO) protocol, which is rarely reported in prior EEG seizure modeling work and highlights the difficulty of patient-independent seizure detection, with a mean LOSO balanced accuracy of 0.558 across 19 subjects. Across datasets and evaluation settings, our multimodal foundation model enabled robust seizure detection and straightforward adaptation to new seizure detection scenarios, while also supporting interpretable seizure localization.

AI.tldr: A multimodal EEG foundation model combining Mamba-based raw signal encoding, ViT-based time-frequency encoding, and text encoding, pretrained with self-supervised learning, achieves state-of-the-art seizure detection (0.874–0.878 AUROC on CHB-MIT) and demonstrates cross-dataset generalization.
AI.motivation: Existing EEG models for epilepsy are narrow in scope, limited to specific datasets and tasks, hindering cross-dataset applicability. Foundation models and self-supervised learning offer a path toward a generalizable EEG backbone supporting diverse tasks.
AI.method: A multimodal EEG foundation model with three encoders sharing a common embedding space: (1) a Mamba-based raw signal encoder, (2) a ViT-style encoder for time-frequency representations, and (3) a lightweight text encoder. Pretraining uses masked modeling, cross-view contrastive alignment, and temporal consistency losses to learn seizure-relevant representations without labeled data. Fine-tuning is performed on CHB-MIT and additional seizure datasets, with evaluation under both standard splits and leave-one-subject-out (LOSO) protocols.
AI.result: On CHB-MIT, the best single model achieved 0.874 AUROC and an ensemble reached 0.878 AUROC (state-of-the-art). Under LOSO evaluation, mean balanced accuracy was 0.558 across 19 subjects, underscoring the difficulty of patient-independent detection. The model demonstrated robust seizure detection, straightforward adaptation to new scenarios, and interpretable seizure localization across datasets.
AI.conclusion: The multimodal foundation model enables robust, generalizable, and interpretable seizure detection that adapts readily across datasets and settings, advancing beyond single-task, single-dataset EEG models.

title: MSBraM: A Multi-scale Self-supervised Brain Foundation Model for Hierarchical EEG Dynamics Learning
summary: Self-supervised foundation models have recently shown strong potential for electroencephalogram (EEG)-based analysis. However, existing approaches struggle to capture the inherently multi-scale temporal structure of EEG signals, where local neural patterns and long-range dependencies jointly encode task-relevant information. This limitation hampers cross-scale representation learning and generalization across diverse downstream tasks. To address this challenge, we propose MSBraM, a Multi-Scale self-supervised Brain foundation Model designed to learn hierarchical EEG representations. MSBraM follows a two-stage pretraining framework. First, a multi-scale neural tokenizer discretizes raw EEG signals into semantic codes at different temporal resolutions via vector-quantized reconstruction. Second, the model is pretrained to predict masked codes using a curriculum multi-scale masking strategy, progressively integrating fine-grained local patterns with global temporal context. We pretrain MSBraM on over 2,400 hours of EEG data and evaluate it across 10 downstream tasks on 12 public datasets. Extensive experiments show that MSBraM achieves superior performance on other state-of-the-art pretrained models, demonstrating strong generalization and transferability. These results indicate that explicitly modeling multi-scale temporal dynamics is critical for effective EEG foundation models.

AI.tldr: MSBraM is a multi-scale self-supervised EEG foundation model that uses a two-stage pretraining framework—vector-quantized tokenization at multiple temporal resolutions followed by curriculum masked prediction—to capture hierarchical temporal dynamics. Pretrained on 2,400+ hours of EEG, it achieves state-of-the-art performance across 10 downstream tasks on 12 public datasets.
AI.motivation: Existing self-supervised EEG models fail to capture the multi-scale temporal structure inherent in EEG signals, where both local neural patterns and long-range dependencies are critical. This limits cross-scale representation learning and generalization across diverse downstream tasks.
AI.method: MSBraM employs a two-stage pretraining framework: (1) a multi-scale neural tokenizer that discretizes raw EEG into semantic codes at different temporal resolutions via vector-quantized reconstruction; (2) curriculum multi-scale masked prediction pretraining that progressively integrates fine-grained local patterns with global temporal context.
AI.result: MSBraM achieves superior performance compared to state-of-the-art pretrained models, demonstrating strong generalization and transferability across 10 downstream tasks on 12 public datasets.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly modeling multi-scale temporal dynamics is critical for building effective EEG foundation models, as evidenced by MSBraM's strong empirical results.

title: Zero-Flow Two-Sample Tests
summary: We propose a new approach to two-sample testing for deciding whether two sets of samples are drawn from the same distribution. The test is built on a statistical discrepancy based on the zero-flow criterion, termed zero-flow discrepancy (ZFD). We prove the validity of ZFD and propose a practical testing procedure, termed the zero-flow two-sample test (ZF2ST). The key idea is to learn how samples from the two distributions are locally misaligned and use the resulting directional pattern as evidence of distributional difference. By separating witness learning from hypothesis evaluation, ZF2ST can use flexible neural networks while maintaining valid statistical calibration. We develop both regression-based and power-maximized approaches for learning the witness. Experiments on synthetic and image datasets demonstrate that ZF2ST can achieve strong testing power for structured distributional changes while maintaining well-calibrated type-I error.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces ZF2ST, a two-sample test based on a zero-flow discrepancy (ZFD) criterion that learns local misalignment patterns between distributions using neural networks, while maintaining valid statistical calibration by separating witness learning from hypothesis evaluation.
AI.motivation: Existing two-sample tests struggle to balance flexibility (e.g., using deep neural networks) with valid statistical calibration (type-I error control). The authors aim to develop a test that can leverage flexible function approximators while preserving reliable hypothesis testing guarantees.
AI.method: The method uses a zero-flow discrepancy (ZFD) — a statistical discrepancy based on the zero-flow criterion — to quantify distributional differences. A witness function is learned (via regression-based or power-maximized approaches) to capture how samples from the two distributions are locally misaligned. Crucially, the witness learning stage is separated from the hypothesis evaluation stage, enabling the use of flexible neural networks without compromising statistical calibration.
AI.result: Experiments on synthetic and image datasets show that ZF2ST achieves strong testing power for detecting structured distributional changes while maintaining well-calibrated type-I error control.
AI.conclusion: ZF2ST provides a practical and statistically sound framework for two-sample testing that successfully combines the flexibility of neural network-based witness learning with rigorous hypothesis testing guarantees.

title: X$^3$-OPD: Distilling Reasoning into Large Audio-Language Models via On-Policy Alignment
summary: While large audio-language models have achieved remarkable progress in auditory perception, they still lag behind text-based large language models in deep logical reasoning, primarily due to the scarcity of high-quality audio reasoning data. To bridge this gap, we propose X$^3$-OPD, a cross-modal on-policy distillation framework that transfers reasoning capabilities from a powerful text teacher to an audio-language student. During training, the student generates reasoning trajectories conditioned on its own acoustic perception, while the teacher provides token-level guidance using matched textual inputs and verified answers. We further construct a three-tier symmetric corpus covering textual reasoning rendered into speech, audio-event reasoning grounded in complex acoustic scenes, and spoken-dialogue reasoning involving paralinguistic cues. This design extends cross-modal distillation beyond textually recoverable content to reasoning grounded in non-linguistic events, prosody, and conversational context. Experiments on MMSU, MMAU, BIG Bench Audio, and MMAR demonstrate that X$^3$-OPD substantially improves audio-grounded reasoning and chain-of-thought quality while largely preserving the model's existing capabilities under domain shift.

AI.tldr: X³-OPD is a cross-modal on-policy distillation framework that transfers logical reasoning capabilities from a text LLM teacher to an audio-language student model using a three-tier corpus (textual reasoning rendered as speech, acoustic event reasoning, and spoken-dialogue reasoning), achieving substantial improvements on audio reasoning benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Large audio-language models lag behind text LLMs in deep logical reasoning due to the scarcity of high-quality audio reasoning data. Existing distillation approaches fail to handle reasoning grounded in non-linguistic acoustic phenomena.
AI.method: An on-policy distillation framework where the student generates reasoning trajectories from its own acoustic perception, while a text teacher provides token-level guidance using matched textual inputs and verified answers. A three-tier symmetric corpus is constructed: (1) textual reasoning rendered into speech, (2) audio-event reasoning from complex acoustic scenes, and (3) spoken-dialogue reasoning with paralinguistic cues. This extends distillation beyond textually recoverable content to non-linguistic events, prosody, and conversational context.
AI.result: Experiments on MMSU, MMAU, BIG Bench Audio, and MMAR show substantial improvements in audio-grounded reasoning and chain-of-thought quality while largely preserving existing capabilities under domain shift.
AI.conclusion: X³-OPD effectively bridges the reasoning gap between audio-language models and text LLMs by enabling cross-modal reasoning transfer through on-policy distillation with a diverse, multi-tier audio reasoning corpus.

title: Logical Regression for Planning with Axioms
summary: In automated planning, logical regression is an operation that returns the most general condition necessary for an action to achieve a particular formula. It has many applications, such as allowing for more robust plan execution and providing compact policies for non-deterministic planning. Although relatively simple to calculate in basic planning settings, logical regression becomes significantly more complex when additional factors, such as axioms, are present. We introduce a methodology for approximating the logical regression of an action in a domain that includes axioms; an approximation that limits conditions to partial states. Our method produces minimal partial states while avoiding the recalculation of axioms. To demonstrate the impact of our methods, we embed our form of regression in an execution monitoring context, a well-established setting that can benefit greatly from logical regression. Our results show that this form of regression can dramatically generalize partial states across multiple domains, reducing the number of variables considered for execution monitoring by up to 70%, and demonstrate that the resulting execution monitor is robust enough to recover frequently in an environment with unexpected changes: several domains recover over 50% of the time in our tests.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a method for approximating logical regression in planning domains with axioms, producing minimal partial states without recomputing axioms. The approach reduces monitoring variables by up to 70% and enables robust execution recovery exceeding 50% in several domains.
AI.motivation: Logical regression is valuable for robust plan execution and compact policy generation, but becomes significantly more complex when axioms are present in the domain. Existing methods struggle to efficiently compute regression in such settings, motivating the need for an approximation technique that remains tractable while preserving utility.
AI.method: The authors introduce a methodology for approximating logical regression in axiom-containing domains. The approximation restricts conditions to partial states and produces minimal partial states while deliberately avoiding the recomputation of axioms. The approach is embedded and evaluated within an execution monitoring framework.
AI.result: The regression method generalizes partial states dramatically across multiple domains, reducing the number of variables needed for execution monitoring by up to 70%. In environments with unexpected changes, the resulting execution monitor recovers frequently: several domains achieve over 50% recovery rates in empirical tests.
AI.conclusion: The proposed approximation to logical regression effectively handles domains with axioms, producing compact partial states that significantly reduce monitoring overhead. The approach yields a robust execution monitor capable of frequent recovery from unexpected environmental changes, demonstrating practical value for real-world planning applications.

title: Graph Learning on Ensembles of Cyclic Peptides: An Investigation of Molecular Ensemble Modeling
comment: Accepted to Graph Foundation Models workshop at ICML '26. Contains 8 pages, 4 figures
summary: Molecular property prediction from structure often uses a single representative conformation, even though many molecules exist as conformational ensembles in solution. We introduce EnsembleEGNN, a molecular ensemble foundation model that encodes an ensemble by first encoding each conformer with shared Equivariant Graph Neural Network (EGNN) layers, then pooling the resulting conformer representations with a Set Attention Block. We pretrain the model on CREMP, a cyclic peptide ensemble dataset, using a multi-task self-supervised objective combining masked token recovery, noisy-coordinate reconstruction, and pairwise distance reconstruction. On the CREMP-CycPeptMPDB dataset, training EnsembleEGNN from scratch fails entirely ($R^2=0.005$). However, the pretrained model reaches $R^2=0.477$ and Pearson $r=0.699$, outperforming the sequence-only BERT baseline ($R^2=0.439$, Pearson $r=0.667$). When EnsembleEGNN is co-trained end-to-end with the BERT sequence encoder, the hybrid model improves further to $R^2=0.538$ and Pearson $r=0.737$. These results demonstrate that encoding conformational ensembles into a single thermodynamically informed embedding improves cyclic-peptide property prediction.

AI.tldr: EnsembleEGNN is a pretrained molecular ensemble model that encodes conformational ensembles via shared EGNN layers and Set Attention pooling, pretrained with multi-task self-supervision on cyclic peptides. It significantly outperforms a sequence-only BERT baseline for property prediction, and fusing it with a sequence encoder yields further gains, demonstrating the value of ensemble-aware representations.
AI.motivation: Most molecular property prediction methods use a single representative conformation, ignoring that molecules populate conformational ensembles in solution. This work aims to leverage full conformational ensembles to improve property prediction, particularly for cyclic peptides.
AI.method: EnsembleEGNN encodes each conformer via shared Equivariant Graph Neural Network (EGNN) layers, then pools conformer representations using a Set Attention Block (permutation-invariant aggregation). The model is pretrained on the CREMP cyclic peptide ensemble dataset with a multi-task self-supervised objective: masked token recovery, noisy-coordinate reconstruction, and pairwise distance reconstruction. A hybrid variant co-trains EnsembleEGNN end-to-end with a BERT sequence encoder.
AI.result: Training from scratch on CREMP-CycPeptMPDB fails (R²=0.005). Pretrained EnsembleEGNN achieves R²=0.477 and Pearson r=0.699, surpassing the sequence-only BERT baseline (R²=0.439, r=0.667). The hybrid model (EnsembleEGNN + BERT) further improves to R²=0.538 and Pearson r=0.737.
AI.conclusion: Encoding conformational ensembles into a single thermodynamically informed embedding substantially improves cyclic-peptide property prediction. Pretraining with self-supervision on ensemble data is essential for learning meaningful representations, and combining structure-based ensemble encoding with sequence-based encoding yields the best performance.

title: PATS: Policy-Aware Training Scaffolding for Agentic Reinforcement Learning
summary: In long-horizon LLM agent reinforcement learning, weak policies often repeat similar failures, producing uninformative rollout trajectories and limiting effective policy optimization. Existing skill-centric methods improve exploration by optimizing, filtering, or internalizing reusable skills. However, they remain centered on the skills themselves rather than being designed as adaptive training-time support for the evolving policy. To address this, we propose a policy-centric training paradigm that reframes skills as a dynamic training scaffold. Our framework, Pats, converts rollout groups from the latest policy into evidence cards and uses task-specific evaluation to adjust the context used in subsequent rollouts. Concrete guidance helps weak policies to complete challenging tasks. As policy improves, redundant context is revised or removed to reduce reliance on explicit guidance while preserving useful rollout variation. The policy is optimized with environmental rewards using standard RLVR, and the training scaffold is discarded at deployment. On ALFWorld and WebShop, Pats improves over strong baselines by up to 18.6%. Across seven search-augmented QA benchmarks, it remains competitive while using 32.1% fewer prompt tokens than the baseline.

AI.tldr: Pats proposes a policy-centric training paradigm where skills serve as a dynamic scaffold that adapts to the evolving policy. Evidence cards derived from recent rollouts provide concrete guidance for weak policies, while redundant context is pruned as the policy improves. The scaffold is discarded at deployment. Pats achieves up to 18.6% improvement on ALFWorld/WebShop and uses 32.1% fewer prompt tokens on QA benchmarks.
AI.motivation: In long-horizon LLM agent RL, weak policies generate uninformative rollouts by repeating similar failures, limiting effective policy optimization. Existing skill-centric methods (optimizing, filtering, or internalizing reusable skills) focus on the skills themselves rather than providing adaptive training-time support that evolves alongside the policy.
AI.method: Pats introduces a policy-centric training paradigm with three key mechanisms: (1) converting rollout groups from the latest policy into evidence cards, (2) using task-specific evaluation to dynamically adjust the context provided in subsequent rollouts, and (3) revising or removing redundant context as the policy improves to reduce reliance on explicit guidance while preserving useful rollout variation. The policy is optimized via standard RLVR with environmental rewards, and the entire training scaffold is discarded at deployment.
AI.result: On ALFWorld and WebShop, Pats improves over strong baselines by up to 18.6%. Across seven search-augmented QA benchmarks, Pats remains competitive while using 32.1% fewer prompt tokens compared to the baseline.
AI.conclusion: Reframing skills as a dynamic, policy-centric training scaffold—rather than static reusable components—enables more effective exploration and policy optimization for long-horizon LLM agents. The adaptive nature of the scaffold ensures strong guidance when the policy is weak and graceful reduction of dependence as the policy matures.

title: Beyond Sufficiency: Time Series Explanation with Counterfactual Necessity
summary: Faithful explanations of time-series classifiers should identify subsequences that are not only sufficient to preserve a black-box model's prediction, but also necessary for maintaining it. However, existing sufficiency-oriented methods can assign high importance to spurious subsequences that support the prediction without being essential to the model's decision. We introduce \textbf{TimePNS}, a necessity-aware framework for time-series explanation. Inspired by Pearl's counterfactual notion of necessity, TimePNS assesses whether a temporal factor is necessary by intervening on it and measuring whether the original prediction is disrupted. The framework adopts a two-stage design. Stage I learns an identifiable causal generative process together with a sufficiency-oriented explanation mask. Stage II performs counterfactual interventions on temporal factors to derive necessity signals, which supervise a temporal gate that refines the initial explanation by suppressing non-essential components and emphasizing counterfactually necessary ones. Experiments on synthetic and real-world time-series benchmarks show that TimePNS more accurately identifies decision-critical subsequences and consistently improves sufficiency-necessity trade-offs over strong baselines.

AI.tldr: TimePNS is a two-stage framework for time-series explanation that identifies subsequences both sufficient and necessary for a black-box model's prediction. Stage I learns a causal generative process with a sufficiency mask; Stage II uses counterfactual interventions to derive necessity signals that refine the explanation, suppressing spurious features and emphasizing causally necessary ones.
AI.motivation: Existing sufficiency-oriented explanation methods for time-series classifiers can assign high importance to spurious subsequences that support but are not essential for the prediction. There is a need for necessity-aware explanations that identify decision-critical temporal factors whose removal would disrupt the model's output.
AI.method: TimePNS adopts a two-stage design grounded in Pearl's counterfactual notion of necessity. Stage I learns an identifiable causal generative process alongside a sufficiency-oriented explanation mask. Stage II performs counterfactual interventions on temporal factors to derive necessity signals, which supervise a temporal gate that refines the initial explanation by suppressing non-essential components and emphasizing counterfactually necessary ones.
AI.result: Experiments on synthetic and real-world time-series benchmarks demonstrate that TimePNS more accurately identifies decision-critical subsequences and consistently improves sufficiency-necessity trade-offs over strong baselines.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating counterfactual necessity into time-series explanation yields more faithful and precise identification of decision-critical subsequences. The two-stage causal framework effectively balances sufficiency and necessity, outperforming existing sufficiency-only approaches.

title: Bridging the Gap Between Plausibility and Admissibility: Constraint-Aware Flow Maps for Dynamic Graph Systems
summary: Generative models can support decision-making under uncertainty by producing ensembles of plausible future system trajectories, but statistical plausibility does not ensure structural feasibility. This study investigates whether post-sampling symbolic constraints can improve the reliability of generative trajectory modeling in dynamic graph-structured systems. A conditional diffusion model generates future graph-state trajectories from partial observations, while an external symbolic layer applies hard filtering, soft weighting, or projection-based repair. The framework is evaluated on two controlled synthetic regimes: a compact graph and a medium-complexity dependency graph, using metrics for structural validity, sample efficiency, diversity, robustness, and calibration. In the compact regime, the model produces an invalid probability mass of 0.002996, indicating an almost entirely admissible trajectory manifold. Under the same architecture and training protocol, invalid mass increases to 0.155929 in the medium-complexity regime. Hard filtering removes all invalid retained trajectories while preserving 84.4% of generated samples, whereas soft weighting preserves effective sample size but yields only limited validity gains. Family-level analysis shows that dependency constraints account for nearly all observed inadmissibility. These results indicate that statistical plausibility and structural admissibility are distinct reliability properties and that symbolic constraint handling becomes more valuable as graph-structural complexity increases.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether post-sampling symbolic constraints can improve the structural feasibility of trajectories generated by diffusion models for dynamic graph-structured systems. While generative models produce statistically plausible futures, they may violate hard structural constraints. The study finds that as graph complexity increases, structural inadmissibility rises significantly, and symbolic post-processing—particularly hard filtering—effectively removes invalid samples, demonstrating that statistical plausibility and structural admissibility are distinct properties requiring separate handling.
AI.motivation: Generative models can produce ensembles of plausible future trajectories under uncertainty, but statistical plausibility does not guarantee structural feasibility (e.g., respecting dependency constraints in graph-structured systems). The authors aim to determine whether adding a post-sampling symbolic constraint layer can bridge this gap, improving the reliability of generative trajectory modeling for decision-making.
AI.method: A conditional diffusion model generates future graph-state trajectories from partial observations. An external symbolic layer is then applied, offering three strategies: (1) hard filtering (discarding invalid samples), (2) soft weighting (down-weighting invalid samples), and (3) projection-based repair (mapping invalid samples to the nearest admissible trajectory). The framework is evaluated on two synthetic regimes—a compact graph and a medium-complexity dependency graph—using metrics for structural validity, sample efficiency, diversity, robustness, and calibration.
AI.result: In the compact regime, invalid probability mass is only 0.002996 (nearly entirely admissible). Under identical architecture and training, invalid mass rises sharply to 0.155929 in the medium-complexity regime. Hard filtering eliminates all invalid trajectories while retaining 84.4% of samples. Soft weighting preserves effective sample size but yields only marginal validity improvements. Dependency constraints account for nearly all observed inadmissibility in family-level analysis.
AI.conclusion: Statistical plausibility and structural admissibility are distinct reliability properties that diverge as graph-structural complexity grows. Symbolic constraint handling, particularly hard filtering, becomes increasingly valuable for ensuring trajectory feasibility in more complex graph-structured systems.

title: Expanding Flow Maps
summary: Flow-based generative models have enabled remarkable progress in fast and controllable generation across continuous and discrete state spaces, yet existing parameterizations are constrained to fixed dimensions or fixed sequence lengths. Here, we introduce Expanding Generative Flows (EFlows), which define flows between distributions of increasing dimensionality along an expanding interpolant that grows the state by augmenting it with conditional noise. Building on this construction, we propose Expanding Flow Maps (EFMs), a new class of flow maps that distill the expanding interpolant into efficient few-step generative models. Each EFM factors the map between any two timesteps into two learnable operations: an expand operator, which augments the state space with new coordinates or tokens conditioned on the current state, and a transport map, which pushes the expanded state forward along the interpolant. Composing these operators yields a single map that jointly expands and denoises the state, recovering existing fixed-canvas flows and flow maps as the special case in which the expand operator is the identity. We further extend the framework to the discrete simplex, enabling variable-size graph generation and variable-length sequence generation. Across both continuous and discrete modalities, we establish EFlows and EFMs as a principled framework for settings in which output size is itself a learned, controllable degree of freedom.

AI.tldr: EFlows and EFMs introduce a flow-based generative framework where the output dimensionality is a learned, controllable variable, enabling variable-size generation in both continuous and discrete domains by composing an expand operator with a transport map.
AI.motivation: Existing flow-based generative models are constrained to fixed dimensions or fixed sequence lengths, limiting their applicability to tasks where output size is itself an important degree of freedom, such as variable-size graph generation or variable-length sequence generation.
AI.method: The authors propose Expanding Generative Flows (EFlows), which define flows between distributions of increasing dimensionality via an expanding interpolant that augments the state with conditional noise. They then introduce Expanding Flow Maps (EFMs), which distill this interpolant into efficient few-step generative models by factoring the map between timesteps into two learnable operations: an expand operator (augments the state space with new coordinates/tokens conditioned on the current state) and a transport map (pushes the expanded state forward along the interpolant). The framework is extended to the discrete simplex for variable-size graph and variable-length sequence generation.
AI.result: The framework unifies existing fixed-canvas flows and flow maps as a special case (where the expand operator is the identity). It successfully enables variable-size generation across both continuous and discrete modalities, establishing a principled approach where output size is a learned, controllable degree of freedom.
AI.conclusion: EFlows and EFMs provide a principled, unified framework for generative modeling where output dimensionality is learned rather than fixed, bridging continuous and discrete domains and recovering prior methods as special cases.

title: Agent-Guided Relational Concept Discovery: Toward Interpretable Surgical Margin Assessment
comment: This paper is accepted to MICCAI 2026, and this is the submission version, not the camera-ready version
summary: Deep learning models can effectively use Rapid Evaporative Ionization Mass Spectrometry (REIMS) data for surgical margin assessment. However, their clinical adoption remains challenging due to limited generalization to operating room conditions. This difficulty arises because models are typically trained on labeled spectra collected from resected tissue samples, while they must operate on noisy, unlabeled data acquired directly during surgery. In addition, the black-box nature of deep learning models makes it difficult to understand and systematically improve their behavior. Concept-based learning offers a promising way to address these challenges by mapping raw measurements to human-understandable concepts. However, supervised concept-based approaches rely on concept annotations, which are difficult to obtain in complex mass spectrometry workflows. We propose Agent-Guided Concept Discovery, a framework that learns meaningful concepts directly from data without requiring predefined concept labels. During training, a reasoning agent refines semantic descriptions of the learned concepts and adaptively adjusts their weight based on diagnostic relevance. These concepts are further grounded using a biochemical knowledge graph to ensure consistency with known metabolic relationships. Across Skin and Breast Cancer datasets, our model improves balanced accuracy and sensitivity over the baseline. In a representative intraoperative case, it shows fewer false positives, indicating better generalization to surgical conditions.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Agent-Guided Concept Discovery, a framework that learns interpretable concepts from REIMS mass spectrometry data without requiring predefined concept labels, using a reasoning agent to refine concepts and a biochemical knowledge graph for grounding, improving surgical margin assessment accuracy and generalization.
AI.motivation: Deep learning models for REIMS-based surgical margin assessment suffer from poor generalization to operating room conditions due to training on clean labeled data vs. noisy intraoperative data, and their black-box nature hinders systematic improvement. Concept-based learning could help but requires costly concept annotations that are difficult to obtain in mass spectrometry workflows.
AI.method: Agent-Guided Concept Discovery learns concepts directly from REIMS data without predefined labels. A reasoning agent iteratively refines semantic descriptions of learned concepts and adaptively adjusts their weights based on diagnostic relevance. Concepts are grounded using a biochemical knowledge graph to ensure consistency with known metabolic relationships.
AI.result: The model improves balanced accuracy and sensitivity over baseline methods on Skin and Breast Cancer datasets. In a representative intraoperative case, it demonstrates fewer false positives, indicating better generalization to surgical conditions.
AI.conclusion: Agent-guided concept discovery enables interpretable, generalizable deep learning for REIMS-based surgical margin assessment without requiring expensive concept annotations, bridging the gap between benchtop training and intraoperative deployment.

title: Detecting LLM-Generated Tokens in Human--LLM Coauthored Text
summary: The rise of human-AI collaborative writing has created a growing need for fine-grained detection methods that support localizing likely LLM-generated content in mixed-authorship documents. Existing methods for detecting LLM-generated text mainly focus on document-level classification and cannot identify which parts of the text are generated by LLMs. This paper introduces a new method to address this urgent need. Our method operates at the token level, the natural unit of modern language models, and builds on existing token-level detection scores. The key idea is to smooth adjacent token scores to reduce their variability, while using an adaptive Lepski-type rule to select the bandwidth according to the local authorship structure. Our method is simple to implement and does not require token-level labeled data for training. Theoretically, we characterize this trade-off and show that the proposed method achieves favorable mean square error performance in estimating the underlying signal. Empirically, we demonstrate strong performance of our method against a wide range of baselines in both synthetic datasets and a realistic dataset. We deploy a publicly accessible website that implements the methods as well.

AI.tldr: A token-level detection method for localizing LLM-generated content in mixed-authorship texts, using adaptive bandwidth smoothing via a Lepski-type rule, requiring no labeled training data.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-generated text detection methods operate at the document level and cannot pinpoint which specific tokens or passages were machine-generated within mixed human-AI documents, creating an urgent need for fine-grained, localizable detection.
AI.method: A token-level detection approach that smooths adjacent token scores to reduce variability, combined with an adaptive Lepski-type rule for bandwidth selection that adapts to local authorship structure. The method requires no token-level labeled training data.
AI.result: The method achieves favorable mean square error performance theoretically and demonstrates strong empirical performance against a wide range of baselines on both synthetic and realistic datasets.
